About this work

Sermones et Exhortationes ad Monachos — "Sermons and Exhortations to Monks" — collects Trithemius's addresses to the monastic community at Sponheim during his reforming abbacy (1483–1506). The sermons are practical spiritual direction for Benedictine monks: on obedience, humility, the discipline of the choir, the dangers of private property, and the interior life that the Rule is meant to form. They sit at the heart of the monastic-reform cluster, alongside De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis and De Triplici Regione Claustralium — less a systematic treatise than the abbot's own voice, pressing his monks toward the observance he wanted for them.

This is the 1516 Strasbourg edition (BSB scan). It is one of two witnesses of the Sermones et Exhortationes in this corpus, alongside the other Strasbourg printing of the same year (prdl-24394); the two differ by print witness and pagination. The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No published English translation is known;

    Sermons and Exhortations to Monks

    Sermons and Exhortations to Monks, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim ... Of these sermons there are two books: the first is called the Book of Homilies, the second the Book of Sermons. Strasbourg, 1516.

    [Source page illegible in the scan; the page image is the authoritative witness.]

    Sermons and Exhortations to Monks by John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, later of Wurzburg. Of these sermons there are two books: the first is called Homilies, the second Sermons.

    Ottomarus Luscinius of Strasbourg: a decastich on the homilies of John Trithemius to monks

    If for anyone it is not enough to follow your gentle laws of right, O Christ, unless he should speak of monks: Serapion, Paul, and Antony once tried the path, which bristles with countless rough places. He strives to show how a rough cloak may torment the body, and does not allow down to be in the bed; so that fasts may drive out the swollen pride of the soul, and brief, [half-slumbering?] rest may cherish the limbs. These things the silent men taught by deeds; but Trithemius is better suited than they, since he is strong in tongue and hand.

    With the grace and privilege of the Imperial Majesty.

    Maximilian, by the favor of divine clemency elected Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, and Count Palatine of Germany, Hungary, Dalmatia, and Croatia, to the honorable and devout man beloved by us, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James the Greater at Wurzburg: imperial grace and every good thing.

    Since you have humbly represented to us that you have composed various editions of both ancient and modern authors, collected not without great labor, vigils, and diligence, which you desired with your whole mind to have brought into the light and published; and since our beloved subject of the Holy Roman Empire, Master Johannes Haselberg of Constance, has offered himself with a most ready spirit to be the agent of such a matter, and for this purpose has procured at great expense the type with which he may print the aforementioned works: we therefore, in order that [unclear] of the aforesaid Master Johannes may shine forth more and more, have given and granted, and by the tenor of the present letters do give and grant, to the aforementioned Master Johannes Haselberg of Constance full power and authority of every kind.

    We decree that he may print, and sell when printed, wherever and at whatever price he wishes, whatever among the treatises and little works edited by you, the aforementioned Trithemius, abbot of Saint James the Greater at Wurzburg, shall have been reviewed and approved by the honorable man faithful and beloved to us, Conrad Peutinger, doctor and our councillor. And we forbid all and singular printers of books, of whatever condition they may be, to dare or presume to print, or to publish, buy, or sell when printed by others, those books that have been published, throughout the whole Roman Empire and in our hereditary lands.

    Moreover, we command all and singular our faithful beloved subjects of the Holy Roman Empire, of whatever estate, condition, dignity, and office they may be, whether ecclesiastical or secular, under pain of our most grave indignation and that of the Holy Roman Empire, and of ten marks of pure gold, to be applied as often as the contrary is done, one part to our fisc and the other part to the aforesaid Master Johannes Haselberg, that they assist the same Master Johannes of Constance with their favor and aid in their places and lands, and by no means permit the said works and treatises to be printed, or, when printed elsewhere, to be sold. Rather, all those presuming to do anything against this our grant and prohibition they shall forthwith declare, in our name, to have incurred the sentence of this indignation of ours and of the Holy Roman Empire, executing therein our express will.

    In testimony whereof, these letters have been furnished with the impression of our seal on the back. Given in our town of Innsbruck on the tenth day of the month of November, in the year of the Lord 1514, in the twenty-ninth year of our Roman reign, and the twenty-fifth of Hungary.

    By the king himself.

    At the lord Emperor’s own command.

    N. Ziegler.

    Corrected by Paul Obersteiner.

    A ii

    Epistle

    John Trithemius, called the Sponheimite, to the reverend father and his teacher, lord Johannes de Colenhausen, abbot of the monastery of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter in Seligenstadt, and formerly my predecessor at Sponheim: reverence and honor.

    I do not know, teacher ever to be venerated by me, under what unlucky star that monastery of Sponheim stands as having been built, since rarely does an abbot die in it; rather, almost all, afflicted by weariness, have, now for almost seventy years, as I find from the annals, resigned of their own will. We are not wholly ignorant why you too, after the example of those who went before, abandoned us poor men before the time: we who rightly accuse our poverty and the rebellious rashness of certain men. I now experience, alas, the cause which impelled your mind to leave the abbacy of Sponheim, utterly barren and unfruitful, over which you presided for thirteen years after the reform, not without continual anxiety of mind and infinite labors. I pass over the wrongs of very many of the brothers which you endured, all of which indeed are daily doubled upon me. You ordered me to send to your fatherhood the book of my exhortations to the brothers, which recently, amid the raging occupations of worldly affairs, I composed by lamplight; and although it is unworthy of your reading, I nevertheless did not wish to resist the command of a parent. Therefore I pray your gentleness kindly to apply the file of correction: if anything is lacking, add it; cut away what is superfluous; and what is unsuitable either hand over to the flames or at least set in order. Farewell, sweetest father, mindful of us. From Sponheim, on the sixth day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1386 [editorial note: likely a printer’s error for 1496 — Trithemius was born in 1462, making 1386 impossible].

    All things. I. Folio III.

    It befits the soldiery of Christians, brothers, and especially of monks, to be subject to the various calamities of this world, and, like gold in the furnace, to be continually exercised and tested by tribulations. For it belongs to monks to surpass the common little rule of the soldiery of Christians by a higher manner of living, and to obey not only the Lord’s commandments but also his counsels. It belongs to monks utterly to despise riches, honors, and all the pleasures of the present world for love of God, and, having overcome fleshly desires, to be continually at leisure for God alone. For a monk is so called as one solitary from unity, who even by the very word of his name is admonished to contempt of the world. Therefore the office of a monk is to remain with himself in solitude, cleansed and purified from vices, and sweetly to love Christ above all things. For the goal of monks, to which regular institution is directed, is Christ; whoever refuses to imitate him is neither a monk nor even a Christian. Hence, my brothers, we ought to know that whoever does not follow our Lord and Savior in true patience and humility gains nothing for salvation from being called a Christian or a monk. For he himself is the one who says in the holy Gospel: Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he shall enter the kingdom of heaven. And what the will of God is, the holy apostle disclosed, saying: This is the will of God, your sanctification. But since the necessary consummation of this sanctification enjoined upon us requires great endurance of evils in all things and humility, since no one is holy by his own strength, we must, my brothers, keep continual consideration of our vocation within ourselves, so that never, growing sluggish in idleness, through

    On Spiritual Warfare.

    It certainly cannot be otherwise than that we too, his imitators, wicked and most vile sinners, ought to suffer many things, since all that we suffer we justly endure by our own demerit. For no one comes to the glory of the city above unless he has first been justified here from sin; but since the tribulations of the just are many, he will in no way be able to be just who has refused to endure adversities for righteousness in this world. Therefore, my dearest brothers, imitate in great patience and humility our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who, having become man for us, voluntarily endured the greatest things, and in this world was never without the bitterness of persecution. For from the hour of his most sacred birth until the departure of his spirit from his body, he was always most patient for us in the bitterness of this present life; and the bitterness of his future passion, foreknown by him, never withdrew from his foreknowledge. For since he was almighty God made man for us, he knew all things, understood all things, foresaw all things; nor could anything of those things which he was going to suffer be hidden from him, who, in order to suffer, was made passible in the world, while remaining God, as he was, impassible. Born, moreover, of the Virgin Mary without commerce with a man, in order to fulfil the law, he is soon circumcised on the eighth day; and he who had no sin is wounded for our offenses. By night the child is led into Egypt from the face of the persecutor; and he who was Lord of all, poor and needy in the midst of the nations, unknown, is exiled for seven years. Finally, through all the days of his life in this world he most patiently endured continual labors, and never refused to undergo any adversities for the glory of the Father.

    For all hard and bitter things the just and innocent one voluntarily suffered for us, most unworthy as we are; by the most bitter death of the cross he redeemed us from the destruction of perpetual damnation, and in his own blood mercifully reconciled us to the Father. Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, as the prince of the apostles has warned, my brothers, let us be armed with the same thought, so that we, suffering together with the innocent one, may diligently recall to memory those things which he endured for us.

    For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign together with him when he triumphs in glory. Behold, Christ calls us to the glory to which he has gone before; he gives the weapons with which he himself first overcame the prince of the world; he prescribed the form by which a soldier ought to follow the king to the crown. Christ calls his soldiers to the palace of heaven; the attendant gifts of virtues lead them through distresses, and the victors receive rewards, to reign forever. Therefore, my dearest brothers, always pursuing our warfare most zealously, let us continually declare war on vices and concupiscences, so that, just as the flesh wars against the spirit, so we too may fight constantly, watching in prayer and fasting against the kindler of vices. For as long as we live in this world we are pilgrims away from the Lord, and like gymnosophists we contend in the stadium, carrying out the necessary course of life in continual struggle. Yet we fight not by our own strength, but supported by the mercy of our king, who said to his imitators in the holy Gospel: Without me you can do nothing. And lest we should flee the battle of the warfare set before us as impossible, he said elsewhere: In the world you will have distress; but have confidence: I have overcome the world. And so that we might know that the Lord Jesus is always present in this world to his little servants, he promises us thus in the apostles: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age. Having received security by this promise, O soldiers of Christ, my dearest brothers, why do we hesitate, why do we not stand bravely against all the insolences of this world? Let us always have our king and protector present with us as we fight; and do we fear to engage against a weak enemy, who overcomes no one except the willing? Gird yourselves, I pray, for the unconquerable Christian warfare, which you have professed under a twofold condition: the one when, at the font of sacred baptism, renouncing Satan, you swore the words of Christian instruction; the other when in the world you solemnly put on the monastic garment of religion.

    A great necessity of making progress constrains you, if you weigh your profession with due consideration, since the obligation of the Christian name commands that you must keep the evangelical commandments, and the vow which you voluntarily emitted requires that you observe the precepts of monastic institution. It is no longer sufficient for our salvation to fulfil those precepts which are set before Christians in common to be observed, unless also most diligently

    All. I. Folio IIII.

    that you keep the monastic institutions which you promised me. “Vow,” says Scripture, “and pay.” And again another Scripture says: “If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it.” For an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him, and it is much better not to vow than, after a vow, not to pay what was promised. And Saint Augustine warns us how necessary it is to pay to God what has been promised, saying: “There are certain things which, even without vowing them, we owe to the Lord. But after we promise them to the Lord, we are constrained of necessity to pay them.”

    But now, my brothers, I ask you carefully to consider what you have vowed to the Lord your God, and diligently to weigh under what necessity of paying what you promised you have been placed. For you vowed to your God, not to man, obedience and the conversion of your morals according to the Rule of our most holy lawgiver Benedict, and perpetual stability in this order of religion. The obedience, however, which you promised to God, you owe to his vicar, a man, whom you have learned from the Rule which you profess to bear the place of Christ in the monastery. What sort the conversion of morals ought to be according to the Rule you see plainly set down in the fourth chapter, on the instruments of good works; in it you are not ignorant of the deed of all monastic perfection [unclear] at the beginning of his profession.

    Indeed, all of you have heard what our divine father commanded to be done concerning novices, and you are not ignorant of what was done in the case of each one of you at the beginning of his profession. For thus he says: “But he who is to be received shall promise in the oratory before all concerning his stability, the conversion of his morals, and obedience, before God and his saints, so that if ever he acts otherwise, he may know that he will be condemned by God, whom he mocks.” Consider now therefore, brothers, under how great a necessity of regular observance you have been placed, since unless you fulfill in deed what you promised in receiving the monastic habit, you will have to be judged before the almighty Lord not as servants of God, not as friends, not as monks, but as mockers.

    Therefore always be mindful of those things which the Rule commands you, according to which you promised to order your morals; and labor as true soldiers of Jesus Christ, continually keeping watch in the fear of the Lord, since, as Scripture says, unless you hold yourselves steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown. Consider your calling: because the Lord has called you not to idleness, not to the pleasures of this world, nor to pursuing the desires of the flesh, but rather to continual labor, to abstinence from all delights, and to the constant mortification of the flesh under the image of the Crucified, so that you may bear his stigmata in your hearts.

    Certainly you have now put your hands to the plough of the holy heavenly agriculture, in which you are commanded to sweat continually in labor, and not only never to look back, but, always advancing from virtue to virtue, to strive toward the summit of supreme perfection. For to live as a monk is nothing other than to shun human company and, in solitude, by the desire of most fervent love, actually to please God alone. Hence Scripture says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth; he will sit alone and be silent, because he will lift himself above himself.”

    Therefore, if you wish to be perfect, you who by regular institution are bound to love perfection, begin from the way of life which Christ taught; and since already for love of him you despise all things, do not neglect humbly to conquer, overcome, and despise even yourselves. But the servant of Christ has nothing except Christ; he loves nothing, cares for nothing, seeks nothing except Christ, so that he may be perfect and may please him whose soldiery he has voluntarily professed. But the monk who has anything besides Christ cannot be perfect, since true love is not divided, nor is the mind truly lived among diverse and contrary things.

    For this reason the Lord says: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me.” You indeed, most beloved brothers, have already, as I trust, left the world and whatever you had in the world; and not only all the goods of the world which you possessed and could have had, but you have also laid aside every desire of having. And you have come to this monastery of the divine prelate Martin, in which the poverty of temporal goods is great; and this alone has been given to us in place of riches: not to find causes of avarice. But just as punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause does, so want does not make a poor man blessed, but voluntary [unclear] for the love of Christ

    On the Progress of Spiritual Warfare.

    ...patience in poverty itself. For in the Gospel the Lord did not proclaim all poor persons whatsoever blessed and to be given the kingdom of heaven; rather, as you know, he foretold that only the poor in spirit were to be blessed. For contempt of riches is not enough for salvation, unless the renouncer of gold also strives with all his strength, through patience and humility, constantly to imitate the Savior. For it is easier to despise the world than to despise and deny oneself. Yet whoever wishes to imitate the Son of God and attain evangelical perfection must become a despiser not only of the world and temporal things, but also of his very self. For the Savior says in the holy Gospel: Unless someone has renounced all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple. And lest we should think this enough for perfection, he again bears witness more openly concerning contempt of oneself, saying: If anyone wishes to follow me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake and the Gospel’s will save it. Christ became obedient to the Father even unto death; if you wish to imitate him, as you have promised, it is necessary, brothers, that you deny yourselves to yourselves. For he cannot be a monk who has not first wholly renounced his own will. You who, before God and all his saints, promised to live according to the monastic rule may not hereafter appropriate your own will, since what has once been consecrated to God must no longer be recalled to human uses. For you serve as soldiers not for yourselves but for Christ the King; hence you retain in your own power neither willing nor refusing. For you are dead, as holy [Christophilus?] says, and your life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, your life, shall appear, then you too will appear with him in glory. If you desire to rejoice with him without end, you must now in this time serve strenuously as soldiers for love of him. For no one will be crowned with Christ unless he has persevered in lawful combat to the end, since one who does not know how to persevere can [not?] conquer,

    On the Progress of Spiritual Warfare: Second Homily

    Most beloved brothers, whenever the recollection of that moment comes to mind, when, though I protested and resisted, you appointed me, unworthy as I am, as abbot over you, so often I am shaken wholly within myself by the bitterness of my heart, and I am compelled to shed tears even unwillingly and unawares. For I know that I was not set over you by my own merits; but whether this was done by yours, I do not know. May almighty God grant that this appointment concerning me was not made because of the demerits of either me or you. Why did you will it so, brothers? You raised me up, young, unlearned, and by no means fit, as leader for the warfare that we profess, so that now it is altogether necessary for me both to teach and to learn, when neither perfection of life commends my teaching, nor consideration of age as yet obtains for the shepherd the necessary authority. In these three years now I have learned sufficiently in how many miseries I am entangled, while I alone am compelled to bear the weaknesses of all of you, and I, unhappy man, am supported by no one. Who will free me from the vanities of this world, into which I have been called back, I who entered the monastery in order to escape every care and anxiety of the present life? Since, however, it is necessary to bear the burden placed on my shoulders, I beg you, brothers: diligently extend to me the helping hands of your prayers, so that, by the Lord’s granting, I may deserve to live among you in such a way that I do not transgress the condition of spiritual warfare which the Rule commands us. For we are professed soldiers of the same warfare, and the vow does not distinguish office, since solemn profession at the beginning of this life made the shepherd bound together with the sheep. Hence, when I speak to you about the spiritual warfare which, by God’s mercy, we have professed, my intention is, insofar as the Lord Jesus shall deign to grant, also to shake myself out from the feathers of sloth and lukewarmness toward the fervor of holy newness...

    Homily II. Fol. V.

    [unclear]: and to summon all of you, according to your strength, to the guardianship of the military order. For we are frail and weak, and we do not long remain stable in holy purpose unless by daily exercises we continually renew the fervor of the spirit. For by reason of my office I am bound to set before you those things which can conduce to your salvation; it belongs to you to hear me speaking, as the shepherd of your souls, patiently in all things. For although, being young, I am not fit to teach so great a multitude of elders, nevertheless, because you have appointed me your shepherd, I am compelled, under the necessity of salvation, to feed the flock which I undertook to govern. What is mine to do, I both do willingly according to my strength and will do as long as I shall live in this solicitude of pastoral care: young though I am, I shall teach you elders, and without interruption I shall show how you ought to serve as soldiers for him in whose arms you have sworn.

    For I am not unaware of the dreadful threat of our lawgiver, who says: Let the abbot know that whatever profit the master of the household may find lacking in the sheep is laid upon the shepherd’s fault. And what follows concerns you, my brothers, if, while I preach and admonish, contempt for the word of God arises. Again, he says, he will be free only insofar as, if all diligence has been applied by the shepherd to a restless or disobedient flock, and every care has been shown for their diseased actions, their shepherd, absolved in the judgment of the Lord, may say to the Lord with the prophet: I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have spoken your truth and your salvation; but they, despising, have spurned me. And then at last, for the sheep disobedient to his care, let death itself be the punishment prevailing against them.

    Here no covering of excuse is left; no place for evasion is afforded; but the danger of both parties is publicly described. For I, holding the place of the abbot, if I have not announced to you the justice of God, if I have not corrected you when sinning according to the Rule, have denied my office, and the whole of whatever is found lacking in holiness among you will be imputed to me. For it is mine, by reason of the pastoral office, to say what is expedient for the salvation of your souls; but yours is humbly to hear those things which I shall proclaim in the name of the Savior, and, so far as each one has strength, faithfully to fulfill them with a great heart.

    You have heard my danger if I do not cry out; you have heard yours also, if you despise me as I preach the word of God to you. But so that by the Savior’s mercy we may all escape secure, let each one of us zealously pursue what is commanded him in this spiritual warfare, taking the greatest care that, made deaf hearers of the truth, we do not lie to the Lord. Let us diligently remember the vow which we have made, and let us preserve inviolate until death the holy order which we profess. Let us hear our king saying in the Gospel to his soldiers: If anyone ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my minister be. We are ministers of the eternal king, priests and Levites, all cloistered monks, and bound by a double reason to great holiness, since we have at once taken up the order of clerics and profess the rule of monastic purity.

    Therefore let us follow our commander, under whom we serve, along the path of the austerity of all virtues; and let us arm ourselves with right faith, firm hope, and the most fervent charity toward God and neighbor, in which the perfection of all holiness is comprised. For whoever is girded with the defense of charity is never overcome by the adversary. For in charity the military service of Christ truly grows sweet; and when its fervor begins to burn in the soldier’s heart, it fears no adversities. For charity, as Saint Gregory says, is never idle, but does great things if it is true; but if it refuses to work, it was not perfect charity. Therefore, beloved cloistered men, you who have promised that you will serve the eternal king perpetually, cast away now the works of darkness, and put on the charity of God and neighbor, which is the strongest armor of salvation for all. If anyone has been clothed with it, he will fear no labors, however hard, no adversities of this world. He will not fear hunger, nor thirst, nor persecutions of men; not reproaches, not mockeries, not prisons, not chains, not any hard and adverse things whatever; but everyone who has once perfectly tasted the charity of God, unconquered against

    On the Progress of Spiritual Warfare.

    [Through] whatever raging of the world, he will remain. The true lover of God rejoices in tribulations, is glad in adversities, exults in persecutions for the sake of righteousness. He follows his king, who is seated in the heavens; there he dwells in mind and in the desire of his soul, where he does not doubt that his savior reigns.

    Whatever pleasure and delights are seen anywhere in the world produce for the servant of Christ, burning in true charity, stench and horror as if they were the vilest dung, because he loves nothing earthly, nothing transitory, nothing perishable, but only him to whom he has devoted himself, with the whole intention of his mind. For the true soldier of Christ thinks nothing of the things of the world; he cares not for the flesh but for the mind, as one who is not ignorant of what is written: No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself.

    Indeed, all who serve an earthly emperor always obey his commands in everything, and immediately go, without contradiction, wherever he has ordered. All follow one leader, and whatever he commands in the king’s name, no one in the whole army contradicts. You also, soldiers of the king of ages, who have appointed me as your leader in his place and as preceptor, hear the command of your emperor Jesus Christ through my mouth, and do what he commands us in the holy Gospel. Hear what he orders, and consider how you ought to serve as soldiers in the observance of regular discipline.

    “He who ministers to me,” he says, “let him follow me.” Listen, cloistered monk, bearing the warfare; pay attention. Christ, to whom you serve as soldier, speaks to you; the heavenly emperor, at whose altar you minister, addresses you. If you wish to be my minister, you must follow the virtue of patience and humility which you have learned from me. For I have given you an example, O my soldiers, that just as I have done, you also should do likewise. Charity, O monk, compelled me to be born in the world as a man from a virgin; may that same charity, for love of me, always preserve you pure and humble in the cloister.

    The work of human salvation which the Father commanded me I strove always to accomplish, for your sake, with unceasing meditation; and you, if you love me, take care to preserve inviolate until death the holy purpose of monastic life which you have undertaken for your sins. I was always, in all things, voluntarily subject and obedient to my heavenly Father, even to the most bitter death of the cross; you also, if you wish to come to me, obey your abbot, appointed in my place, humbly in all things and always according to the rule.

    I never transgressed in any respect the command which my Father gave me; and unless you preserve inviolate until death the three principal vows of the monastic institution, you are by no means to be numbered among my ministers and soldiers. Though I was rich, for the sake of your salvation I became poor and needy; but unless you, for love of me, have despised and abandoned all things, you will not be able to be my disciple. Poverty, hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and continual labors in the world I endured for your sake; unless in these you have followed me according to your rule, as far as you are able, patiently and voluntarily, you will certainly be neither my minister, nor my soldier, nor my monk. For in your patience you will possess your soul.

    In this world I desired nothing, had nothing, loved nothing earthly; but poor, humble, and meek, [unclear], I most perfectly subjected myself always in all things to the will of the Father, ready to receive injuries and blows. But you, O cloistered monk, who profess the monastic rule under an abbot or prior, if from now on you have followed the desires of your flesh, if you have possessed a private purse or property of your own in the monastery, if you have loved anything besides me, if you have despised the commands of your preceptor, if you have not served me perseveringly in humility, know for certain that I shall not hold you as a soldier, I shall not count you as a monk, a minister, or a disciple, but judging you a fugitive, an apostate, faithless, false, a mocker, and an unfaithful perjurer, I shall condemn you without mercy forever, as you have deserved, with my betrayer Judas and the fallen angels.

    What your lips vowed to me is no longer yours but mine. But if you have usurped for yourself what is mine, you do not wish to be a monk and my faithful servant, but a thief and a perverse robber, impious and unjust; have no doubt that when I come I shall judge you as such. But if you have persevered faithfully in the holy purpose until death; if you have kept inviolate, under the authority of my vicar whom I appointed shepherd for you, the will which you solemnly consecrated to me; if obedience, poverty, and

    All. II. Fol. VI.

    If you have kept chastity with humility for the love of my name even to the end; if you have always striven to please me alone in all your actions; if you have taken care to follow me without interruption along the steep path of the virtues: knowing without doubt, know most certainly that I shall hold you, made from a servant into a very dear friend, as a soldier to be crowned with me in my kingdom; I shall love you; I shall cherish you; I shall set you gloriously forever in the midst of my saints. Hear me now, my servant, you who, out of reverence and honor for my name, have enrolled yourself in the warfare of monks; and with a great and perfect heart follow the footprints of my feet, just as that blessed teacher of yours, once your friend, taught you and strove with all his efforts to imitate. Let not the enticements of the flesh deceive you, O my strenuous soldier; let not the vain and pernicious dealings of this world seduce your soul, dedicated to me; [unclear] of the unclean spirit, which no mortal has ever been able to escape. Let those last things which you must necessarily undergo always remain in your memory; and from their swiftest passage take up for yourself the necessary dread and contempt of the pleasures of the flesh, which are passing away, and of the future things of this sojourning. Just as brief labor borne patiently and charitably in the world for my sake prepares eternal happiness for my soldiers, so the desires and pleasures of the flesh, which quickly pass away, sink the soul of a sinful man down to hell to be tormented without end. Therefore let all your desires be toward me, monk, you who serve me and who follow me along the steep path of regular observance. Give me your heart if you desire happiness; seek me alone if you love your own life and salvation. When you have loved God, you are tranquil and holy; when you have followed him, you are blessed and glorious without end.

    What would you do, my brothers, if it should happen to you to hear these words which we have spoken from the mouth of our savior and king as he spoke them? What, I ask, would you do? I certainly believe that there would be great compunction in your hearts, if you heard Christ speaking personally in this way. But we, holding Christ’s place in the monastery, speak the words which he has given, and you do not attend; we declare to you the necessary contest of salvation, and you show no signs of compunction. If you do not know what cause there was for my saying these things, I now beg you to understand. I see certain of you abhorring sacred readings, given over to vanities, and caring for nothing less than the perfection of spiritual warfare; their god is their belly, and their glory is in confusion. Do you suppose, most worthless scoundrels, who have no taste for anything spiritual, that Christ will come again from heaven to speak to you those things which he entrusted to his preachers to be spoken? Have you not heard Paul saying: Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God. Once Christ was seen on earth; once he appeared visibly among mortals; once he preached the way of eternal salvation; he will not add a second time. He appointed pastors and vicars over his household to teach the ignorant; wishing to manifest their authority, he said in the Gospel: He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me. Therefore hear those whom Christ has set over you as rectors, to whom he entrusted the distribution of spiritual wheat, as he said in the holy Gospel: Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the lord appointed over his household, to give them wheat in due season? [unclear] fruits, while it is granted to you at the proper time, lest, if you neglect to repent, the time be cut off. For you know what divine Scripture says to us: The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. Beware, I beg you, of delaying the good, because none of you knows when he is to die; rather, attend to that true saying of the wanton poet Naso, who admonishes thus: But hasten, and do not put yourself off to coming hours; he who is not ready today will be less ready tomorrow. No one [unclear] life for himself

    On the Progress of Spiritual Warfare.

    let him promise the brothers long life; but rather let each one think that death is near at hand, and therefore let him live prepared, as though he were to depart from the body tomorrow. For the hope of a longer life has deceived many, and, holding them back from the fervor of their holy purpose, has suddenly plunged them down to the lower world. Therefore complete your service, which necessarily will be ended before long, in such a way that you may not fear to appear before your king when he comes. Always be mindful that you have no abiding city here, nor can you remain long in this mortal life, but death will come quickly and compel you to depart.

    For whoever is a true monk and desires to be a faithful soldier of Christ despises all the delights of this world; he always thinks of his Lord as present to him; and, casting away from himself every impediment and every little burden, he cares above all how he may be able to please him. He ought not to be anxious in seeking the necessities of life, since the providence of the shepherd arranges all these things for those subject to him. Let the whole care of the monk be to keep himself clean from this age, so that, free and released from all things, he may seek nothing but God, think of nothing but Jesus crucified for us.

    O happy soldier of Christ, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised, if faithful, prudent, and vigilant in the love of God he shall remain even to the end. Certainly nothing is happier than a good monk, to whom the Son of God promises himself as a reward; nor anything more laborious, since, placed in the arena of battle, he is daily in peril concerning his salvation; and nothing is stronger than the monk who conquers the world together with the devil, nor anything weaker than one who is overcome by his own flesh.

    Therefore, O monk, you must always keep watch against the hidden enemy of your salvation; for he is never more easily conquered than if he is kept far from the entrance of the mind. Hence, if you desire to escape victorious against him, do not allow the engines of his deceit and fraud to be brought nearer to you. First of all, guard your senses, lest death enter through the windows; and take the greatest care against the enemy's snares when for a time he has allowed you to be secure in your devotion. Never forget the admonition of the wise man, who says: If you do not hold yourself constantly in the fear of the Lord, your house, that is, your conscience, will quickly be overthrown. Therefore Solomon said in Proverbs: Blessed is the man who is always fearful, but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil. For the monk who is presumptuous through security is without doubt tending toward destruction.

    It is therefore necessary that the soldier of Christ always be prepared against his adversaries, so that as long as he lives in this mortal body he may not trust that he has perfectly overcome them. For the flesh always desires against the spirit; and lest the soul at any time be overcome, as long as one happens to live, it is necessary to fight. Whenever you have conquered your invisible enemy, he rises up again and again, having gathered greater [unclear] for you, so that he who cannot obtain victory by strength may at least bring on despair by persistence. But you, most valiant soldier of Christ, take care that you do not fail in the arena of this very brief combat; take care that before the battle has been completed at the end, you do not lay down the arms of necessary defense. For the Savior says: He who has persevered to the end will be saved.

    Do not give rest to your soul as long as it has been granted to you to remain in this miserable pilgrimage, but always do something good, lest the devil ever find you idle. Always remember the admonition of Scripture, saying: Whatever your hand is able to do, work at it earnestly, because neither work nor reason nor wisdom nor knowledge will exist in the lower world, to which you hasten. There is no one who lives forever, but we all die, and like waters we fall away into the earth, which will not return again to their former state. Then there will no longer be time to do good for the merit of eternal happiness; but whatever a man has sown here and now in this present time, then he will receive as recompense. Therefore holy Scripture says again: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand cease. And Saint Paul, admonishing Timothy, says: Labor like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. For no one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has approved himself. For even of those who contend in the arena, no one will be crowned unless he has contended lawfully. But everyone who contends in the arena abstains from all things. In another place also the same lover of Christ says: I want you to be without anxiety.

    You therefore, soldier of Christ, who contend in the arena of daily battle so that at last you may appear glorious forever before your God, [unclear] the corruptible [unclear] who, contending in the arena, indeed for a corruptible

    [unclear], lest he be defeated, abstains from everything, so that naked and free he may run the more swiftly. Therefore, if you desire to walk the way of God in true purity, if you wish to defeat the enemy in the contest of a steadfast mind, cast from yourself all the garments of fleshly pleasures. For whoever has learned to run naked, having thrown off hair and clothing, carries around nothing besides the unencumbered body by which he can be held by the adversary. For he who runs naked has stripped himself of every anxiety over the things clamoring round about, and thinks of nothing other than victory; nor does he care meanwhile what is being done at home with wife or children. Nothing present calls him back from the course; the agility of his companions does not frighten him off. Among many he contends as though alone; he hastens breathless toward the prize as though certain. Imitate him, soldier of Christ, in the spiritual struggle: naked, contemplate the naked Savior hanging on the cross, so that you may be able to cast down the adversary the more easily, the less he sees you to possess of the vanities of the world. Therefore fight naked, light, and unencumbered on every side; naked and freed from everything, fly into heaven. Naked you came into this world; naked you are to return to the earth. Pondering these things diligently, my brothers, so run that you may obtain eternal life with all the saints. Amen. The homily ends.

    What the Armor of Spiritual Warfare Is. Homily III.

    Most beloved brothers, today we have heard the holy apostle writing in the epistle to the Ephesians: Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil; for our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against princes and powers, against the rulers of the world of these darknesses, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, that you may be able to resist on the evil day, and in all things to stand perfected. He then adds what the armor of God is: Stand therefore, having girded your loins in truth, and having put on the breastplate of justice, and having shod your feet in preparation for the gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, praying at all times in the Spirit with every prayer and supplication, and in the same keeping watch with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints. To the Thessalonians likewise he says: But let us, who are of the day, be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and charity, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.

    These are the arms, brothers, with which the soldiers of Christ, once clothed, vanquish the savage adversary; these are the monks’ signs of virtues, without which no one attains victory over vices. The instruments of human warfare, which very many mortals pursue too eagerly, are helmet, shield, breastplate, sword, dagger, cuirass, belt, lance, and many other things of that kind. Men about to proceed to war are armed with these most carefully, and unless they have been most diligently protected over the whole body, they are certainly judged less fit for battle. But the arms of our spiritual warfare are faith, hope, charity, patience, humility, obedience, chastity, together with each of the holy virtues of the soul enumerated by our holy teacher Benedict under chapter four, where he makes beautiful mention of the instruments of good works. And would that, my brothers, we were as careful and diligent concerning these spiritual arms of our warfare as we see worldly men to be anxious about their corruptible armor.

    But now, which I say with too much grief, since we shamefully cast aside the arms of salvation with which we ought to have overcome all our adversaries, what else remains except that we succumb to our enemy in the struggle? But perhaps you will say: If the Christian faith, as the apostle testifies, belongs to the arms of spiritual warfare, we certainly intend to remain in it. But granted. What then does Saint James say in his epistle? What will it profit, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith, but does not have works? Can faith save him? For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. Therefore, whenever Scripture speaks of faith, it must always be understood not as common and dead, but as formed by good works and illumined by the sweetness of divine love. For no one will be saved by faith so [unclear].

    What the Armor of Spiritual Warfare Is.

    With the greatest zeal always strive that you may be able to hold this shield of faith, formed by holy works, in your hands against all the attacks of your enemies, because he is never conquered by the adversary who is protected by this impregnable shield. Confirming this, the blessed Augustine also says, from the words of the Lord:

    There are no greater riches, no treasures, no honors; there is no greater substance of this world than the Catholic faith, which saves sinful human beings, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores the penitent, increases the just, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins and widows and married persons in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, and places believers in the eternal inheritance with the holy angels.

    Thus in the root of a tree there appears absolutely no form of beauty, and yet whatever beauty or comeliness there is in the tree proceeds from it; so also from the humility of faith, whatever of merit, whatever of blessedness the [unclear] soul has, all proceeds from the foundation of faith. For as the Apostle says, whatever, or everything, that is not from faith is sin, since without faith it is impossible to please God. For one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is the rewarder of those who seek him. But the more anyone loves, the more fully he advances in faith. For faith without charity is like something cast away as useless, and a shield without a strap.

    O faith, a treasure richer than all things: when formed in the mind of mortal man, you make him equal to the immortals; you conquer demons and strongly overcome all hard and adverse kingdoms. Faith is the foundation of all virtues, without which no spiritual building stands. Faith is the illuminator of the mind and the principal instrument of spiritual warfare. For without the shield of faith the devil is not conquered, nor do you overcome the [unclear] of wanton flesh. Therefore, brothers, let us consider how necessary faith formed by charity is for us, and [unclear], because in this warfare, while we fight, neither is victory granted to us nor is confidence preserved. For faith is a shield, with which we very easily conquer the enemy of our salvation, if we are bound to it by the handle of divine love. For the blessed Pope Gregory says: We are truly faithful if we fulfill by works what we promise in [unclear]. In this armor, since faith is the foundation of all good works, all our prayers

    All Things. III. VIII

    [unclear] must precede, so that the mind may be able to arrive at love. For unless faith is first held, one in no way reaches spiritual love. For charity does not precede faith, but faith precedes charity, because no one can love or hope for a good which he refuses to believe.

    But since now you faithfully believe what he also commands, and have placed the foundation of the spiritual building upon a firm rock, it is now necessary that without delay you also do the remaining things that are needed for perfection. Therefore love peace and truth, so that in the faith of Christ, as true soldiers, you may be able at all times to remain stable and most steadfast. For, as Scripture bears witness, truth is great and stronger than all things, nor is there anything unjust with it. Whoever loves truth is a true disciple of Christ, and loves Christ himself, who says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” All the ways of the Lord likewise are mercy and truth; from this Satan fell through pride, because he did not remain in everlasting truth.

    Therefore the holy Christ-loving Paul commands the soldiers of the Lord to gird themselves in truth; in this he wished to show the state of perfection toward which cloistered persons especially ought to strive. For what else is it to love truth than to be a human being as one is commanded to be, and so to live according to the norm of justice, true and solid, such as holy perfection requires of nature through grace? Hence Firmianus Lactantius says: “Let those who devote themselves to truth cast away the pleasures hostile to it and troublesome, which bind the soul to themselves and do not allow it to be free. But let eternal things always be preferred to false, useful things to pleasant. Let nothing be pleasing to the sight except what can be done justly, piously, and religiously; nothing sweet to the hearing except what makes the soul better.”

    Therefore soldiers have their loins girded in truth when, having despised the enticements of the flesh and the vanities of the world for the love of God, they strive with all their strength so to conduct themselves and live that they may be able in all things to please the highest Truth, which is God. After this the soldier of Christ is commanded to put on the breastplate of justice, without which no one can rightly and fruitfully serve the Lord as a soldier. Justice, moreover, is to preserve and distribute to each person what is owed to him according to law or nature. And this is the most excellent of all virtues; without it there can be no piety, no religion, no holiness, and no discernment of good and evil. For it is light and a great splendor, from which the force and dominion of every good rises up among mortals. Justice is the mother of innocence, the nurse of concord, the parent of friendship, the begetter of piety, and the preserver of religion. Justice, as Scripture bears witness, is perpetual and immortal; injustice, however, is the acquisition of death.

    In what ways the Christian soldier ought to put on this breastplate of justice, our Savior himself declares in the holy Gospel, saying: “All things whatsoever you wish men to do to you, do you also likewise to them.” Therefore, my brothers, keep this manner of living in the monastery: that each one should do for his fellow soldier in all things just as, according to the right judgment of reason, he desires at all times to have done to himself by others. For this is the first duty of justice, that one harm no one; then, that one use common goods without any harm to another; and, what our warfare further requires, that one do for a brother what, by just reason, conduces to salvation as to one’s own.

    O how great a peace mortals would enjoy if they followed the exhortations of the apostle, by which each is commanded to bear the burdens of the other. “Everyone,” says Scripture, “who does justice is born of God.” This is the breastplate [unclear]: to show worship and piety to God, holiness to ourselves, and brotherly charity to our neighbor. We all serve Christ as soldiers under the trophy of justice; if anyone is unjust, he shows that he belongs not to the soldiery of Christ, but rather to the company of demons. For justice is the greatest virtue, which distributes to each what is his own; if you lack it, you lose the name of soldier. Therefore render worship and piety to God; to your superior [unclear]. For this indeed, brothers, is the true justice of monks: that each one should conduct himself without offense according to the prescribed norm of the law, assigning to each his proper dignity: reverence to his superior, concord to his equal, discipline to his inferior, worship and obedience to God.

    and holiness for himself; patience for an enemy; mercy for the poor; brotherly charity in the Lord for all. Therefore the holy Christ-lover says: “We are debtors, brothers, not to the flesh, that we should live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” He therefore fights rightly who gives to each what is his own. Next we are commanded to have our feet shod in preparation for the gospel of peace, so that the good which, by the Lord’s generosity, we ourselves have come to know, we may also gladly communicate to others. For our law, brothers, according to which we are commanded to serve as soldiers for the Lord, is the gospel of Jesus Christ, to which all the rule and constitutions of cloistered persons are ordered. For our monastic constitutions have not been established as the gospel, but the statutes of monks have been made on account of the gospel. For a Christian can be saved without being a monk; but a monk cannot be saved unless he is a Christian. Let certain excessively superstitious and foolish cloistered persons be ashamed, who value their own rules and statutes more than the gospel of Christ; who observe the traditions of men even to prisons and chains, but do not heed the constitutions of God and of holy universal Church. To these the words of our Savior, speaking to the Jews according to Matthew, rightly apply: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?” And the evangelical teaching is to be preferred by far to all the constitutions of the whole world. After the gospel, however, the statutes of the universal Church hold the first place of authority, and neither the constitutions nor the rules of monks are compared with them in dignity. Let us take care to live according to evangelical purity, and we shall be perfect in the monastic way of life of the fathers. Let our feet always be shod in preparation for the gospel of peace, so that we may mortify in ourselves the desires of the flesh, and through love of God and neighbor may have peace with all. For without peace and the concord of brotherhood, mortification of the flesh is of no profit, as Saint Jerome says: “Whoever afflicts the body but abandons concord does indeed praise God on the timbrel, but does not praise him in the choir.” Hence Solomon says: “Better is a dry morsel with joy than a house full of victims with strife.” And again he says: “It is an honor for a man to separate himself from contentions; but all fools are mingled with insults.” The holy Christ-lover also, a lover of peace, admonishes us, saying: “Follow peace with all, and holiness, without which no one will see God.” Hence also the prophet Zechariah: “Love peace and truth,” says the Lord almighty. And our Savior says in the holy gospel according to Mark: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.” “There is no peace for the impious,” says the Lord. But he is truly a soldier of Christ who has peace with God, with his neighbor, and within himself. A man is said to have peace with God when, moved by good will and turned toward him through the continual desire of love, despising transitory things, he directs the gaze of his mind to things above, and most diligently keeps all the things that the Lord has commanded. For when the Son of God was born in the flesh, the holy angels sang glory to the Lord, who sits above all things in the heights, and announced peace to men of good will. But impious and unjust men cannot have this peace with God, because they have turned their wills away from the Lord. He has peace with his neighbor who does injury to no one, who, when injured, does not repay vengeance, but, overcoming evil with good, never abandons brotherly charity. If any of his neighbors unjustly murmurs against such a man, the soldier of Christ has not on that account abandoned peace, because perhaps another has begun an unjust murmuring without just cause. A just man, who has peace with God and desires to harm none of his neighbors, will rightly be called peaceable, even if someone, disturbed unjustly, rises up against him. For the just man says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they fought against me without cause.” Hence Saint Augustine speaks: “Among the true worshippers of God, even wars themselves are peaceful, because they are waged not from greed or cruelty, but from zeal for peace, so that the evil may be restrained and the good relieved.” He has peace within himself who, enlightened by purity and holiness, lives secure in his conscience without error, whom anxious synteresis does not bite back, nor any unjust or wicked thought disturb. Hence again Augustine: “Peace is serenity of mind, tranquility of soul, simplicity of heart, the bond of love, the fellowship of charity.” For it removes enmities and rivalries; it restrains wars.

    All. III. Fol. IX.

    It restrains anger; it treads down the proud; it loves the humble; it quiets the discordant; it reconciles enemies. It is calm toward all, burdensome to none, troublesome to none, onerous to none; it does not know how to exalt itself, it does not know how to be puffed up. Whoever receives this, let him hold it; whoever has lost it, let him seek it again; whoever has let it go, let him search it out, because whoever is not found in it is disowned by the Father, disinherited by the Son, and, no less, is made alien to the Holy Spirit. He can never come to the inheritance of God who refused to observe the testament of peace. For the place of God is in peace, but the devil’s dwelling is in anger and disturbance.

    Therefore every person who does not have this threefold peace in his heart, who does not offer it in his mouth, nor show it in his works, is to be called neither a monk nor a Christian. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. If those who make peace are called sons of God, beyond doubt those who confound peace are sons of Satan. Therefore, my dearest brothers, have among yourselves that peace which the world cannot give, which is the peace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, concerning which Isaiah the prophet said: And the work of justice shall be peace, and the service of justice silence, and security forever. For God is the Lord of peace and love; therefore whoever violates peace and brotherly love shows that he is not a true lover of God. Let the true peace of Christ be in your hearts, and you will fear no adversities of this world.

    Let true peace also be among you, not feigned, because Christ desires peace not from the mouth but from the heart, and wishes one’s neighbor to be greeted by affection rather than by the lips. Therefore if any one of you has in anything saddened his brother, let him make satisfaction to him as soon as possible before the setting of the sun, and take care, all of you, that the sun not set upon your anger before him; and, falling at his knees, ask pardon. And the sword, says the Spirit, which is the word of God, through every prayer and supplication, let us, soldiers of Christ, always hold in our hands. The word of God, which is contained in the holy scriptures, is a victorious defense against all assaults of demons, as we are admonished by the example of our Savior, who, when tempted by the devil, with tranquil gentleness hurled the testimonies of the divine scriptures in his face, saying: It is written, Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

    And you, monk, serving as a soldier for Christ, whenever you are tempted by the devil, at once impress the sign of the holy cross upon your forehead, and say with Saint John Chrysostom in a certain homily: I renounce you, Satan, with all your iniquities, and I join myself to you, Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, because it is written: The soul that has sinned, it shall die. This is the sword of the Spirit, most sharp on both sides; if, from the very beginning of temptation, you always brandish it in your hands against the enemy, with God protecting you, you will easily overcome all his contrivances and snares. For scripture says: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

    And so, rising from bed in the morning, at once make that protestation which I have described against the adversary of your salvation, and neither the devil nor any perverse person will be able to harm you by incantation or sorcery, whether that be [unclear] or something else. Do this same thing when you are about to sleep at night, and whenever you perceive some temptation of the malignant spirit rising up in your thought. And thus you will be safe in all your ways, and the devil will flee far from you and will not dare to come nearer to you, unless your own sloth first trips you up, so that either you cast away the sword or immediately commit some mortal sin. For scripture says: Those who commit iniquity and sin are enemies of their own soul. Solomon also says in Proverbs: His own iniquities seize the impious man, and by the cords [unclear]. If, therefore, brothers, you wish to be secure under the protection of Almighty God, flee sin, because sin separates us from the help of the Lord, just as purity and cleanness of conscience join us to God, as Isaiah the prophet says: Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened so that it cannot save, nor is his ear heavy so that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he would not hear. Jeremiah also says: Our iniquities have turned away these things, and our sins have kept good

    On the reading and study of the divine Scriptures

    by us. For everyone who sins mortally opens the door of his heart to the devil and closes it to God; nor can he trust in the aid of the Most High as long as he has remained lying in wickedness without repentance.

    Here ends Homily III.

    On the reading and study of the divine Scriptures: Homily Four.

    Since every Scripture, divinely inspired, as the holy [apostle of Christ?] says, is useful for teaching, or for arguing, for correcting, for instructing in justice, so that the man of God may be perfect, instructed for every good work, we ought gladly to direct to the reading of the divine Scriptures some portion of the zeal for secular literature in which we once labored. For in the divine Scriptures whatever saving knowledge requires is found expressed most abundantly, so that what you do not find there is by no means necessary for salvation. For the majesty of the divine Scriptures far surpasses all the knowledge and teaching of the whole world, which the Holy Spirit poured into the men of God so that it might be written, and, so that it may be understood, he bestows the grace of his illumination upon studious readers.

    This Scripture, my brothers, turn over diligently with purity of mind and the fervor of twin charity, for whoever truly loves God spends all the time he can find free in sacred reading. Let the frenzied deeds, so to speak, of fleshly lovers be incentives to you, I pray, toward the wholesome study of the Scriptures: they, receiving letters and little pledges from their mistresses, do not cease to read them, and often reread and kiss them; and, what is a greater sign of love, they hang them either from the neck or at the breast, so that the beloved memory of her whom they desire may never depart from the mind.

    Consider, brothers, the madness of carnal men in love, and blush at your own lukewarmness concerning the love of God. Which of you is affected toward the holy Scriptures of God with so great a love of heart as a blind lover, insane with affection, is inflamed toward the filthy and utterly vain love-letters of one little harlot? He, because of love for the absent woman whom he desires, guards her letters and little gifts with frequent kisses; pondering every single stroke with excessive love, he examines them again and again; in all that he does he is always thinking of the absent woman; anxiously he hastens to come into her sight.

    O if we who are called Christian monks, who serve the supreme and immortal king Christ Jesus, who are commanded to love our God above all things and are enjoined to love nothing in this world except him, if, I say, we were to pursue our creator with as much love as carnally minded men observe and love their corruptible and mortal girlfriends. The holy Scripture read daily brings God before us, manifests his will to us, instructs us what we ought to do, and discloses what we ought to avoid. Through it the almighty speaks with us, and, instructing us by an invisible teaching, consoles us, as the holy apostle says: For whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.

    Therefore the true soldier of Christ, and especially the cloistered one, who loves God in his whole heart and longs to please him alone, embraces the divine Scriptures, and above all the holy Gospel, with affection, and is constantly occupied in its reading and meditation. But whoever neglects readings of the divine Scriptures clearly shows that he is not a true lover of God. But what does Scripture itself say? He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the laws, his prayer will be detestable. But blessed are they who examine the testimonies of the Lord; with their whole heart they seek him.

    And so you, my brothers, if you truly love the Lord Jesus in your whole heart, if you desire above all things to please him as true soldiers, if finally you wish to advance toward the perfection of the monastic life, you ought always to occupy yourselves with fervent affection in the reading of the divine Scriptures. How useful the reading of the Scriptures is, blessed Jerome intimates, saying: Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. For after God nothing in this life is taken in more pleasantly, nothing is felt more sweetly, nothing separates the mind more powerfully from love of this world, nothing so strengthens the soldier of Christ against all the temptations of adversaries, nothing disposes and confirms a monk so much for every good work, as frequent reading and ardent study of the Scriptures. Indeed, if the benefits of the almighty which

    Homily IV. Fol. X.

    ...he has bestowed upon the human race, when by reading through the whole breadth of Scripture we recall them to memory with studious devotion, they will furnish us the greatest material and occasion by which, burning more greatly in the love of God, we may make progress. For what else does the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures contain than a certain right order of the good things which God has either already bestowed on men or has promised that he will also give? Or what is there that can so strengthen us for the endurance of evils and render us willingly patient, as if we read in the Gospel that the Son of God suffered innocently for us, and after him the victories of the holy martyrs?

    For sacred Scripture contains the things necessary for us for saving knowledge, and it admonishes us what, as soldiers in this pilgrimage, we ought usefully to seek, and what also to avoid. Hence again Saint Jerome says: “Our riches are to meditate on the law of God day and night.” Let us therefore prepare strength for ourselves; let us assume perfect might, so that amid the darkness of errors and the confusion of night the light of the knowledge of Christ may appear, and days and nights may have a protecting light, so that, with Scripture as our guide, we may be able to arrive at the holy land.

    For what is better than this learning, what discipline sweeter? What is sweeter than our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true salvation and sweetness of faithful souls? Let Christ be our banquet; let sacred reading be our food and drink. For what can the life of a monk or priest be without knowledge of the Scriptures? We know Christ not by sight, not by hearing, not by touch, but by reading the Scriptures; and the more we advance by reading toward true knowledge, the more we are delighted in the holy Scriptures.

    For what is sweeter than to know the will of God and not to be ignorant of the rewards of his promises? For, as Jerome says, the field of the divine word is most rich: it has in itself all delights, and whatever you wish springs from it, just as the Jews report that manna in the desert, when it was eaten, tasted in the mouth of the eater according to his will and desire. Therefore, my brothers, read the divine Scriptures often; through them you can plainly know the will of God and arm yourselves most strongly against the snares of the devil.

    For if, according to the apostle Paul, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, he who does not know the Scriptures does not know the power and wisdom of God; and how will he know Christ? Ignorance is of Christ; and he who does not know Christ will not belong to his fellowship, as Saint Christophilus says, because if anyone is ignorant, surely he too will be ignored.

    Moreover, the more constant anyone has been in the study of the divine Scriptures, the greater understanding and sweetness he receives from reading them. But it especially befits you, brothers, to turn over the divine Scriptures daily by reading and learning, since both abundant time, free from occupations, is granted to you, and a place sufficiently suitable is offered by the rarity of those who come by.

    Therefore I exhort and admonish you, if you love your salvation, always to have the divine readings in your hands, so that all the time which, after the worship of prayer, is permitted to you without labor may be spent on the study of sacred Scripture. Let no day pass, my brothers, on which a monk serving Christ as a soldier does not read something from the sacred volumes that may make him better in his holy purpose. Rather, let him follow the counsel of Saint Jerome, who says: “Let the divine Scriptures always be in your hands and be continually turned over in the mind; nor should you think it enough to store up the commandments of God in memory, unless you strive also to fulfill them in works.”

    For God, my brothers, requires two things of us. First, he wishes us to know his most holy will; second, that, once known, we do it. But we cannot know his commandments if we are ignorant of the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Nor does he do the will of God who is ignorant of it, nor has he known it who has not learned it. Learn, therefore, what is the pleasing will of God, that you may do it; do it once known, that you may understand more fully.

    For no one understands the will of God better than he who, once he has known it, does it from love. And so, if you desire to become a most learned interpreter of the divine Scriptures, learn to begin the pursuit of knowledge not from words but in holy works. For then you will comprehend the rich knowledge of sacred reading, if you have kept your heart clean from every sin, and, struck and pierced in holy compunction in the love of God, you continually turn over Scripture. For the knowledge of the divine Scriptures is a high mountain on which Moses speaks with the Lord; to which the [unclear] of vices...

    Of the delight in and study of the divine Scriptures.

    A man polluted with filth is forbidden [the mount]. For so it is read in Exodus: "Beware that you go not up into the mount, nor touch the borders of it. Everyone that toucheth the mount shall die the death. Whether it be beast or man, it shall not live." For a man touches the mount and dies as often as anyone, puffed up with secular learning, is scandalized at the simplicity of the divine Scriptures. But a beast touches the mount and is overwhelmed with stones as often as a man, immersed in the carnal fury of the passions, proceeds to the study of sacred Scripture with a soul unpurged. If, therefore, you wish to unroll the readings of the divine Scriptures wholesomely, if by reading you desire to attain to true knowledge, take care first of all to put off all relation of pride and the rashness of perfidy, and then to purge the chamber of your heart from all the uncleanness of carnal pleasures. For God, as the canonical Scripture says, "resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." No one proud, puffed up, arrogant, and rash—no one carnal in mind, lustful or restless—is held fit for the study of sacred Scripture, but only the humble, the meek, the gentle, the modest, the chaste, the tranquil in body and mind. Hence Prosper says in an epigram: "The commands of God a mind not quiet cannot search out." Therefore, that religious study may be exercised, the quarrels of the malignant must be cast away. The quiet can in some measure search out the law, if, free from the noise of the world, they are at leisure. That the mind, then, intent on pious studies, may be helped, let divine love conquer the wars of the flesh. For the temple of the Lord grows by sacred silences and is silently built—a house not to fall. With minds cleansed, therefore, and the heart compunct in the love of God and humbled in true contrition, proceed to the study of the Scriptures; for the Lord will not enlighten you unless he has first made you purged from all iniquity. For, as Scripture itself says, "perverse thoughts separate from God; but virtue proved corrects the foolish, since wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins; for the holy spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding." And therefore we must cry out with holy David, more frequently, to the Lord: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my bowels."

    For no one usefully understands the sacred Scriptures of God who does not turn himself with his whole heart to the Lord through [his] power. And therefore, if you wish to understand the divine words both rightly and wholesomely, take care above all, with [your] study, to keep yourselves clean from all pollution of sin according to your strength. Let not the insane folly of certain monks seduce you, I pray—who try to excuse their ignorance with a trite proverb, saying: "What is the knowledge of the Scriptures to us, who have no office of preaching?" [Rather] let us embrace the counsel of the wise man, who says in the book of Proverbs: "He that walks simply walks confidently." "It is enough for us to live simply"—since the servant who knows the will of his lord and does it not shall be beaten with many stripes, but he who did not know [and] committed [things] worthy of stripes shall be beaten with few. O most hateful and abandoned scoundrels, who despise saving knowledge, and love the ignorance of the divine Scriptures rather than the understanding [of them]! Will affected ignorance render you liable to fewer stripes? Or will you therefore, sinning, be guiltless before God, because you are voluntarily ignorant of the commands of God? You shall be tortured with a double penalty: the one, that you despise to know the way of God's commands; the other, that you keep not his words. It is not the simplicity which you allege, but rather a twofold impiety. For if, according to the prophet, "blessed are they that keep the testimonies of the Lord," who would doubt that those are accursed who neither seek out God nor heed his Scriptures, but rather with a hardened mind the more despise [them]? Hear

    Homilies, four.

    ...those who are unlearned will die in poverty of heart. What is more wretched than an unlearned priest? Even if he does not have the office of preaching, nevertheless by reason of the order he has received he is bound to knowledge of the Scriptures. For God wills that every human being fulfil his holy will; and no one who is ignorant is able to do this. Therefore the Lord first commands that you learn what is pleasing to him, and secondly that you do it. How, then, will you think ignorance of the law excusable, through which you have become transgressors of the first will of God?

    Why do you think almighty God handed over the scrolls of his Scriptures to men? Was it so that they should be read by them and understood, or so that, unread, they should be despised? Certainly the Scriptures of God’s commandments were given to mortals so that they should read them, and afterwards so that they should fulfil them in deed. But you, who with deliberate mind wish to be ignorant of God’s Scriptures, how can you do the will of him which they teach? Or in what way will you be able to be doers of the law, who have not first been hearers? For it can happen that someone who knows the will of God either observes it or neglects it; but it cannot happen that someone ignorant of it fulfils it. Indeed, someone will more easily fail to do a good thing that he knows than carry out in deed what he does not know. No one does a good thing that he does not know.
