    Saint Augustine says of the ignorant in a certain place: “Not everyone who is ignorant is free from fault. For that ignorant man can be excused from punishment who found no way to learn. But pardon cannot be granted to those who, when they had from whom they might learn, did not devote labor to discipline.” Hence also Saint Leo the pope says: “If ignorance seems intolerable in laymen, how much more in those who are in charge; nor is it worthy of excuse or pardon.” Therefore, brothers, do not think yourselves excused before God by ignorance of the divine Scriptures, but rather doubly guilty, since, lest you should have to do God’s will, you desire to be wholly ignorant of it. For a human being ought not to be ignorant of the divine will, since he is placed in the world for this purpose: that through illumination of the understanding and purity of affection he may merit the everlasting enjoyment of the vision of him. For both kinds of knowledge, namely of God and of oneself, are necessary for every mortal for salvation, and he will nowhere find this without knowledge of the Scriptures. Indeed, just as from knowledge of oneself there comes into a man the fear of God, and from knowledge of him love is born, so from ignorance of oneself there proceeds pride, and from neglected knowledge of God contempt, with despair of salvation.

    Nothing is more unhappy than an unlearned monk who neglects or despises the study of the holy Scriptures, because he can never abide pure with himself in true tranquillity of heart, but is compelled by his own restlessness, contrary to the integrity of monastic life, to occupy his mind with external and useless things. We see among you certain men who are ignorant of the Scriptures, and who are the less inclined toward discipline. It is indeed shameful not to know what you are commanded to know; more shameful not to learn it; but most shameful to despise it. And there are among you certain men who do not know saving knowledge; there are also those who neglect to learn. What if I add that there are still others who utterly despise knowledge of the divine Scriptures? Certainly I am not lying; you know that what I say is true. For some of you have resisted my studies bitterly, even to the point of envy, cavilling that you would rather have a ploughman set over you than a man of prayer. Did they not also try to draw the visitors into their opinion, wishing by their encouragement to lead me away into renunciation of the Scriptures, so that they might make me a field-worker and a keeper of pigs rather than of souls? But in vain do they try to hinder the divine oracle; under its impulse I have resolved, as long as I live, to set all the honors and riches of the world after the study of the Scriptures. I am your abbot for as long as he who called me shall will it; if one of the two must be chosen, I prefer to give up the abbacy rather than renounce the study of holy Scripture. For I know truly that nothing more salutary can befall a cloistered man in this life than if he begins truly to love the divine Scriptures.

    Whoever of you wishes to follow this instruction of mine will have me alike as leader and companion of the journey. But whoever despises me as I learn will nevertheless be compelled to hear me as I teach, even against his will. I have said these things against those who, savoring earthly and perishable things, cast the fear of the Lord away from themselves; who, being utterly ignorant of everything, despise learning. I know the faces of my flock, and I believe that I am not wholly ignorant of the inclinations of the hearts of each of you. Therefore I shall not cease to exhort you to the holy studies of the Scriptures, knowing that a lover of sacred reading cannot be a practitioner of carnal vices. For how much...

    On the daily renewal of one’s purpose.

    ...the more zealously a monk has devoted himself to thoroughly learning the Scriptures, the less he is inflamed by the fires of carnal pleasures. For although, according to the saying of Saint Jerome, the monk’s office seems not to be that of one who teaches, but rather of one who mourns, nevertheless, because he professes the warfare of Christ, it is fitting, indeed necessary, that he should know the well-pleasing will of almighty God, to whose words and arms he has sworn. But just as a soldier cannot know the will of his lord who is far absent except through messengers and letters, so the monk will not understand the precepts of the eternal King except through sacred readings and sermons, the evangelical Scriptures. The reading of the Scriptures opens the gate of salvation to those who do not know it; it leads the diligent reader by the straight path to the knowledge of God; it makes the lover of it despise all worldly things and love nothing other than true wisdom. But nothing is more shameful than for a monk in the spiritual life to be unwilling to make progress, and knowingly to wish to be ignorant of the will of God. Let no one flatter himself on account of his weakness or ignorance, since he who is ignorant will be ignored, and he who hates saving knowledge is deservedly condemned. The [Lord?], about to send the preachers of the Lord into all the earth, warned them beforehand, saying: Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves, lest either you be supplanted by someone through ignorance, or you devise injury against someone through deceit. For there is little difference in vice between being able to deceive and being deceived. Therefore I beg you, dearest brothers, that you be willing to attend to the Rule of our holy father Benedict, which admonishes you in very many places to labor frequently in readings of the divine Scriptures. For in the Scriptures we are taught, instructed for every piety, how we ought to live in this very brief pilgrimage of our sojourning, so that we may be able to please the Lord our God above all things. For it belongs to monks, for the love of God, to despise the world and all pleasures of the present life; manfully to restrain the illicit motions of the flesh; to apply themselves also to prayer, reading, and meditation on the Scriptures; and continually to lift the mind from earthly things to heavenly. Blessed is that monk who has not gone away in the counsel of the impious, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the chair of pestilent men, but meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, learning here

    On the Daily Renewal of the Holy Purpose: Fifth Homily.

    We have heard, dearest brothers, the reading recited to us from the book of holy Job, in which he laments the misery of the human race, and the calamity of this life, and at the same time its unstable brevity. “Man,” he says, “born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state.” “Behold,” he says, “the brief years pass by, and I walk the path by which I shall not return.” “All flesh shall fail together, and man shall return to ashes.” What, brothers, do you notice among these things, or what do you think? Is there any man among us who does not know that he is mortal, who can say with truth, “I shall not be moved forever”? Alas, my brothers, how blind we are while keeping our eyes open; how forgetful and sluggish travelers we are, who know most certainly that we are going to die, and yet place such confidence in the vanity of the present life as if we were not mortal. But “what man is he who will live and not see death, who will deliver his soul from the hand of hell?” Behold, Scripture says, “we all die, and like water we flow away upon the earth.” Therefore remember, my brothers, that death does not delay, and all that has passed will be counted brief; because, as the holy lover of Christ Paul says, “it is appointed for men once [to die].” If, then, with the eyes of the mind we were always to place before us the coming of death, and were so to order our life and [unclear] that we might always be found prepared, how blessed and secure our departure could become. Did not also the King of the living and the dead, Christ himself our Lord, wishing us always to be ready for death, warn us beforehand in the holy Gospel, saying: “Therefore you also be ready, because at the hour you do not think, the Son of Man will come.” But how much it profits for

    Homily V.

    Fol. XII.

    for purity of mind, frequent meditation on death: the wise man in Ecclesiasticus gave warning, saying: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Thought of future death brings fears; but fear necessarily [unclear] the mind; like a nail driven by a hammer, it fastens the impulse of the flesh and proud movements to the wood of the cross. In consideration of this, many of the pagan philosophers used to say that the whole life of a wise man is a kind of continual meditation on death. Hence Saint Jerome says: “Nothing will profit you so much toward temperance in all things as frequent meditation on this brief and uncertain life, which, like a leaf seized by the wind, passes away; and when it is not feared, it falls into death. Therefore keep the memory of your death, which by no counsel can you escape, and you will easily be able to overcome all the movements of the flesh. For he who sometimes thinks that he is going to die despises present things, and, unless he is utterly foolish, will prepare himself for future things.”

    For I know, and in part I confess that I have experienced, that the will of the human mind cannot long remain uniform in the holy fervor of spiritual life; and for that reason it has pleased me to recall the memory of death more often before your eyes, so that the mind, struck by fear of future things, may be renewed daily in a holier purpose. The human soul, bound through the exercise of itself to the eternal body [unclear], is very small and wavering and unstable; now it is carried off to one thing, and now it is moved to another. Therefore the wisdom of God says through Solomon in Proverbs: “My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes keep my ways.” As if he were saying: Unless you have bound the whole love of your heart to divine wisdom, you will never be stable and confirmed in keeping the Lord’s commandments. For just as the heart is the first principle of motion in man, so the greater is the watch kept over it for the preservation of life, since if it is struck by the assault of diseases, the whole life of the body is already in danger. Hence it is written: “With all watchfulness keep your heart, because life proceeds from it.” By the name of the heart, however, we understand the affection whenever it inclines toward the love of some thing, clinging to it so much that it entangles the whole will. Hence the psalmist says: “If riches abound, do not set your heart on them,” that is, do not love them with the desire of the will. Nothing is more changeable than the human heart, because it is altered by almost every single thought and can with difficulty remain in the same purpose, unless it restrains itself by a certain forceful intention. Saint David, not ignorant of this, said to the Lord: “But I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever. Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled.”

    Therefore, my dearest brothers, if there is any one of you who desires to serve our Lord and Savior in true purity of heart, if anyone wishes to be a monk in deed as well as in name, let him learn first to trust not in himself but in God; and let him take care to renew the good purpose of holy conduct with an ever-new institution, not only every day, but, so far as he is able, even at each hour and in the moments of his actions. The fervor of spiritual conduct, to whose experiential operation the institution of the cloistered life is understood to be wholly ordered, cannot long remain at the same point, because if it does not always advance toward what lies ahead, it necessarily slips back toward lower things, and, what is worse, weaker things. There is no stationary, lingering standing-place in the arena of spiritual exercise, because it is the property of the human heart by its own natural motion always either to advance toward better things or to fall back into that which is evil. Hence, if you do not advance in spiritual conduct, you necessarily fail; if you do not progress toward holier things, you certainly go backward. Since experience has made this clear to us, I do not cease to admonish your charity that you always stretch the desire of your heart in good conduct toward further things, lest there you perilously incur the danger of failing, where you have not found an opening for becoming perfect. The fervor of spiritual purpose must be directed toward the love of God, and cannot otherwise be preserved in him. For the love of God is not absurdly compared to fire: just as fire, when the fuel of wood is withdrawn, is necessarily extinguished, so the love of God, if continuous exercises in good works are lacking, is endangered as it vanishes away. Hence there is that saying of the Savior in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” O monks, happy is that conscience in whose breast nothing burns except the love of Christ, which loves him above all things and despises all pursuits of vanity. Now consider, brothers, your consciences most diligently, and examine precisely whether you love God above all things.

    On the daily renewal of holy purpose.

    If the fire of divine love is now burning in you, apply fuel, lest at any time, through your lukewarmness, you feel the little sparks of holy fervor utterly extinguished. Believe me, brothers, for experience has taught me: while the fire of divine fervor is burning in you, you will preserve it with easier exercise than, once it is extinguished, you will kindle it again. Therefore whoever now experiences the love of God in himself, whoever has received heavenly charity in his heart, let each one take care with solicitude not to fall back into the negligences of his former life, and let him apply the necessary fuel of spiritual exercises, so that he may be able to preserve the fervor of God as it advances within him. Let him beware not only great sins, but also small negligences, and, as far as he can, the least ones; for he who despises the least thing falls little by little, and he who does not always fear danger will soon feel the loss of spiritual fervor and of his former purpose. For Scripture says: If you do not steadfastly hold yourself in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overturned.

    Blessed, therefore, is the man who is always fearful, who does not presume upon the virtues he has received, who knows with certainty that he is about to fail whenever he does not find that he has advanced at every moment toward higher things. But truly, brothers, I fear greatly, unless the estimation of works somehow deceives me, that in some of you the fire of this holy fervor is not yet present, since they seem to love little the true pursuits of monks; and this, from their manner of life, although it is clear to anyone, none of you can be ignorant of. I have not thought it wholly superfluous to admonish them, since thus far they seem to have advanced little, for the hand of the Lord has not been shortened so that it cannot save the penitent. For I trust in the mercy of the living God, that, on account of my charity toward them and the exercises of piety of those among you who walk according to the purity of the rule, he will grant them at some time to come to their senses and to love more ardently the pursuits of holy fervor.

    What is this, brothers, that you do not live monastically in the monastery, and, having professed a spiritual manner of life, walk according to the flesh? Do you not know how dangerous it is for a monk to live secularly in a cenobium, and to violate by a lukewarm manner of life the vow of ancient purity which we have all made? Acknowledge, I pray, that the last things of all cloistered persons are nearest to the extremes, and that good and zealous monks, lovers of their own salvation, receive in heaven not the common rewards but the very greatest rewards of the saints, while those who live badly or lukewarmly in monastic religion are punished not with a moderate or common torment, but with the gravest torment of demons. For the higher the state in which someone sins, the heavier will be the punishment of the offender in it.

    Therefore, if anyone among you has already learned to walk the way of divine love with spiritual sweetness, it is necessary that he go forward, so that he may advance more each day. But he who still lies in the torpor of a sluggish mind should strive as quickly as possible to rise again, since just as punishment is promised to those who lie fallen, so the crown of victory is denied to those who do not persevere. Beware, therefore, lest ruinous lukewarmness overturn the mind, for it is exceedingly dangerous to cloistered persons, because it is most grievous and full of miseries and sorrows, and plainly very near to hell; from its abyss a monk who has once fallen into it rarely rises up. And alas, how many faint-hearted cloistered persons are found today, lax and idle, who frequently succumb under the burden of spiritual warfare and rarely rise again to true fervor of spirit. Their condition is truly to be pitied: they have a name that they live, and they are dead; neither the memory of death has been able to lead them to true compunction of heart, nor has the remembrance of hell set before them been able to soften them.

    Monks of this kind, thereafter, so long as they remain thus growing torpid in sloth, are either oppressed and overcome by evil habit, or they are in a certain sense in hell, so that they never breathe fully again in the light of the mercies of the Lord, nor do they come to the liberty of the spirit, which alone is nearest to the kingdom of heaven and makes the yoke of the Lord sweet and the burden light. These evils befall them for this reason: because their will has not yet been purged of carnal passions, nor do they will the good as they have known it, having been enticed and drawn away by their own concupiscence. For they love the perishable consolations of the flesh; even if at times they interrupt them, they nevertheless never break them off completely. Hence it is that they very rarely direct their affections toward God, and if at any time they are moved to compunction for an hour, they do not persevere long, but soon, through sloth and inertia, are wearied by sleep, suddenly loathing, out of sadness and melancholy, the good which they had begun. But unable to be filled with the fervor of divine love, twice agitated

    Homily V. Fol. XIII.

    storms: for just as flesh placed by the fire and repeatedly removed is never well cooked, so the soul that has repeatedly fallen back into acedia is by no means truly enlightened by the divine Spirit. For Scripture says to the Lord: “Those who distance themselves from you will perish, and you have destroyed all who work iniquity.” For the farther the mind has withdrawn through acedia from the fervor of divine love, the nearer it is to hell and despair, and the more rarely and with greater difficulty does it recover strength for true penitence.

    Whoever among you, therefore, my brothers, desires to flee from the midst of Babylon, whoever longs to come to the inward fervor of the spirit, let him always strive with the greatest effort to drive from himself the torpor of mind and acedia, and daily to renew the holy purpose of divine love. It is very hard, I confess, to resist the depraved habit of the flesh, and in an old heart to think new thoughts against custom. Certainly, brothers, no one can rise from the depths of hell with a lukewarm will, nor will anyone be able to overcome an evil habit without great violence and a long-lasting contrary habit.

    Therefore, even if no one becomes holy by his own powers, but it is God who works all things in all, nevertheless it is plainly clear to us that the kingdom of God suffers violence; and he who neglects to bring violence upon his own fleshly impulses does not attain to the fellowship of the saints of the Lord. Hear now, monk, whoever you are who are lukewarm and acedious toward the love of God; hear, I say, and tremble, because unless you immediately rise from the evil habit of a torpid life, unless you inflict force upon yourself through a contrary habit, unless you earnestly prepare your heart for the fervor of divine love, you will never see the face of God in glory.

    Acedia is the root of despair; and not only its root, but also its nurse and mother. If it has once oppressed the mind of a person dedicated to God, it at once closes off every way to salvation. For the kingdom of heaven is not promised to sleepers; the blessedness of eternity is not prepared for those growing torpid in idleness and sloth. Rather, the crown is laid up for those who manfully command the impulses of the flesh, and those who live by the spirit, not by the flesh, are endowed with the glory of eternal felicity.

    No virtue is acquired without labor; no enemy is overcome without battle. If you wish to be crowned, conquer; if you desire to conquer, it is necessary that you fight bravely and perseveringly. “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” Solomon cries to you. “When will you rise from your sleep? If you are diligent, your harvest will come like a spring, and poverty will flee far from you.” For he who gathers at harvest is a wise son, and he who snores in summer is a son of confusion. For he who works his land will be satisfied with bread, but he who follows idleness will be filled with want.

    Now, brothers, is the time for doing good; now the opportunity of meriting eternal blessedness is granted to us by the Lord God, and it is suddenly cut off in death. For Scripture says: “Whatever your hand can do, work at it earnestly, because neither work nor reason, nor wisdom nor knowledge, will be among the dead, to whom you are hastening.” If the good of eternal blessedness that is promised delights you, the labors of the struggle that are set before you ought not to frighten the mind. For no one will be crowned by the Lord unless he has contended lawfully; no one will come to the summit of eternal height unless by the fervor of the spirit he has overcome the illicit impulses of the flesh.

    We must always fight, brothers, against the threefold battle-line of the devil as long as we live in this pilgrimage, because here he becomes insuperable to this extent: he is not overcome little by little by one who grows lukewarm. Hence Saint Augustine proclaims: “No one ought to be secure in this life, which is wholly called temptation, lest he who was able to become better from worse should at some time become worse from better.” And so Solomon too in the Book of Proverbs says: “Desires kill the sluggard.” For just as constancy bestows perfection in every work, so acedia is the destroyer and stepmother of all religion and of the spiritual progress of the soul.

    For, as blessed Jerome says, nothing in a holy purpose is worse than idleness, which not only does not acquire new things, but also shamefully consumes what was previously acquired. The rule of a holy spiritual life advances and grows with joy by continuous progress; by cessation, however, it grows torpid and fails. Therefore, brothers, the mind must be renewed by daily and fresh increases of virtues, and this journey of living is to be measured not by what has passed, but by what remains.

    Therefore flee idleness above all, since it is the mother and nurse of all vices; but overcome acedia not by fleeing it, but by resisting it bravely. Scripture says: “Idleness has taught much evil.” For every idle person is occupied with vain and pernicious desires. And so the monk who desires to serve Christ in true purity of mind should always be occupied in some spiritual exercise, lest idleness beget vice, and

    On the daily renewal of holy purpose.

    Let pernicious thoughts find a place where they may be strengthened. Just as rust consumes iron, and a garment is gnawed by worms, so idleness weakens the mind; and virtue of the soul, long neglected, gradually ebbs away and is utterly overthrown. Therefore flee idleness, and overcome sloth. But since we cannot remain firmly and without change of mind in one state of divine love, it is necessary for us, lest we ebb away entirely, to renew our holy purpose daily, so that as often as, through the negligence of human weakness, we begin, however slightly, to grow dull in spiritual fervor, so often, examining ourselves by the memory of things to come and by contemplation of the Lord’s Passion, we may at once recall our conscience to its former purpose of making progress.

    But this we must guard against with the utmost care: that we not put off this holy effort to make progress until tomorrow, since it has often done harm to have postponed what could have been [unclear]. Hence the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not delay to be converted to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For suddenly his wrath will come, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” Augustine also says: “Why do you put off the good until tomorrow, saying: life will still be long? For who knows whether it will be long? And if it is not good, what profit is there that it will be long?” Without a good life, the conduct of a monk should be called death rather than life.

    The remedies of a more amended life, therefore, must not be deferred by any delays, lest the time for conversion perish through tardiness, when already no postponement of repentance is granted. For he who promised pardon to the penitent did not promise tomorrow. No one who fears concerning himself delays being converted to repentance, nor extends today’s salvation into tomorrow. But every man who knows that he is set in tepidity of mind and who defers amendment of life from day to day is deceived by hope of a longer [life], since if he knew that he would die tomorrow, today without doubt he would change his purpose. Hope of a longer life has miserably deceived many, who, while they daily defer the amendment of their conduct, suddenly fall into the depth of death.

    Which of you is there, brothers, who does not resolve in his mind to assume the purpose of a more amended life before he dies? For I believe that each one of you intends to exercise still greater devotion toward God before he falls into the danger of death. And why do you wait so long for the day? Why do you put it off from day to day? Behold, you who now live in health and do not give yourselves to the spiritual exercises of divine love when you can, and when the Lord patiently waits: the last day will come for each of you, and now it is hastening, on which, with the angel of death pressing hard, the power whose effect you delayed so long is taken from you. Therefore again and again I ask you, brothers, and with what diligence I can I admonish you: turn yourselves to the Lord our God with your whole heart while you live healthy and unharmed; and do not further defer the will, lest you lose also the power granted to you. Think often and think again that we are not citizens of this world, but strangers and pilgrims; nor do we have here a lasting city, but we seek the one to come; and every day we hasten toward death, not even knowing it.

    On the love of quiet and solitude: Homily Six.

    Two intellects were created from the beginning; Holy Scripture does not plainly disclose [this], but by the teaching of the fathers it is known to lie hidden, brothers, that the angels are the work of God, and it counted them among the works of the six days. But there are some who write that the angels were created long before this visible world; and just as we cannot prove this by the testimony of the divine Scriptures, so neither do we rashly attack it. For there are several grave and holy men who placed the creation of the angels long before the beginning of the world.

    But the angelic intellect was made at once from the beginning in the act of all things knowable, and it knew all things that it could know, and thereafter admitted nothing toward its own perfection. For, created by the Lord in its perfection, it did not require an increase by which it might understand more. For indeed, since pure intellect was made joined to God without intervening medium, it was made such by nature, nor did it need practice in order to understand after our fashion, since its being admits no corruption. And so, cleaving to its object through the affection of love, God, whom it understands to be the center of its blessedness, immediately and

    immutably contemplates and loves; he is blessed and fears no alteration of himself. But the human intellect, which our teachers have called the soul, was indeed created at the beginning in complete ignorance, and knows none of those things which the angelic intellect understands by nature. These two intellects differ as act and potency, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, possession and privation, beginning and end, simple and composite, substance and accident, nature and art, truth and likeness. For, as divine Scripture bears witness, all things that are present in the angelic intellect by nature and from the beginning the human intellect will attain through the arts at the end, as the Lord Jesus says in the holy Gospel: “In the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God in heaven.”

    For in order that the mind may be exercised toward understanding through many labors, as though through the arts, it has been placed for a brief time in the workshop of the body. If there, turned toward God, it duly completes its craft through love, then at last, departing from here, it becomes equal to an angel. But if, consenting to the impulses of the flesh, it has not kept its order, then disturbed and wretched, like the apostate spirits who fall, it will depart from the body to be tormented forever. For since our mind, or soul, was created in ignorance and privation of all things, it must by continual action, movement, and art come to knowledge of things. The end indeed makes the human intellect equal to the angelic, changing its potency into act, and will make from privation possession, from empty full, from imperfect perfect, from deprived possessing, from dark luminous, from nocturnal diurnal, from lunar solar, and from earthly heavenly. This end, my dearest brothers, is the beginning of eternal salvation; no one can happily come to it who does not strive with all his powers toward the summit of perfection.

    But since it is difficult, in the midst of crowds, always to keep unbroken this necessary effort of advancement, where a thousand occasions for sinning are offered, the holy fathers who founded the monastic order taught us by word and example to flee the world, and not only in mind but also in body to avoid frequent intercourse. Of those who were stronger in spirit, many flew to the hermitage, so that they might become nearer to the Lord in mind the farther they withdrew in body from the world. Of these we read what was said by the prophet Isaiah: “The wilderness will rejoice and will blossom like the lily; sprouting it will sprout, and it will exult, rejoicing and praising.” Others, wishing to profit many, established cenobia, in which they placed a multitude of monks, whose manner of life would be separated from the peoples and yet would be social among themselves. For it does not suit all to sit in the hermitage, for whom it is more fitting to serve the Lord in the midst of brothers. For our monasteries too have their own solitude, so that whoever wishes to be solitary can be so in the midst of brothers, provided he maintains the privacy of the cell in which he dwells. For a monk, according to the interpretation of his name, is called solitary, because in mind and body he is separated from the tumults of this world.

    Therefore, as I am about to make today’s sermon to your charities, I desire to admonish you, as much as I desire your progress in spiritual life. I ask you, I say, and exhort you in the bowels of brotherly charity, to love the quiet of the cell as the workshop of your salvation, in which there is great peace for those who love God, and great advantage for perfecting the intellect toward knowledge of the highest truth. For the prophet Isaiah says: “In silence and hope will be your strength.” Whoever does not love the solitude of the cell and the quiet of silence by no means loves purity of mind, but, wandering in body, always draws new vanities into his spirit. Hence blessed Jerome says: “Why do we desire the crowdedness of cities, we who are reckoned from singularity? For to me the town is a prison, solitude a paradise.”

    If, brothers, the hermitage and solitude delighted us, this place would afford great advantage to our purpose, where, apart from poor peasants, a guest is rarely met; no one disturbs our quiet, no one troubles us, no one brings in spectacles or rumors of momentary novelty. But I see few among you who love inward quiet, and I grieve vehemently, because I know very well that a monk cannot make progress in spiritual life when it is clear that he does not love the quiet of the cell. But he who knows how much good the privacy of solitude confers upon the soul loves his cell and does not easily go outside, always fearing in tumult

    On the Love of Quiet and Solitude.

    to lose what he has gathered with great hidden labor. For, as Saint Augustine says, he is less goaded by pleasures who is not where there is an abundance of pleasures; and he suffers less trouble from avarice who, placed far from human beings, does not see riches. Since, therefore, the holy Spirit of God loves the secrecy of the mind but shudders at publicity, it belongs to you, brothers, to love the solitude of cells as the workshop of all virtues, and never to estrange yourselves from its dwelling without a reasonable cause. For a monk who loves secrecy, not an idle one, who has learned to remain steadfastly in his cell, sometimes enjoys many holy consolations, of which the wandering and restless man is necessarily deprived.

    Just as a fish dies if it is kept too long outside the water, so all the devotion of a monk perishes if he wanders too often outside his cell. Let us imitate John the Baptist, whom Chrysostom says is the chief of monks: he, a monk, as soon as he was born, lived in the desert, was nourished in the desert, and as a monk awaited Christ in solitude. For just as it is difficult for a tree placed beside the road to preserve its fruits until maturity, so it is difficult for a monk who often wanders outside his cell and is occupied in the affairs of the world to keep the fruits of righteousness unstained until the end.

    Let us therefore withdraw, monks of God, from tumults, and let us plant ourselves in the secrecy of monastic solitude, so that neither the world may have anything in common with us, nor we with it. For a mind that is shaken by the cares and anxieties of the world is rarely truly rooted in the love of God. Indeed, movement of the body often alters the state of the mind, and a person who is always immersed in outward things is never illuminated by the fervor of the divine Spirit. For quiet of mind is born from the firm steadiness of the body, and the man who loves solitude for the love of God remains stronger and united with himself in holy exercise.

    Whoever among you, brothers, is an eager lover of his own salvation should learn to remain quiet in his cell, and, as far as he can, should strive to occupy himself continually, with desire, in the works of divine love. But be quiet in your cell, not idle; tranquil, not drowsy; always devoted to spiritual exercise, not slackened by torpor of soul. The instruments of spiritual exercises in the cell are four: to read, to write, to pray, and to meditate. A fifth, however, is granted to few, who after true purity of heart are raised to the mountain of contemplation of the Lord.

    Finally, these four exercises of monks dwelling in the solitude of the cell must be so moderated that they produce neither weariness nor torpor of mind, but that a suitable time be assigned to each activity, so that, while alternation lightens the mind, the little body is not burdened beyond its strength. Therefore the reading of the divine Scriptures should have its own suitable hour for study; when it senses that a desire for devotion is present, it should at once be changed into fervent prayer. Manual labor, moreover, which is enjoined on the monk dwelling in the tranquility of solitude, is very useful, lest harmful lukewarmness arise in the mind.

    For the reading of holy Scripture stirs the monk to the charity of God; meditation on the Lord’s passion and on the benefits of God inflames the mind to the fervor of most ardent love; prayer strengthens the weak soul; and manual labor, continued temperately, preserves one from torpor and weariness. When we pray earnestly and devoutly, we speak with our God, who is present everywhere; but when we read in the holy Scriptures, we are taught by the Lord himself what we should seek or flee. Prayer, if it is ardent in the love of God, purifies the mind from sins and vices; reading, however, instructs and forms it, as Saint Isidore says: “By prayers,” he says, “we are cleansed; by readings we are instructed. Both are good, if possible; if both are not possible, it is better to pray than to read.”

    Therefore the monk who wishes to spend his time in the cell usefully and fruitfully should strive continually to occupy mind and body in these exercises by turns, because a soul that keeps watch in such labors gives no entrance to perverse thoughts. Hence the divine Jerome, admonishing a monk, says: “Always do some good thing, so that the devil may find you occupied.” For he is less assailed by the enticements of the flesh who, always usefully occupied, admits no weariness of mind. Indeed, while each monk, a careful guardian of his own soul, is carried by alternation from the exercise of one good work to another with desire for holy fervor, his striving is strengthened toward constancy in all virtues, and he falls into weariness so much the less

    Homily VI. Folio XV.

    ...how much more accustomed study is to be varied, and to make use of alternations against weariness. Hence Jerome again says: “Let prayer often interrupt reading, and let the pleasing alternation of holy prayer come upon the soul continually cleaving to it.” The monk who does not love the secrecy of the cell is not a true soldier of Christ, since he bears the name and habit of a monk without the works; and he who ought to have been solitary for the love of God, having turned back in mind to the world, loves the pursuit of vanity. Hence the blessed pope Gregory says: “He who lives removed bodily from men, but plunges himself in thought amid the tumults of human intercourse through desire for earthly things, is not solitary, although he dwell in solitude. But if someone is pressed bodily by the crowds of the people, and yet suffers no tumults of secular cares in his heart, he is not in the city, even if he dwells in the midst of men.” And this is what holy Jerome says against Jovinian: “The wise man,” he says, “can never be alone. For he has with him all who are good and who have been good; and he has a free mind, and whatever he wishes he brings forth, and he transfers himself wherever he wishes. For what he cannot do in body, he embraces in mind; and if there is a lack of men, he speaks with God.” Therefore a good man will never be alone.

    And so, remaining in your cell, always beware of idleness, since nothing so enfeebles all the powers of the mind as idleness, after it has produced acedia from itself. If you have loved God ardently, you will never be idle, because true love of Christ does not allow torpor to arise in the soul, but always impels the lover toward the delight of the beloved. And just as a certain man wise according to the flesh truly said, “Let him love who does not wish to become slothful,” so experience has taught us in spiritual love that the mind which it has begun to inhabit it does not allow to grow torpid with idleness and sluggishness. For divine love always impels one toward better things; and the more it has advanced by burning, so much the greater increase of itself it takes on. But the [workshop?] of this love is a clean conscience; if a monk desires both to have and to preserve it clean, it is necessary first of all that he despise the vanities of the world and the business of temporal things. For it is not possible that a double love reside in one breast; nor can a man succeed in loving Christ who does not wish to despise the world. For God, although in the Trinity of persons he is one in the essence of substance, is either loved by us alone, or is not loved with a partner.

    Therefore, so that the conscience may remain clean in all purity, and so that the mind may have strength to love God above all things, let the monk love the secrecy of the cell, and never withdraw from the exercise of inner sweetness. For in the cell of a good and wise monk there is the greatest tranquillity; and if anywhere there is an earthly paradise, it is in the monastery of those who are converted to the purity of the cenobitic institution. There is peace there, piety, goodness, light, virtue, honorableness; there is joy there, purity, sweetness, and great tranquillity of life, where the devout praying monk speaks with the Lord, and the future sweetness of the heavenly kingdom is tasted beforehand by the contemplative soldier. O cell of monks truly serving God, paradise: you are indeed the little garden of most honorable delight, in which the mind is joined to God through love and is sweetly raised up through desire. The monk who loves, venerates, and cultivates you is a true soldier of Christ, and serves the Lord in the fullness of virtues. But he who abhors and deserts the secrecy of the cell despises the workshop of his own salvation. Therefore, my dearest brothers, I beg you to begin to inhabit the secrecy of the cell with desire of mind; without love for it no one will be able to come to the perfection of virtues in the cenobium.

    On the manual labor of monks. Homily VII.

    “Because you shall eat the labors of your hands,” says the prophet of the Lord, “blessed are you, and it shall be well with you.” If all are reckoned blessed who live from the proper labor of their hands, certainly no one idle eats bread without guilt and fault. For almighty God imposed this punishment upon the first-formed Adam for the transgression of the original command, announcing to him that in the sweat of his face he would work food from the earth with his hands. But since in Adam we have all sinned, we are necessarily subject to the same punishments to which it is agreed that he was subjected. He labored with his hands for the food by which he might live, nor did he eat bread idle. Hence the blessed father no

    Father Benedict, detesting the idleness of monks, says in the Rule which he handed down to us: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul; and therefore at fixed times the monks ought to be occupied in manual labor, and again at fixed hours in divine reading. For then they are truly monks, if they live by the labor of their own hands, as our fathers and the apostles also did.” Hence also the holy Christ-loving Paul says in the epistle: “He who does not work shall not eat.” In the beginning of the monastic state this was the custom of monks, that they admitted no one into their fellowship without labor, not so much on account of the necessities of food as on account of the salvation of the soul, lest through idleness an opportunity be given to pernicious thoughts.

    At that time monks had no assessments, no tithes, no revenues, no annual proceeds of any kind; but all, living together in common, procured food and clothing for themselves with their hands, burdening no one with the exaction of what was owed. The holy apostles also of our Savior, although they had the right to live from the preaching of the gospel, preferred to labor with their own hands, lest they should seem to have burdened any of the faithful, and so that they might have not only the means by which they themselves should live, but also something with which they might furnish necessities to the needy.

    But after monks began to have assessments and revenues, the former pursuits of simplicity soon failed; and little by little, together with riches in temporal things, pride grew, to such an extent that in time monks refused all manual labors. As long as the monks were poor and humble in birth, they worshiped God in truth; but after they began to abound in riches, duplicity put simplicity to flight, and the exaltation of the nobles extinguished the humility of the monks. Once the integrity of regular observance had been taken away, soon also in many monasteries the wealth of temporal things failed by the just judgment of God.

    Of their number was the present monastery of Sponheim, brothers of mine, neither the last nor the first, which for many years in both states remained miserably desolate, to such a degree that the five monks only who were living in it a dissolute life did not have the means from which they might take the necessities of life for themselves. Hence, by the mercy of God at last providing for it, Frederick, duke [unclear], having invoked the counsel of the fathers of the reformed order, in the year of the Christians 1469 expelled the monks deformed in life, deposed the abbot, named Otto of Cologne, and placed in this monastery four others, called from the observance of Bursfelde, from the monastery of Mont Speciosus. Over them he set as abbot John, from the noble family of Budisbach, which they commonly call “of the Carbonaria house,” a man such as you have seen and heard, worthy of eternal memory; he found this place in extreme poverty, and, presiding over it for almost fourteen years in great patience, brought it back to the state in which we now live.

    Therefore, since scarcity of temporal things still presses heavily upon us, there would be need of continual labor, by which we might nourish ourselves with necessary food and free the house of God in which we dwell from debt. But what are your labors, or how much can they contribute to us for such great matters? We are few in number, and unfit for rustic labors; nor does the institution of the priestly order permit us to spend the whole day in the field turning stones with our hands, and to interrupt the divine service.

    We are wretched, weighed down by excessive poverty and lack of all necessities; and if we have labored much, we gain little from it; and if we have worked little, surely we fail still more in spirit. For man, as Scripture bears witness, is born to labor just as a bird is born to fly. Therefore, lest you eat your bread idle, you will always have to be assigned to some honest and useful labor, by which both the mind may be relieved from weariness of regular observance, and our grave poverty may be repaired, at least in some small measure.

    In harvest time for hay, and on the days of autumn for the vintage, we have been accustomed to occupy you outside the monastery only when, evidently, the labor is very necessary and the dearness of hired workers increases the price and wages of servants. For the rest of the time we have decreed to keep you in the monastery, because your labors, in comparison with the expenses, contribute little to the monastery’s uses, and, as it seems to us, very few of you willingly present yourselves as volunteers for rustic pursuits. There is also another consideration which stirs my mind, lest you, by external

    Homily VII. Fol. XVI.

    to be occupied readily with works of the hands without reasonable cause and manifest necessity; for I find that labors of this kind do not accord in you with regular observance, but rather destroy than promote the integrity of monastic discipline among you. I am ashamed to say it, and nevertheless I am compelled to utter it: your labors outside the monastery and the cell bring more destruction than salvation to the purity of the soul. For how do you labor, and what are your pursuits in your labors? Is it not to wander about, run here and there, indulge in [unclear] and cups, and occupy the rest of the time in vain and useless talk?

    You do not have in yourselves that fervor of the Holy Spirit of God by which we read that the ancient monks of our institution were once inflamed; and for the common necessity, with such desire, such zeal, such effort, all and each labored with their hands that you would have thought the business of the whole monastery was placed in the prudence of each one. For each one labored as though he alone had had to feed the whole congregation with his own hands. Amid these things they paid the services of divine worship with such eagerness by day and night, as though they were in no way occupied by the labors of the hands. Which brother among you is an imitator of such men, so that he either reckons our common want as his own, or strives, according to his strength, to relieve it by laboring in the sweat of his face? They, laboring with their hands, continually besought God with their hearts; but you, intent on tales, neither satisfy the duty of the hands nor [unclear] as monks.

    In the time of the regular fast, too, they either carefully kept the measure of abstinence appointed for them, or, if they could not do so because of the greatness of their labors, they ate for this reason: so that they might be rendered fit and capable for their labors. But you do not eat in order to labor; rather, you labor in order to eat what, according to the Rule, ought to have been fasted from. You take occasion from labor to relax the fasts.

    Again, how foully and most basely some of you treat their garments: what zealous lover of regular discipline could bear this with equanimity? [Unclear], my brothers, [unclear] are handled so wastefully. Everything that belongs to the monasteries of the servants of God is the patrimony of Christ, and the whole is said to be dedicated to God; nor is anyone permitted to abuse the things of Christ, or to turn them to another use. Do you not know what our holy lawgiver Benedict says to you in the Rule? “If anyone has treated the things of the monastery filthily or negligently, let him be corrected. If he has not amended, let him be subject to regular discipline.” And in the chapter on the cellarer of the monastery: that he should regard all the substance as if it were the sacred vessels of the altar.

    Finally, I cannot and ought not be silent about how filthily and negligently most of you treat everything, as though either you would not be seen by God, or no loss would come to our property from sloth. Know, brothers, that I announce this to you beforehand as a warning: for these things, as also for your other sins, you are to render account to the Lord God.

    For this reason I have reduced for you the labors outside the monastery, lest by working badly you should sin more gravely; and manual work is to be enjoined upon you: to write books, to bind them, and these and similar things which you can perform within the enclosure of the monastery with tranquility of mind and body. Would that you at least did these manual works [of yours?] with diligence for the love of God, so that you might not eat bread altogether idle. There is no manual work which, in my judgment, better befits a monk than to write books of sacred reading, and to prepare the necessary things for others who write. For it will generally be permissible to interrupt this holy labor with prayer, and to keep watch for the food of the mind no less than of the body.

    Necessity also compels us to apply ourselves diligently to writing books, if we desire to have at hand that with which we may mutually occupy ourselves profitably in spiritual study. For you see that the whole library of this monastery, which once was distinguished and large, was [unclear] by the monks before us, sold and alienated, and that no more than fourteen volumes were found here by us. Indeed, the industry of the printing art, recently invented in our days at Mainz, daily brings many volumes to light; but it is by no means possible for us to buy everything new, since we are still weighed down by the greatest poverty.

    Wherefore I advise and exhort you that, since you do not come very gladly to external manual labors, you should at least labor diligently in writing volumes for the honor of God; for just as idleness is the enemy of the soul, so moderate labor is the spiritual preserver of life. A monk, since he is a soldier of the eternal King, ought never to be idle. For idleness begets acedia, and that brings upon the soul the destitution of pernicious death. The labors of monks, however, are to be so moderated that [unclear]

    On the Manual Labor of Monks

    ...that they may be free for divine converse; but amid the works of the hands let meditation on the Scriptures burn in the heart; and after it has brought the mind into the ardor of the spirit, let it be moved into most devout prayer. Therefore let the monk, Christ’s soldier, be like the clean animal of God that chews the cud, always having in the mouth of his heart the fodder of the holy Scriptures, lest the mind lie open to vain and pernicious thoughts, or a foul or idle word burst from the speaker’s mouth. Let him always remember, while working, the Scripture that says: Blessed is the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. For everyone who loves the Lord Jesus in truth daily turns over in his heart, with tears and prayers, both his teaching and his passion. For he is not a true lover of God who forgets his commandments even for a moment. Indeed, as Scripture says: Those who love the Lord seek the things that are pleasing to him, and those who fear his holy name shall be filled with his law. Hence one of the saints says to the Lord: In my heart I have hidden your words, that I may not sin against you. The spirit, therefore, must always be stirred up and renewed daily by spiritual goads, lest it grow numb through sloth or languish in uncertain idleness. The labor of monastic discipline, the practice of reading and prayer, and the diligent keeping of vigils are true incitements to virtue. Nothing, however, is more harmful to the holy purpose of the monk than idleness, since it both excites the flesh to lust and weakens every strength of the mind and extinguishes the fervor of the spirit. For idleness in the cloister is the tinder and nourishment of all evils. Wherever, therefore, you may be, whether in the field or in the cloister, always flee idleness as the most pernicious plague of the soul, adorning and exercising the mind either with prayer or with meditation on the Scriptures. Converse gladly with the good and zealous lovers of God; but avoid the negligent and the despisers of their own salvation. For he who touches pitch will be defiled by it, and he who makes himself a companion of sinners will not be free from crime. Consider your words carefully, so that you detract from no one at all, nor listen to another who is detracting, since both the detractor and the willing hearer serve the demon: the one by speaking, the other by listening. Labor like a good soldier of Christ Jesus, and diligently do with your hands whatever is enjoined upon you by obedience; nor let it seem hard to you to obey another’s command, for which eternal happiness, a crown for your spirit, is prepared in heaven. Therefore no labor, no length of time, no observance ought to seem hard to a monk, by which the glory of eternal blessedness is acquired. Consider, my brothers, the brevity of this life and do good while it is permitted, since he who now sows sparingly will also after death reap sparingly, and each one will receive a fitting reward for his own work, not for another’s. The time for laboring is very brief, but the recompense that is owed to good works is everlasting. Consider, my brothers, men entangled in the world, and all lovers of this age, how strong they are in earthly and perishable matters, but weak and feeble in heavenly things; so that you may take care to please God as much as they labor continually to appear rich and glorious to the world. For for temporal glory many have not refused to sweat even unto death; but for the hope of future happiness they despise even doing or enduring a little. For earthly gains they most patiently tolerate all sorts of injuries; and for a heavenly reward they refuse to endure the insult of even a very slight word. They can stand all day before an earthly king, prince, or judge; but in prayer before the almighty Lord they cannot continue for the space of one hour. They gladly tolerate many adversities for the acquisition of perishable riches; but they neglect the more to seek heavenly goods, the more pleasantly they are occupied in love of earthly things. Let their way of life, dearest brothers, admonish you all the more to flee all the cares of this world, inasmuch as you are now permitted to handle fewer of the affairs of earthly things. Always devote all your solicitude and care to the acquisition of heavenly goods, and labor most diligently at all times for the reward of future blessedness. For, as Scripture testifies, your life upon earth is a warfare, and whatever a man has sown, this he shall also reap. Know that death hastens daily, and at every moment a part of life, never to return, is extinguished. Watch, therefore, my dearest brothers, watch, for you do not know when the Lord our God will come to the judgment of each one’s death

    Homily VIII.

    whether at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning, lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping. Therefore watch at every time, praying that you may be accounted worthy to escape all the evils that are to come, and to stand with confidence before the sight of the Son of God, who judges all things. For, as the divine lover of Christ bears witness, we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body, according as he has done, whether good or evil.

    Blessed is that monk whom the Lord shall find watching in good works, who has prepared himself for the wedding of the heavenly Lamb in true purity of heart, who will not fear to meet the judge. Let that memorable saying of divine Jerome on the Gospel according to Matthew always be in your hearts, when he says: Whether I eat or drink, or do anything else, that voice always seems to sound in my ears: Rise, dead, and come to judgment.

    As often as I think of that day of the future examination, I tremble with my whole heart and body. Therefore, if there is any joy in the present life, my brothers, it must be so conducted that the bitterness of that dreadful judgment never withdraw from memory. O that great, terrible, dreadful, exceeding and very bitter day, on which the sun and moon will be darkened, not by diminution of light but by comparison with majesty; where every argument of excuse will cease; where all things will be manifest, and nothing will be able to lie hidden from the judge, because he who knows the hidden thoughts of minds will then judge openly; who is neither anticipated by favor, nor bent by mercy; is not corrupted by gifts and presents; will not be softened by prayers; nor thereafter will he be appeased by any satisfaction.

    Therefore, brothers, while you are placed in this life, let each of you do as much as he can for his soul, because penance for sins done here alone is useful and fruitful, so long as there is room for pardon and the sentence of justice is still delayed. He who postpones doing good and performing penance until death is very near to damnation, because the good that he neglects when healthy and unharmed he will rarely restore when sick and already about to die. For holy Pope Gregory says: Whoever does not fear to defer the fruits of penance until the hour of death is himself a witness against himself that true repentance was never in his mind. Now therefore turn yourselves to our Lord with your whole heart, doing penance before him, and live, I pray, in such a way that, when you must depart from here, you may not fear to appear before his face.

    That one must pray without ceasing. Homily IX.

    Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, brothers, in the Gospel according to Luke, wishing us to be continual in prayers, admonished us thus, saying: It is necessary always to pray and never to fail. This counsel of the Lord befits, before all mortals, monks most of all, and all cloistered persons in whatever religious life, whose every action and whole life, indeed whatever they do, ought either to be prayer or at least conformed to prayer. For all who profess the monastic service are called spiritual, not without reason, in order that they may be admonished by the very word to despise the pleasures of the flesh for the love of God, and to walk through true charity in the ardor of the spirit.

    For the holy apostle of Christ says: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; for if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live. Knowing, however, that without constancy in prayer the fervor of the spirit cannot long endure in us, he likewise says to the Thessalonians: Always rejoice; pray without ceasing; in all things give thanks, because this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you.

    But what the manner of praying is, the Savior taught us in the Gospel, saying: But you, when you pray, enter into your chamber, and with the door shut, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. And in another place he said to the Samaritan woman: Woman, believe me, because the hour will come [unclear] the Father seeks such as will adore him. God is spirit, and those who adore him must adore in spirit and truth. It is manifest from Christ’s teaching that prayer is of the heart rather than a lengthy speech of the mouth, because, since God is spirit, he must be adored in no other way than by the innermost fervor of the spirit. For the prayer of the heart in the fervor of the spirit has great power; but the multiplication of words without attention of mind

    That one must pray without interruption.

    ...no usefulness at all. Hence Saint Jerome says: God is to be prayed to not in words only, but with the heart. Therefore the chanting of five psalms with purity of heart, serenity, and spiritual cheerfulness is better than the singing of the whole psalter with anxiety and sadness of heart. And the holy pope Gregory says: True petition is not in the sounds of the mouth, but in the voices of the heart, that is, in holy thoughts. For it is not words but desires that make the stronger voices in the ears of God.

    Except, therefore, for those prayers which we are bound to say either by decree of the Church or by the institution of the monastic order, [prolixity?] in the rest and multiplication of words contribute nothing, or little, to true and inward devotion of the mind, since where there is no fervent desire in the love of God, an excessive extension of speech is introduced in vain. For sacred Augustine says: Let much speaking in prayer be absent, but let fervent attention persevere; for to speak much in praying is to handle a necessary matter with superfluous words. For prayer embraces many things in few words, so that the simplicity of faith might quickly learn the sufficiency of its salvation, and the prudence of the ingenious might stand amazed at the depth of the mysteries.

    But for those in whom, because of hardness of heart, the compunction of inward fervor has been lacking, when they prostrate themselves in prayer there is need of more extended speech, shouting, and tears, so that by long exercise of the mind they may at last strike forth within themselves the burning fire of divine love, until they rise in the affection of holy prayer in the Spirit of God. But afterward, when the fervor of divine love and compunction has penetrated the mind, there is thereafter no need for the exercise of words, but the continuation of spiritual nourishment is required, lest the fervor of the spiritual fire be extinguished. To this end our most holy father wished prayer in the assembly to be shortened, so that if anyone wished to pray apart in the spirit, he could do so.

    There are, however, some who are so hard of heart that while praying they find little or nothing of spiritual compunction; for them freedom brings ruin, and solitude often brings despair. Attend, I pray you, dearest brothers, to what I say to you, and consider how greatly you are bound to pray without interruption. It is not enough for a monk, striving toward perfection in the school of Christ the eternal king, to discharge the canonical prayers; nor is it sufficient for a man solemnly dedicated to God by vow to fulfill the common prayers of the order in the convent, since one who is commanded always to pray without interruption is bound beyond verbal prayers also to spiritual prayers. For prayers instituted by the Church or by the order fall under the merit of obedience, and under the law of necessity by reason of a precept; but that manner of praying which is called spiritual is strengthened in the freedom of the spirit as useful and necessary for a monk at every time for perfection.

    Hence it must be noted that for prayers which are by precept of the Church or the order, the utterance of words is required as a matter of necessity, together with the intention of satisfying the statute by which anyone is bound to pray. Let those see how they satisfy the command of the Church who do not express the seven canonical prayers by the utterance of words, but with closed mouth run through the sequence of prayers by thought alone, with their eyes assisting. But in those prayers which we undertake to say not by command but by our own will and from devotion alone, the fervor of the mind toward God suffices without the utterance of words, because, as we have said, God requires such worshippers as adore in spirit and truth. But the canonical prayers, which they call the hours, we are bound to say, and not merely to think. In both cases devotion of mind toward God is useful; without it no prayers are believed to be effective.

    And so, my brothers, when we stand for prayer, we ought to watch with the greatest zeal and attend to the prayers which we pour forth, lest we pray without the fruit of inward compunction. Therefore let every thought of the flesh depart far away; let no occupation with household affairs hinder the mind; nor let the soul then think anything else at all except this alone which is being said. Therefore also the priest, after the preface has customarily been sent before the sacrifice, prepares the minds of the brothers, saying, Lift up your hearts, so that when the people answer, We have them with the Lord, he may admonish them that they ought to think of nothing other than the very God whom they invoke. Let the breast therefore be closed against the adversary and lie open to the Lord alone; and in the time of holy prayer let no one admit any occupation of the world at all.

    Great is the usefulness of pure prayer, which, like a faithful messenger, carries out the command of the fervent mind, and, flying, ascends into heaven, where flesh does not reach. For prayer is sustained by two wings, so that it may fly up into heaven; one of these is called fasting, and the other is named almsgiving. Hence Saint John Chrysostom says: Nothing is more powerful than a person praying, who prays with

    Homily VIII. Fol. xviii.

    [fasting?]: because it has two wings, and neither strays nor grows sluggish. Let us therefore pray in the highest fervor of spirit, and let us live with as much purity of conscience as we can, because that prayer is perfect and pleasing to God whose cause and tongue alike cry out, whose deeds and speech agree with its supplication, whose life and thought lend patronage to its petitions. For without the justice of truth every prayer will be fruitless, because we know that God does not hear sinners, and that salvation is far from sinners, as Scripture says: “He who turns away his ears so as not to hear the laws, his prayer will be abominable.” The holy prophet also says in the psalm: “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me.” For just as in a wound no medicine is of any benefit unless the iron is first drawn out, so the prayer of that man is of no benefit while deceit still remains in his mind or hatred in his breast.

    But in order that God may hear your prayer, first of all the conscience must be cleansed from every stain of mortal sin, and the mind must take on a true purpose of amendment. To pray much and at the same time offend in many things: what else is this than to mock God? For in two ways prayer is hindered, so that it is not heard by the Lord: one, when the one praying still commits evil by sinning; the other, if he has not, for God’s sake, forgiven his debtor the debt. Therefore you who desire to have the fruit of your prayers, who wish to come with the penitent to God’s mercy, take care that you do nothing evil against God’s will, and diligently see to it that you truly forgive from the heart all things committed against you by men. For you know that the Lord said: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven.”

    But after you have cleansed your conscience from evil and forgiven every offense to your neighbor, then you will be ready to entreat the Lord, casting yourself humbly down in his sight; and pray with purity of heart and fervor of spirit, nor cease from prayer as long as you live in the flesh. Let your prayer be pure, simple, clear, and manifest; let it be full of gravity and weight, and adorned with the beauty of true humility. Do not ask anything in prayer contrary to the salvation of the soul, nor pray too importunately for a temporal thing, because it is shamelessness to ask riches from God, which furnish the greatest occasion for pride and often defile Christian purity. It is not shamelessness if you ask for daily bread, because it is one thing to ask for material by which you may become proud, and another to ask for necessary nourishment by which you may live.

    Do not justify yourself when praying, lest like the Pharisee you go away condemned; nor ask anything from the Lord as if by debt owed to your merits, but humble yourself in all things, so that you may deserve to receive grace. Remember the humility of the publican, and pray with such humility that you may find with him pardon for sins and justification of the soul. For God’s grace is more abundant than the prayer of the suppliant, and he grants us more when we pray than we ask. You will not pray with a cry of the voice to him who knows the hidden things of the heart, but in the fervor of spirit and the inward cry of the mind strike the ears of the divine majesty. Nor should you draw out a length of words before him who is spirit, because God will be appeased not by much speaking but by the devout mind of the one praying.

    At the time of prayer cast away from yourself every malice and unrest of heart, and, as we often say, forgive if you have anything against your neighbor. For unless for love of the Savior you forgive your neighbor every debt, you will obtain nothing from the Lord by your prayers. It is said that there is a certain kind of serpent which, when it wishes to go into the water to drink, first vomits out all its poison. You also, monk, imitate this serpent in this respect: vomit out all the poison of anger and bitterness, forgiving your brother a hundred denarii, so that the Lord may forgive you ten thousand talents. As you desire the Lord to be toward you, so also show yourself toward your fellow servant. Call upon the Lord with your whole heart and you will find him; let your prayer be ardent and most pure, so that your mind may be joined to him in most holy love.

    Strive for this throughout your whole life: that you may offer pure prayer to the Lord God at all times. He does not act with levity, nor is his judgment easily moved; what he promised is fixed. If you pray earnestly, you will see a miracle. Remember that you stand beneath the gaze of God, who understands all the secrets of hearts and knows the hidden things of minds. Therefore stand watchfully in the sight of him who knows all things, and pray with as much fervor of spirit as you can, that [unclear] liij

    That one must pray without ceasing.

    ...that you may deserve to obtain mercy. For by holy prayer the conscience of the penitent is cleansed; and he who raises his heart to the Lord in true purity, his prayer does not return empty. O, if you knew, dearest brothers, how pleasing to God are the prayers of a pure mind, and how much benefit they confer upon the soul, you would allow no time to pass without prayers. For our prayer, if it is pure and burning in the fervor of the spirit, is a most faithful messenger to God; it speaks to God on our behalf, and obtains all things that are necessary for our salvation while it prays.

    Therefore I admonish you and exhort you in true charity to pray without ceasing, and never to cease from the fervor of the Holy Spirit. Let there be no time for you empty or idle in sluggishness of mind. In the fear of the Lord, I beg you, always be watchful and attentive, so that you may be able bravely to conquer and overcome the temptations that threaten. As soon as foul thoughts begin to knock at the mind, run back to the practice of prayer, and they will be in no way able to prevail against you. For prayer is a great fortification of the soul; in its presence all the contrivances of the opposing side fail. For through the purest prayers all useful things are granted to us by God, and all adversities are driven far away.

    The mind is powerfully kindled in the love of God by pure prayers, and whatever occurs of a lighter stain is cleansed by praying. By holy and continual prayers the world is conquered; the plagues of the soul are healed by devout petitions; by tears and weeping the devil is overcome; and he for whom a thousand cohorts are not sufficient for battle is weakened by the prayer of one poor man. Just as wax, melting before the face of fire, is dissolved, so at the fervor of pure prayer all the power of demons, crushed, is enervated.

    If a base thought has been cast into your mind by demons, then at once, with the sign of the cross impressed upon your forehead, say: Save me, Jesus Christ, mediator of God and men, and drive away from me all the wickedness of the ancient enemy through your most innocent passion. What can be briefer than this prayer, or more powerful? For as soon as it has been uttered with fervor of mind against the presence or suggestion of demons, every contrivance of iniquity withdraws. For the power of pure prayer is very great, since it both penetrates heaven and by its steadfastness overthrows the powers of the air.

    Prayer illuminates the mind, purifies the affection, obtains pardon for sins, and strengthens the spirit in the love of God against all adversaries. Nothing so raises the mind from earthly things to the love of heavenly things; nothing so quickly and powerfully destroys the pleasures of the flesh; nothing so illumines the understanding; nothing likewise so greatly confounds the adversary of truth, as pure prayer, which is poured out to God with the fervor of divine love and is adorned by the testimony of a good conscience. If you desire to be terrible to demons, if you wish to be a friend of God, have a pure conscience and never interrupt spiritual prayer.

    For devout prayer can do all things, if it is [offered?] with uprightness of faith and purity of life. Prayer puts demons to flight, enervates the power of the malign, heals the soul languishing in tepidity, and strengthens the spirit that is weak and infirm in the fear of God. Pure prayer makes one near to God, and him whom it had received as a servant it makes to be a friend of God. Pure prayer, fervent in the love of God, penetrates heaven, wonderfully illuminates the understanding of the one praying, closes hell, opens paradise, and brings in the souls of the faithful.

    For Truth does not lie, who in the holy Gospel promises, saying: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to the one knocking it shall be opened. Which of you has ever turned to the Lord with his whole heart and prayed, and has not been heard? Or who has called upon the Lord, who cast down Amalek, trusting in his own strength, not by fighting with iron but by praying with holy prayers? For the continual supplication of the just man avails much, and the prayer of one humbling himself penetrates the clouds.

    Elijah was a man subject to suffering like us; and he prayed with prayer that it should not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months. And again he prayed, and heaven gave [rain?], and the earth gave its fruit. By prayer and tears King Hezekiah obtained fifteen years of longer life, and by prayers changed the prophet’s sentence. By prayers holy men shone with miracles, and, supplicating the Lord, recalled the dead to life. To the purity of prayer also all things are subject, and there is nothing in us so difficult that devout and fervent prayer

    Homily VIII.

    Folio XIX.

    to obtain. Then, when we pray, we receive confidence of obtaining from the Lord what we ask, when no perversity of life contradicts our prayers. For the Lord is the hearer of a righteous prayer, namely when integrity of life commends the prayer, and no guilt of conscience makes the one who prays hesitate. Friendship will not stand between those unlike each other, and between God and a sinner there can be no communion. If you wish to be heard when you pray, take care first that you do not differ from the will of God. Live in the spirit most like to God, and you will suffer no rejection in prayer. For indeed purity of conscience, in the fervor of divine love, makes a man like to God in understanding; likeness causes love; love introduces familiarity; familiarity, confidence; and upon confidence there follows the easy obtaining of one’s petition. For just as there is no union among things unlike, so between God and an evil man prayer avails nothing.

    Therefore whoever among you desires to obtain the effect of his prayers, let him first, through true penitence, cleanse the dwelling-place of his heart from every fault; then let him strive to inflame himself by the exercise of holy compunction; afterward let him continually feed his mind in the pursuit of the love of God, so that the good which he begins he may thereafter at no time interrupt.
