But afterward, when, with the desire of divine love always increasing in him, he has by long effort brought the exercise of holy purity into habit, and the mind has conceived the necessary firmness in its good purpose, then for the first time the likeness of divine communion is gradually introduced, and prayer is formed to its due state. For the more the mind, stirred up in the love of God, has advanced, the more quickly will prayer obtain from the Lord what it asks. For the love of God alone makes one powerful in prayer; and in it, the more fervently the mind has burned, the more easily it will obtain the effect of its petitions. For if you love much, you can do much. For God is charity, and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. But in him in whom God remains, there is nothing stronger than he, except God himself alone.

    There are among you certain men weak and feeble in spirit, who already consider themselves strong and perfect in the way of the Lord; their devotion is both rare and fleeting, and they boast that without the wedding garment they have approached the kingdom of heaven, although they still lie far off in the lower places. To these I say again what I have often said: that no one suddenly becomes the highest, and unless a monk has subdued all his animal passions through the mortification of the flesh, he does not reach the very high mountain of divine contemplation. For whoever, placed in a monastery under authority and obedience, follows his own will against monastic discipline, is not worthy to be heard by the Lord in his prayers.

    But those of whom we speak are great and wise in their own eyes: loving their own will, they murmur at everything, and whatever they themselves have not arranged they think badly done. They examine the actions of their brothers with curious inquiry, but are content to neglect discerning their own negligences. In their morals they are lax and disorderly; in words frivolous and loud; unwilling toward obedience, and always slow in good works and full of sloth. They neglect the common exercises of the order and attend to private ones according to their own will. And as long as they remain in their own rashness, they do not rise up to the true love of God. Let monks who love their own will hear what the Lord says: “I came not to do my own will, but that of the Father who sent me.” Brothers, attend to this teacher; unless you live in imitation of him, you will pray without fruit. For the Lord gladly hears the prayer of him who keeps his commandments in truth. But he who transgresses the commandment of God, who follows with desire the pleasures of the flesh and the consolations of the world, his prayer is not heard.

    For God, just and upright, is believed then gladly to hear your prayer when a good mind and a good life make supplication together. But if a man’s conduct displeases God, how will his prayer please him? For God is spirit, and a man who walks not in the spirit but in the flesh certainly does not approach God at all. Therefore you, monk, who do not walk according to the purity of the Gospel and the Rule, who love your own will and not God’s, know that you will not feel the efficacy of your prayers unless you first amend your life. For unless your conduct agrees with your prayer, you will not obtain what you ask. Then you cry to the Lord with one great voice, when even with the tongue silent you cry out with good works. For good prayers and evil conduct merit nothing good. Therefore do what a certain wise man advised: and if you have sinned, do not cast yourself away again, but pray also concerning your former sins, that

    …may be forgiven you. Before [your] prayers, prepare your soul, and be not as a man who tempts God. Let the mind be pure and ardent in the love of the Lord; let the conscience be clean and strengthened in the purpose of a holy way of life; and the prayer will be pleasing to the divine ears. If you pray otherwise, you will obtain nothing. He prays well who lives well; and he easily obtains who prays with holy works. Finally, prayer is rendered much effective and pleasing in the sight of God, if it be at all times consonant with the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. For Christ is God and man, the mediator between God and us, through whom we have safe access to the Father, as he himself testifies in the holy Gospel: "No one," he says, "comes to the Father but through me." Whence let no day pass on which you do not at least once give thanks to Christ by praying—who by the pain of his wounds healed the languors of your soul, who shed his blood for you, and by his most innocent death redeemed you, wretched, from the destruction of perpetual death. Truly a man is most ungrateful, and unworthy of the Christian name, who is so far forgetful of Christ's so great benefits that he does not daily, or at least once, render thanksgivings to him. But let the monk—who, dead to the world, is bidden to live for God alone—carry continually in his breast the memory of the Lord's passion, always giving thanks to his Redeemer, always blessing, always adoring; and daily—nay, as much as can be done, in every single moment—let him with tears, compassionating, turn over [in his mind] the bitterness of Christ's wounds. Every day, after the several regular prayers which the Greeks call canonical, with knees bent and mind raised to heaven let him say: "I give thanks to you, and blessing [you] I adore you, O mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus, most sweet God and man, for your most holy incarnation, for your nativity from the Virgin, for [your] circumcision, for the flight into Egypt and the seven years in exile which you endured for us. I adore you, Lord Savior Jesus Christ, for your labors, for [your] hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness; for your journeys, for your teaching and preaching, for your miracles, for the calling of the nations, and for the justification of sinners. I give you thanks, Lord, Son of the living God, for the pain of your wounds; I bless you for the shedding of your most holy blood; I adore you for your death which you most innocently endured; and I beseech you, by your whole passion, [your] piety and clemency, have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death." This most brief prayer the devout monk will recite at least seven times a day, so that as often as he passes before the image of the Crucified, in like manner, with fervor of mind, he may adore Christ. He who is a true lover of Christ always thinks of Christ, speaks of and venerates Christ, [and] does not doubt that Christ is everywhere present to him. The passion of Christ is never absent from his memory; and through the greatness of love he forgets himself, and in Christ is wholly occupied in mind and desire. Whoever is fervent in soul in the love of Christ despises earthly things, conquers the flesh, [and] desires only heavenly things. Waking, he ever thinks of Christ with desire; sleeping, he dreams of Christ; and, continually sighing, with the divine Ignatius he cries: "My love is crucified." He joins sighs to sighs, and Jesus—whom he loves with his whole heart—he discerns present, not with his eyes but with his spirit. With the desire of love urging [him], as often as he gazes on the Crucified, he soon dissolves into tears, and, glowing with the fire of charity, cries out: "O love stronger than all strengths! How sweetly he burns who is inflamed with the desire of Christ!" Rightly did he speak who said: "Love is strong as death." For what can be stronger than the love of Christ, by whose ardor the holy martyrs, despising so many thousand kinds of death, overcame [them]? O my crucified love, have mercy on me; grant me to feel that sweetness of your love of which I speak, that I may always carry about in my heart your most bitter passion. I know, my brothers, I know that there is no more effective mode of praying, nor more useful to us who are still weak, than to be in the memory and power of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Whence, since it is manifest that without a mediator there is no ascent of the mind to God, every good work must be begun in the name of Christ; for then we usefully pour out prayers to God, when with purified conscience we pray through his only-begotten Son.

    Of the custody and origin of thoughts: Homily Nine.

    Solomon, that once most wise king, in the book which he entitled "of the Proverbs," [addresses his] son

    Works, IX. Fol. xx.

    ...having exhorted him to true wisdom. Among other things he said: “My son, attend to my wisdom, and incline your ear to my prudence, that you may guard your thoughts, and that your lips may preserve discipline.” For it is no small part of wisdom, dearly beloved brothers, if a monk knows how to discern his thoughts prudently and to guard their movements carefully at all times. It is a great thing to think nothing evil, but it is not a lesser mark of prudence to be able to repel evil thoughts from their very beginning. For the deep reflection of the human heart is ever shifting, varied, manifold, and unstable; to observe its beginnings and restrain its movements is the height of prudence and a great sign of wisdom. If I have called the heart of man a mill, driven by perpetual motion, I have not strayed from the truth, especially if anyone should wish to examine its restlessness most closely. For what else is the human heart than a kind of mill, always in motion, always grinding something? The human heart is never idle, never rests without movement, but is always doing something; and just as an empty mill consumes itself by its own motion, so the heart of man shamefully runs down from itself when thought of the good does not constrain it. It is always moved toward some object with the desire of its love; it is always grinding, always acting, always occupied with something delightful, whether it be good or evil. As the body is not moved without the soul, so the mind of man does not remain fixed in the good unless it has been continually restrained by holy exercises. Therefore the wise man said in Ecclesiasticus: “Joyfulness of heart is the life of man, and the treasure of holiness without failing; and the exultation of a man is length of days. Delight your soul in what is pleasing to God, and hold it in, and gather your heart in his holiness, and drive sorrow far from you.” What is the gathering of the heart, if not the diligent guarding of thought? For he gathers his heart in the holiness of the Lord who continually observes, in the fear of God, the movements of his thoughts. And therefore Scripture says: “With all custody guard your heart, because from it life proceeds.” But thoughts take the beginnings of their movements from those things which are presented by the senses; these wander the more dangerously the less they are examined from the outset by the judgment of reason. Therefore whoever desires to be watchful over his thoughts, whoever wishes to gather his heart in the holiness of the Lord, should first of all guard his outward senses with the greatest diligence, and set the bridle of prudence upon each of them. Hence Scripture commands thus concerning hearing and sight: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue; and make doors for your mouth, and bars for your ears.” “Blessed is the man who stops his ears lest he hear bloodshed, and closes his eyes lest he see evil.” We also read thus in holy Job: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think of a virgin.” But against those who have fallen into the pit of sins through the service of their senses, the Lord thus bears witness through the prophet Jeremiah: “Because death has climbed in through your windows; it has entered your houses to destroy the little ones outside, and the young men from the streets.” Death enters our houses through the windows whenever a wicked thought is let into the mind through the service of sight or hearing. For the house is conscience, of which Scripture says: “Unless you hold yourself constantly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown.” [unclear] guards it. Therefore the house of conscience must be fortified by the fear of the Lord; the senses too must be restrained with the greatest diligence, because he does not sufficiently guard his thoughts who does not turn his ears and eyes away from the occasion of evil. And so, if you wish to be a prudent guardian of your thoughts and a true gatherer of the heart in the holiness of the Lord, hedge your ears with the thorns of compunction and of the fear of God, lest they hear evil; and turn away your eyes, lest they introduce sin through sight. What it is not lawful for you to desire, do not look upon with desire; and what it is not expedient to have, do not think upon. Many have perished through the service of the senses, and because they proceed incautiously to see outward things, they have often shamefully lost their inner goods. He who does not fear danger is already surely near destruction; and he who presumes on his own virtue runs hastily toward the ruin of sin. He who flashes his eye into the brilliance of lightning will be blinded for the moment; and he who gazes upon the beauty of women will not be free from danger. I praise the prudence of that monk who is alone in the midst of crowds, and sets a censor over his senses, lest he admit anything evil to his lady. He sets guards beside the gate, who with sword and club repel those who rush in disorderly. Fear [unclear]

    Works, IX. Fol. xx.

    On the Custody and Origin of Thoughts

    The holy fear of the Lord never deserts the mind of a wise man; but, just as a strong and ever-watchful champion always stands at the prince’s side, so it guards the [house?] of the heart. He turns his ears away from all scurrility of words, and closes his eyes lest they see evil. He always walks according to the twelfth degree of humility, with his gaze fixed upon the ground, praying to the Lord with the prophet: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; in your way give me life, O Lord.”

    Go, I admonish you, brothers: direct your senses in the fear of the Lord, so that you may always be able to keep the dwelling of the heart clean and inviolate. Remember the Scripture, which says: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord.” Consider, I pray, with how great a cleanliness and purity of mind you ought to shine, you who not only, by reason of the priestly order, carry the vessels of the Lord, but, what is more, are even yourselves the vessels of the Lord. For the holy lover of Christ, Paul, says: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” And again he says: “Or do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own?” And elsewhere: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are.” And concerning that same Paul, in the Acts of the Apostles, the Lord said to Ananias: “Go, for this man is a vessel of election for me.”

    The monk who performs priestly office in the Church of God is bound by a double reason to the observance of most holy purity. For the soldier of Christ, because of the vow which he made to God, must be pure, holy, and continually tireless in good works; and by reason of the priestly ministry, circumspect and most diligently watchful. For it is written: “Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently.” You are ministers of almighty God, who daily sacrifice his Son at the altar; his work is entrusted into your hands, and therefore great purity of mind and body is demanded in your manner of life.

    Therefore, in order that the chaste purity of the mind may remain, the instability of thought must be restrained. The senses must be guarded at all times, for through them the integrity of the mind is corrupted. For you are dead to the world and have now begun to live for Christ; it is not lawful for you to think anything except what is holy, nor is it fitting for you, ministers of God, to love anything earthly. For it is God whom you serve, O monks; it is the Almighty whom you minister to, my brothers. Live pure, holy, and innocent, because it is not fitting for you to be occupied with the business of the world, you who have been called to the soldiery of God.

    Let love of God and purity of heart grow in you with time, so that the longer you live in this world, the holier you may become. Always turn yourselves away from every evil, so that you may be able to persevere without failing in good thoughts. Always raise the eyes of your mind to heaven, and do not occupy the sight of the flesh with perishable things. Also always close your hearing to every useless, vain, and foolish speech, and always think with fear on the future judgment of God. Do not pollute your hands with the unlawful and shameful touch of any things whatever, so that you may be able to sacrifice the Son of God with a clean body and a pure conscience.

    In food and drink it is not the part of monks to distinguish flavors, nor is it fitting for the soldiers of Christ to love bodily delights. Nature requires few things, and rustic foods by which it may be nourished; appetite, however, unless it is restrained by the command of reason, is dragged toward unlawful things, through which the simplicity of nature is violated. Therefore flee excess in all things, and observe regular moderation in your way of living. Let none of you patiently listen to one who detracts from his brothers or speaks evil of his neighbor. Let each one of you restrain his tongue from useless speech, and let good monks blush to speak evil of any Christians.

    Never let that warning of the Lord depart from your memory, spoken in the holy Gospel: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. A good man from a good treasure brings forth good things, and an evil man from an evil treasure brings forth evil things. But I say to you that every idle word which men shall have spoken, they shall render an account for it on the day of judgment.” O sentence too greatly to be feared. If an account is demanded for idle speech, what do detraction, scurrility, and filthy speech deserve? Or if a useless word is judged guilty under the strict reckoning of examination, what will he answer who so readily speaks what is evil and harmful? An idle word is every utterance of men which has been spoken without just usefulness and lacks the reason of lawful necessity. Therefore, brothers, consider your words, and let no one speak a word not pertinent to the matter, or to just usefulness, or to necessary [unclear].

    Homily IX.

    Fol. XXI.

    of [unclear]. For you have heard the fearful sentence of the Lord, and you are not unaware of the command of our holy lawgiver, who says in the Rule: “Buffooneries, idle words, and words that provoke laughter we condemn to perpetual exclusion in all places, and we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth for such speech.”

    Here holy father Benedict forbade three kinds of words to monks, and condemned them to perpetual exclusion in all places: namely, buffoonish, idle, and laughter-provoking words. What buffoonery is, the interpretation of the grammarians has declared to us. For the vice of buffoonery is opposed to refinement and modesty, and is a certain wanton jocularity provoking the laughter of hearers, without shame or honor, immoderate in words and gestures, which do not accord with reason, do not befit a good man, and are not suitable for a wise man. Buffoonery is so called from a buffoon, who follows the houses of the rich, provoking his hearers to laughter by wanton and dishonorable words and gestures for the sake of a reward or a coin.

    And this kind of words holy father Benedict forbade to monks and condemned utterly, because those who serve God are rightly commanded to abstain perpetually, in his sight, from foul and dishonorable words. Between buffoonery and much-speaking there seems to be this difference: the former exceeds by reason of dishonor, the latter by reason of excess. The former is foul and dishonorable; the latter is superfluous without virtue.

    Foolish talk is rightly joined with these, since it is forbidden not only to monks but also to all Christians. Hence the holy apostle of Christ says: “But fornication and all uncleanness or covetousness, let it not even be named among you, as befits saints; nor filthiness, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery, which are not to the purpose, but rather thanksgiving.” Idle words are likewise forbidden to all monks, because they are prohibited by the Lord, as you have heard, in the holy Gospel. Words that provoke laughter also do not befit Christian people, and much less are they suitable for cloistered men. For the monk, who is dead to the world, is commanded always to think on his last things; but he is bound everywhere, for love of God, to despise laughter and every insolence of the present life. Laughter is a confused voice, declaring the inward joy of the mind with immoderate cheerfulness. But nothing

    [unclear] humility, reverence, and subjection are required, lest anyone seem to speak more than is fitting. A man is known from his words, and he who multiplies utterances in his mouth is foolish in heart. A man’s speech is the witness of his conscience, and for one who loves modesty and innocence of heart, his words ought to be modest and without vanity. For you are ministers of the living God, my brothers: let no vain, useless, and idle word go out from your mouth, but only what is good for the edification of the hearers, so that it may increase charity in their minds, toward the illumination of the heart in the knowledge and love of the highest truth. Precious is the tongue of the monk that speaks nothing at all except what is holy, and worthy of blessing is the mouth from which nothing is brought forth except what is divine. Let each one keep his heart clean from every wicked thought, since he who is good in heart does not speak an evil word, and he who truly loves God does not utter idle speech. Apply every care and consideration to your thoughts, since evil must be watched there with principal attention, where it takes the beginning of its proceedings, so that as soon as it has begun to arise it may be cut off by the roots. For there is no thought of evil so weak that it does not grow with time, if it is nourished by the consent of the thinker. Therefore evil, while still weak, must be conquered immediately at the beginning, because when delay intervenes, even a very small evil gains strength, though in the beginning it may seem [unclear]. A great fire often arises from a small spark, and from a lesser thought a great sin sometimes rises up. When thought gives birth to delight, it is accustomed soon to burst into consent, and consequently into deed also, if it can cast itself headlong. But when the will, through delight, has granted consent to an evil thought for the deed, even if what the soul desires is not completed, nevertheless the sin has already been consummated before God. But what does Scripture say? Sin, when it has been consummated, brings forth death. For almighty God regards the will of man, whether he wills good or evil. Therefore he says in the holy Gospel: Whoever has looked at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. God reckons the will as the deed whenever a person cannot bring into effect what he wished. Therefore again and again I admonish you, brothers, and with as much diligence as I can I solemnly urge you, that according to the holy Apostle you walk cautiously, not as fools, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Watch most cautiously for the snares of the evil demon, and resist evil and unclean thoughts immediately from the beginning, because remedy is considered far too late when the disease has gained strength through long time. Accustom yourselves at all times to dwell upon good and holy thoughts, and you will easily be able to overcome the insolence of evil ones. For just as vessels filled with good liquids receive no external corruption, so minds filled with good thoughts do not admit the intemperance of evil ones. Since the eye of the heart is that by which God is seen, and through purity of conscience one arrives at the glory of eternal happiness. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God. A clean heart is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, and where evil thought is not admitted, God without doubt abides. A clean heart is the seat of wisdom, and where purity of mind is guarded, no perils of adversity will harm. Be mindful of Scripture saying: Perverse thoughts separate from God, but tested virtue corrects the foolish. For wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor will it dwell in a body subject to sins. For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding. But a perverse thought is any thought admitted that is contrary to evangelical purity; by commerce with it the mind of the thinker is defiled, whenever by thinking about and turning over those things that are opposed to God it takes delight in them. And those perverse thoughts separate the mind of the thinker from God and little by little cast it down into the depth of evils. For an evil and perverse thought, when it has penetrated, first poisons through the venom of delight; then it clouds reason; afterward it draws the will into consenting to the evil suggestion; finally it consummates sin in deed. From then on, an evil once presumed is practiced more freely, and all shame or fear is removed through habit. Sin is joined to sin, and little by little the habit of doing evil is strengthened. But when time is granted to an evil habit, a certain

    Homily IX. Folio XXII.

    ...generates the necessity of sinning. Here is the hardest dominion of death; here the deepest depth of evils. Whoever has once entered this abyss of sins rarely, indeed not easily, rises again to purity of heart without the special grace of God and the greatest labor of repentance. By his own will the sinner has fallen into this pit of death; but without God’s mercy he will not be able to rise again. Most harsh is the yoke of evil habit: if anyone has once submitted his neck to it, he rarely recovers his former freedom of spirit.

    All these things are wrought by perverse thought when it is admitted into the mind and, through delight, is changed into consent and deed. For no thought is so small that it does not gradually grow if it is not driven from the mind. Blessed, therefore, is that monk who casts all his thought upon the Lord; who always and everywhere denies a place to wicked thoughts; who despises all the perishable riches of the world; who scorns all comforts of the body. He prepares the cleanness of his heart for his Lord; he loves nothing in this world except the Lord; he orders all his thoughts to the glory of the Savior, and observes his commandments with the utmost diligence.

    What is happier than that monk who presents himself to the world not as a citizen but as a pilgrim? He lives in the world as if he were not in the world; indeed, greater than the world is he whose whole conversation is in heaven. Consider now, therefore, dearest brothers, the shortness of this time, and always remember that you are mortal and will soon pass away. For we have here no abiding city, but seek the one to come; and since we know that so many thousands of men have gone before us through death, let us consider how soon we too must necessarily die.

    Now indeed a short time is granted to us, but one very acceptable, in which we may work the fruits of eternal life. For now is the time for laboring; now is the hour for sowing good, because after death each one will receive the reward of his labors, when no further opportunity for laboring is granted. Therefore, my brothers, anticipate this hour of death with holy works, and do not fail now in the seedtime of labor, so that in eternal recompense you may rejoice without end. Let no day pass on which each one of you has not become better, and has not added some new good work to those he has already performed. Always think on the price of the harvest to come, and let no greatness of labor terrify you.

    On The Daily Struggle Of Temptation: Homily Ten.

    In yesterday’s sermon, dearest brothers, I admonished your charities to resist the beginnings of evil thoughts, and with all your strength to prepare yourselves by good and holy works for the prize of the future reward. But since, as Scripture bears witness, the life of man upon earth is temptation, I have thought it necessary to discuss this same matter in your hearing, as much as the Lord shall grant, so that, having been forewarned, you may be able to fight more strongly against the invisible adversary.

    You know the words of the wise man, who says in Ecclesiasticus: “Son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice, and prepare your soul for temptation.” Let no one think himself free from temptation, brothers, so long as he walks in this mortal way of life; but the more anyone advances in the fear of God, the more cautiously let him know that he must live. For Saint Pope Gregory says: “The more our enemy sees that rebellion is made against him, the more fully he strives to attack. For he neglects to strike those whom he feels he possesses by undisturbed right.” The devil pursues the one fleeing from him and endeavors to overthrow the one who rebels against his command.

    You, O men, the more you advance in the spiritual way of life, the more urgently you must keep watch against the adversary of your salvation. For, as Saint John Chrysostom says, our adversary never sleeps, but always keeps watch for the destruction of the human race; none of us can resist him except the one who has learned to keep watch at all times in the fear of the Lord. And Saint Leo, pope of the city of Rome, says in a certain sermon: “The ancient enemy does not cease to spread everywhere the snares of temptations, so that in whatever way he may be able, by corrupting the faith of believers, to blacken it. He knows to whom he should offer the enticements of the flesh, into whom he should pour the poison of envy, before whom he should set the incitements of lust. He knows whom he should disturb with sorrow, whom he should deceive with joy, whom he should oppress with fear, whom he should seduce by admiration [unclear].”

    On the Daily Struggle of Temptation.

    [unclear]. He examines the characters of all; he scrutinizes the affections of all. There he seeks occasions for doing harm, where he has seen anyone to be more diligently occupied. There are no works of virtue without the trial of temptations; no faith without disturbances; no contest without an enemy; no victory without an encounter. Hence Saint James the Apostle says in his epistle: Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him. Hence again Scripture says: The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men. But lest anyone think that the devil is permitted to tempt men as much as he desires, Saint [Christophilus?] cries out: But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will also make with the temptation an outcome, so that you may be able to endure it. And Saint Augustine says: The devil is permitted to tempt only so much as is profitable for you: that you may be exercised, that you may be proved, that you, who did not know yourself, may be found by yourself. For the devil, with God’s permission, can stir up the motion of temptation; but it lies in your most free power, if you wish, to give or deny consent to the tempter. Hence, when he tempted the Son of God in the desert, he did not drive him, did not touch him, did not compel him, but only said: Cast yourself down; so that you may understand that he cannot conquer except one who wills it. Therefore the divine chief apostle of Christ said: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. For the devil can suggest evil; he cannot compel, nor overcome unless you consent.

    Our life, as Saint Augustine bears witness, in this pilgrimage cannot be without sin and temptation, because our progress is increased through temptations; nor does anyone know himself unless he has been tempted; nor can he be crowned unless he has conquered; nor can he conquer unless he has fought; nor can he fight unless he has had an enemy and temptations. For Scripture says: He who has not been tempted, what does he know? For no one will be crowned except one who has fought lawfully. Therefore, brothers most dear, as you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear; and so long as you can be conquered and subjected by the adversary, do not boast of security. You know that he with whom you have entered the contest never sleeps, does not rest, does not cease from persecution, and, always lying in wait for you, is never wearied. But if at any time he has been overcome, immediately he rises up for a new contest, nor does he desist from assaulting the good until, defeated, he altogether falls back, or else by untimely perseverance conquers the combatant. Hence also Saint Pope Gregory says: The ancient enemy, when from the first contest he sees that he is falling back, renews other wars of temptations. The wary adversary of the human race observes the character of each person, and whatever vices they are nearer to, these he places before the face of the heart; and he uses great strength to overthrow the state of the mind.

    Stand firmly rooted in the fear of the Lord, and you will easily overcome all the temptations of the enemy. For it is written in the Book of Proverbs: In the fear of the Lord is confidence of strength. And again: Through mercy and faith sins are purged; but through the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil. In Ecclesiasticus, moreover, the wise man said: The fear of the Lord drives out sin. For he who is without fear will not be able to be justified. For the anger of his animosity overturns him. Therefore, by Solomon’s testimony, that man is called blessed who is always fearful; but he who is of a hard mind will fall into evil. Prepare your souls also, through zeal for holy conduct, for temptation, so that when it comes you may be able to resist and stand the stronger for it. For you will easily overcome the devil if you always come prepared for battle. Behold, your adversary, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; you must resist him in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ if you desire to obtain victory. No place for flight is granted here; no little delay of security is allowed to those who fight; but it is necessary that you engage: you will overcome the enemy if you have stood bravely, or be conquered by him if you have fought badly. By this law we have all entered the world, that by fighting we may conquer; on this condition we have been made men, that, having overcome the allurements of the flesh, we ought to become equal to the holy angels. Contests are never lacking to monks, since for as long as they live in the flesh, we are necessarily exposed to temptations. For Scripture says: Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them. But in all our temptations that saying of the prophet Isaiah [is to be brought] to memory

    Let us recall all the words of him who says: “You who have been weaned from milk, you who have been drawn away from the breast, expect tribulation upon tribulation, hope upon hope, yet a little while, because of the wickedness of lips, because of the malignant tongue.” Those weaned and drawn away from the breast are men advanced in age, whose part it is to receive tribulation upon tribulation for God’s sake, so that they may deserve to bring back hope upon hope, as sacred Scripture says: “But we glory also in our tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience; and patience, trial; and trial, hope. And hope does not confound, because the charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” For through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. For by temptations we become known to ourselves, and we find out whether we truly fear God. Hence the Lord speaks through Moses to the people, saying: “The Lord your God tests you, that he may know whether you love him with all your heart and with all your soul.”

    This world, dearly beloved brothers, is to be compared to a furnace, in which the fire of temptation and adversity continually burns, and through which we must necessarily pass. In this furnace of tribulation the chaff is burned up, but gold and silver are cleansed of every stain. The chaff is turned into ash; the gold is kept for the ornament and beauty of the royal palace. The furnace, I say, is the world; the fire is temptation or tribulation; the gold is righteous men; the chaff, however, is the unrighteous and sinners; the craftsman who purifies the gold is almighty God himself, who favors our progress and cooperates by grace toward the merit of virtue. Therefore let us do what God wills; what he imposes, let us patiently bear for love of him, since, as the holy [apostle of Christ?] says, “the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that shall be revealed in us.” Hence Saint Jerome says: “Who would not wish to be troubled? Who would not desire to be reviled, that he may gain being praised by Christ’s voice and be rewarded with an abundant heavenly recompense? Would that, because of the name of my Lord and because of justice, the whole crowd of unbelievers might persecute and trouble me. Would that this whole world might rise up to my reproach, provided only that I may deserve to be praised by Christ and hasten toward the reward of his promise.” And the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men.”

    Therefore, whichever of you, my brothers, desires to come to the kingdom of heaven, whichever of you cares above all to please God, let him learn gladly to receive the tribulations of temptations for love of him, and joyfully to endure whatever adversity shall occur. For there is none of us who does not need daily purification, none who does not offend almost at every moment. If, then, we love our own salvation, if we demand that our sins be forgiven us and that we be cleansed from every stain of heart, let us patiently sustain whatever adversity happens to us, since the evils of tribulation, which the soul patiently tolerates for love of God, cleanse it more than the good works which it now performs of its own will in this world.

    Great matter for suffering has been left to us in this place: we who are heavily pressed by need, weighed down by poverty, and also constrained by the debt of borrowed money. What adversity do we not experience in this monastery? What storms and tempests do we not suffer, brothers? By what inconveniences are we not harassed? How desolate all the goods of this monastery were when, fifteen years ago, regular observance was introduced, none of you can be ignorant. But the tribulation of common want rages more severely against me, who must provide the necessities of life for you, and very often do not sufficiently know from what source I may pay. Yet your patience consoles my spirit, and the hope which you have conceived in the Lord, the savior of the humble, so that I do not doubt that his mercy will be present in time; and I hear him saying to me through Isaiah the prophet: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.” Gladly, then, I shall have patience in the poverty which, God thus ordaining, we now suffer, so that after death we may deserve to come to the riches of eternity. For the more, in this our pilgrimage, we shall have been afflicted by persecutions, poverty, need, labors, and tribulations, the greater rewards we shall obtain in the future recompense of the righteous, when God grants them. Therefore with me, my brothers, patiently endure whatever almighty God has preordained us to suffer, since, as the holy pope Gregory says, confidence in almighty God is then certain

    On the daily struggle of temptation.

    [unclear]: when adversity is added for a good work, and in this world the scourge of God is received with joy, so that a fairer reward may be kept for the future recompense of the saints. Again also he says: Those whom the adversity of temporal life humbles take joy from the hope of the everlasting inheritance, because divine dispensation would see that they were not to be saved forever if it did not restrain them, to be instructed under the rule of discipline.

    When afflicted, we lose earthly things; but by humbly enduring affliction we multiply heavenly goods for ourselves. For the present life is a road, by which we hasten toward our homeland; and for that reason we are often touched in it by disturbances, lest we think that our homeland is here. Therefore let the monk rejoice in his adversity; let him who is tempted, to whom the world has been crucified, be glad; let him trust that he belongs to the fellowship of God, who with a pure conscience always does good and receives the contrary in tribulation.

    For it is the truest sign of divine compassion if a Christian man is struck in this world by various adversities, who, serving God with a pure conscience, has prepared [unclear] in heaven. Knowing that some can sin greatly, he forestalls them with bodily weakness lest they sin, and mercifully scourges them for their salvation, seeing that it is more useful for their souls to be broken by illnesses unto salvation than to live unharmed unto damnation. Others he wills to be poor, whom he foreknew could not use riches unto salvation. For to many the wealth and [unclear] of this world [unclear]; and the unexpected enemy struck them the more heavily, because he found them negligent through long habit of quiet.

    Hence holy men, when they trust that they are making much progress by the prosperity of virtues, rejoice that by a certain governance of heavenly dispensation they are also exercised by temptations, because they guard the glory of the virtues they have received all the more robustly when, shaken by the assault of temptation, they recognize their own weakness more humbly. The way of tribulation is a short road to Christ, and he is found in it more quickly than in tranquility. For the holy bishop Ambrose says: There are many who seek Christ in leisure and do not find him; and there are those who seek him in persecutions and quickly find him. He is present in the dangers of his faithful, just as in the psalm he speaks of the just man, saying: I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him.

    Let purity of conscience keep guard in adversity; let the inviolate integrity of life always be preserved; and whatever adversity there is will undoubtedly be for us to the merit of salvation. The ancient enemy can overcome no one by fighting, unless he has first found him to have fallen away from himself. He seeks out those who are sluggish in idleness; he trips up the unwary soldier, and he most easily lays low the one whom he finds stripped of arms. Therefore, my brothers, always keep watch in holy prayers; always persist in good works, so that whenever the tempter approaches, he may never find you idle.

    Remember the words of our savior Jesus Christ, saying in the holy Gospel: Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands; and be like men [waiting for their lord, when] he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him. He keeps watch who, standing firm in the fear of the Lord, is never drowsy with sluggishness of mind. He keeps watch who preserves his soul against whatever adversities of this [unclear] by the tireless constancy of a holy purpose. He keeps watch, whoever does not cease to make progress daily in the love of the Lord.

    He carries a lamp in his hands, whoever adorns the purpose of holiness with fitting works. He also holds a lamp in his hands, whoever, purified in mind and body, shines for his neighbor by works of holy piety. Hence the holy lover of Christ, Paul, says in the epistle: I beseech you, most beloved, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God. He who, chastising his body by the pursuits of holy abstinence, brings it under servitude to the spirit has consecrated a living sacrifice to the Lord. But whoever has now learned to preserve his heart clean and pure from every pollution of sin has undoubtedly sacrificed a holy offering to the Lord. Whoever indeed perseveres in the purpose of holiness to the end has without doubt offered a pleasing sacrifice.

    But we gird our loins when we keep ourselves pure and unstained in body and mind from every form of lust. The virtue of holy chastity is of great merit before God, and, in proportion to the greatness of the struggle, is to be granted a singular reward in the recompense of the righteous, as the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my sabbaths, and choose the things that I have willed, and hold fast my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name, which shall not perish.” And concerning these the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; and there are eunuchs who were made so by men; and there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He who can receive it, let him receive it.”

    But why did he say, “He who can receive it, let him receive it”? I think that this introduction of eunuchs, who castrate themselves for love of the kingdom of heaven, is not to be referred to the cutting off of the genital members, in which many, so thinking, have wandered from the truth of the Gospel, but rather to the command of the mind, by which chastity is preserved entire, conceived from love of Christ. For those castrate themselves for the sake of the kingdom of God who keep true chastity of mind and body inviolate for love of God. And just as bodily no one is easily castrated without the great pain of torment, so no one can arrive at the perfection of chastity without the utmost exertion of labor. And certainly no one is modest by his own powers, no one modest by his own merits. It is God who gives the good will; he it is also who joins strength to the will, so that it may be able. But because it is not for many to live chastely, he leaves each one to his own judgment, saying: “He who can receive it, let him receive it.” The cutting off of members does not make the mind chaste, since the root of lust is interior, and cannot be removed by the amputation of the shameful parts. But if the mind has been chaste and whole, it will easily restrain the insolence of the members. For nothing is stronger than the mind of a man [unclear]. [Unclear] Lord, most venerable [unclear] of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

    Whoever, therefore, flees from the labor of the struggle will never attain the height of honor. Brief now is the time in which we labor, resisting the devil; but very soon the eternal time will come, in which, reigning without end, we shall exult with Christ. Let the body be chastised with discreet abstinence, lest it kick back against the command of the mind; let the concupiscence of the flesh be broken by holy exercises, so that it may always obey the counsels of reason. If at any time it begins to strike the mind with wanton impulses, let it even be restrained with blows, because it is better that the back, humbled by useful stripes, should be subdued than that the petulance of the flesh should hurl the soul down into hell. For Scripture says: “He who delicately nourishes his servant from boyhood will afterward find him insolent.” The flesh is the servant of the mind, which must always obey the command of reason. But if the flesh has been nourished too indulgently, then, accustomed to pleasures, it will refuse to bear the command of the spirit. For a servant becomes insolent toward his master whenever he is nourished delicately by him through habit. And it is difficult to bring a rebellious and insolent servant back to humble obedience after he has long been accustomed to kick back.

    For it is written: “A servant cannot be instructed by words, because he understands what you say and scorns to answer.” Therefore the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “Fodder and a rod and a burden for an ass; bread and discipline and work for a servant. He works under discipline and seeks rest; loosen your hand for him, and he seeks freedom. The yoke and the strap bend a hard neck, and constant tasks bow a servant down.” If we begin to borrow these testimonies of the Scriptures from the literal sense for the moral sense, we shall find that all the things said about the servant and the ass fit very rightly with lazy and delicate flesh. For truly the flesh is the servant of the soul, which always rises up against its mistress unless it is wearied every day by discipline and work.

    Indeed, he who keeps this flesh delicately at all times in idleness and pleasures will necessarily feel it insolent against spiritual impulses, because while the flesh is lifted up into pride, the spirit, languishing in idleness and lukewarm, is weakened. Therefore unless you, brother monk, continually humble this servant of yours, namely the flesh, through work and abstinence; unless [unclear] its illicit movements [unclear].

    [unclear] of continence and sobriety you have imposed: with it going before, you will go wholly into the abyss. For we know, as the holy apostle says, that the flesh lusts against the spirit; and unless by the spirit we have put to death the works of the flesh, we shall die in its corruption. Nothing casts the soul down into the pit of sin more than the insolence of the flesh, which, when it is allowed to live by its own will, struggles back like a stubborn servant against its lord. Unhappy flesh, you who by the desire of vanity cast down the soul: it will not pass unpunished for you if anything, at your malicious suggestion, [unclear]; for God will judge both. Woe to you; I have sinned with her, because while Adam, a transgressor of the commandments, is driven from paradise, Eve, the inciter of evils, necessarily accompanies the wretched man. Be consenting to the spirit, O flesh, because the apostle says: “But those who are Christ’s have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” And you, O men, brothers, who profess the warfare of Christ, who have voluntarily sworn yourselves to the law of monastic life, who have promised to imitate the footsteps of the Savior: consider your calling, so that you may walk carefully, not like fools who are driven by every wind, but as true lovers of Jesus Christ, who by the spirit have put to death the deeds of the flesh. You, I say, my most beloved fellow-soldiers, always keep watch in good works, mortifying for the love of Christ our bodies which are upon the earth, constant in fasts and prayers, and continually occupied in meditation on the divine Scriptures. Always stretch yourselves forward to what lies ahead; every day renew with fresh zeal the fervor of your holy purpose. Flee idleness and all sloth, and diligently consider how brief is the time of this life. Let the brief and moderate labor of the hard contest not frighten you; let the wickedness of the enemy not make you fainthearted, since every labor is quickly overcome by voluntary endurance, and the devil, however savagely he rages, is overcome as soon as you call upon Christ. Remember the words of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, saying in the holy Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” But what, my brothers, is our cross except a life of temptation [unclear]

    Homily XI. Folio xxv.

    Let him think that he has spent that day uselessly on which he has not sent ahead some good work for which he may expect reward. Let the good monk strive at all times to cultivate the field of his heart, and, so far as he can, utterly root out all the thorns and briars of evil affections. Let him learn to love the Lord Jesus above all things with a pure mind, and to keep most diligently whatever he commanded. Let him sow in tears of devotion and constancy what he may reap with all the saints in exultation. Let not the continual difficulty of labor frighten his mind; let not the hard struggle of the flesh break his spirit, since he who labors little gathers little fruit at harvest, and he who now sows much in tears for love of Christ brings back on that day a most abundant fruit. For this, brothers, is the appointed end of our journey which we undertake in the present pilgrimage: that, purified by continual exercise in labors and adversities, we may go forth from here clean and pure to our homeland.

    On fleeing the company of the wicked: Homily eleven.

    [unclear] The company of the wicked has drawn many back from the way of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; therefore, my most beloved brothers, we do not cease to admonish you to walk in the way of the Lord with the good and holy, so that by their instruction and example you may daily become better. For, as the blessed apostle of Christ says, imitating a senarius of a certain Greek, Menander: evil conversations corrupt good morals. He does not truly desire to be good whom the conduct of the wicked delights. Remember [unclear]. No one speaks wicked things unless he is first found corrupt and depraved in his own heart against the purity of the evangelical tradition. As each person is, and as are the things he turns over and performs in the secrecy of his heart by reflection and thought, so such speech more often proceeds from his mouth. For the speech of one who speaks is the truest witness of the heart, as our Lord and Savior says in the holy Gospel, that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. For a good man brings forth good things from the treasure of his heart, and an evil man likewise brings forth evil things.

    Since, therefore, he who speaks evil is not good, we must beware of all who use depraved, scurrilous, and pernicious speech; in their talk certain shameful things frequently resound, while words of holiness are either never or very rarely heard. Foul speech is the sign of an immodest heart, even if deeds do not follow. Therefore you, my dearest brothers, who have promised, according to the rule and statutes of the holy fathers of the Church, not only to preserve chastity and every kind of modesty in deed until death, by both implicit and explicit profession, but also ought to be far removed from every unclean thought: flee the company of wicked men and the assemblies of the malicious, and at all times avoid those who speak unjust, foul, or idle things. Remember the Scripture which says: He who touches pitch will be defiled by it, and he who associates with a proud man will put on pride. Hence holy Pope Gregory says: The weak ought to avoid the society of the wicked, lest the evils which they frequently see and are unable to correct should delight them to imitate. And Saint John the bishop says: If a good man is joined to an evil one, either they are made equal, or they are quickly separated from each other. For friendships either seek equals or make them. Indeed, the nature of things is such that whenever a good man is joined to an evil one, the evil man is not improved by the good, but the good man is contaminated by the evil. For diversity of things can never have concord, and wicked society troubles many.

    There are among you certain brothers, I say it groaning, professors very forgetful of regular discipline: to them the cell is a prison, the choir a siege, prayer nausea, silence punishment, the reading of Scripture weariness. The love of God either never or rarely raises upward the hearts of those whose whole way of life consists in lower things. Whenever I happen to be absent, they immediately gather among themselves, not about Christ, nor about the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, nor about the integrity of regular observance, but they bring forth a long discourse about the vain and useless affairs of this world; and by conversing they involve themselves in tales of kings and wars, matters about which it is not lawful for a monk to think. But whatever I say to these men, whatever I speak, whatever penance I impose

    On fleeing the company of the wicked:

    [to make progress?] those whom evil habit has corrupted from the beginning of their instruction. Nothing, however, is worse than an evil habit. For the monk who, as a novice and a young man, neglects [discipline?] spends all the days of his life in torpor and sloth. For Scripture says: “A young man walking according to his own way, even when he has grown old, will not depart from it.” Therefore I say to you, venerable elders, I beseech you, I admonish you, and by the mercy of God I beg you with what urgency I can: from now on live thus, conduct yourselves thus, walk thus, so that your conduct may agree with the years of old age; and you who have already advanced far into old age, offer an example of holiness for the instruction of the younger men.

    To you, without doubt, is ascribed whatever is found in the conduct of these younger men. For you ought to go before the younger men in all holiness, in word and in deed; you are commanded to display to them an example of all perfection, so that, when they see in you all the works of virtue made perfect, they may be moved, as it were, by a certain impulse of shame, and be stirred to imitate your holiness. For the manners of elders provide the younger with an example of living, as is said in the proverb: “What the old men have sung, the young men have learned.”

    But you younger men, show reverence with humility to the elders, considering their gray hair; and those whom you know to be more fervent in the observance of regular discipline, rejoice to have as teachers by keeping their company. Avoid those who either walk restlessly or observe the purity of regular discipline too negligently. Not all who are called elders are worthy of the imitation of younger men; nor do years make a monk venerable, but conduct established in the love of God with prudence makes him worthy of veneration.

    Therefore, whichever of you, dearest brothers, desires to be a true lover of God, whatever progress he desires to make in the holy monastic way of life that he professes, let him always flee the companionship of undisciplined brothers, and seek fellow-soldiers who agree with his purpose in good. For the prophet says in the psalm: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverted.” For evil company has harmed many; and he who delights to dwell with the reprobate will not be free from the contagion of sin. For everyone who [unclear] with carnal men: out of the abundance of the heart they speak nothing other than vain and carnal things.

    Homily XI. Fol. XXVI.

    For evil conversations corrupt the good morals of young men. All their pursuits are vain, and their words useless, indeed destructive, who, being carnally minded, have not known the exercises of divine love. For truly, just as one diseased sheep gradually corrupts the whole fold, so one slothful and perverse monk in a congregation often becomes the cause of many transgressions. As [unclear] says, a little leaven corrupts the whole mass of flour into which it is mixed with its odor; so young monks and novices who associate with lukewarm and slothful elders are imbued with their evil ways, and never thereafter are reformed to the integrity of holy fervor.

    Therefore I say to you elders: be, by good works and by chaste and always modest speech, a pattern of life for the young, so that whenever they are corrected for their faults they may not defend themselves by the examples of elders. For it is most shameful for elders to be culpable in those things for which younger men are rightly rebuked. Live, I beg you elders, so that in your presence the younger men may presume neither to say nor to do anything that seems reprehensible. Let the wicked fear you as judges, not as men acting the part of patrons, because as many as have sinned by your examples are reckoned to have perished by your instruction.

    Let there not be among you anyone lukewarm or slothful, because desires kill the lazy man, and vanity destroys every idle monk. Let there not be among you a verbose man, a wandering monk, a circumcellion, murmuring and restless, because whoever delights in such things and pursuits both ruins himself by evil work and kills his brother by his examples. Let there not be among you a mocker of the simple, nor a despiser of the humble, nor anyone rash and censorious; because he who is quick to mock will be consumed in his own folly and will not be glorious. He opens his mouth against the humble, always seeks quarrels, and rejoices to be talkative about the deeds of others. He will not prosper in his counsel, and if he has been raised to some honor, he will quickly fall into the depths. His pride is hateful to God, because, though he is foolish and witless, he boasts that he is learned and wise. Soon his foolishness will be laid bare, and a grievous [destruction?] will seize him within.

    On Avoiding the Company of the Depraved.

    ... he kicks against his superiors, never [unclear] a friend by his own judgment. Whomever you see violating the rule of fasting without the elder’s blessing, flee as an enemy of salvation; and [flee] the man who by talkativeness, [unclear] when there is no cause, overturns peace and stirs up quarrels. Flee a rebellious monk, disobedient to his elders, as from the face of a snake, because, filled with the poison of malice, he seethes, and in the pride of his mind has lost his soul. He who does not obey the elder’s command is perverse; and he who, when corrected, is not humbled is an apostate. Let not one who disparages his brother and speaks against him be in conversation with you, for he is far worse than a thief. Him whom you have seen wholly zealous in regular observance you shall love as a father and venerate as a most loving teacher. You may confidently make use of the familiarity of him whose friendship always makes you better in the love of God. Imitate good men with all zeal, and follow the habits of those who live in conformity with monastic perfection. Have as a friend a brother of good will; but from him who is hard-hearted turn away your ears. He who is light-minded and dissolute in morals should be to you like a man who destroys a hedge in a field. Do not be the companion of one who despises the Rule and silence, who does not distinguish places or times, who without the prior’s blessing multiplies words everywhere. Avoid as fuel of lust and a spring of all vices the monk given to wine and drink, who too often exceeds the monastery’s canonical measure. A monk who, by the counsel of his own head, strives against the elder’s command is near perdition, and hastens breathlessly into danger for his soul. Do not share in the works of a stubborn monk, and do not have the friendship of one who, with his own rashness, laughing, speaks against his superiors [unclear]. Be continually in the midst of the disciplined, and let your soul gladly walk with the humble. For he who joins himself to [unclear] men will never be exalted. He who raises his voice in speaking and cries aloud, [unclear] of voice, cannot hide the folly of his heart, and he will glory in his vanity.

    The friendship of good men is the firm salvation of the soul, and in the company of the depraved the innocence of the simple is corrupted. The best company is that of those whose fear of God has confirmed examples of good works. Nothing is more precious than a friend who fears God, and nothing more dangerous than a companion who is of depraved will. A brother who fears God with his whole heart will be a wall of strength for his friend; and he who is joined in soundness of mind with such a one is sanctified at all times by the blessing of the Spirit of God. He who walks in the midst of those who fear God is upheld as though by a very strong wall round about him, so that he may not fail. From his words the servant of the Most High will be known, and works of holiness mark out the good monk. No foul, scurrilous, or idle word comes forth from the mouth of one who fears the Lord; and he who is a true lover of Jesus does nothing that offends goodness. In the mouth of a monk who loves God, Christ always resounds; and he who is a true worshipper of God displays the speech of righteousness both in his mouth and in his work. He who fears God is the best counselor, and he who walks according to the canon is a prudent judge of thoughts.

    An elder who fears God and has been proved and experienced for a long time in regular observance is the director of youths; and he who has no stain on his garment knows how to be a good instructor of novices. He who is an understanding teacher and expositor of the divine Scriptures, keeping his soul in humility: gladly receive all the words of his mouth as though they were golden, because they have [unclear] and the solidity of future eternal happiness. He who is truly learned has compassion on the weak; and he who loves Jesus encourages the man wavering in soul toward strength. He who walks with a talkative man will not escape contention; and he who delights in lying will never be a friend of wisdom. He who is constantly occupied with external things will not be making progress, and glories without cause that he is a monk. The purpose of holiness is quickly corrupted when a monk wanders too frequently outside his cell with desire. He who abandons the secrecy of his cell without the elder’s command does not strive toward the perfection of the holy purpose. Beautiful is the company of good men who fear God, and he who has become accustomed to dwell with them will not experience confusion. The heart of a young monk is a clean tablet, upon which the conduct of elders is inscribed, never to be erased. The worst writer upon a beautiful heart is the elder who either does or says shameful things before a youth. He who infects the minds of youths with rash speech is like impious Herod, who

    All twelve.

    ... killed boys. The evil that a young man receives from a foolish and negligent old man, even when made a priest he will not amend. Every vessel that is filled with vinegar is spoiled; and a monk who is neglected in the novitiate, when he grows old, is not amended. Cursed is the old man by whose evil conduct young men perish, since one who has left bad footprints for those who follow is like one who with his own hand has cast a blind man headlong into a pit. Before the inward judge, each man is worthy of as many deaths as the innocents who have perished through his depraved example.

    Young man, seek an old man as the guide of your life: not one who has completed many years in his lax and lukewarm conduct, but one whom the fear of the Lord and knowledge of the divine Scriptures commend. Better is the company of a young monk who fears the Lord than the fellowship of an old teacher whose life does not have the light of divine love and of intact regular observance. An old man disordered in his morals, lacking cleanness of mind and devoid of discipline, is like one injured in the shin, led lame to the grave. An old and lax monk is like a foolish man who, not knowing the end, is seized with robbers at a drinking banquet. An elder without maturity is like a little pipe of elderwood crushed under the feet of those at play.

    Vainly does he boast that he has been a monk for many days, who has not perceived the beginning of inward conduct. He who loves the cleanness of his heart keeps himself at all times from the company of undisciplined brothers. As a stain of pitch clinging to the garments of those dancing saddens virgins, so a good young man blushes at the foul words of elders. Wanton speech is not that of a man who fears God, since from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; and he who utters foul words is not clean before the Most High. If sinners begin to hate you because of the fear of God, do not be saddened, because unless you displease the wicked you will not attain the perfection of the good. For to displease the wicked because of justice is praiseworthy, and a manifest indication of divine love. If you love your soul, flee the counsels of the undisciplined, and do not have fellowship with mockers. Walk with the good, and let him who fears the Lord be your counselor.

    On monks sent on the road. Homily 12

    Folio 27.

    It belongs to monks to flee the world and, for love of solitude, to avoid crowds of people at all times as far as they can. A monk is so called from solitude, just as one is named from unity. He cannot be a monk who seeks the throng of peoples; and he who delights in cities has not yet tasted monastic sweetness. If you are a monk, you must not leave the solitude of the monastery without reasonable cause; and you who are bound to silence must not take delight in the conversations of worldly people.

    Whoever loves wandering courses in the city has abandoned his conscience; and he who is often outside his monastery does not keep the purity of inward progress. He who goes about the houses of his parents and delights in the feasts of his neighbors does not regard himself as a monk; and he who goes to the banquets of drinkers kills his soul. He who sleeps in the house of his kinsman seeks comfort; and he who avoids the assemblies of religious men follows a pernicious liberty. A monk in the house of his father and mother is like a lamb in the midst of wolves, and like a hare surrounded by the hounds of hunters.

    If you are a monk, if a servant and soldier of God, what are you doing in the house of your parents? Or what are you seeking in the midst of peoples? A monk remaining long outside the monastery among secular people is like a man who has buried his only-begotten son beneath the depth of waters. For just as there is no life for fish on dry land, so there is no salvation of soul for monks in the world. Outside the river the fish dies; and the purity of a monk’s conscience is quickly defiled outside the monastery. The life of monks is in the monastery, and the death of souls in the midst of secular affairs.

    It is a great virtue of the soul to flee the crowds of men, or, if it is altogether necessary to be among them, nevertheless to withdraw in mind. We are sometimes compelled by necessity to make a journey through the world; but the purity of conscience is so much the less polluted by meeting people, the less the desire of the mind is drawn away from the secrecy of the cell. Therefore every good monk among us must be warned that, whenever by command of his superior he is sent on the road because of the necessity of some matter, he should never wander abroad in mind.

    He who does not guard the senses is quickly corrupted when evil is set before him; and he who casts away the fear of the Lord returns to the monastery impure, neces-

    Concerning monks directed onto the road.

    [unclear] will return. When the [stream?] flows out, by its muddiness it stains the beauty of the meadows lying open round about; and when a monk gives attention to the tales of secular people, he defiles the purity of his conscience. Therefore, before you set your foot outside the monastery, fortify yourself with holy prayers; and before you go out, do not neglect to commend the road to the Lord with prayers. Then carry out what the lawgiver commanded, and entrust yourself to be protected by the prayers both of the abbot and of all the brothers.

    Prescribe for yourself the canon of the strictness of regular observance, under the steady remembrance of which you may guard your mind from every [unclear] of vanities that meet you. Do not go anywhere out of the monastery without the abbot's blessing, because, since you ought to be dead and buried to this world, it will no longer be lawful for you to do anything without the command of your superior. Recognize yourself as a soldier of King Jesus Christ; let your [unclear] be governed by command. For the monk who goes anywhere out of the monastery without the abbot's permission is like a little sheep in the darkness, which [unclear] is burned up in a house fire.

    But the true monk of Christ, even when he is outside the monastery in body, remains in the cloister of the mind; and he is no less alone with many than he has been accustomed to be solitary in his cell. The lover of Christ thinks of Jesus even in the midst of a crowd; and he who is a true worker of virtues keeps his heart firm in the fear of God in every place. For even if in body he is not in the monastery, nevertheless through the vigor of his mind he always stands steadfast, as if alone in the cloister. The spirit is not polluted by the body's movement, when the solitude of the mind is preserved.

    You must live on the road, O monk, with the same holiness with which you are commanded to conduct yourself in the monastery, and you must walk with a certain greater caution, lest you scandalize anyone by a more lax example, where there seem to be as many judges of monks as there are observers present. The eyes of all secular people look up to monks, and they look in their works for the holiness which they hear them profess. A monk gives more offense by one reckless word than a man given to the world does by ten thousand. For however frivolous and buffoonish a worldly man may seem, nevertheless he has not learned to tolerate calmly the insolence of monks, since with rustic simplicity he believes all cloistered men to be not as they are, but as they ought to be. Hence among them an evil word or deed is charged to a monk for condemnation, whereas it is imputed to a worldly man for pardon.

    And not without reason. For a monk who has professed the holy and approved canon is bound to direct his whole effort toward perfection, and in word and deed to surpass by far the conduct of secular men in all purity of mind and body. For a frivolous or idle word which is granted to secular people for pardon is judged for cloistered men to be destruction.

    Gold is more precious than all metals and is more greatly desired by mortals; and in nothing is a stain or corruption of falsity more quickly detected. And a defect which is discerned in gold with judicial severity is overlooked in the other metals because of the baseness of their nature. Gold delights the eyes with its beauty, and strengthens the innermost parts of life by its virtue. Gold, fused in the fire, is not diminished; and a true monk of God is not changed from the purpose of holiness in the tribulation of persecution. A small stain on a golden vessel greatly displeases in the sight of a powerful man; if an earthen vessel is crooked, no one detests it. When a monk offends in small things, a great outcry of many arises against him, because his way of life is compared to gold. The canonical life of monks is a golden mirror. Gold in the midst of mud receives no stain upon its nature, but preserves all its beauty inviolate.

    So too the true lover of Christ, such as he has learned to conduct himself in the secrecy of his little cell, such also he stands among men when directed onto the road, because he walks pure in mind as well as body before the Lord. For if he is a true monk, he is not polluted by the dust of another's way of life, nor is he changed from the rectitude of his holy purpose by anyone's presence or conversation. Amid the tumultuous talk of worldly people he thinks elsewhere, and the dissolute conduct of others does not delight his mind. He who is single in heart is not divided even in the midst of those making an uproar. Therefore, monk, you who desire to be good, gather your mind back to yourself, and before you leave your cell for the journey, dispose your heart. Let the fear of the Lord always be the companion of your road

    All XII.

    and let the keeping of monastic discipline never depart from your side. Fence your ears with the memory of the last things, lest hearing vain speech pollute the integrity of your mind. Humbly cast your eyes down to the earth, lest they look up at what it is not fitting for a servant of God to desire. Do not take part in the conversations of carnal men; if you have sought to avoid their presence, take care not to lend them your mind. Even in the midst of ribald men, do not transgress your rule, and do not abandon your accustomed maturity. Do not fear insults and the reproaches of [unclear], and let your heart not be troubled by the words of dark men. The preservation of monastic discipline is righteousness; and those who despise the simple pursue the innocent with laughter.

    Keep your holy purpose in all things, and the Most High will avenge the injury. Do not say in your heart, “I suffer violence,” nor be ashamed at the words of those who deride you. The glory of a monk is to endure insult, and the crown of beauty is to rejoice in reproaches. He who is patient under injuries is stronger than Atlas, and he who is not saddened when mocked is greater than all. If you fix your desire in heaven, nothing on earth will disturb you; and if you are a true monk, your heart will exult at injuries. There is a judge in heaven who knows all things, and there is the Most High God, who cares for all things. He is the just repayer of merits, and he will remember his poor. The more, now in this life, you cast your soul down into the depth of humility for love of him, the more in future glory you will be exalted above the rest. For by patience heaven is climbed, and by humility the kingdom is reached. For Christ himself also had to suffer, and so to enter into his glory.

    A self-indulgent soldier is one who seeks delights while his emperor endures insults and mockeries, and while he hangs on the gibbet of the cross for his army, he himself follows pleasures. A soldier who goes out naked to war without weapons, and a monk who disdains to embrace patience and humility amid insults: the destruction of both is swift. The monk who is a sincere lover of Christ is not angered at injuries, does not threaten those who bring insult, stands fixed in holy purpose, and, however wicked they may be, is not moved.

    Just as timely rain increases the hay in the meadows, so merit grows for the monk from the humble endurance of injuries. Humility is the sinew of all virtues, and constant patience under injuries for the love of God is the mine of good works. Therefore, when you are about to go out on the road from the monastery, prepare your heart for the endurance of injuries, and strengthen your mind against the insolences of those who mock you.
