When scoundrels have shouted after your back, repeating the name of monk, remember Christ mocked and spat upon before the governor, who did not answer a word, but in silence preserved patience. Imitate him as your leader, O monk; always listen to him as your teacher, who was meek and humble of heart. Do not answer a word to those who mock you; do not turn your face backward, but say with the prophet: “Those who sought evils for me spoke vanities, and all day long they meditated deceits. But I, like a deaf man, did not hear; and like a mute man not opening his mouth. And I became like a man who does not hear, and who has no reproofs in his mouth.”

    Christ did this; Jesus taught this; the king of all commanded this. If you wish to be his disciple, you must always be ready for every injury. When set upon a journey, do not neglect to say your canonical prayers with what devotion you can, and always turn over something good with yourself in your mind, either by praying or by meditating. [The Lord’s eye?] goes with you, and his holy angels accompany you as you walk. And therefore preserve a clean heart in all things, lest you offend the majesty of such great companions. The Lord is wholly eye and ear; from his knowledge nothing is hidden. Apply constant guard to your words, and let deliberation of the heart precede every word of the mouth, so that you speak nothing at all for which you could repent. The mouth of a monk will speak both few and reasonable things, and his lips never exceed in speech. His whole conduct is set toward the edification of his neighbors; and he who teaches very many by his morals, even when silent, speaks useful things. He who is a true lover of God walks most humbly on the road, and he who fears the Most High restrains his mouth from loud laughter. In your whole life, think of yourself as mortal, and live as one dying, as one who is already breathing out his last breath. Happy is the kingdom, and rich before God the province, in which monks rise [by night?], since where there is no fear of God the theaters are filled with cloistered men. The monk on the road

    Concerning monks sent on the road.

    He who has God as his friend easily disdains human familiarity; and he who speaks with angels takes very little delight in the conversations of mortals. Whenever on the road you see a sign of the Lord's Passion or of the Crucified One, do not pass by unless you say: I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, for the pain of your wounds, for the shedding of your most holy blood, and for your most innocent death, which you endured for us on the altar of the cross; and I beseech you, by your bitter Passion, have mercy on me now and in the dread hour of my death. Repeat this very short prayer often as you go, and never pass by an image of the Crucified One unless you have given thanks to the Savior.

    Do not quarrel with the man who walks with you on the road, lest, having returned to the monastery, he falsely say some evil thing against you. He who provokes his companion on a journey to impatience is like one who drives a rabid dog to barking with a blow. The wicked man is overcome by gentleness, and he who is humble of heart calms one stirred up in mind. Among secular men do not pour forth speech, lest perhaps they take occasion to mock you.

    We permit [unclear] to speak good things among young men; but let the one who is lower in rank listen to [unclear]. The weary ploughman hastens to rest; and the monk, sound in mind, hastening by byways, returns with longing to his cell. Let the word be held in the mouth until reason brings forth the judgment of equity; and speech that can instruct its hearers should not be hidden.

    Do not trust the songs of flatterers, for when they have [unclear] the innocent man, they soothe ears with disordered speeches. A monk who is nourished on contentions is like [unclear], and like a man afflicted with spasms who stirs up quarrels under the name of religion. Do not presume to speak before the learned, lest perhaps, when you do not understand the parable, you be laughed at by those standing around. He who recognizes himself as a monk does not use profound speech; and he who teaches little ones makes questions plain.

    When you go to men unlike your profession, do not boast in anything; but if you are questioned, answer humbly in few words. When set on a journey, always think of God, and regard reverence for your senior as your companion. Do absolutely nothing that you would wish not to be known to him; for, as the holy [unclear] says

    Homily XII.

    The servant of Christ is believed to act in Christ's stead in the monastery, and therefore he is deservedly honored by all. Live, then, as though you always had him present before your eyes; and whatever you would not presume to do or say with him looking on, do not attempt in any way when he is absent. For it is a foolish consolation, when conscience is gnawing with guilt, for a sin to be hidden from men and for one who knows himself to be sick unto death to flee the judgment of his shepherd. A monk who does evil and wants it to be hidden from his prelate has violated the integrity of the monastic rule and has gravely sinned against the fifth degree of humility. For thus it commands: The fifth degree of humility is this: if he has not concealed from his abbot, by humble confession, all evil thoughts coming into his heart and evil deeds done by him in secret.

    These are the admonitions of father Benedict; these are the holy teachings of monastic instruction. If you, monk, despise or neglect them, you will be shown to be unmindful of your own salvation. It is a sure sign of humility if a monk has not refused to open his heart to his senior, and wants none of the evils he has committed to be hidden from his shepherd. He who confesses his offense with humility will be strengthened against the adversary of his salvation; and he who hides his thoughts will advance into evil. For there is no evil thought so small that it will not gradually grow if neglected, and no vice so slight that it will not gain strength if it is dissembled.

    Therefore evil thoughts must be repelled at once from the beginning, because when a depraved thought is not immediately extinguished it gives birth to delight; delight, repeated, gives rise to consent; consent to habit; habit to necessity; necessity then brings in despair; despair, contempt; contempt, obstinacy; and obstinacy gives birth to the eternal death of the soul. For Scripture says: When the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises. Is not your abbot, O monk, the shepherd and physician of your soul? Am I not, my dearest brothers, after God, the one who feeds your mortal bodies with necessary nourishment? Am I not compelled to minister to you the word of salvation? If you, the sheep, flee the shepherd, what pastures of the spirit do you expect from us? The sick man who flees the physician despises his own salvation and willingly kills his own soul.

    A monk, therefore, walking in the way of wickedness and turning aside from the paths of justice, is near to death; and he slips so much the more into the depth of vices as he reverences less the judgment of the one correcting him. But he is truly a monk who guards his soul from every iniquity and does absolutely nothing that he would wish his shepherd not to know. He who conceals his way is not pure, and he who flees the presence of the judge increases suspicion. Like a sheep you walk in the desert, to be snatched by the wolf, negligent and impure monk, who withdraws himself from the knowledge of his shepherd and is devoured by demons. A sick sheep running to destruction, and a monk hiding every sin: there is no salvation for them unless they return to the physician.

    Monks returning from a journey should immediately, on that very day, according to the monastic rule, prostrate themselves before the sight of all the brothers, so that whatever has been committed on the way through negligence may be expiated by the prayers of the community. For the common prayer of many avails much for washing away sins, if it has been poured out to the Lord with the fervor of devotion.

    Here ends Homily XII, On monks sent on a journey.

    On the daily expiation of sins.

    Homily XIV.

    Since for a long time in this corruptible life we are established, dearest brothers, we offend daily in many things; and however holily we may seem to conduct ourselves

    On the Daily Expiation of Sins.

    We are not without sin. For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and an earthly dwelling depresses the understanding that thinks on many things. For Scripture says: “There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin.” The blessed evangelist John also says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Indeed, through intercourse with the flesh the soul, excessively delighted, sins, and its strength is diminished by [unclear] of the spirit. For the mind is deceived by the presentation of sensible things, and readiness to do wrong is strengthened by long habit. The weakness of the flesh weakens the fervor of the spirit, and the frailty of the will resists the holy purpose of the mind. Hence Solomon, the most wise king, says in the book of Proverbs: “Seven times in a day the righteous man will fall and will rise again; but the wicked will fall into evil.” By the testimony of this saying we are warned not to grow lukewarm in the purpose of holiness, even if it should happen that we have fallen seven times in a day. As often, O monk, as you have fallen through sin from the purpose of holiness, so often rise again to repentance, thereafter never to return. But however often people have fallen, they can always rise again to repentance and obtain by tears and prayers the grace of God which they had lost by sinning. For the heart of man is flexible; it can be moved in either direction, because never can a man in the flesh become so evil, if he makes use of the grace of the Lord. Since these things are so, my brothers, you will have to be warned by my exhortation today to walk carefully, so that he who, with conscience as witness, already walks in the paths of righteousness may persevere in it by advancing daily, and that he who understands himself to be guilty before the Lord may amend his life as quickly as possible. If human frailty daily drives you on, or, to speak more properly, hurls you down and makes you do wrong, let the love of God and of your own salvation also stir you daily humbly to expiate your fault through true contrition. For thus the righteous man falls seven times in a day and rises again, because, even if he slips through human frailty, yet, persevering always in the purpose of holiness, he is strengthened more and more in mind in the love of God. For, keeping his conscience free from grave sins, he is unwillingly polluted by daily negligences; and when he sees that he cannot live without faults, recognizing his weakness humbly, he groans the more deeply. But if he should also have been overtaken by a graver offense, he soon rises again to amendment through repentance. Therefore the ancient governors of monastic discipline, considering the condition of human frailty, established various kinds of expiation, by which both monks of good will might daily advance toward the better, and the wicked might be compelled to the observance of the regular life. For in the Rule the holy father Benedict gives this command, saying: “With all solicitude let the abbot take care concerning delinquent brothers, because it is not the healthy who have need of a physician, but those who are ill.” For this reason the first leaders of regular observance, with provident consideration, established that every day after Prime, in an appointed place, a chapter of faults should be held, in which, with the abbot or prior presiding, the actions of all the brothers are brought into the open with equal discussion. This place, my brothers, bears the figure of the purgatory of souls, since here not only are past sins expiated, but we are also fortified against future ones. For in this place, which we call the chapter room, whatever wrongs you have committed openly are corrected and expiated through salutary repentance. Here daily, as the paraphrast pronounces it, you learn your monastic law, according to whose integrity you have promised to live; here every day you hear the exhortatory word of salvation; here you listen as the victories of Christ’s martyrs and their many sufferings for the orthodox faith are briefly recited. This is the school of monks, necessary for the consideration of regular discipline, in which everything is learned that is commanded to be observed by those in the cloister. There are two things, my most beloved brothers, which this place requires of you: the one, that in correction [you be] always humble

    Homily XIII. Folio XXX.

    hold patience; and the other, that you willingly receive our exhortation, such as it is. For the first, our holy lawgivers, desiring you to be prepared, command that the brave deeds of the martyrs, whose imitators you ought to become, be read; and then, that you may be teachable in mind, they ordered [unclear] to be subjected to regular discipline. Thus, too, that you may be brave and patient, in imitation of the holy martyrs, under necessary rebukes, the account of their passion is read here in your ears, so that, your minds having been prepared for saving doctrine, a reading from the Rule which you profess may be recited to you at the same time. The holy martyrs of Christ encourage you by their example to patience; and blessed Benedict admonishes you by his teaching that you also be ready for injury.

    Therefore let none of you, most beloved brothers, refuse in this place humbly to receive penance every day for his negligences; let no one disdain it. This place is the public one for expiating sin, in which the severity of judgment is so tempered that the kindness of discretion is not violated. For I wish to be the physician of your souls, not their destroyer. Therefore approach the examination of our judgment without fear, so that, when accused concerning negligences committed openly, you may humbly proclaim them. I am unwilling to burden you beyond the Rule, so as to transfer the most secret offenses of conscience from sacramental confession to the public examination of the one accused, which we know certain persons have done, to the grave detriment of the souls of their subjects. For thus says our teacher Benedict in the Rule: “But if the cause of the sin has lain hidden in the soul, let him disclose it only to the abbot or to spiritual elders, who know how to heal their own wounds and those of others, and not to uncover or make them public.”

    There are two places in the monastery for the expiation of sin: one for those things that are manifest, and the other for those that are hidden. For manifest sins are to be expiated publicly before all in the daily proclamation of faults; but hidden sins, and those whose manifestation would scandalize the weak, are to be referred to confession. For when sin is manifest it must also be punished publicly; and he who has offended in secret must also be corrected in secret. There are certain rulers of cloistered persons who [bring] the hidden sins of their subjects to public examination

    On the daily expiation of sins

    To endure. For we must make satisfaction for our sins; but if we neglect to do this in this life, in the life to come we shall necessarily do it under compulsion. There are among you some who take corrections badly; to them we announce [unclear], since it is necessary that in the future they endure very grievous things, those who here refuse to endure small and light ones. But I, considering their weakness and ignorance, am grievously tormented within myself, because I see their minds wounded and yet I am afraid to apply the necessary medicines. For if I apply remedies suited to their ailments, I fear that, becoming fainthearted, they may fall into despair; or certainly, given over to a reprobate sense, they may withdraw entirely from their holy purpose. Therefore I use as much discretion as I can, as all of you will bear me witness, preferring to send the weak, through patience with charity, to purgatory, rather than through [just?] severity to have them descend in despair to hell.

    For who in this mortal life has ever been able to make satisfaction for sins, who has applied the good will of penance? For good will alone commends the works of penitents. But since many are punished unwillingly, they are still far removed from perfect satisfaction. Believe me, my dearest brothers, that satisfaction for sins is commended more by suffering than by doing. For so our Lord and Savior himself, Jesus Christ, expiated the sin of the whole world by suffering on the altar of the cross. Would that you knew what an effective medicine it is for a soul befouled by sins to receive proclamations and corrections with humble patience, and also, for the increase of perfect satisfaction, to bear injuries and insults with equanimity. I am certain that humble patience in adversity far surpasses every kind of satisfaction; and the readier the mind has been to bear insults and injuries for the love of Christ, the more easily and quickly it will obtain from the Lord pardon for all its sins and a fuller indulgence.

    For this place in which we now speak is the workshop of purgation and expiation, in which zeal for regular discipline holds chief place, discretion presides over examination, and charity directs and completes all things. Therefore in this very place patience is very necessary for you; without its presence no satisfaction will be consummated. Whatever monk is a zealous lover of his salvation and loves this place and workshop of expiation never goes forth from it without having been made better than himself. For this place is to be feared by demons and is terrible to them, but dear and greatly venerable to the holy angels of God; in it the fault of humble monks is washed away, and whatever is committed openly is also expiated publicly before all. But if any guilt of hidden fault has been committed by anyone, the secret confession of the penitent will likewise purge it away. In both cases pure confession with humility is required, and both here and there patience is declared necessary for you.

    Therefore, whoever you are, monk, who desire to be good, prepare your soul in all patience, so that both in adversity and in prosperity you may keep the tranquility of your mind most constant. When you have been proclaimed by some fellow-brother for your negligences, bear it patiently with all humility, faithfully bringing to memory how innocently the Son of God was accused for you. For if that just and innocent one, who committed no sin, suffered insults, why should you not patiently bear rebukes from a senior, you who offend daily in many things? He most patiently endured innumerable injuries for your salvation; and why should you not, for your sins, humbly and patiently endure brief and few admonitions? For if you are justly proclaimed in judgment, and are blamed for fault, you must necessarily be patient, since you yourself have deserved what you suffer; and the humble toleration of rebukes will be imputed to you as satisfaction for sins. But if you did not deserve the proclamation in judgment, nevertheless bear it patiently for the love of Christ; now it will be reckoned to you not only as satisfaction for preceding sins, but much more as justification. Therefore whether a monk is proclaimed justly or unjustly, he has no just cause for defense, because if he has sinned, he suffers according to his deserts; but if he is innocent, he is the more bound to patience. For no one unless patient and humble will be able to imitate Christ; but since a monk of Christ is especially bound to be his disciple and imitator, it is most fitting for him to be patient. Without

    All Things. XIII.

    By sword and fire a monk can be a martyr, if for the love of God he has preserved true patience everywhere in his soul. For the true monk is neither puffed up by praises nor saddened by reproach; he shows himself patient under injuries; in the face of insults and reproaches he is glad and humbly keeps silence. No one is stronger than the patient man, who knows how to conquer himself and humbly to endure any adversities whatever, for the love of God, with a tranquil mind. But every impatient man is proud and arrogant, since he does not follow Jesus, the teacher of humility, and therefore he is indignant at the just rebukes that he has deserved. As the furnace tests gold, so insults and injuries test the monk, whether he truly loves Christ. Humility and patience in adversity are the true marks of monks; whoever is not clothed with their adornment boasts of the name in vain. He who is not humble cannot truly be a monk; and he who does not preserve patience in adversities cannot be a true disciple of Christ. Hence King Solomon said in the Book of Proverbs: “A patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than a conqueror of cities.” For a man’s teaching is discerned through patience, and his glory is to pass over wrongs. The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests just men. A monk who follows Christ in truth is patient under all injuries; and he who is not forgetful, but a mindful meditator on the Lord’s Passion, exults and rejoices in his soul at insults. For all, as holy [Christophilus?] says, who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution, and whatever evil befalls them they overcome with the greatest constancy. And although patience is necessary for a monk in every place and time, nevertheless in the daily examination of faults it must be guarded more diligently with especial attention, where the correction of morals is in question, and whatever has been committed in each person against the norm of monastic purity is amended by the senior. Therefore before we enter this place in the morning, all things must be considered, and the mind must be strengthened against those things that can happen, so that if perhaps a rather harsh rebuke occurs, it may not overthrow the mind from the state of tranquillity. For even if we have resolved never to offer insult or do injury to any of you, we do not deny that it can happen that whoever weighs our fatherly correction by the words rather than by the intention may think himself rebuked beyond what he deserves. As God knows, in all things we seek your salvation and nothing else; to cut away vices by the root, according to the statutes of our religion, and not to harm anyone, is what we sincerely intend. We cannot please all men in all things; but we are especially compelled to displease those who, sinning daily against the canon, promise themselves impunity for their crimes. Of them King Solomon said: “Evil instruction belongs to those who abandon the way of life, and he who hates rebukes will die.” The pestilent man does not love him who rebukes him, nor does he go to the wise. He who deliberately does evil flees the light and hates correction, because he is a fool; but he who is sensible in mind will give thanks to his corrector. Therefore in this matter I do not fear the hateful murmurings of subjects, knowing that I have undertaken the care of sick sheep, to whom, whether they wish it or not, I am bound to apply the remedies of salvation. If it were possible, brothers, I would most earnestly wish not to disturb any of you in anything, even slightly, but to live among you with the greatest tranquillity, and cheerfully to serve the Lord our God in peace of mind and body. But because not all of you seek in truth the things that are God’s, I must rebuke and sometimes disturb the restless, lest impunity for small crimes give boldness for greater ones. For I know what necessity of danger I undergo through the care of pastoral office, and therefore I neither can nor ought to be silent for you, [unclear] by the danger of your sins. We ask you by our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us, that for the love of God, for the remission of your sins, you sustain our fatherly and necessary rebukes at all times patiently and with true humility. Let each one think within himself that there is no day on which he does well and does not offend in something; and let him know that in a short time he will receive the reward of his works: good things for good, and likewise evil things for evil. Therefore let him strive, as much as he can, in this life to make satisfaction for his offenses

    On the daily expiation of sins.

    [unclear]: and humbly to expiate all their iniquities by the daily chastisement of the body. Know, my brothers, that there is no sin so small that the justice of almighty God leaves it unpunished. Therefore, since there is none of us who has not offended in many things, arm yourselves, I beg you, with patience and humility, so that whenever you are corrected for sins, you may endure it with all gentleness. For in this time of freedom of choice you can, with a small expiation, make satisfaction for many debts, whereas after death in purgatory the soul will be tormented for a long time and most grievously even for small ones.

    Indeed, voluntary satisfaction avails greatly; but what is done from necessity earns less toward grace. Altogether, brothers, it is fitting and necessary for the soul to be purged of fault, if it is to reign in heaven and rejoice with Christ. But the soul that has neglected the purgation of its faults in the present life will be punished more heavily in the life to come. Let none of you say, my dearest brothers, what many ignorant people are accustomed to say: “It is enough for me, if my soul shall have reached the punishments of purgatory.” Believe me, brothers: whoever has said this word from the heart does not weigh what purgatory will be. For he does not know what he asks who desires purgatory.

    Just as he is foolish who, when he could pay his debt as a free man, scorns to do so and willingly goes to prison, so he is deservedly to be judged the most foolish of all men who, when he can make satisfaction to God for his sins in this life, postpones it to the future. The repentance of this life is fruitful, and voluntary satisfaction is also very meritorious; but after death there will be no place for repentance, but then each person will receive according as he has done in his body, whether good or evil. Think on these things, brothers, while you live in health, lest, forestalled by the command of death, you at last grieve too late. Let today’s salvation not wait for a doubtful tomorrow; and he who can, with grace and in freedom, pay his debt, should not allow himself to be dragged to prison with torture.

    As much as each person can throughout his whole life, so much let him take care to make satisfaction for sins, since the spirit returns securely to the Lord when, while still existing in the body, it is daily purged by the fire of divine love. Here you have a place in which the daily expiation of public offenses is carried out; if you hold true and humble patience in your mind, without doubt you will obtain certain remission of them all. As for secret and hidden faults, not only does the Rule admonish you what you ought to do, but daily sacramental confession also instructs you in all things. For at the altar we are each accustomed daily to offer devoutly the Son of God; and none of us approaches that most holy mystery unless he has first confessed according to custom, since the highest purity is required where the salvation of the whole world is renewed through the Mass.

    Amid these things, most beloved brothers, who among us would not daily make progress in the love of God, unless he shamefully and utterly laid aside every desire for progress? For I dare to say that the monk who does not make progress in this holy congregation is proved to have utterly forgotten his own salvation. Believe me, brothers: God will save no one unwillingly. If you neglect your own progress, it will be imputed not to him but to you. For God is the intellectual light that enlightens every man coming into this world, as John, soaring aloft, says; but those who do not receive the light necessarily remain in darkness. He who turns his mind away from the faith that is in the Son of God remains in darkness; and for him who does not do the works of light, faith will profit nothing toward salvation.

    Outside the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ there is no salvation, and he who thinks otherwise is not a Christian. Do not let the consideration of foolish piety seduce you, O man, so that you believe [unclear] outside the Christian faith; there is no salvation for anyone unto eternal life. For Christ, the only Son of God, is the sole Savior of the world; whoever does not believe in him, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he will be condemned with the devil. But you, my brothers, who now believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, I beg you, live hereafter in such a way that, Christians in name and deed, you may be able to come to his fellowship: he who lives and reigns with God the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever.

    On true repentance.

    Homily XIII. Folio XXXII. Of monks. Homily XIV.

    Although our whole way of life, my dearest brothers, may rightly be called penance, since we seem both dead to ourselves and already buried to the world, yet because we are surrounded by mortal flesh and sojourn in the midst of a sinful nation, it cannot happen that, by the impulse of our own frailty, we do not daily offend in some matter. For the expiation of this, satisfaction must be made by doing penance not only generally but also specifically. For penance is necessary for all mortals, by which they both lament the evils they have committed, with the intention of amendment, and thereafter resolve, so far as can be done, to live without sin.

    It is proper to monks to do penance without interruption, and continually to pray both for their own sins and for those of others. For the monk does not have the office of teaching, as Saint Jerome says, but plainly that of mourning: either, if he is weak, he mourns himself, or, if perfect, the world, and in fear awaits the coming of the Lord. If you are a perfect monk, do penance for the sins of others; but if you are weak, it is right that you repent the more for your own. Therefore the monk must always do penance, for he is appointed before God as intercessor not only for his own sins but also for the offenses of others.

    But who among you, brothers, is not weighed down by his own offense? Who, I ask, among you does not need penance? I see you offend daily in many things, and I grieve; I perceive how you neglect penance for past things, and I tremble. Do you not recognize that you are mortal? And why do you not make satisfaction for the name of monk, by doing the penance necessary in time? Remember, I beg you, the threatening Scripture, which says: Do not delay to be converted to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you. For you will not escape death, which is at the door for all of you; and it lies hidden in ambush for the younger also, but when you least expect it the spirit, compelled from the body, will depart.

    Therefore, if you recognize that you are sinners, if you desire thus to come to the mercy of God, now, I pray, take up penance at once, and amend your conduct in all things according to the purity of the rule. Let it be enough to have neglected true penance up to this point, to have continued for so long a time in a way of life too lukewarm. For God, who overlooks the sins of men on account of penance, has not promised prolongation of life to those who defer repentance. Consider the long-suffering of God, who has mercifully borne with you sinning daily for so long, and do penance, so that you may find the remission you desire.

    For the Lord says through the prophet: I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that he be converted from his evil way and live. Likewise in the holy Gospel he says: Do penance; for the kingdom of heaven will draw near. Penance is a great good for mortals: it cleanses filthy souls and recalls minds from destined destruction. Here blessed Augustine says: Penance heals infirmities and raises the dead; it increases health; it preserves grace. Penance restores movement to the lame, sight to the blind, abundance to the barren, strength to the weak; it drives away vices, adorns virtues, fortifies and strengthens the mind.

    But that is true penance, brothers, which its necessary parts truly commend as a whole: where contrition pierces the mind; where the hidden sin is reported in humble and pure confession; where obedience makes satisfaction according to its powers; where the penitent so grieves over past things that he truly takes care at all times against future ones. True penance is that which love of God adorns with groans and tears, where the sinner grieves more over offense against God than he fears the torment of hell.

    And who of us, most beloved brothers, would not grieve? Who would not groan that he has sinned against the law of monks of the Most High, from whom we have not only life, but also await the promise of eternal happiness? Woe to us, brothers, if in this life we have neglected to do true penance, which, as monks, we ought always to do. Not pleasures, not delights: our way of life ought to be occupied in the crucified Jesus Christ alone, and we ought to keep ourselves estranged from the consolations of the world. The consolations of the world do not befit you, O monk; not laughter, not guffaws, not any consolation of the flesh, but sorrow and bitterness with tears. If you do not give yourself continually to these, you have lost the name of monk. It is not lawful for you to rejoice with the age, you who are dead to the world; nor ought you to seek any comforts of the present life, you who promised the Lord, according to the monastic rule, to serve in solitude. It is yours, monk,

    to despise always and everywhere the joys of this world for the love of God, and not to refuse to undergo any adversities or hardships for the honor of your Savior. For thus the canon admonishes you; thus the monastic institution commands; thus reason necessary for salvation advises. You are commanded to be content with every lowliness and extremity, and always to be [ready?] for all things. But I see very many of you perverting the rule of salvation and living in the monastery otherwise than one ought. Monks now do not fear to seek delights in the monasteries, they who came from the world to conversion poor and beggarly. For the things they could not have outside, now, if they are lacking in the monastery, as though they had suffered the gravest insult, they rebel against humility. Woe to the monks whom not the love of God but want made cloistered, whose god is the belly, and who think of nothing less than poverty. It is not for you, O monks, henceforth to seek in the monastery the delights which the rule commands to be wholly renounced. It befits you to spurn all the pleasures of the present life and to love absolutely nothing in this world except God. For your whole way of life ought always to be given over to divine services, since you promised to live by the spirit and not according to the flesh. No one who is a true monk lives without penance, but whoever truly longs for the feasts of eternal happiness daily chastens his body through abstinence. For it cannot be that a monk enjoy the delights of the present life and the eternal ones; but if he longs for those, he must despise these. For the monk who professes the cenobitic canon is commanded to be a disciple of Christ the Savior; if he desires to please him in truth, he must become his imitator. Thus he says to him in the holy Gospel: He who wishes to be my disciple, let him follow me. And what it is to follow me, John the Apostle, knowing this, teaches in a certain epistle, saying: He who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked. And the Lord himself again says in the Gospel: He who wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And he who loves son or daughter above [unclear] is not worthy of me. Your master has not spoken obscurely, O monk, nor wrapped his meaning in riddles, but has set forth plain speech, by which you can pretend no excuse. For Christ himself is the example and rule of a good and perfect way of life for every Christian, and especially for the monk; if the cloistered man does not follow him with his whole heart in [unclear], he glories in vain in the profession of faith. For just as a Christian is named from Christ, so a disciple is named from imitation of the master. Therefore imitate the master in your conduct, so that you may prove yourself a true disciple of Christ. For the Lord Jesus Christ, whose discipline you profess, O monk, though he was rich, became poor for us; but you, though you are lowly and needy, seek abundance of all things in the school of poverty, and although the teacher commands everything to be despised for love of him, again you desire to possess everything in the monastery. The Lord and your master was obedient to the Father for us even unto the death of the cross; but you, full of pride and impatience, either refuse to obey your superiors for love of him, or you obey unwillingly and with indignation. He, for your salvation, not only endured most patiently throughout his whole life the words and insults of wicked men, but also, for love of you, bore blows and livid wounds and dreadful gashes. Nor did he refuse to undergo the most shameful death, in order to call back your soul from the error of death to the life of eternal light. From the day of his birth he lived in the world poor and humble, and, [unclear], filled with tribulations and reproaches, so that by teaching and benefits he might restore you, a most ruined man, to knowledge and love. For what would we be, if the Son of God had not appeared as man, except utterly ruined? And what are we, if we do not imitate the master according to our strength, except ungrateful? Woe to monks, ungrateful mortals, who contemptuously refuse to follow our Lord and Savior in humility. Let us examine our way of life, brothers, and compare the disciples with the master whose name has been invoked over us, and we shall plainly understand how far we have withdrawn from the paths of our most kindly teacher. But let us return [unclear] with our whole heart, I pray, and do penance, because we have withdrawn far from the way of salvation, serving the flesh rather than the spirit. Let no one deceive himself by the vanity of hope; let no one wait for the last hour of this life as penance, because he cannot sin, for neither does the length of life have certainty

    All things: nor does delaying repentance bring security. He who does not repent while healthy is foolish; and he who does not amend his faults when he can, by the just judgment of God, loses the power that has been deferred. For repentance is then fruitful when, by freedom of choice, it has been voluntary; but when the danger of death is already pressing, it seems rather to be necessary than undertaken by the repentant person's own choice.

    Let no one say in his heart, my brothers, let no one think that the labor of repentance is hard, and therefore that it should be put off until the very last particle of this life. That thought is exceedingly dangerous, since the fixed end of life, which divine providence has appointed for each person, just as he has wished it to be hidden from all, so he will not prolong it for anyone who intentionally defers repentance.

    If we wish to be safe and secure in conscience, let us do penance while we are healthy, while we are able to sin, while no necessity of approaching death yet presses us. For it is a very doubtful matter to do penance when necessity already compels, and the imminence of death makes you no longer able to sin, when, that is, not you have dismissed your sins, but they have dismissed you, powerless before them.

    O how many, deceived by the hope of a longer life, descend into the abyss of eternal damnation, who when healthy scorned to do penance. For the longer you have deferred repentance, the less disposed to repent you will always be found. For wickedness gains strength with time, and there is no sin so small that it does not grow when neglected. Therefore embrace repentance while you are healthy, and do not put it off from day to day, since you understand what you possess today, but you do not know what will be tomorrow. For each new day brings its own inconveniences, and he who today is not disposed toward repentance will perhaps be less fit tomorrow.

    But let none of you say, “What have I sinned, that repentance should seem necessary to me, when my whole life is nothing other than a certain hard and prolonged necessity of repenting?” You have heard Scripture testify that there is no man on earth who does good and does not sin, since no one is clean before God. For even if you do not commit the great crimes of human impiety, such as homicide, theft, adultery, fornications, and things like these, nevertheless, because you have been established in that calling in which you ought with all your strength to raise every effort toward the state of perfection, sins that are small for mortals living in the world are certainly imputed to you as more serious.

    For all sins, so far as possible, must be avoided by cloistered men, not only those that impede salvation but also those that stain the perfection enjoined upon them. And who among you lives with as much purity as monastic perfection requires? It is a great sin for a monk if he has set down his effort from perfection, if he has lived negligently in the monastery, if he has transgressed even one commandment of the canon and the Gospel. And who among you is there, brothers, who loves the Lord God with such sincerity, such charity, and such fervor of love as a man is bound to love his maker and redeemer? Or whom will you give me from among all of you who does not at times exceed, either in taking food or in drink, more than befits the integrity of monks? Which of you does not offend in speech, or who is not sometimes troubled by evil thoughts? Whom among you has acedia not struck, and whom has sad sloth not disturbed? Who is there in this small congregation of yours whom pride does not touch, and whom impatience has not quite often made murmuring?

    Let each one of you consider the paths of his way of life, and he will find that he fails in many things, even at any moment. For what if a monk has committed no evil? What if he has kept himself clean from this wicked age? He will not be able to be perfect unless he has both turned away from evil and done the good that his perfection requires. For one without the other does not suffice, but from both perfection rises up in a man.

    Therefore, brothers, we must always keep watch with the highest zeal, so that we may satisfy the institution of the holy fathers, according to which, by public profession, we have solemnly obligated ourselves to live, in order that without interruption we may direct our effort toward the perfection set before us. Let not the consideration of our own weakness draw us back from holy effort, since we are aided no less by the grace of the creator than we run by our own desire. Just as every day, in many things, by living rather negligently, we fail on any occasion, so also at each moment, rising from the torpor of mind, let us renew holy effort in a good purpose. Let us join tears to holy prayers, and always [unclear] the help of God with devout

    On the True Penitence of Monks.

    ... let us invoke [him] with supplications. Let us preserve charity inviolate in all things, because it is charity that covers a multitude of sins. Each day the good soldier of Christ, who desires to be a faithful soldier to his Lord, should examine himself by scrutiny at least once, and should consider more carefully how much on that day he has advanced or fallen back in holy desire. Whenever he finds that he has sinned in anything, let him at once do penance, and with tears ask mercy from the Lord. Let him not wait for the doubtful morrow: salvation is for today; and he who can immediately find pardon should by no means introduce delay. Let him at once grieve in his heart that he has sinned against the Lord; let him also renew his holy purpose with new fervor; and let him judge that he has utterly lost that day on which he has not become better by making progress.

    Prayer should always be on the monk’s lips; continual compunction should be in his heart; tears of devotion should continually flow from his eyes; and the exercises of inward love should never depart from his memory. Let the most bitter remembrance of the Lord’s Passion often be in the mind of the cloistered man; and let all the prayers that he makes to the Father be [unclear] in the power of the blood and wounds of our Lord, and let either prayer be offered to God or meditation on his words be turned over in the mind. Let the devout monk turn away from evil and do the good that he can, with cheerfulness and discretion of the Spirit of God; because, as has been said, for doing penance it is not enough to change one’s ways for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also strives to adorn one’s conscience with good works.

    Therefore, my brothers, as you know, four things are required for true penitence. The first is true contrition for sins, which is sorrow of heart voluntarily assumed in detestation of the evils that one has committed. Of this Scripture says: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” And again: “Those who sow in tears” [unclear]. The third [unclear] is the sorrow of contrition: the greater it is, the more fruitful penitence will be. For true contrition is that which both sorrow of mind commends and continual cleansing by tears bears witness to. Great is the usefulness of tears, because there is no sin so grave that contrition, accompanied by tears, does not wipe it away.

    Hence the holy doctor Augustine says: “O humble tear, how powerful and virtuous you are, because yours is the kingdom, yours is the power. You do not fear the gaze of the judge; you impose silence on accusing enemies; you alone enter before the king, but you do not depart alone; you conquer the unconquerable and bind the omnipotent.” He likewise says: “The holier anyone is, and the more full of holy desire, the more abundant is his weeping in prayer.” True compunction has sorrow; sorrow is shown by tears; and penitence is adorned by these as by certain ornaments. True compunction makes the soul shudder at sin, and when it has begun from fear, increased by its own advances, it gradually rises into love, whose virtue is great and whose power is truly admirable; before it every enormity of sins soon yields. For whoever true compunction of heart has made to supplicate, the merciful Lord soon hears him.

    O happy tears, O saving affliction and truly sweet bitterness, [unclear], through which the compunct soul rises to the mercy of God. For, as the holy [unclear], [unclear] is renewed. The second thing that pertains to the truth of penitence is a firm purpose of amendment, because whoever has the word of confession in his mouth and does not have in his heart the purpose of amendment is either deceitful or vain. But whoever has it in the heart and not in the mouth is either proud or timid, and in no way fit for true penitence. For Scripture says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” This judgment, lovers of Christ, especially [holds] at the time when the statute of the Church decreed confession necessary for salvation. The third, therefore, is confession of the mouth for the truth of penitence; contrition of heart alone, especially from that [unclear], is sufficient neither [without] the purpose of future amendment. But what this saving confession ought to be, I know that none of you is ignorant.

    Homily XIV. Folio XXXIII.

    I say, however, that perhaps it will not be useless: that confession ought to be one’s own, complete, free, humble, spontaneous, and shamefaced. For the holy bishop Ambrose says that shamefaced confession greatly avails with God for remitting sins to human beings, and the penalty that we cannot avoid by defense we relieve by humble shame. A great thing is the due confession of sins, since it immediately restores to spiritual health the soul of the confessor wounded by offenses; it also justifies the humbled mind and grants pardon for sins. For all our hope after the fall of sin consists in the humility of confession, because guilt is not forgiven unless it is revealed in confession, through the priest, to God who knows all things.

    For in confession there is a place of mercy, as Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: “He who hides his crimes will not prosper; but he who has confessed and abandoned them will obtain mercy.” It is also written in the Psalm: “I said, I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my sin.” The holy evangelist John also says in his first epistle: “If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just, so that he remits our sins for us; and he will cleanse us from all iniquity.” And the holy bishop Augustine says: “Confession is the salvation of souls, the disperser of vices, the restorer of virtues, the conqueror of demons, and the heap of all goods. It closes the mouth of hell and opens the gates of the heavenly paradise.” Cassiodorus also, commending the power of true confession, speaks thus: “O blessed confession, which takes away everlasting reproach, since whatever guilt penitence has found, it renders absolved for eternal ages.”

    Fourth, satisfaction is necessary for true penitence; by it, namely, we remove all causes that cut off sins, and for those things that we have wrongly committed we placate the Lord with holy works. Hence the divine Pope Gregory says: “We do not truly make satisfaction if we cease from iniquity, unless we also pursue with opposed acts the pleasures that we have loved.” The most holy Pope Leo also says in a sermon: “By prayer God’s propitiation is sought; by fasting the concupiscence of the flesh is extinguished; by alms sins are redeemed; and at the same time through all these the image of God is renewed in us.”

    Confession, moreover, is the voluntary accusation of the offender, from blushing shame, and, through the keys of the Church, making satisfaction for sins, with the obligation, through penitence, of chastising in himself the things he has brought forth, by the command of the priest. Confession ought to be simple, humble, pure, faithful, frequent, naked and open, discreet, voluntary, one’s own, shamefaced, complete, secret, full of tears, made at the due times, strong and [secret/secure?]; voluntary, secret, full of tears, made at the due times, strong and secure; voluntary, secret, full of tears, are held. For true penitence requires all these things: it so laments past sins that henceforth it does not commit further things to be lamented.

    On the abstinence and fasting of monks. Homily XV.

    A great and necessary good for a monk, dearest brothers, is abstinence with fasting: namely, that he not offend in mind through the concupiscence of the flesh and evil thoughts, and that in body he abstain from foods and drinks that beget wantonness of spirit. For the concupiscence of the mind is quickly kindled into lust if the body is nourished too carefully. Considering the very great usefulness of this good, the most holy fathers of old, who handed down precepts of living to monks, all with one judgment established for us a fixed measure of fasts; under its moderation the body should take such refreshment of foods as nature required, not such as the intemperance of the will might desire.

    Holy Scripture also commends fasting to us in many ways, and so often mentions it with praise. For the Lord God says through the mouth of his prophet Joel: “Be converted to me with all your heart, in fasting, mourning, and weeping.” In the book of Judith too one reads thus: “Know that the Lord will hear your prayers, if you remain steadfast in fastings and prayers in the sight of the Lord.” Similarly in Tobit we read: “Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving, more than to store up treasures of gold, because almsgiving frees from death, and it is that which purges sins.” Our Lord Jesus Christ also said in the holy Gospel to the disciples: “Blessed are you who now [are hungry?], for you shall be filled.” But the best fast of monks is to abstain from all things that can pollute the soul, that is, idle

    On the abstinence and fasting of monks.

    ...to bear speech: to admit no vain, useless, or foul thoughts; to commit nothing that is unbecoming to a servant of God; and to omit nothing that pertains to the consummation of righteousness. For unless the mind has fasted from vices and sins, bodily abstinence will profit nothing toward the salvation of the soul.

    Hence the holy priest Jerome says: “Your abstinence and fasting are pleasing in proportion as they are offered with holy conduct, so that what in others are coverings for vices may in you become ornaments of virtues.” For what good is it for the body to be made thin by abstinence, if the spirit swells with pride? Or what virtue is there in not drinking wine, and being drunk with anger, lust, hatred, and envy? Or what will it help us for eternal salvation, brothers, that according to the rule of our holy father Benedict we do not eat meat, if we do not subdue the vices of the flesh?

    For the thrice-holy pope Gregory says: “In vain is the body worn down through abstinence, if the mind, divided by disorderly movements, is scattered among vices.” Hence Scripture commands: “Sanctify a fast.” To sanctify a fast is, with other good works joined to it, to show abstinence of the flesh worthy of God. Indeed, if abstinence from foods alone made a man virtuous, there would have been no need to add “sanctify”; but because fasting alone does not suffice for the sanctification of the soul, it is necessary that it be adorned with the ornament of all virtues. For those who abstain from foods and do evil imitate the demons, for whom there is always fasting and never any lack of sin.

    A fast acceptable to God is to restrain the body by abstinence from the desire of evils, and by the spirit of compunction to mortify the deeds of the flesh for the love of Christ. Let the mind of the one fasting be fervent in the love of God; let his conscience always be clean from vices, and the fasts of humble servants will please the Most High. Let the monks’ fasts be daily, as the canon of the holy teacher Benedict established; let their hearts be clean, as the Lord Jesus commanded in the holy Gospel; let their refection be moderate, fleeing satiety, because just as from excessive fullness the body is corrupted by diverse and various illnesses, so too an unregulated movement of lust is aroused in it. For modest and moderate food is both medicine for the body and a support of virtue for the soul.

    For Saint John Chrysostom, bishop, says: “Nothing is so pleasant as food well digested and cooked; nothing so healthful; nothing so sharpens the senses; nothing so drives away sickness as moderate refection. For sufficiency with moderate nourishment produces health and pleasure together. But abundance makes disease, brings on troubles, and generates various illnesses. For what excessive hunger does, immoderate fullness of foods is also accustomed to do. Hunger indeed in a few days takes a man away and frees him from this penal life; but excess of foods consumes and makes the human body putrefy and rot, torments it with long illness, and at last consumes it with a cruel death.”

    Therefore, that you may live sound in mind and healthy in body, my most beloved brothers, keep this rule of living which the holy fathers prescribed for you by word and showed beforehand by living example: fleeing all luxury of foods and drinks, grant to the body only so much as, nature requiring it, is enough for good health. Let food quiet hunger, but not stir the body to lust; let drink quench thirst, not [unclear] the mind. [unclear] expelled our first parents shamefully from the kingdom of paradise and innocence: they did not devour a bird, a fish, a calf, or a pig, so that you should think food was in fault; rather, against God’s command they presumed to take a very cheap apple, so that you may know that not food, but appetite, is liable to the vice of sin.

    For it can often happen that some man takes more lavish foods without fault, provided he regulates his appetite, while another receives cheaper foods not without guilt of conscience, when through immoderation he exceeds the measure of temperance. Therefore let none of you think himself secure from the vice of gluttony because he eats neither luxurious nor delicate foods, since it is not food but the appetite for food that is held in fault. For it is quite possible for one eating beans and vegetables to contract the guilt of sin, and for another taking the most delicate birds as food not to sin.

    Hence one of the holy fathers says: “A belly filled with any foods at all brings forth seedbeds of lust, nor can a mind choked by the weight of foods govern the rudders of discretion. For not only excess of wine is accustomed to make the mind drunk, but also the excess of all foods, while it is unsteady.”

    and renders it wavering, and strips it entirely of all contemplation of integrity and purity. Therefore great discretion is needed, so that food necessary for the support of life alone is supplied to the body, and no excess of indulgence occurs. Hence the holy Pope Gregory says: “It is a great labor of discretion to give something to the demanding body and to deny it something; by not giving, to restrain gluttony, and by giving, to nourish nature.” For through abstinence vices are to be extinguished, not the flesh; and through food the body is to be nourished, not sins. Thus, then, it is necessary that the monk maintain the art of continence in his diet, so that he kills not the flesh but vices. For often, while we pursue the enemy in the flesh, we severely slaughter, through immoderate abstinence, the spirit of devotion which we love. More often also, while we have compassion on the [unclear], as though sparing a fellow-citizen, we nourish an enemy for battle against us. But when the vice of gluttony rules, men lose everything they have done bravely; for when the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are overthrown together. For one does not rise up to the conflict of spiritual combat if the enemy placed very near within us, namely the appetite of gluttony, is not first subdued by us, with God’s help; because unless we overcome the things that are nearer to us, we hasten in vain to fight against those placed farther away. For war is waged in vain in the field against foreign enemies if within the walls of the city there is a citizen lying in ambush. We never overcome the assaults of demons unless we first overcome gluttony in ourselves.

    Let no one, brothers, deceive himself by empty persuasion, so as to believe that there is no sin among beans and vegetables, if the mind loosens too far the appetite of receiving by excessive pleasure. For in taking food one can everywhere be [unclear], when appetite is extended beyond the rule of nature. See, we never eat meat either in the monastery or outside it; here in this open countryside we see fish very rarely; no one among us has ever seen more sumptuous foods; we neither can nor indeed ought to have delicate fare. Our foods are barley, oats, beans, peas and vegetables, milk also, cheese and eggs. From these we receive the daily supports of our life; and hunger stirs appetite so that disgust for them may not arise. Outside the time of the Lenten fast, fish are so rare for us that scarcely once in a month a few are brought from the river Nahe, and those very small. In the whole Bursfelde reform there is no monastery less provided with the necessity of fish. But can we therefore not fall into the vice of gluttony, because we cannot find more sumptuous foods? Indeed, since the vice is not in the food, as has already been said, but in the appetite, the eater of peas or beans can sin no less in eating than he who is accustomed to eat the most sumptuous and choice foods. Poverty does not make us wholly [unclear]; [unclear] simple and rustic [foods], by which nature may somehow be sustained. This, my brothers, I pray, let us take care of: that in that which produces loathing of delicacy our conscience not be polluted by excess. Let us take with patience and thanksgiving, from what the Lord has given, as much as necessity itself requires; and let us not think that the snares of the devil cannot harm us, since he overthrew the first men in paradise not by more sumptuous food, but by a small and common apple. For the vice is not in the food but in the appetite, when either we desire things forbidden to us, or, eagerly gaping after permitted things, we use them otherwise than we ought.

    Nor does abstinence befit anyone more than a monk, who, since he has been specially called to the soldiery of Christ, ought not by his profession to have leisure for any delicacies. Our poverty imposes upon us a certain necessity of abstinence; for we can restrain ourselves to temperance all the more easily, since the less we overflow with foods, the more purely we fast in holiness of mind. For temperance is more easily preserved in poverty, but in riches it is indeed more quickly endangered. What the food of monks ought to be, blessed Jerome makes clear, saying in a certain letter to Paulinus: “Let your food be cheap and taken in the evening: namely vegetables and legumes; and sometimes consider it the height of delicacy to eat a few little fish. He who desires Christ and feeds on that heavenly bread does not greatly seek what dung he may make from precious foods. The lover of Christ loves abstinence; he cultivates fasting as the one remedy of soul and body; he takes the greatest care that his heart not be weighed down by surfeiting, nor does he take more food than nature, content with little, demands.” But the monk who rejects fasting, who [rejects] abstinence, the nurse of virtues—

    On abstinence and fasting for the monk.

    [unclear]: he who gulps down foods with greed, who drinks wine or strong drink and whatever can intoxicate to satiety, is unworthy of the very name of monk; he cannot be a disciple of Christ. Woe to our times, in which already very many clerics and monks have shamefully cast away the virtue of abstinence, who ought to have shown the people of God the way of salvation no less by example than by word. Given over to gluttonies, and immersed in continual drinkings and pleasures, contrary to all clerical propriety, they hasten to go before [unclear] into the perdition of eternal death. Scripture says: The beginning of a man’s life is bread and water. But now our monks and cloistered men buy for themselves at great cost whatever is sold more dearly, whatever they find more sumptuous; by gorging their bellies they bury it, and through intemperance corrupt soul and body alike. Amid banquets they debate fasting, and when they have become drunk they praise temperance. There each one boasts that he is victorious over vice, although he has already been conquered by gluttony and drunkenness. Our Lord Jesus Christ says in the holy Gospel according to Luke: See that your hearts are not weighed down in excess. It does not befit a man dedicated to God to eat or drink to satiety; nor is it lawful for a monk to eat more than nature requires. Let eating still hunger; let it not induce fullness. Let belches be far away, which satiety is accustomed to produce at feasts; let vomiting and undigested [unclear] not be heard among monks. It is necessary that all of us cloistered men use great moderation of discretion, so that one nourishes the body with foods and drinks in such a way that, serving the spirit, it may be able to live, and not, having grown fat, begin to grow wanton against the command of the mind. Let satiety always be far away, for nothing so inflames the body and stirs the genital members as undigested food and a belly hot with wine or beer. Hence Saint Jerome, admonishing Eustochium concerning temperance, the preserver of all virtues, says in a certain letter: Let the bride of Christ flee wine as poison; for wine and youth itself, more prone to gluttony, are weapons against adolescence. Avarice does not so shake adolescence, nor does pride puff it up, nor does ambition delight it, as do those [unclear] which seem to us innate in pleasure.

    Homily XV. Fol. XXXVI.

    [unclear] could [unclear] anew. For what condemned our first parents except the transgression of the commandment? For God’s concern was not with food but with obedience. For if man had abstained as almighty God had commanded him, surely through this obedience he would have merited, in his innocence, the enjoyment of eternal happiness. For it is established by the tradition of the Scriptures that man cannot be saved without the merit of free will, since, although the grace of God works all things in all, it will save no one without the cooperation of his own will, except only infants baptized in the name of the Trinity, and those who cannot have the free use of reason.

    For just as free will accomplishes nothing toward salvation without the grace of the Savior, so the grace of God will not save an adult without the merit of a good will. But the first man, placed in paradise and having transgressed God’s commandment through lack of temperance, did not have the merit of obedience in a good will; therefore, wretched and unhappy, he was cast out. But the compassion of almighty God determined from eternity to restore him who had fallen through weakness, whom he knew to have been deceived by the envious suggestion of the serpent rather than by his own malice. He remitted this guilt to the passion and death of his only-begotten Son, born in time of the Virgin, so that he who had fallen by his own rashness might be restored to salvation through the obedience of the mediator. For it was impossible for the human race, lost through disobedience, to reach the mercy of the Creator except through the obedience of such a mediator, who would be God and man, in whom there would be both the strength of power and the innocence of nature. For we were blind through ignorance and mute through silence. The mediator of God and men, Christ Jesus, came, sent to enlighten every man coming into this world; he handed down the knowledge of God to mortals, and, dying for the lost, he sealed for the redeemed the greatest cause of love. He instructed the intellect through faith, by which we know God; he stirred the affection through his passion, by which we rightly love him above all things.

    And so, if we love our Lord and Redeemer with the whole integrity of sincere charity, it is plainly fitting that we chastise our body for love of him. For our abstinence will conduce to merit for us for a twofold reason: namely, when by fasting, through obedience to the statutes of the fathers, we offer sacrifice, and when by abstaining through the charity of God we show ourselves grateful to our Redeemer, who endured death for our sake. Abstinence merits or bears [unclear]; it commends obedience; it supplies wisdom and instruction; it purges the affection; it enlightens the intellect; it grants victory against demons; it perfects religion; it obtains forgiveness of sins; it tames the unlawful motions of the flesh; it wins efficacy for prayers; it displays to one’s neighbor an example of virtue. Abstinence purifies the mind, adorns the soul with virtues, and heals the weak little body. He who loves abstinence is wise, and he who loves fasting is a mighty ruler. A sober mind is the dwelling-place of wisdom; but he who pursues banquets will die in poverty of soul. It is difficult for a man to become wise who lives his life in pleasures. [unclear] is content with the gifts of nature, and in modest things preserves a holy life. Continuous voracity over a long time has harmed many, and more have perished by gluttony than by the sword. For habit seems to alter nature, and the longer it has prevailed, the more strongly [unclear].

    There is among the Helvetians a man named Nicholas, whose abstinence turns the men of all Germany to admiration, and today, as you have heard, he is named in [unclear] with the title of sanctity. He, once a farmer living in a certain village of the Helvetians, was accustomed, in the manner of the country people, to pronounce judgment among fourteen disputing villagers. It happened at one time that he could not revoke a decision of his companions which he thought unjust; and, fearing danger to the salvation of his soul, he left his house, wife, children, and all worldly business and possessions, and withdrew alone into a neighboring wood for the love of God, in which he lives a solitary life. And behold, today is the twentieth year since he entered the solitude without taking human food. I speak of things known to all, nor do I think there is any man living in Germany who has not heard the report of this miracle. And lest perhaps in future anyone believe that we have been deceived by pretense, we cite Helvetia, together with the prelate of the church of Constance, as witness; they observe his ways and life with the greatest care:

    On the abstinence and fasting of monks.

    He is a man of very keen intellect; although he is wholly ignorant of letters, nevertheless, like another Antony, the hermit of old, he understands the meaning of the Scriptures exceedingly well. We have seen how most eloquently he disputed with a certain master about the sacrament of the altar, a thing at which anyone who has not in the least tasted heavenly things through the pursuit of contemplation will not be able to marvel enough. I have introduced these matters, brothers, so that you may understand that nothing is so difficult that habit, continued over a long time, does not make it easy.

    This holy man, as he himself confesses, did not suddenly arrive at the height of this abstinence, but over time, by successive degrees, little by little withdrawing a small amount of food from himself, until at last he was able to abstain altogether. For, as we have said, he has abstained from every corruptible food now for almost the twentieth year. By the example of this man, my brothers, let each of you learn daily to subtract something from his food and drink for the love of God, and let him accustom himself to provide for his body not as much as he can, but as much as is sufficient for the support of nature. For nature, as Boethius bears witness, is content with few and very small things; if you try to force its satisfaction with superfluous foods, what you pour in will become either unpleasant or harmful.

    Many dishes beget many illnesses, and gluttony of the belly dulls the mind and torments life. For the wise man says: "Sweet is the sleep of the worker, whether he eats little or much; but the fullness of the rich man does not allow him to sleep." The belly is to be filled without satiety, and one must rise from the table without disgust, so that, clearly, we may eat not as much as we can, but as much as we ought when nature requires it.

    For monks, however, variety of foods is especially to be avoided; for anyone who uses various dishes, attempting to put more into the stomach than nature raises up [unclear], feasts not without the vice of gluttony. The strength of our body is to be restored by moderate and simple food, not shamefully oppressed by many and various foods, because the body was not created for food, but food for the body. That variety of foods brings various diseases upon the body we prove from the temperance of the ancients, whom a uniform simplicity of foods preserved for a very long time in this life.

    But our most holy founder, Benedict, the most modest hierophant of all the leaders of monks, prescribed for us a rule adorned with the highest discretion; in it, wishing to show monks the measure of foods, he says: "We believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for the daily meal, whether at the sixth or the ninth hour, for all tables, because of the infirmities of different people, so that one who perhaps cannot eat from one may be refreshed from the other. Therefore let two cooked dishes suffice for all the brothers. And if there are fruits or fresh legumes there, let a third also be added."

    If I understand the mind of our lawgiver correctly, he granted monks two cooked dishes where the necessity of infirmity requires it, not for the filling of the appetite of the healthy. For the monk who is healthy is rightly excepted from this indulgence, so that he may be refreshed by one cooked dish only. But in my judgment the infirm man is rightly permitted to be refreshed from both, since excess is feared in no respect.

    Yet since not all of us can do all things equally, and one person needs more food, another less, it is impossible to prescribe one form of abstinence for everyone; but it is left to the judgment of each person's discretion, that he should take as much as necessity requires, not as much as the pleasure of appetite commands. This must especially be guarded against: that immoderate satiety of foods should not creep in, for it stains the soul when either disgust follows the meal or heavy sloth follows the mind. Vomiting that proceeds from satiety belongs to dogs rather than to monks.

    The Christian religion especially detests a man who is a glutton, because the delights of the servants of God are not food and drink, but piety and justice, by which God is both worshiped in purity of faith, and to each person what is his own is administered justly. Therefore whoever you are who desire to please God with your whole heart, whoever you are who hasten to arrive at the joys of eternal happiness, impose upon yourself a manner of fasting with a measure mixed according to your strength, and apply the greatest care that, while fasting, you be constant in prayer, just in judgments, outstanding in brotherly love, patient in injuries, humble under rebukes, circumspect in speech, clean in conscience, fervent in the love of God, and, with prudence accompanying you, fearful in all your actions.

    Flee useless and idle words, and be persevering in good works at all times, having constancy in adversities, watchfulness in temptations, continence at meals, and simple purity in heart. Let your fasts be moderate and holy, in all humility of mind;

    Homily XV. Fol. XXXVII.

    which so weaken the body that they do not lift up the mind into pride, lest the exercise of humility become material for vices. Fasting detests idleness; it does not love wordiness; it cherishes secrecy; it devotes itself to prayers and tears. Fasting, as Saint Ambrose bears witness, is the death of fault, the destruction of sins, the remedy of salvation, the root of grace, the foundation of chastity. By this step the righteous Moses came to God; by this gift Elijah, before he died, ascended into heaven in a chariot. Those who walk in the Spirit love fasting, and those who profess chastity necessarily flee an abundance of delights. For hunger is a friend to virginity, an enemy to wantonness. Fullness, however, betrays chastity and nourishes wantonness. For fasting extinguishes the burning arrows of the devil; the urgency of prayer restrains them; and the continuation of vigils in the love of Christ repels all the snares of demons. Hence Saint Leo the pope says in a certain sermon: What can be more effective than fasting, by the observance of which we draw near to God and, resisting the devil, overcome [his] alluring enticements? For fasting has always been food for virtue, and abstinence the nourishment of holy chastity. From abstinence, indeed, proceed chaste thoughts; it begets reasonable desires, and also modest counsels; and through voluntary afflictions the flesh dies to concupiscences, while the spirit is renewed in virtues. Let us therefore love fasting, my brothers, for love of virtue, on account of him who did not refuse to undergo death for us; and let us abstain not only from unlawful things but also, as far as can be done, from permitted ones, so that we who in many ways have offended against the commandments of salvation may, as recompense of satisfaction, henceforth restrain ourselves from every pleasure. Let us fast from every sin; let us take no food of malice; let us devour no banquets of pleasure, nor be made drunk with the wine of luxury. Let us fast from all perversities; let us abstain from evil works, and let us not speak harmful things; and let us always beware of hurtful and perverse thoughts, which separate us from God. Let us always keep most zealous watch in prayers to God, knowing that he whom we invoke with prayers is everywhere most present to us. Let his praise always be in our mouth; and since we cannot praise his magnificence in speech, let us adore him in the heart with the desires of a most chaste love. For then our fasts are pleasing to him, when they have been adorned with holy works and continual prayers. For the prayer of the righteous man, as sacred Scripture bears witness, penetrates the heavens, and it becomes the more effective, the more it is found adorned with charity and fasting. Let us join to it, as it were, two wings, fasting and charity, and it will obtain for us from the Lord whatever conducive to salvation we shall have asked.

    On the Lenten fast of monks: Homily XVI.

    Because, by the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearly beloved brothers, we have begun the Lenten fast, reason demands that we say something briefly about its observance. For although you have many writings of the holy fathers on this most sacred exercise of fasts, nevertheless, because I know by experience that my sermons among you are not wholly fruitless, I gladly impart to your edification what the Lord has granted. For, as blessed Jerome bears witness, the act of the living voice has within it a certain hidden operation, which in Greek speech he more elegantly called energy; and the discourse of a teacher, uttered by the mouth, is stronger for persuading. But I, set apart in your midst only by the name of pastor, confess that I am a young man, unlearned and lacking both the experience and the discretion necessary for the governance of souls; whence it happens that I speak with a certain blush and shame, a young man among elders, an ignorant man among the learned, a disciple among masters.
