Therefore I beg that none of you despise the simplicity of my speech; let no one take it ill that I speak, because even if I am not fit for speaking, nevertheless by reason of the office of pastoral care entrusted to me I confess that before God I am bound to admonish you. Your charity gives me boldness to speak, and the readier you show yourselves to hear, the more you move me to speak. Nor will the labor be burdensome to me, however great it may seem, by which the salvation of your souls is perfected. Help me with your prayers, that the Lord Jesus may speak in my mouth, and may grant strength to my poor little talent to bring forth in your midst whatever can produce in you an increase of holy fervor. For as much as I desire to benefit your charity by my sermons, I am unable to do so, because I am compelled to be too much occupied by the care of secular business. Whence

    On the Lenten Fast of Monks.

    only by day and in that part of the night which, after the night lauds, I am accustomed to pass sleepless, do I devote myself to exhorting you, setting down on little sheets what occurs to me to say. And so I have wished to introduce today’s conference from the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, who says thus concerning Lenten observance: “Although at every season the life of a monk ought to have the observance of Lent, nevertheless, because this virtue belongs to few, we therefore advise that in these days of Lent they guard their life in all purity, and that all alike wash away in these holy days the stains and negligences of other times. This is then done worthily if we restrain ourselves from all vices, and devote ourselves to prayer with tears, to reading, and to compunction of heart.”

    If this virtue belongs to few, that they should at every season lead a life of Lenten observance, it is now plainly evident that few monks in religion live according to the purity of the Gospel, since all who profess the soldiery of Christ are bound to direct their effort toward the summit of perfection. For the monk, according to the interpretation of his name, is solitary; and he is then rightly believed to live in the cenobium according to the Gospel and the rule which he has professed, when, having despised worldly possessions and honors for the love of God, he conducts himself in all purity of heart before God and men: vigorous in work, clean in thought, sparing and peaceable in speech. This is the life of a monk, having Lenten observance at every season: to chastise the body for the love of God through abstinence, and to nourish the mind through inward compunction. He lives rightly who lives justly, who loves God above all things, who with the greatest zeal and the greatest diligence observes his commandments in words and deeds. For he is the true monk of Christ who imitates Christ with all his powers.

    But if you wish to imitate Christ, O monk, observe most carefully what I am about to say. Flee the world and all comforts of the flesh, so that you may deserve truly to be solitary. Never permit vain, useless, foul, and harmful thoughts to dwell in your heart, but always think something good, and let the memory of the Lord’s Passion never depart from your mind, so that each day, with thanksgiving, you may contemplate the Lord hanging on the cross. Consider God present to you everywhere, who sees, knows, and understands whatever you have either thought or done, since nothing is hidden from him. Keep your heart clean from every defilement of sin, and always have a pure conscience, fervent in the true love of Christ. Let no idle time fly away from you, but let thought always find you engaged in good works. Do not grow sluggish with much sleep, and keep yourself far removed from every sloth of tepidity. Embrace moderation in food and drink, and live as sparingly as is permitted, so that the body, moderately sustained, may always serve the spirit in humility and in no way rise up against the command of reason.

    As soon as you perceive some sluggishness arising in you, flee to the memory of the most bitter Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, and bring back [unclear] whatever can more swiftly drive away sloth. Break off, I beg you, all delays, since sluggishness of mind, when dissembled, grows suddenly; and sloth, which is not at once extinguished by the new fervor of the mind, is immediately strengthened into the grave destruction of the soul. For of all evils in a monk this is the worst: if through sluggishness and sloth he has offered a place in his heart to the seedbed of vices. And you, O monks, must keep watch against this beast not only every day, but every hour and moment, since, once admitted into the heart, it never enters alone; but when it has been stirred, a mass and spring of all vices accompanies it. There is no more destructive plague of the monk than the sluggishness of sloth, through which all fervor of devotion is extinguished; and, faithful service having been interrupted, the mind, driven by laziness and idleness, is cast headlong into the pit of despair. Whoever permits delay from sloth quickly falls away from the purpose of holiness.

    Against this Solomon admonishes you in the Book of Proverbs, saying: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom. Though she has no leader, nor instructor, nor ruler, she prepares her food in summer and gathers at harvest what she may eat.” And again he says: “Desires kill the sluggard, because his hands have refused to work at anything.” Nothing is worse than idleness for those who profess the purpose of holiness, because it not only accumulates nothing good, but even consumes and scatters everything previously accumulated. For the fervor of holy devotion rejoices and advances by progress, but through cessation it grows sluggish and little by little, not to say suddenly, vanishes,

    All things. XVI. Fol. XXXVIII.

    For sloth is the root of despair, and the mother and nurse of all vices. For just as a garment both produces and nourishes the moth, so the most pernicious plague of acedia both gives birth to and fosters despair. This beast is accustomed to vex no one more than monks, and especially those who lead their life withdrawn in solitude. Therefore, monks, you must beware with the utmost care of this enemy of the salvation of souls, and it must be fought not by fleeing but by resisting bravely; and one must diligently consider that no one has attained the honor of holiness by torpor and sloth, nor has anyone deserved the kingdom of eternal happiness without great and continual labor.

    Therefore the mind must always be renewed by daily and fresh increases of virtues, and this perilous journey of living must be measured not by what has passed, but rather by what remains. Let no one promise himself security in this life, which is named wholly a temptation, full of as many dangers as there are affections in the soul; but let each one take care that he who could become better from worse does not become worse from better. And especially in these holy days let us all take care, as much as we can, to become better, adding for ourselves, by the counsel of our divine teacher, something to the usual measure of our service: namely special prayers, abstinence from foods and drink, so that each one, beyond the measure prescribed to him, may offer something to God of his own will with the joy of the Holy Spirit, that is, may subtract from his body something of food, of drink, of sleep, of talkativeness, of ease, and may await holy Easter with the joy of spiritual desire.

    For a monk is proved to be little religious at other times if in these holy days he is not found more religious, more fervent in the love of God, and more devout. Hence the divine pope Gregory says in a certain homily: Lent is to be observed with the highest observance, so that the fast in it, on account of the Lord’s days that have been subtracted from abstinence, unless sickness has hindered someone, is by no means relaxed, because these days are the tithes of the year which we are commanded to offer to the Lord. Saint Ambrose also says: He keeps Lent who by fasting and keeping vigil ascends to Easter. For just as at the remaining time of the year to fast brings a reward, so in Lent not to fast is a sin. The former fasts are voluntary, and these are necessary; the former come from choice, but these from law. To the former we are invited; to these we are compelled. And therefore he who passes beyond the appointed number by eating on one day is accused not as the violator of one day, but is charged as the transgressor of the whole of Lent.

    In these sacred days all desires of the flesh must be restrained; the body must be chastised through abstinence, so that if perhaps at other times we have lived less temperately, we may in some way make compensation by this Lenten fast. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us follow the admonitions of our most holy father Benedict, and with as much diligence as we can let us exercise ourselves in holy works, subtracting something daily from our body, for love of God, from food and drink, so that we may prove ourselves true servants of God.

    Next, however, our holy founder adds, saying: Yet this very thing which each one offers, let him report to his abbot, and let it be done with his prayer and will; because what is done without the permission of the spiritual father will be imputed to presumption and vainglory, not to reward. Therefore all things are to be done with the will of the abbot. The words of our holy lawgiver are plain, brothers, so that no one could have recourse to the covering of ignorance. For if all things are to be done with the will of the abbot, then without his permission absolutely nothing is to be done.

    Indeed, the more a good work is adorned with more virtues, the more it must be considered of greater merit before God. Therefore, when a monk, by the license and blessing of his abbot, subtracts something of foods or drink from his body for love of God, he will receive not only from that abstinence itself the reward of eternal satiety promised by the Lord, but also the kingdom for humility, and for holy obedience: he has resigned his will to Christ in the hands of the abbot; and if he thereafter usurps it again by his own decision, he has now shamefully denied Christ. For what else is a monk who usurps his own will, except the unjust possessor of another’s property? Therefore let the monk be humbly subject to his abbot for love of Christ, always in all things; let him presume absolutely nothing

    On the Lenten fast of monks.

    ...to act against his command; let him omit or neglect nothing that has been enjoined on him by him. Let him beware of troubling or saddening his shepherd by a restless manner of life; nor let him murmur against him, nor disparage him, nor say any evil whatever against him. Rather, let him reverence him with the sincere affection of charity, as the vicar of Christ, and not sadden his spirit either by importunate or disorderly words or deeds. Moreover, let him aid his labors as much as he can, and intercede for him with continual prayers before God. Monks sin greatly against God who do not fear to sadden their abbot by their importunate disparagements and wicked behavior.

    Therefore whatever monk desires to be good, whoever truly wishes to be devout in the Lord, let him always and everywhere venerate his abbot with pure love as the vicar of Jesus Christ in the monastery; let him humbly obey his commands in all things, and in no way depart from his direction. But let the abbot strive to show himself in all things a worthy shepherd to his monks, one who feeds the sheep of Christ entrusted to him by word and likewise by example, in all gentleness of charity. Let him not disturb the brothers without just and reasonable necessity; let him not be a despiser of the holy community; let him recognize himself as the steward of the monastery's goods, not their lord. Let him not be a mocker of his subjects, not turbulent, not importunate, not a tyrant, but their sincere lover, gentle in speech, mild and upright in conduct, holy in his way of life, clean in conscience, always devoted in mind to God.

    Let him at all times bear solicitous care for the souls entrusted to him, and neglect nothing of those things which seem able to conduce to their salvation. Let him not therefore raise himself up on high because he has been placed as ruler of others, but let him remember that he must fear so much the more, inasmuch as he is most certainly bound to render account for all in the dread judgment of God. Let him correct the proud, rebellious, and contumacious as a lord; let him kindly cherish the humble, obedient, and governable as a most gentle father, and wisely distribute to each one his right without acceptance of persons. Let him always consider himself the mother and nurse of the monks; and therefore those whom he can bring back to better things by gentleness he ought not to exasperate with importunate words and harsh invectives. Let him always bear solicitous care for the weak, and provide for all in such a way that they have no just cause for murmuring. In his own weaknesses let him learn how he ought to have mercy on his subjects. For he cannot be a good shepherd of souls who disdains to suffer heartfelt compassion for the necessities of his ailing subjects.

    But he can become a good abbot among monks who knows how to adapt himself to the persons of the weak in such a way that, whenever a brother asks something of him, taking upon himself the condition of the person asking, he says in his heart: What would I wish to be done to me in this matter, according to the right judgment of reason, if I were in the person of the one asking? Indeed, if the abbot imagines himself a subject, he will let no one go away from him saddened. We have now said, brothers, what sort of men it befits you to be toward us for the love of God, so that, existing as good monks, you may please the Lord Jesus in truth. You have nevertheless heard what sort of shepherd I ought to show myself to you; whether I do this or not, you yourselves will judge better than I.

    For we shall fast in vain and find no fruit of Lenten observance unless we all are concordant before God in the true charity of ecclesiastical union. Or what good will it do to abstain from richer foods and defile the conscience with evil works or thoughts? For in order that the fasts we have begun may be pleasing to God, it is necessary that they be not only alien and remote from vices and sins, but also adorned with the fullness of all virtues. For holy Ambrose says: What profit is it to fast in the belly and to run riot in hunting, to abstain from foods and to wander in sins? Do you think, brothers, that he fasts who at first daybreak does not keep watch at church, does not seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises in the morning, gathers his servants, arranges the nets, brings out the dogs, ranges through glades and woods, and, I say, drags along with him servants perhaps hastening rather to church? To his own pleasures he adds the sins of others, not knowing that he will be guilty both of his own fault and of the ruin of his servants. And Saint Pope Leo: The chief fast of ours does not consist in abstinence from food alone

    [Homily?] XVI.

    For food is by no means fruitfully withheld from the body unless the mind is recalled from all iniquity. Saint Jerome also says: What does it profit for the body to be made thin by abstinence, if the soul swells with pride? What virtue is there in not drinking wine, and being drunk with anger, hatred, and the other poisonous cups of the soul?

    Therefore let none of you promise himself sanctity from abstinence from food alone, since whatever is required for true penitence is judged necessary also for fasting. For fasts profit unto salvation for those who are contrite for their sins in a true purpose of amendment, who fervently devote themselves to good and holy works. Hence all who fast from food and drink must also abstain from [unclear], so that the mind, adorned with the beauty of the virtues, may sweetly burn in the love of Christ and may in no way grow lukewarm from progress in inner conduct. For the virtue of abstinence is nothing if it has not been adorned with works of charity.

    Therefore, monk, listen to my counsel: if you wish to make your fast fruitful before God, first cleanse your conscience from every stain of sin, so that no desire of evil may intervene; so that the mind may become fervent in the exercise of divine love and be laudably adorned with the remaining virtues. By the remedy of contrition and confession wipe away past sins, and by standing firm in prayers with tears strengthen your mind against all temptations with God’s help. Toward God, as much as you can, be fervent in the exercise of love; toward yourself, tranquil in a pure conscience; toward your brother, ordered in true charity. Always be foremost in humility, firm in constancy and obedience, shining in chastity of mind and body, pious in meekness, a monk in conduct, continually inflamed with desire for perfection. If you commend your abstinence by this kind of cleanness and purity, you will fast rightly.

    Exercise your mind diligently in meditation on the passion of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, so that no day passes in which you do not run through his life and death at least once with thanksgiving. I will not say irreligious, but ungrateful, is the Christian who is so immersed either in temporal affairs or occupied with the pleasures of the flesh that he does not call to mind, at least once each day with thanksgiving, the most bitter passion of his Redeemer.

    Fol. XXIX.

    But the monk who forgets the benefits of our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not recall his passion once every day with thanksgiving, who does not meditate every day on the law of the Lord or on the Gospel, is rightly considered the most ungrateful of all men. Nothing is more powerful for him than that prayer which is offered to God the Father in union with, and in the power of, the Lord’s passion. Too justly is that spirit to be condemned which, though redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ, is led astray by the pleasures of its flesh so as not to remember such great benefits of God toward itself.

    For there was no reason that the Son of God should become man except that he willed to justify us sinners: born in the world for us, suffering in the world for us, and cruelly dead on the wood for our crimes. That just one came into the world to justify us who were sinners; the pious one came to the impious, that we might learn piety, humility, and patience from him. The physician came to the sick, life to the dead, mercy to the desperate; it was not our merits that drew him down from heaven into the world, but our sins.

    It is fitting, therefore, brothers in [unclear], that we celebrate with all devotion this Lenten fast dedicated to his most holy passion, who first deigned to do such great things for our salvation, who, in order to rescue us from the destruction of death, did not hesitate to give himself for us unto death. Let us do, for the love of Christ, whatever good we can; let us endure, in consideration of his passion and death, every adversity that happens to us in this world, since the Lord Jesus, who in charity willed to suffer for us, has truly shown himself most worthy that we love him with all our heart.

    For if, brother, you recognize yourself as a sinner, Christ saves you by his death. Contemplate him as it is fitting, hanging on the cross, and you will be healed from every bite of sin. For nothing in this world is found more effective for cleansing and curing the wounds of conscience than meditation on Christ. For the most precious blood of the Lord, poured out, has become sufficient medicine for sin. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: Brothers, that we who are wounded by sin may be healed, let us behold Christ crucified. For just as those who looked upon the bronze serpent in the desert did not perish from the bites of serpents, so those who

    On the Lenten fast of monks.

    [Unclear] with devotion beholds the death of Jesus Christ: he is healed from the diseases of sins. But if you trust that you have been justified from sin, all the more and more fervently must Christ hanging on the cross be contemplated by you; without the merit of his passion no one lives righteous on earth. For outside faith in Christ there is no righteousness. However religiously a man may live, if he does not believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, he will by no means attain eternal salvation; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he will necessarily perish forever. The death of Christ opened the gate of salvation, through which no one else can enter except one who faithfully believes in Christ. For this reason Christ humbly subjected himself to the condemnation of death, that he might free believers from the yoke of perpetual damnation. O infinite charity, O immeasurable loving-kindness: who, believing in you, eternal majesty, would not marvel at such astonishing benefits granted to us? For your passion, Lord Jesus, is the price of our salvation, the refuge [unclear] of sinners, the singular remedy of infirm minds, the fountain, origin, and end of all good things. Therefore, now, dearest brothers, let us recall and diligently bring back to memory the bitterness of the Lord’s passion, so that, since we necessarily acknowledge ourselves to be sinners, we may at last be able to be justified through the merit of that very savior of ours. For meditation on the Lord’s passion surpasses all exercises of this kind, if it has been continued for a longer time with the fervor of inward devotion. That mind of a monk which, kindled by zeal for divine love, has been accustomed every day, at least for a little hour, to keep the memory of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ with tears, does not easily lie open to the suggestions of demons. For that heart which the love of Jesus possesses always remains inaccessible and closed to all evil thoughts. Truly blessed is that monk, and never to be named except with honor, who meditates day and night with loving zeal on the teaching and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; who never forgets his Savior; who, whether he eats or drinks or does anything else, always beholds with the eyes of the mind the Lord Jesus hanging on the cross. No pernicious thoughts have their course in his heart; no evil or idle word proceeds from his mouth; he thinks of nothing except Jesus crucified for us, and whatever

    Homily XVII. Fo. XL.

    he restrains: he calms avarice, [unclear] sloth, mitigates [unclear], uproots pride by the roots. Moreover, no passion of a carnal thing wearies the mind of a man whom the passion of Christ truly occupies. O how sweetly he burns whom the memory of Jesus’ passion sweetly inflames. O how blessed is the mind that embraces the continual meditation of Christ’s death. O good Jesus, my love of the cross, who are the salvation and health of faithful souls, grant us to keep continual memory of your passion; grant to your servants always to commend the fasts begun with good works, because then our abstinence will be most pleasing to your uncircumscribable majesty, when it has been adorned with meditation on your precious blood; who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for all ages of ages.

    Here ends Homily XVII.

    On the sleep and wakefulness of monks. Homily XVII.

    The monk who always thinks that he is going to die should permit his eyes to pass no time [unclear]. For Scripture says: “Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Against the forgetful and uncertain, however, it is written: “A people without counsel and without prudence. Would that they were wise and understood and provided for their last things.” The remembrance of death brings watchfulness into the soul and extinguishes every disordered thought of the mind. He who rightly fears death never grows sluggish in good work. For the wise man says: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly; for neither work nor reason nor wisdom nor knowledge will be in the lower world to which you are hastening.” For the monk who is a true worshiper of God spends no moment of time uselessly, but by nights and days, in the exercise of good work, always performs the watchfulness of the mind with the highest devotion; and while sleeping in body, steadfastly in [unclear] he says to the messengers of God: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.” Sleep is the image of death and the binding of the senses of the body; but he who is a true lover

    On the sleep and wakefulness of monks.

    [unclear]. For indeed they mercifully allowed monks in community a space of five hours before the night praises, and likewise added two, or two and a half, after matins for sleep. He for whom this time, namely seven hours, is not sufficient for rest shows himself a very sluggish and slothful monk. Hence we are admonished to keep watch not only in mind but also in body, since he who disdains to keep watch bodily in the service of God is scarcely able to preserve his body in true purity.

    Let us keep watch, therefore, most beloved brothers, especially in these holy days of Lent, in which we have declared war on vices and are firmly prepared to conquer and overcome the ancient enemy, the devil. For you have heard the holy prince of the apostles admonishing in these words: “Brothers, be sober and keep watch.” Why did he give this warning? Because, he says, “your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith.”

    And so, my brothers, let us keep watch as long as we are set in battle, lest at any time, weighed down by drowsiness or idleness, we be overcome by the adversary of our salvation. For as long as we live in the flesh, it is necessary that by watchfulness and chastisement of our body we fight bravely against the enemy. Let the labor of the contest not frighten you, because although our adversary is troublesome, nevertheless he is so weak and feeble that he can overcome no one except one who is willing, and one who has utterly cast off all guard over himself.

    But the Lord Jesus Christ is our strong helper and protector, who grants strength to those who fight eagerly and will bestow on the victors an unfading crown in heaven with all his saints. As dust is scattered by the wind, so our adversary the devil, confounded and terrified by the voice of those singing psalms with humble devotion, is driven away. Therefore let none of you, most beloved brothers, act negligently; let no one in the time of prayer grow dull through sluggishness of mind and drowsiness; let no one fear the contest with the devil with disordered fear.

    Stand manfully for the perpetual salvation of your souls, fighting against a weak adversary, and hold your own flesh no less suspect than demons. For you know, as not only Scripture testifies but also long experience teaches, that the flesh desires against the spirit; and therefore the monk who is not harmed by the wantonness of his own flesh is rarely overcome by demons in the contest. Walk, therefore, in the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.

    Let him who is watchful and a strong fighter rouse the weaker brother, who is sluggish in devotion, and restore him as far as he can, both by words and by examples, to the holy fervor of the spirit. Let him who is spiritual among you not despise his disorderly brother, but rather bring him back through humble admonition to the pursuit of piety. For Scripture says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

    For indeed, if, consenting together in brotherly love toward one another through faith in Jesus Christ, you have always been of one mind, without doubt you will easily conquer your adversary the devil. For where the true charity of Christ makes monks living in a monastery of one mind, there God is worshiped in all holiness; there the invisible presence of holy angels is believed to be present, through whom the rashness of malignant spirits is restrained. In such a congregation of saints God dwells, whom the army of the heavenly kingdom praises together with the voices of the monks singing psalms. A multitude of monks fervent in the love of God is the paradise of the delights of heavenly graces. A city adorned with a multitude of towers is a congregation of monks thinking the same thing in the Lord.

    Keep watch, my brothers, I beseech you, keep watch in holy prayers, and especially at that time shake off drowsiness and dullness of mind when you stand in church before the Lord to sing psalms. For if, standing before God in psalmody, you are fervent in prayer, you will without doubt feel his grace present with you. For he is estranged in mind from the purpose of a monk who while praying thinks of something else, and offers his mind to be stirred not by divine things but by transient matters or occupations. For you know what our holy founder Benedict says in the Rule: “If,” he says, “we wish to suggest anything to powerful men, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence; how much more must supplication be made to the Lord God of all with all humility and devotion of purity; and let us know that we are heard not in much speaking, but in purity of heart and compunction of tears.” Since, however, for us singing psalms

    Homily XVII.

    [unclear] we believe God to be present everywhere, great reverence is needed in prayer, so that our mind may agree in every respect with our voice. Let us therefore consider, brothers, before whom we stand, and to whom, in the sight of the angels, we recite the psalms in prayer; for the monk who, at the time of prayer, [unclear] vain thoughts [unclear] are very necessary to him: but, summoned by his servant, he leaves the king and turns himself to the servant’s vain and useless conversations. Truly anyone who did this would be judged foolish by all, and would rightly seem deserving of the severest punishments.

    But what does the monk deserve who, standing before the highest king of all things and speaking with him about the things that pertain to the salvation of his body, admits into his mind thoughts that are harmful, or even destructive? If one who mocks and despises an earthly king is punished by beheading, what does one deserve who despises the heavenly emperor? Therefore I admonish you, brothers, and with all the sincerity I can I ask that, having purified your hearts, especially at the time of prayer, from the stain of wicked thought, you receive in the mind only what you sing aloud with the mouth.

    As the angels stand always before God with fear and the greatest reverence, singing an everlasting hymn of praise, so let us also take care, my brothers, to stand before him with a pure heart, a clean conscience, and most fervent devotion, so that we may be able to sing his praises much more in spirit than in body. Let us therefore separate our minds from all earthly affairs; let us cleanse our consciences from all enticements of the flesh; let us put on the fervor of the Holy Spirit; and let us drive far from us all sluggishness and idleness. For just as a heavy load weighs down the back of a slothful man, so drowsiness at the time of psalmody is accustomed to oppress the minds of monks.

    Nothing harms monks more than sloth, which little by little enfeebles all the powers of the mind and extinguishes the whole fervor of the spirit. For when a monk has begun to fall away from the fervor of holy devotion, countless evil thoughts enter the mind; and he can now drive them away so much the less, the farther he is convicted of having withdrawn from his former fervor. Hence drowsiness arises [unclear] by the display of services; the mind is burdened by sadness and melancholy, which the monk, growing lukewarm in spirit, strives with all effort to relieve not by spiritual but by earthly and fleshly little consolations. And as he proceeds longer in this alienation of mind, he is hardened, now almost insensible, against the exercise of compunction; and the more he longs for the consolations of the flesh, the farther he wanders from the inward fervor of the spirit.

    For what makes you drowsy at the time of psalmody except sloth? For the mind that has fallen into torpor soon makes the body doze. But again I admonish you, brothers, as I have more often been accustomed to do, that you especially avoid idleness and drowsiness at the time of prayer, since, just as drunkenness brings forgetfulness into the soul, so also drowsiness makes the mind unsound and foolish before God. Wash away this vice of drowsiness, O you young men, by which we grieve that some of the seniors have long since been infected through long habit; among them dozing in choir is familiar, and compunction of mind toward God is exceedingly rare.

    Beware, I say, this evil habit of sleeping, which, after it has once led a monk away captive, rarely allows him to be free. Therefore at the beginning of conversion young men especially must fight against this most pernicious enemy of religion, as someone said in verse: “Resist at the beginnings; medicine is prepared too late when evils have gained strength through long delays. But on that account do not put yourself off into coming hours; he who is not ready today will be less ready tomorrow.” For it is difficult to cure a sickness that has become old through long duration.

    Let us see with how much diligence and attentiveness servants stand before earthly kings and princes, so that we may not be ignorant of how it befits us to stand in prayers before God, who alone is king of all and lord of the universe. The eyes of all look to the lord, and all and each hang most attentively upon his nod, lest anything commanded by him escape those standing by through negligence. From this, then, let us consider with how great purity we ought to stand before the Lord God in the assembly of prayer, day and night, from whom we desire to obtain the kingdom of eternal happiness. Not the voice, not

    On the sleep and wakefulness of monks.

    [unclear]; but the intention of one who is fervent in the love of God deserves to be heard. Therefore flee drowsiness and torpor of mind as a deadly poison, because sleep and idleness are the wellspring of all vices. A watchful eye, however, is the servant of inward devotion, and the monk who truly loves Jesus Christ guards himself from every excess. He who is watchful sharpens the mind with understanding; but the monk who sleeps much shamefully blinds his soul. A monk watchful in prayer and fasting is fearsome to the devil; but he who is sated with food and sleep is not allowed to rest by the spirit of fornication. For wakefulness dedicated to prayers breaks the frenzy of luxury, and powerfully extinguishes the fire of desire; it purifies the inmost parts of the heart, enlightens the mind, and inflames the affection toward the love of heavenly things. Wakefulness is the mother, nurse, and guardian of good thoughts, the certain victory over the temptations of the ancient enemy, the flight of phantasms, the death of vices, and the life and fountain of all virtues. Sleep, however, is the companion and fosterer of lust for many, the robber of human life, the image of death, the procurer of oblivion, the partner of sloth. Immoderate sleep corrupts the stomach, harms the brain, and dissolves both body and soul. A monk frequently given over to sleep despises wisdom, prostitutes chastity, neglects the salvation of the soul, loses precious time, kills the mind, and nourishes vices. Therefore whichever of you, dearly beloved brothers, desires to arrive at the rest of heavenly felicity, let him forcefully repel from himself all torpor and sloth of mind; let him learn first to conquer himself, so that thereafter he may be able to overcome the devil, the enemy of his salvation. For unless you have first exterminated the evil that is in you, when will you overcome that which comes from outside? Learn to command your passions, and, with the Lord’s help, you will easily overcome all things that happen outwardly. Cleanse the mind from every disordered desire, so that in truth you may love Jesus alone above all things, with whom you hope to rejoice forever. But no one will reign with Christ in heaven who does not imitate him with holy conduct while living on earth, as sacred Scripture says: He who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked. For the Lord Jesus, who by his death freed us from the destruction of eternal damnation, himself voluntarily became mediator of God and men; he himself is the way by which the path of life must be continued for us; he himself is the norm and rule of saving conduct for Christians. No one comes to God except through Christ; no one will see the Father except through the Son. Therefore, if you wish to come to salvation, you must pass through the Savior. For he himself said in the holy Gospel: No one comes to the Father except through me. And that other saying: I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will find the pasture of eternal life. And again: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Through this way, I pray you, my brothers, always walk by pious and holy conduct; fervently love this truth with a pure heart; hasten ardently toward this life, which alone is lasting. Let the teaching of Christ never withdraw from your hearts, but remain in memory at all times, since he refuses to become his true imitator who has not been exercised day and night in meditation on his words. Therefore, always watchful in prayers, live with such purity of mind that, when Jesus Christ our Lord calls you in the hour of death, you may deserve to hear him with joy: he who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, one almighty God, forever and ever. Amen.

    On patience and meekness. Homily XVIII.

    Among all professors of the Christian faith there is today no class of men for whom the virtue of patience seems more necessary than for the company of monks. For in these our days, as the charity of many grows cold, to use Paul’s expression, we have been made a spectacle to mortals, so that wherever a monk comes among worldly men, he is marked out by the fingers of almost all who see him to be mocked and derided. Why I have said this you know, you who are not ignorant of what recently happened in the town of Bingen. A drunken crowd of young men and boys received a monk

    Homily XVIII.

    Folio XLII.

    ...someone passing along the public road, and, as though he had presented himself as a traveler because of the rain, threw him into the mud; and by treating the man with injury he made him a pitiable spectacle of his own shamelessness. No one was present to restrain the insolent men; yet the monk’s patience overcame the raging men, and, full of the love of Christ, while he was being mistreated he answered nothing other than “Thanks be to God.” Thus the more he showed himself tranquil in mind and spirit, the more the scoundrels dragged the innocent man about, thinking that he was heated with wine, whom the love of Christ had made joyful and glad.

    He left to all monks a great lesson in patience: when he could have avenged himself, he did not wish to do so though wronged. Would that, my brothers, for love of God and for our sins, we were as patient in the smallest things as that good man was in the greatest. There are among you certain men, I say it unwillingly, too insolent and impatient, who are moved to anger by a word, even one not insulting; and while they are justly corrected for their negligences, they unjustly murmur, adding sin to sin through impatience.

    But to what end do I set before them the patience of the man just mentioned, when they do not heed Jesus Christ, the most patient of all men? Indeed, whoever does not embrace patience and humility after the example of the King of heaven is brought back to gentleness by the imitation of no man. For the Son of God is the highest and supreme example of patience and humility; whoever is not bent to endurance by the recollection of his passion is rightly judged hardened and a companion of demons.

    No good Christian doubts that the words of our Lord Jesus Christ are true. But Christ says in the holy Gospel: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. If the meek are to be called blessed, what prevents the rancorous, wrathful, and unmeek from being named accursed? Certainly nothing. And if, as the Lord himself and our Savior Jesus Christ bears witness, we possess our souls in patience, there is no doubt that we lose them through impatience.

    It is therefore especially fitting that monks be meek, gentle, and patient, who have solemnly devoted themselves to the imitation of Christ and the apostles. But Christ, the meekest of all, commands his disciples and imitators in the Gospel, saying: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: If you wish to reign with Christ in heaven, first learn from him to be meek, patient, humble, and gentle; for unless you have lived in this world after the imitation of his life, you will by no means reign with him forever.

    The divine Ambrose also says: When I have laid aside every sin, and stripped off every malice, and, content with simplicity, have been poor in evils, it remains that I temper my morals. For what does it profit me to be free of crimes, unless I have been meek and gentle? But he is meek who yields to wickedness and does not resist in evil, but overcomes evil with good. And he is gentle, as Chrysostom bears witness, who, when he has been provoked by injuries, neither thinks of doing evil nor does it.

    Cassiodorus, however, says: We call the gentle “accustomed to the hand,” that is, patient and meek, who tolerate the iniquities of others and do not presume to burden anyone. Of such persons it is said in the psalm: My soul shall be praised in the Lord; let the gentle hear and rejoice. He did not say, Let those skilled in the law rejoice, nor those who fast, nor those who sing psalms, but the gentle, who, together with charity, have been accustomed above all to have moderation in all things.

    But those are truly meek, gentle, and patient who harm no one, injure no one, offend absolutely no one, but, standing firm in their simple humility, always bear all injuries, insults, and mockeries evenly for the love of Christ, and are moved by no pain of spirit against those who harm them, just as we have already said that monk was, whom at Bingen the raging boys treated with exceedingly insulting behavior.

    But it is easy to be meek, patient, and gentle so long as nothing is done except according to the will and judgment of the one who is patient. Yet it will become clear how far he is from true gentleness if a slight occasion arises. It is a great virtue if you do not harm the one by whom you have been harmed; great strength of soul if, for the love of God, you forgive injury to the one who inflicts it; great glory if you observe the commandment of Christ and pour out prayers for those who injure you. No one has known the powers of his own soul whom a notable insult has not yet burned; let no one boast himself meek or patient who has not been sated with reproaches. There is no patience without adversity, nor gentleness without insult, since if due

    On Patience and Gentleness

    If you wish to keep the bounds of endurance, first of all there will have to be someone present who inflicts an insult. “If I had lived,” says the lazy and sensual monk, “in the days of the martyrs, I would have feared to undergo no kinds of punishments for the love of Christ; I would voluntarily have exposed my body to the torturers, so that I might carry off the crown of martyrdom.” Great is the rashness of folly. You have never been able to suffer a word patiently for the love of God, and do you promise the steadfastness of the holy martyrs? You fear a light correction, you who promise that you will give your body for Christ.

    If martyrdom delights you, hear what the most blessed pope Gregory says. If, with Christ helping us, we strive to preserve the virtue of patience and live in the peace of the Church, we also hold the palm of martyrdom. For we can be martyrs without sword and flame, if we truly keep patience in our soul. To die at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in open deed; but to bear insults and love the one who hates you is martyrdom in hidden thought. Patience, however, is to endure another’s evils with equanimity, and not to be gnawed by any grief against the one who brought the evil.

    What now will you say, lazy monk, who, incapable of suffering the very light martyrdom of words, boast so insolently of steadfastness in shedding blood? Learn, wretch, to have patience in light matters, and consider that, as Scripture says, if a man is unfaithful in a little, who would entrust to him what is greater? You murmur at everything that happens in the monastery; when rebuked, however gently, for your grave offenses and negligences, you bear it most impatiently. In your eyes no one walks rightly in the monastery; no one except you, in your estimation, conducts himself religiously. You alone, as it seems to you, are holy in the monastery; you, most learned of all, concede that no one knows what you alone do not know. You think yourself, above all others, worthy of all honors, because you not only lack patience, but retain neither true humility nor obedience.

    This is not the way by which one goes to the kingdom of heaven: when in the school of humility a monk is proud, and by his conduct a Christian lives contrary to Christ. But a monk, the solemnly sworn servant of Jesus Christ, in order that he may imitate his Lord, ought not to be proud but humble, obedient not rebellious, gentle not cruel, nor insolent but mild. But a monk who is proud, wrathful, contentious, and a lover of his own will, such as, alas, those set over temporal affairs often are, whom among us according to the Rule we call cellarers: their pride has made for many a road to destruction.

    Grief compels me to speak, and shame forbids me, although you all know the fall by which the devil lately brought shame upon us in the case of a brother. Who in our whole congregation was prouder than he? Who went about filled with greater insolence? But because he seemed among us to have greater experience in temporal matters, on that account he considered himself superior to all. The Almighty permitted him to fall, so that he who, [unclear], had refused to recognize his own weakness, at last confounded, not without the scandal of many, might understand that God is the adversary of the proud.

    I grieve vehemently, and more than can be said; the fault of the man who fell seems to me heavier, because by his fall we are all confounded. May God grant him to do true penance, so that those who had been scandalized by his fall may be edified by his satisfaction before God and men. Pride has always been destructive to monks; and the mind of a man which it has once invaded it sinks into the pit of all vices. Beware pride, my brothers, because it is the beginning of every sin; it is that which through the envy of the devil introduced death into the world. Pride is the death of all virtues, and the source and spring of all vices. Humility, however, the nurse of virtues, most befits monks, because it makes them both mild and gentle. For every proud man is impatient, and every arrogant man an enemy of gentleness. He who is humble of heart has patience in adversities for the love of God; and he who is tranquil in soul in the face of injuries merits a double crown.

    A patient man in adversities becomes close to God; but he who is proud and impatient gladdens his enemies. For Scripture says: Better is the patient man than the strong man, and he who rules his own soul than the conqueror of cities. Likewise the holy bishop Augustine says: The just and pious man ought to be ready to endure patiently the malice of those whom he desires to become good, so that rather the number of the good may increase, and not that by equal malice someone should add himself to the number of the evil. For patience is very necessary for us, brothers, so that, doing God’s holy will, we may receive in Christ

    All things. XVIII. Fol. XLIII.

    Promise. Daily there are adversities at hand for us by which we may be exercised; therefore, just as a cause for endurance is never lacking, so, I pray, may necessary patience always be present. We are oppressed by want and poverty of necessary things; we are burdened by traffic with the weak flesh; besides, the world tempts us in order to entice us; the devil tempts us in order to seduce us. Among so many adversaries of our salvation, it is necessary, brothers, that we keep watch in all patience and humility, since in this pilgrimage, as long as we live, we are placed, so to speak, in the midst of evils. Our poverty ought to suffice us, because it does not belong to monastic religion to be exalted in temporal things, but rather to be cast down, so that monks, poor in imitation of Christ, who was made poor for us, may deserve to glory with him forever in heaven.

    What if we see certain wicked men and sinners in the world abounding in riches? If good and just men are rich in this world, provision is made by God’s providence not for their strength but for their weakness, so that by benefits they may be called forth to better things. “I was young,” says the prophet, “and have grown old, and I have not seen the just man forsaken, nor his seed begging.” “Cast,” he says, “your thought upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you; he will not forever give wavering to the just.” The Lord Jesus knows what is fitting for each one of his little servants for salvation, and therefore he dispenses the gifts of the present life unequally according to the capacity of individuals. For all things are not fitting for all; therefore, among the just in this world, with respect to temporal goods, some are poor, while others are wealthy. Concerning the poor the Lord Jesus says in the holy Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And through the prophet he speaks, saying: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.” For it does not conduce to eternal salvation for all to possess the riches of this world; rather, it is expedient for some to be poor and for others to be wealthy, according as the Lord of all has provided what is more useful for each.

    Concerning just and good rich men. The blessing of the Lord makes men rich, and affliction will not be joined to it. But if the wicked and reprobate abound in riches in this age, this ought not move the good to indignation; rather let them fear him who leaves no good unrewarded and no evil unpunished. For the wicked, whom he cannot reward in heaven because of their iniquity, he rewards in this life for their good deeds; and for the good, whom he nourishes here in poverty, he preserves eternal rewards in heaven for the merit of justice. But just as not all the poor in this world are just and good, so not all those rich in temporal goods in this life are wicked. The reward of the wicked on earth should rightly be borne without indignation, since not love of God but justice has willed it to be present. Hence, just as the wicked have nothing in heaven, so you who have professed monastic poverty ought to have nothing on earth; but in hope of that good toward which you strive, whatever adversity befalls you on the way, you ought to bear it most patiently. For, as Paul, the holy lover of Christ, says: “The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that will be revealed in us.” Let those who are rich in Christ join mercy to humility; but those who are poor, let them take patience with innocence for the love of God. For the soldier of Christ is neither cast down by poverty nor lifted up by riches, but, standing firm in himself, with tranquil spirit he serves the King of heaven and cares nothing for transitory things. Thus the true monk is neither exalted by praises nor broken by reproach; he is not swollen by an abundance of necessary things, nor contracted by poverty; he despises both prosperity and adversity alike, because, as the prophet had said, “the sun shall not burn him by day, nor the moon by night.”

    But we, dearest brothers, let us make a virtue and a good will out of necessity, and out of the disadvantage of poverty, which we must necessarily endure, let us acquire for ourselves a great and useful patrimony of goods; this can at last be done if, for the love of God, we bear this very want manfully and with tranquil spirit. The deformed conduct of our predecessors brought upon this monastery the poverty that we suffer; but the mercy of almighty God, if we have kept his commandments with a perfect heart, will without doubt relieve it in time. For almost two hundred years back, as far as we can ascertain both by conjecture and from the writings of those who preceded us—

    On patience and gentleness

    [unclear]: the purity of monastic institution in this monastery of Spanheim, as also in almost all others, failed; and the disordering of the life of the monks utterly dissipated the entire substance of earthly goods.

    Indeed, when, in the Christian year one thousand four hundred and sixty-nine, Frederick, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, a most Christian man who resided in Simmern, held the corrupt life of the monks in his principality in very great hatred, he reformed three monasteries after expelling the deformed monks, and introduced men very well trained from other monasteries. And first indeed he brought back two monasteries of regular canons of Saint Augustine to the observance of regular discipline: Ravengiersburg, namely, among the [unclear], and Schwabenheim among the [unclear], in the district of the Nahegau. Lastly, in the aforesaid year of the Lord, he also renewed this present monastery of ours, Spanheim, for the reform of the order; and, after removing the abbot together with five monks, he restored in their place four others by observance, over whom he set my predecessor Johannes of Kölnhausen, now serving as abbot in Seligenstadt.

    But they found the place oppressed by such poverty and burdened with another’s debt that there was no one who believed it could be restored, since all the annual revenues had either been sold or alienated under title of redemption; nor was anything at all left from which they might live. Present as reporter and witness of the things we say is our brother Heinrich, one of the first four reformers sent from Mainz; from his mouth you will learn everything more fully. And behold, the seventeenth year is now passing since this place began to be restored under the chapter of the reformed union of Bursfelde, and still we are being tried by no small poverty.

    I have said these things for this reason, brothers: that you may know that we do not bear alone the necessity we suffer, since those four men who first reformed the monastery endured heavier things; for beans and peas had satisfied their bellies, and a thin drink of pear-cider furnished them drink by measure. The mercy of God called us to this place, that through patience we may overcome the [unclear] of our salvation, so that, according to the counsel of the divine apostle, having scant food and a garment with which to cover ourselves, content and giving thanks to the Lord, we may serve in cheerfulness of mind.

    For we are not called to feasts of the flesh, nor to the delights of this world, not to pleasures nor to the comforts of the present life, but to serve as soldiers for the Lord and our emperor Jesus Christ in abstinence from all the delights of this age, in a pure conscience and humility of heart. Attend now therefore to your calling, monks, and do not corrupt the purpose of holiness, if you desire to come to the glory of God.

    Woe to you, faithless monk, who, made a despiser of your calling and a transgressor of your vow, live in the monastery not monastically; you who were called to tolerate tribulation patiently for love of God, and inquire about refreshment. For your profession commands you to go humbly content in every vileness and extremity of clothing, and you do not fear to devote effort to curiosity about garments. You have been called to thirst, and you, despising drinking water, delight in drinking wine to satiety, against the monastic canon. You were made a monk to fight bravely against the adversary of your salvation, and you, having cast away from yourself the arms of the virtues, proceed lazy, idle, and naked; indeed, what is more serious, accompanied by a troop of vices. You were invited to keep watch in holy prayers, and you are dissolved by sluggish sleep and base idleness. You were called into the subjection of humble obedience, and you, swollen with pride, despise obeying the commands of the elders. You were called into charity, and you do not fear to carry hatred against your brother in your breast. You were called to weeping and tears, and [unclear] with deep, disordered laughter. The Lord called you to penitence in the monastery, and you, dissolved into wantonness, join sin to sin. You were called to meditate day and night on the law of our Lord Jesus Christ, and you walk after vanity, applying yourself to tales and perishable things. You were called to heaven, and you, loving the world, pursue earthly things. The Lord called you into the meekness of humility, and you proceed full of rancor and pride. You were called by the Lord to the perfection of the purest monastic way of life, and you, like beasts of burden, rot away in the dung of vanity and negligence. To the observance

    All things. XVIII. Folio XLIII.

    ... you have been called by the gifts of God; and you, given over to the pleasures of the flesh, think of nothing less than Christ. You have been invited to love the Lord Jesus above all things, and you walk according to the evil desires of your heart; you show yourself ungrateful to your Redeemer. You, who ought to have lived by the spirit, savor earthly things, and, sunk in pride, despise all the holy exercises of spiritual conduct.

    And what will you answer on that day of judgment to the Judge, who will say to you, most ungrateful one: I, who am Lord of all things, humbled myself for your sake, taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a man; I poured out my blood for you; for you I endured blows; and for you I underwent a death exceedingly bitter, by my own free will. I, O monk, loved you with my whole heart; I redeemed you by my blood from perpetual death; I called you in love to the heavenly kingdom, if you had kept my commandments. But you lived in opposition to my precepts, and, what is worse, though you had sworn upon my words, you were not afraid to show yourself an apostate and impious traitor against me, your Lord. Now therefore render an account of your stewardship.

    What then will you answer, O lazy and idle monk, who now consume this acceptable time so fruitlessly, and despise living in true monastic purity according to the rule? What, I say, will you answer? Will you deny the works of depravity that you have committed, and show deceitfully the good works that you now scorn to perform, so that by a lie you may circumvent the Judge and thus escape the punishment due to your demerits? But you must not be ignorant that all things that you have done, said, or thought throughout your whole life, good and evil, are manifest in the sight of the Judge, and nothing can be hidden from him, who alone knows all things. For all things are written in the book of God, and your conscience will bear open testimony against you concerning all things badly done, so that not even the least thought will be able to be hidden. For the scripture of the prophets says to God: “Because the thought of man shall confess to you.” You are before the tribunal of the all-knowing Judge, before whose terrible judgment every creature will stand with very great fear and trembling; there no excuse at all is admitted, but each shall receive the sentence due to his merits, with appeal set aside. Thousands of thousands and ten hundred thousand holy spirits will attend him; and do you trust that you can deceive the Judge by a lie?

    But hear my counsel, and, rising from your ruinous sloth, at last, while there is time, return to righteousness. Do not put it off from day to day, because it is exceedingly dangerous for one remaining in sins to be confident, and to reject the remedy of salvation that is offered. Remember that you are going to die, and when you do not expect it you will be called to judgment. Consider, I beg you, how uncertain the time of life is, how it slips away, and how quickly all mortal things are corrupted. Nothing among human things is stable, nothing fixed, nothing firm; but all things that we see are corruptible, and are changed with time.

    Consider also where now our brothers Valentius, Martin, and John are, who in the present year, living with us, were healthy, unharmed, and glad; they spoke with us alike, ate, drank, and labored, thinking of nothing less than that they would die this year. Behold, when they did not think it, death came and seized them, and set their souls before the tribunal of the fearful Judge, who rendered to each according to the works of his hands. Behold, now learn by the example of your brothers that you too are going to die, and perhaps you will pass from this world much sooner than you can estimate.

    Come to your senses, wretched man, while you still can; do penance in the time of your health, when the Judge promises mercy, and do not put off today’s good into the uncertainty of tomorrow. Rise up, even now, late though it is, at last from the sloth of your too negligent past conduct, in which you have hitherto shamefully rotted; and cleanse your conscience from every stain of sin; wipe away with tears the evil that you have committed; and from now on live innocently, as befits a monk. Take up the perfect resolution of amendment, and understand that the kingdom of heaven is promised not to those who begin the good, but to those who persevere unto the end. Know also that heaven is not reached by sloth and torpor, but by great labor, by the very great effort of a will to make progress, and by unwearied zeal for spiritual exercise.

    Therefore, wishing to serve the Lord and to please him in truth, always remain within yourself, fearful in dread, and prepare your soul for temptation. One must resist strongly disordered impulses and desires

    On patience and meekness

    of the flesh: one must resist, with a most steadfast mind, all the allurements and vanities of the world; through prayers and greatness of spirit the demon, the adversary of our salvation, must be put to flight. No drowsy, lazy, and slothful person has ever come to the kingdom of God; no one has obtained heaven without continual labor and much sweat. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent, that is, those who have learned to resist steadfastly the evil desires of the flesh, seize it.

    Review the deeds of all the saints, and nowhere will you find anyone made holy without great and continual labor. For although no one becomes holy by his own powers, nevertheless, by the gracious mercy of the almighty Lord, which grants to those who struggle both the will to do good and the strength, no one is sanctified without works of a good and right will. Since, therefore, God wishes all human beings to be saved and none to perish, we, my brothers, must take the greatest care not to receive his grace in vain, but rather must strive with all our powers, so that, as [a field?] [unclear], we may always respond to the free gifts of so great a sower with worthy fruits from works of good will.

    Let us therefore arm ourselves with the shield of faith, and put on the breastplate of steadfastness and saving patience, so that, prepared against all things that can befall us, through humility and the fervor of the Holy Spirit, with our Lord Jesus Christ helping us, we may conquer. In all these things patience is very necessary for us; without its aid there never was, nor could there ever be, perseverance in good and holy works. For there was no other road to heaven for the saints than patience, nor could anyone ever be sanctified who cast patience away.

    Indeed, all who have pleased almighty God from the beginning of the world down to this our age have triumphed over the prince of the world in no other way than through patience. Hence all of them could most rightly say that saying of the psalmist: For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter. The most holy apostle of Christ, Paul, also, commemorating the patience of the saints of old, says among other things: They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves and caverns of the earth. For all who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution, because, as the prophet says: Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them.

    Patience, therefore, is necessary for all mortals, and it especially befits cloistered persons, since just as adversities are never lacking to the righteous in this world, so no one will be justified without patience. There are, moreover, three principal degrees of patience, as the diligence of the ancients has distinguished them. The first, and weakest, is that of those people who neither seek adversities nor willingly endure them, but when they occur are weighed down in spirit and cast down by sorrow. They even complain at times and murmur for a while against those who inflict them; but after the inflamed agitation of the mind has passed, they return to themselves, and seem to endure patiently, without vengeance, the insult inflicted upon them. Yet the patience of these people, being of no great virtue, is always very near to the fault of an unquiet mind, and therefore must often be judged of no merit, and sometimes of lesser merit.

    And although such people in our times are said to have the virtue of patience, who, though they do not seek to suffer evils, nevertheless when they come receive them willingly and kindly, and embrace them most patiently as a gift sent from God. And such people are truly to be called patient, who, kindled by divine love, endure with equanimity whatever adversity may come, and in tribulation preserve the same disposition that they had before. I would not doubt that the most holy Job the Idumaean was of their number: struck not only by extreme adversity, he bore all things patiently, but even when placed in the abyss of evils, giving thanks, he blessed the Lord, saying: The Lord gave, the Lord took away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord.

    It is fitting that all Christians, and before others especially cloistered persons, observe this degree of patience. For the wise man says: The learning of a man through

    Homily XVIII. Fol. XLV.

    patience is discerned. For the more learned each person has been in the law of the Lord and in knowledge of the ordinance of rational nature, the more patient he will be in adversity. What if, as a lover of truth, I speak more boldly: adversities profit us more than prosperous things, if we are learned and not forgetful weighers of our own condition. But the third degree of patience, certainly the highest and most perfect beyond the rest, is rightly granted to those who not only, when there is need, endure contrary things with equanimity for the love of God and the benefit of the brethren, but who also, more fervent and inflamed with the spirit of charity, thrust themselves forward of their own accord and hasten gladly to receive insults and injuries. And this kind of patience is divided in two ways, just as a twofold account of martyrdom is found. For some, though they could have lain hidden in the persecution of believers, with the charity of Christ burning in them, under no compulsion but by their own free will, presented themselves to the tribunals of persecutors; publicly confessing him as redeemer of the world, they received with joy the torments inflicted on them. Others, however, did not thrust themselves forward of their own accord, yet gladly received the martyrdom offered them, always prepared to endure for the faith of Christ whatever the cruelty of tyrants could inflict. To this degree hasten the most shining confessors, by merit very near to them; and if the cruelty of the impious, by persecuting them, did not take them away, nevertheless they in no way lost the glory of martyrdom. For, crucifying their flesh in this world for the name of Christ, they endured both a voluntary and a lasting martyrdom; through abstinence and humility they were made glorious, always remaining steadfast in spirit and most patient, and most ready to receive martyrdom bodily. Therefore take care, O monks, to be imitators of these according to your powers; and since enemies who kill the body for Christ are now lacking, by struggling against the desires of the flesh and by patiently enduring adversities for the love of God, show yourselves martyrs in mind and spirit. The best kind of martyrdom in the peace of the saints is to afflict the flesh for the name of God through abstinence, to desire nothing in this world, always to make progress in good works, and if anything evil should befall, to bear it in all things gladly and patiently with cheerfulness of mind. Henceforth, dearest brethren, live according to this rule of patience, if you desire to reign eternally with Christ. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ: let each person gladly bestow upon his brother what he desires to be done for himself.

    On the True Humility of Monks: Nineteenth Homily.

    It is almost the opinion of all the learned, dearest brethren, that the highest and chief virtue of monks is none other than humility, because it is itself the mother and nurse of all virtues. For humility makes the monk; pride destroys and corrupts him. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: To whom shall I look, if not to the poor little one and the contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my words? For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, because pride is the beginning of every sin, and without true humility no one can obtain salvation. Since this is so, I think it necessary for me, brethren, to exhort you without ceasing that, fleeing pride, you always preserve profound humility in all your works. Indeed no good work is believed to please the Lord God if it is presented without the seasoning of humility. For humility is the most healthful medicine of faithful souls, which provides for all, because it presses down the swollen ulcers of the spirit, restores what is wasting away, corrects what is depraved, and removes what is overgrown. O humility, mother and parent of all virtues, you strengthen patience, stir up compunction, illuminate charity, adorn chastity, make prayer fruitful, and commend fasting and abstinence. O holy humility, truly beloved of God, you justify the impious through penance; you preserve the just man in the purpose of holiness; you powerfully open heaven to your lovers; you close hell to the penitent. O humility to be venerated, exceedingly pleasing to God, you compelled the Son of the eternal Father to descend from heaven into the womb of Mary, the most chaste ark, the perpetual virgin; you made him appear visible to us, and you laid him, wrapped in poor cloths, in the manger, so that he might adorn us with the ornaments of perpetual blessedness in heaven. You [unclear] the Son of God by the circumcision of the flesh

    On the True Humility of Monks.

    you impelled [him] to undertake, so that, circumcised in mind, we might be able to enter into the promised inheritance of the saints. O humility of great power, which made the king of heaven and earth withdraw from the face of one most worthless little man, and dwell in seven years’ exile in the land of the Egyptians. You compelled Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, to assume a human body for our salvation, and made him undergo the most bitter passion and death by his voluntary will. Great is your dominion, O venerable humility of holiness, since to you the kingdom of heaven is promised; to your worshippers the gift of everlasting blessedness is granted; and whoever keeps to your footsteps is raised to the height of the angels, as Christ says in the holy Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” The [unclear] of heaven taught [unclear] when he said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” Likewise the most blessed mother, the inviolate Virgin Mary, in her own sweetest canticle of praise, speaks thus of the Lord God: “He has cast down the mighty from their seats, and exalted the humble.” And the prophet says in the psalm: “The Lord has looked upon the prayers of the humble, and has not despised their petitions.” O prayer of one who humbles himself: it penetrates the clouds, and until it draws near it will not be comforted, and it will not depart until the Most High looks upon [what is] good. Humility makes the monk pure in his conscience most pleasing to God; and the more he casts himself down by humbling himself for the honor of God, the more glorious he will appear in the kingdom. The monk who truly humbles himself is made a son of the Most High through participation in grace, and will rejoice forever with the king of heaven, Jesus Christ. He who truly desires to imitate Christ should also assume true humility; clothed and fortified with it as with a breastplate of strength, he may do great things, and, thinking nothing of himself except humble things, may not incur the stain of vainglory. For this is the true perfection of monks: always humbly to recognize one’s own imperfection, and rather to reflect diligently on what good is lacking to him than on what he has. For true humility, through the desire of charity, is always stretched toward the things before it; and, a cautious rememberer of things past, it fears lest it lose what it has, and, desiring to acquire through the zeal of devotion what it does not yet have, in the fervor of holiness

    All things, xix. Fol. XLVI.

    [unclear] is raised up; it is sustained by the rock of humility alone. Indeed, if true humility is lacking, the whole gathering of the other virtues will be nothing other than a kind of ruin of a house built without foundation on sand. For in the spiritual building humility lays a stable foundation; charity orders the breadth of that house; the wall is raised on high by the continuous joining of good works in the fervor of the spirit; in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ and in firm hope of the promise of eternal protection and blessedness it is set straight at the summit; and its length is arranged in the most beautiful order in the long-suffering of patience.

    Therefore, my brothers, again and again I admonish, adjure, and beseech you to take care to found the building of spiritual exercise in the depth of humility, because no good work is pleasing to God that has been offered outside true humility. Now there are many things which are accustomed to stir the servants of God to true humility. For the consideration of their own worthlessness humbles some within themselves before God, because, when they consider that they have already often experienced themselves to be wretched and weak, they place all their hope and confidence in God, humbled. Others, weighing the multitude of God’s benefits toward them, fear the judgment of ingratitude; and therefore in the sight of God, with great fear and reverence of gratitude, they always walk humbly.

    And who among us, brothers, is there to whom the compassion of almighty God has not granted many benefits, even singular ones? If we wish to be grateful for them, above all we must be humble. Others, converted by divine mercy after a multitude of sins to penitence, diligently recall to memory how many evils they have committed against the law of the almighty; and for these, humbled in bitterness of spirit, they detest their own impieties with horror. But we offend in many things; hence it is necessary that we humble ourselves always in mind and heart, and even in body, so that grace may abound where sin previously abounded.

    Often, moreover, the providence of divine mercy permits certain persons to sin enormously for a time, so that afterward, converted to penitence, they may learn to remain in true humility. A humble penitent is higher than one who has not sinned but is proud, because humility justifies penitents, while pride condemns the arrogant eternally, even if they have done nothing else evil than this alone, that they are proud.

    Others, carrying in their heart by daily meditation the bitter passion of Christ Jesus, humble themselves so much the more, the more they know that they are very insufficient debtors for such great and wondrous benefits of their Redeemer. The Son of God humbled himself, being made man for us, and, filled with many reproaches, voluntarily underwent the most shameful death of the cross, to free us from the destruction of perpetual death. What Christian man, and especially what monk, will not greatly humble his soul before God when he has recalled to memory such great humility of his Creator and Redeemer? Indeed, the man whom Christ’s humility does not stir to meekness: no admonitions of men will profit in him. In vain are we called monks, unless according to our strength we have humbly followed Christ. For this reason he said in the holy Gospel that he is the way, so that we may imitate his humility, and the way of life of so great a master may become the spiritual form of the disciple.

    And so, brothers, as much as we can, let us labor with all our strength, since for us he humbled himself into such great humility. Therefore the highest medicine for inducing true humility in the servant of God is this: if daily and very often he recalls to memory the most bitter passion of Christ Jesus.

    Tribulations, adversities, and illnesses, together with poverty or want, have also made many humble who perhaps in prosperous and favorable circumstances would have perished, puffed up. And we trust that the poverty which we often say conduces to our salvation does so, since we have a great cause of humility, but find no matter at all for elation and pride. Others, by continual exercise of virtues and by the memory of the death which they must necessarily suffer shortly, have come to great humility. Whom, even the proudest, would not the intent meditation of death humble?
