Or who is so fierce in spirit that he would not little by little lay aside his swelling pride, if he considered more diligently that he will die shortly? Therefore the conscience of a monk must by no remembrance drive from itself the thought of future death, so that he may remain both humble and sorrowful, so that, standing firm in humility, he may not [unclear].

    On the true humility of monks.

    Let continual sorrow forbid every wantonness to the heart. God’s gratuitous compassion also anticipates some men, and by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit makes them humble. Everyone who is led by the Spirit of God utterly detests pride. He who truly knows himself is most wise, and cannot depart from the meekness of humility. But everyone proud and arrogant is ignorant, even if he seems great and renowned among mortals. For true wisdom rests in the dwelling-place of holy humility, and it is shown the more clearly through the lesson of patience. From the knowledge of God and of oneself humility is born, and this is rightly called true wisdom. He who has truly known himself now has nothing from which to grow proud, because, knowing his own vileness, he thinks nothing lofty, but, placed in sorrow of soul, cries to the Lord: What is man, that you are mindful of him? or the son of man, that you regard him? Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow. Why then is earth and ashes proud? Why does the spirit of frail and mortal man swell against God?

    Humble yourselves, therefore, my dearest brothers, as it is written, under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation. For humility with chaste fear greatly pleases the Lord God in his servants, since he approves no virtue of man without it unto salvation. Therefore, if we desire to climb to the throne of the high kingdom of heaven, we must be very humble, because there is no other road to heaven except that of deepest humility, by which both the Son of God himself and all the saints ascended. But all who tried to enter the kingdom by another gate, struck back on the threshold of humility, with the head of pride [unclear], could by no means enter. For the gate of humility does not admit the proud, and [unclear] the narrow way to the kingdom [unclear], he undoubtedly falls into the depth of perdition and death.

    For humility is the ladder of heaven, beautifully marked off by twelve steps; concerning its ascent our lawgiver Benedict says in the Rule: If we wish to attain the highest summit of humility, and to come swiftly to that heavenly exaltation, we must set up for ourselves that ladder which appeared to Jacob in a dream, by which angels were shown to him ascending and descending. Without doubt that descent and ascent is understood by us as nothing other than to descend by exaltation and to ascend by humility, as divine Scripture indicates to us: Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted. But that ladder set upright is our life in this world, which, when the heart has been humbled, is raised up by the Lord into heaven. For we say that the sides of this same ladder are our body and soul. Into these sides the divine calling has inserted the various steps of humility and discipline to be climbed.

    Thereafter he enumerates those twelve steps themselves in order with a sufficiently beautiful arrangement; since they are entirely well known to you, it would be superfluous to be occupied at greater length this time in reciting them. For it is enough in this place to remember the holy canon, upon whose words all of you long ago swore voluntarily, so that you may know that humility is no less necessary for your salvation than love of God and at the same time of neighbor. For the greatest virtue of a monk is said to be humility, and by reason of his profession it is so necessary that without it he cannot be saved. A monk lifted up in spirit and proud will not have Christ, the Son of God, in heaven, but with the demons in hell he will be tormented without end. For Christ, the master and teacher of humility, detests all the proud, and admits into his fellowship only the humble, the mild, and the meek. But the devil is the head and inventor of pride; his servants and disciples are all who follow his pride and haughtiness. For he himself, the king of the proud, cannot bear humility; he flees the meek, and does not presume to stand in the sight of those meek in heart. For in the assembly of the humble servants of God Christ dwells; but in the midst of the proud the devil stirs up quarrels and disputes among those at discord. Where humility has been, there is true peace and the highest tranquillity; but where pride rules, wrath, anger, disturbance, and discord without interruption throw everything into confusion.

    Therefore beware pride, my brothers, because if it cast down the angels from heaven when they were lifted up, when would it not condemn poor cloistered men? It made demons out of angels; without doubt it makes companions of demons out of monks. To those who follow humility

    All things. 19. Fol. 47.

    [unclear] at all times, with all your strength and as much as you can, flee all pride and ostentation, for unless you greatly humble your souls, you will not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Always walk before Jesus in the simplicity of your heart, having a pure conscience in all things, lest your humility become bestial; for it contributes nothing to salvation for a sinner to acknowledge himself publicly and, by persevering in evil, not amend his fault. For the true servant of Christ sanctifies his humility by good works, and amends every guilt of his past life by continual penitence. Daily he recalls to memory the evil that he remembers himself to have committed, and groans that he has gravely offended the Lord. Let him walk very cautiously, and so lament past sins committed that he in no way commit further things that must be lamented.

    The monk who is truly humble follows the Lord Jesus with a pure conscience, and fears nothing in this world more than to offend the teacher whom he imitates. Whatever he does and wherever he goes, he always thinks of the Lord Jesus as present, and by continual meditation examines how he may please him alone. For this is true and Christian humility, and humble Christianity: to wash away sin in true compunction, and to preserve the conscience in all purity at all times, not only from fear, but rather from love of Christ. The true humility of monks continually does whatever good it can for the honor of God, and thinks that it will do nothing that it knows to displease Christ. The true humility of monks neglects none of those things which God has commanded, and always flees as deadly those things which he has forbidden.

    The penitent monk, humble in compunction of tears and serving the Lord in the fervor of charity, is a companion of the holy angels, a friend to the citizens of heaven, and very formidable to demons. For demons fear and flee nothing more than the humility of the servants of Jesus Christ, because, since they themselves are most proud by their vicious will, they are most violently tormented by the devotion of the humble. For where there is true humility, demons cannot remain; for as ice is dissolved by fire, so malignant spirits are scattered from the presence of a humble monk.

    O venerable mother and preserver of all virtues, humility: yours is the kingdom, yours the power; you confer the kingdom on the humble; you bestow the glory of eternal felicity on the meek; without your guidance no one comes to heaven; he who follows you does not fear hell. Whoever gathers works of virtue without you is like one who carries dust into the wind. You are the seasoning of all good works, for just as food in the mouth of the eater is not savory without salt, so without your companionship no one is established as a friend of God.

    Humility made the Son of God man. Humility will make the servant of Christ equal to the holy angel. An angel, through pride in his own judgment, became a devil; and the Christian man through humility becomes an angel. Humility opens heaven to the meek servants of God, and pride plunges exalted men down to hell. Humility makes friends of God, and pride makes companions of demons. Humility illuminates the mind to true wisdom, and pride blinds the understanding of the one whom it has possessed. Humility, once all disordered affections have been purged, [unclear] the man whom it possesses; and pride fills its worshiper with all crimes and filthiness. Humility makes its lover a servant of God, but pride makes him a slave of the devil. Humility makes a man wise in the law of the Lord, but pride renders a man foolish in the knowledge of the Most High. Humility brings the poor man into fellowship with God, and pride makes the rich man a member of the devil. Humility is the mother and nurse of all virtues, and pride is the source of all vices. Humility, with charity mediating, covers a multitude of sins; but pride alone brings in the fullness of all vices. Humility makes the good works of monks most pleasing to God, but pride renders the pursuits of the proud idle before the Creator. Humility receives from the Lord whatever it has asked; but God almighty resists the prayers of the proud. Humility always has, in the mercies of the Lord, a pious confidence with gladness of mind; but pride, by the sting of despair, generates disturbance in man. Humility always has joy of spirit in the love of Christ; but pernicious fear always occupies pride. Humility, the fosterer of good works, neglects none of the spiritual exercises; but pride despises all pursuits of salvation. Humility justifies sinners; but pride condemns its followers. Humility makes one near to God; but pride makes one alien from the grace of God.

    On the true humility of monks.

    Humility eagerly obeys the commandments of God with a peaceful will; pride struggles against the precepts of the Most High. Humility heaps up the merits of everlasting happiness; pride, however, prepares for itself the most grievous torments of hell. Humility affords security at the point of death; but pride brings horrible fear and calamity to the dying man. Humility frees the soul of its worshipper from every distress in the dread judgment of God; but pride accuses before the Judge all the haughty whom it deceived in the world. Humility will place the servants of God at the Judge’s right hand; but pride will set those to be damned on the left. Humility will plead the cause for its own and will prevail in the judgment; but pride, utterly confounded, will hand over the haughty to the devil. Humility will repay its friends with the reward of eternal happiness; but pride will give the perpetual torments of damnation to all the haughty. Humility will be crowned in heaven without end; but pride in the lower world will suffer forever with the demons an inestimable torment. Humility, crowned, will reign with Christ in heaven; and pride, despised, will be tortured with the devil in punishments. Humility, [glad?] and glorious, will sit forever at the right hand of God; but pride, sad and ignominious, will lie without end in the torments of hell.

    Then the humble will exult in glory, and all the proud, because of exceeding pain, will cry out in punishment for everlasting ages. There the humble will stand in the sight of God and of all the saints in great joy and everlasting exultation, receiving, for the voluntary poverty of this life, unfading riches; for meekness, a kingdom; for sadness, joy; for love of God, dominion; for contempt of the world and voluntary chastening of the flesh, heaven. But when the proud and arrogant, placed in hell, see the great glory of the humble whom they despised in the world, they will marvel at so sudden a change of the saints, and they will be troubled with horrible fear, groaning under the very great anguish of spirit and saying in the fury of pride: “These are the poor and humble monks, formerly clothed in vile garments, separated from men, abstaining from the eating of meats and from all uncleanness of the flesh, whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach. Senseless, we judged their life madness and their end without honor. Behold how they have been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints.

    Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice has not shone upon us, and the sun of understanding has not risen for us. What now does pride profit us, by which, then puffed up, we despised the humble? And what does the boastfulness of riches possessed in the world confer on us? All things have passed away, and we, because of obstinacy, have been counted among the demons, since we always held humility in hatred; and without end we suffer inestimable torments. But the humble will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the thought of them is with the Most High.”

    Always think on these things beforehand, my brothers, since without doubt they will be so; and therefore seek true humility of mind, so that you may merit to obtain the rewards of eternal life. Amen.

    On the true obedience of monks: Homily 20.

    If the humility of monks is true and perfect, it brings forth the whole fullness of the holy virtues. But if it lacks the splendor of virtues, there has never been true humility in the mind. For first of all it brings forth true obedience, and a profound subjection in all things for love of God. For the monk who in truth humbly sojourns shows himself in all things an eager disciple of our Savior Jesus Christ; for love of him, content with every advantage and extremity, he rejoices that he is subject to his abbot, obedient in all things. True [unclear] of the monk is a great virtue, which is rendered to the commands of superiors not through servile fear but through the affection of inward charity; which, persevering even unto death not from fear of punishment but from love of justice, performs good with cheerfulness of mind. There are two very beautiful wings of the mind by which the monk flies from earth to heaven; one of them is called humility, the other is marked as the obedience of subjection. The monk who has not been adorned with these wings has utterly lost both the name and the merit of his dignity. Nor should anyone be called a monk, but a lying and most deceitful apostate, whoever lives and dwells in the monastery without hu

    Homily 20. Fol. XLVIII.

    obedience of humble subjection. For a monk without obedience is a monster of the devil; and he who resists the commands of his superiors will inherit the punishments of hell. From the beginning the disobedience of the first man destroyed the way of eternal happiness, which the obedience of Jesus Christ restored. For he was made obedient to the Father for us, even unto death; and by his most innocent passion he restored to us the happiness we had lost. Hence the way to salvation is humble obedience, as our holy lawgiver Benedict cries out in the Rule: “Listen, my son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive the admonition of a loving father and carry it out effectively, so that by the labor of obedience you may return to him from whom you had departed by the sloth of disobedience.”

    Obedience is the tree of eternal salvation, which grows in the garden of monastic humility. Obedience is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, and the quiet tomb of one’s own will. Obedience is the merit of heavenly happiness, and the sole lesson of monastic discipline. Obedience is the extermination of all pride and arrogance, and the persecutor of all vices. Obedience conquers every malice, and extinguishes every disordered pleasure of the flesh. Obedience makes the conscience pure and clean, and preserves true humility in the mind. Obedience is the remedy for the wound of the soul, and the foundation of all monastic observance. Obedience is the faithful guardian of all good works, and the discipline of a sincere mind. Obedience is the beginning of mortification, and the glorious ornament of monks. Obedience is the preserver of peace and concord, without which the vigor of monastic discipline perishes. Obedience always directs the edge of the mind toward God; and he who is truly mortified in spirit despises all the consolations of this world. Obedience makes a monk close to God, and far removed from all filth of soul. Obedience is the adornment of the soul and the garment of beauty; without it no one will come to the kingdom of eternal brightness. Obedience is the mother of victory; and whoever knows how, for the honor of God, to be subject in humility will obtain the crown of martyrdom in heaven. Obedience separates the monk from the world; and he who follows it with his whole heart will be great before the Most High. Obedience is the consummation of Christian perfection; in its humble workshop, the more a monk advances, the holier he becomes. Obedience is sure security at the hour of death; for a monk, when he is about to depart from here, will fly forth more securely the more ready he has been for obedience to commands. Obedience is the rewarder of the humble, and the chief emblem of merits. Obedience is the rule of Christian gentleness, and the strongest inner nourishment of charity. Obedience is the shelter of chastity, and the ornament of most pure innocence. Obedience is the wisdom of monks; and to acquiesce in the commands of prelates is the highest philosophy of cloistered men.

    Obedience and humility are the wealth and riches of monks; and to possess continually in the mind the memory of the Lord’s passion is a sweetness greater than all the feasts of the world. Obedience and humility make the monk; but he who is rebellious and proud wears the monastic habit without cause. Obedience in the mind is the voluntary mortification of the members while they are alive; its merit is of such dignity that a man has nothing greater that may be offered in honor of God. Let each one offer for the love of God what he can: without doubt, he has offered more than all who has slaughtered his own will for God through obedience. It is indeed a great good to distribute one’s resources for Christ’s love to the uses of the poor, and to relieve by alms the want of the needy. But by as much as the whole outweighs the part, by as much as the free choice of the will is nobler than necessity, by as much as heaven stands apart from earth, by so much more has he offered who, for the love of God and by laying aside his will, has forever denied himself. For whatever temporal substance you have offered to God is not yours but another’s, and is of less value than what is proper to you, both in esteem and in reward. You have one thing proper to yourself which, offered to God, is pleasing above all things. What is this, if not free will, which the almighty Creator placed in your power? A good will is greater than all riches, for nothing richer can be offered to God, nothing will be judged more acceptable.

    This most precious gift, my brothers, you once offered to God when, denying yourselves and all worldly things for Christ’s honor, you put on the monastic habit. I beseech you, be mindful of the prayers of your holy profession, and let that solemn promise never depart from memory, which each one of you made in the sight of God before us, saying: “I, brother Johannes, promise stability, and conversion of my ways, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery which was built in honor of blessed Martin, in the presence of lord Johannes, abbot.” Behold the bond by which we have voluntarily bound ourselves to obedience; behold

    On the True Obedience of Monks.

    ...the warfare which we have professed. For these are the vows which our lips declared; these are the sacrifices of pious devotion which we offered to God. Certainly, my brothers, the things we have promised are great, and a greater necessity lies upon us to keep what we have professed. For unless we faithfully observe everything that the Rule of our blessed father Saint Benedict commands us, the justice of almighty God will judge us severely as perjured and impious transgressors. For it is very dangerous not to render to God what has been promised, and through forgetfulness of the holy institution to violate one’s purpose.

    Therefore, to satisfy the duty of pastoral care, I am accustomed daily to admonish you to the observance of regular discipline; nor hereafter shall the necessary word of salvation ever be lacking to you, so long as my spirit remains in this prison of the flesh. But you, I pray, take care not to be fruitless hearers, since the matter concerns the soul, which, once lost, is never recovered. Therefore, all of you who have come together in the monastery to run the course of intellectual combat, all of you who for love of Christ have once renounced your own will and the world: take up holy obedience as the helmet of salvation, and you will carry off a sure victory over the enemy.

    For obedience is the strongest armor of monks, which no adversities will be able to harm. For Scripture says: “He who keeps the commandment will experience no evil.” In Proverbs also it is said thus: “The obedient man will speak of victories.” Obedience makes a monk invincible in all temptations; and he who follows in all things the counsel of his elder will never suffer loss to the salvation of his soul. For obedience is a short and rough road, by which one quickly ascends to the summit of perfection. But the monk who is a true soldier of Christ never trusts his own judgment, but in all things follows and observes the direction of his pastor.

    Indeed, he who is a true lover of Christ, the monk who wholly desires to be faithful, loves his abbot as the vicar of God, and, always obedient to his commands, counsels, and ordinances in all things, submits cheerfully. In order that a monk may be able to do this confidently, no boy, no unlearned man, no carnal man, no one lacking discretion, nor anyone light-minded or inexperienced in spiritual combats, is to be ordained abbot, but a man mature in character, learned in the divine Scriptures, walking in the spirit in the true way of life of holiness, pious, gentle, tranquil in mind, and discreet, one who knows how to show judgment to the wicked and mercy to the well-disposed.

    For whenever a restless, turbulent, indiscreet, and inexperienced man is appointed abbot over monks, the integrity of regular discipline is at once shipwrecked. Subjection, and with it the obedience of humility, must perish when subjects cannot have firm confidence in their pastor. For if the abbot is a mocker of his brothers, or an over-harsh despiser of the weak, who will open to him any secret whatever of his heart? Therefore the greatest care must be taken at the beginning that such a pastor be appointed for sheep bereft of one, who seeks nothing other than the honor of God and the salvation of souls.

    The monk who has obtained such a pastor should give thanks to God, for in these times of ours he rarely occurs who knows how to show himself in all things a worthy and suitable prelate. He is deservedly to be loved by all his subjects and, as the vicar of Christ in the monastery, honored with continual veneration. Let the thoughts of all be opened to him without fear, since he seeks nothing other than the progress of each one. If the physician of sick bodies must be prudent, experienced, and endowed with the highest discretion, how much more fitting is it that the abbot be an excellent man, since he is the physician of souls?

    Blessed are the monks to whom God’s mercy has granted a useful and suitable pastor, provided that it has not also denied them the ability to understand this very thing. Otherwise a good pastor of bad sheep is not recognized in his uprightness, but rather, through the ingratitude of the depraved, is tormented with the Lord. For often the judgments of monks are blind whenever an opinion is sought about prelates; and those who by their conduct corrupt the integrity of the order rarely judge truly and rightly about pastors. Because of the ingratitude of subjects, rulers are very often changed for the worse; and monks who despise a good and useful pastor in the present life have received, by the just judgment of God, a foolish and useless successor.

    Those who are subject in simplicity walk rightly, and those who truly imitate Christ do not pass judgment on the one presiding over them. For we have as the shepherd of faithful souls the one whom we should follow, our Lord Jesus Christ; looking faithfully toward him in spirit, we shall not rashly judge the visible pastor. “On the chair of Moses,” he says, “the scribes and Pharisees have sat; what they tell you, do; but what they do, do not imitate.” Hear these things, O monk, and [unclear]. But this is true: that all sins are the common cause of death, and all good things are the cause of life; therefore if anyone does good, [unclear], and if anyone has sinned, [unclear]. And therefore the Apostle says, “[unclear]”

    Homily XX. Fol. LIX.

    O lover and student of your own salvation, consider the form of obedience which you are to follow. The abbot holds the place of Christ’s vicar in the monastery, whether he be good or bad; he deserves the obedience of all who are subject to him not by his own merit but in the name of Christ. For we understand the saying, “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me,” not only of the apostles, but of any prelate in the Church of God who has been appointed guardian and ruler of souls.

    Therefore, if you have an abbot who is good, suitable, and holy, hear his voice as the command of God, since he bears God’s place; and whatever he commands you, be obedient to him in all things. If his teaching is for you a rule of life, and his holy conduct an example of purer instruction, then he is a friend of God and the vicar of Jesus Christ: in the one respect he deserves that you love him, and in the other that you obey him in all things when he commands.

    But if you have obtained a shepherd who is rude, unlearned, or certainly less suitable, take care not to sin by wishing rashly to examine his actions, but rather consider that your sins deserve to have a useless shepherd. Consider him not as what he is, but as what he is called; honor the shepherd because of love and reverence for him whose vicariate marks him out. Remember at all times that the obedience which you promised to God must be shown purely and simply to his vicar; for if the abbot is bad in his manner of life, nevertheless he does not lose the vicariate of Christ unless he is deposed in fact. Nor does the shepherd’s wicked and blameworthy life absolve you from the obedience promised in religion.

    The meaning of our word must be upheld. Bad monks do not deserve to have a good abbot. Do not think, beloved brothers, that this example is being hurled at you. For I do not think myself a bad shepherd, although I cannot deny that I am rude and unlearned; nor have we admitted any suspicion of evil about you, since indeed we seek nothing more than to nourish and enlarge brotherly charity in all things.

    Frequently monks come to us, wandering either with reason or without cause, who for the most part turn the matter of their own instability back upon their abbots. But I, who desire you to be instructed in all things that are holy and useful, exhort and warn your charities in fatherly fashion that hereafter you not lend your ears to these wanderers, who slander the characters of their own shepherds and strive to hide their own crimes by accusations against others. This is not the necessary integrity of monastic life: to turn the cause of the rebellion and disobedience of subjects back upon the head of the shepherd.

    He who is a true monk does not judge another rashly; and he who is a son of humble obedience does not investigate causes of rebellion. But he who grants consent to the passions of the flesh can never be at rest; and he who scrutinizes another’s life is a despiser of his own salvation. A monk founded in the love of God does not pass judgment on the command of his superior; and he who always beholds Christ present venerates his own shepherd as an angel of God. Boldness makes a monk degenerate, and presumption has cast many into prison.

    A monk who is wanton, too lascivious, and insolent has lost the purpose of holiness; and unless he is recalled to his senses by the hard chastisement of the flesh, he has already set his foot upon hell. He who examines the command of his superior with curious rashness is not obedient; and he who resists an order is not a true disciple of Christ. For true obedience does not murmur, does not hesitate, is not sad, does not seek a byway, does not delay, does not excuse itself, nor does it show the least sign of lack of resignation. At the superior’s command, for the love of Christ, it always rejoices; it runs to meet it gladly, and obeys cheerfully with haste.

    For what else is a monk than a constant combatant, who, armed with the virtues of humility and obedience, always keeps watch in the arena of struggle, and, victorious under a threefold battle-line, fights more strongly against himself? Blessed is that monk who, doing violence to himself, has learned to overcome the will of the flesh, and by the continual practice of spiritual warfare climbs the steep mountain of true obedience. Truly blessed is that monk who, having despised all the comforts of the world, has placed his whole self in the love of Jesus Christ, and now desires nothing further among visible things. It is not for monks to seek riches, honors, and pleasures in this world, nor is it fitting for the soldier of Christ to think of anything except Christ. O monk three and four times blessed, who, for the love of Christ, mortifies his own will until the end of life, and in true obedience has humbly [unclear].

    How great a good humble obedience is before God, my brothers, no one can sufficiently declare; for the divine testimony wished to prefer it to all victims. It is obedience that reconciles the soul to God, and through the shedding of blood crowns the martyrs.

    On the true obedience of monks.

    For the monk who, for God’s sake, of his own free will binds himself to the perpetual obedience of religion, if he lives rightly according to his vow, surely bears a prolonged martyrdom. Obedience, therefore, is martyrdom without the shedding of blood; and voluntarily to subject oneself to a man for God’s sake is a great torment [of the flesh?]. The soul that truly loves humility and obedience undoubtedly advances to the crown of martyrdom. It is a hard work and an exceedingly laborious contest for a free man to despise himself, and to resign himself wholly, and all his will, perpetually under the command and power of another. But let us behold with faithful eyes the reward of this contest, and we shall reckon all the hard and rough things of this life to be like a certain childish game, which is now seen for an hour [unclear] will appear afterwards. Hence the apostle, speaking in the person of a lover of Christ, says: The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory that shall be revealed in us. The crown that martyrdom once bestowed on the saints for Christ, humble obedience will today prepare for the true lovers of Christ. For a monk who is truly humble and obedient for Christ dies secure, without fear, since, serving faithfully under the command of his elder, he is freed from every demand for an account. For he who, living at the nod of his shepherd, walks uprightly in all commands, can commit nothing that may be brought before the judge. He is defended by the testimony of the abbot, according to whose direction he has lived rightly and without complaint. Consider, brothers, the law of obedience according to which you have promised to live, and know that you have made necessary what had been voluntary, when you solemnly consented to the sentence of monastic tradition. It is no longer lawful for you to withdraw from your holy purpose, nor can you revoke a vow once uttered. If you do everything according to the holy Gospel of Christ and the rule of father Benedict, which you have vowed, let there be no doubtful hesitation for you: you will be blessed, and you will receive from the Lord the reward owed to the saints. But if, unmindful of your promises, you violate the vow of holy purity made to God, if you live according to the flesh in contempt of spiritual conduct, then I now denounce to you by your own law that you are most certainly to be condemned by our Lord Jesus Christ, the judge of all, whom you have mocked and despised. For it is much better to promise nothing /

    Homily XXI.

    [unclear]: for love of him you have set me, an unworthy man, over you as abbot. For I shall not be troublesome to you if you run well; but if anyone turns aside from the way of truth, I am compelled, even unwillingly, to meet him as best I can.

    Let the monk always think on his entrance into the monastery, and never forget the first purpose of his profession. In all your works also, O monk, always consider that you are not long-lived upon the earth, but will shortly depart from this life, and that perhaps when you do not expect it, you will die. Therefore keep inviolate the purpose of holiness, and always be watchful in good works, so that when the Lord comes and calls you, he may find you prepared. Remember that you are a pilgrim on earth, and do not have here a lasting city; but just as a traveler hastens quickly toward the end of his journey, so death draws near to you daily without ceasing. Therefore, while you are healthy, set the house of your conscience in order, so that you may not fear death; for rarely does he die well who is not prepared as though he were to die daily.

    How securely the monk departs from this life who, keeping his conscience clean in all purity, lives at all times, without reproach, according to the full integrity of the rule of our most holy lawgiver, even unto death. Let your mind continually hold in memory our Lord Jesus Christ as present, indeed as nowhere absent; and let no hour pass in which you do not think with thanksgiving of him suffering for you. Stand in humility and true obedience, and no adversities will ever prevail against you. Just as a tree sending many great roots into the earth is not easily torn from its place, so the monk who possesses charity and obedience in humility, together with the other virtues, is by no means overcome by demons. Obedience, brothers, is a great virtue, which brings the other virtues into the mind, and, once brought in, preserves them through the ministry of humility. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who became obedient for us unto the death of the cross, illumine your hearts by his grace, and sweetly inflame your minds at all times for the observance of regular life; who lives and reigns with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, unto all ages of ages. Amen.

    On continence and true chastity: Homily XXI.

    I would most earnestly wish, my dearest brothers, that I had obtained from God that grace by which I might be for you a worthy and suitable shepherd, both in deed and in speech. For I know, and it does not escape me, how perilous the governance of souls is for a young and inexperienced man such as I am, when one who has not yet learned to direct and govern himself according to the rule of justice presumes to approach the instruction of others. I blush to open my mouth among you to teach, since, having been a disciple for a short time, I am compelled before maturity to be a teacher. But since it so pleased you, and you wished to have me, a young man, as master, pardon me, because necessity compels me to fulfill, as best I can, the office committed to me.

    Assist me with your prayers, I beg you, brothers, so that the mercy of God may grant the strength that the command of authority denies. For I desire you to walk before God in all purity of mind and body, so that you may please him to whom you handed yourselves over from the beginning. Having taken him as the leader of the journey to heaven, look upon our Lord Jesus Christ, who, born of the ever most chaste Virgin Mary, perpetually preserved the most perfect chastity of mind and body. Imitate this teacher, into whose service you have consecrated your hands, so that you may preserve not only in body the continence enjoined upon you, but also with a mind brighter than sapphire and carbuncle may perpetually guard chastity.

    For chastity is a most beautiful virtue, especially fitting for cloistered men, so that under the yoke of reason it may restrain every assault of lust, and, the madness of vices being extinguished, the bearing of the body may preserve all honorableness. An incontinent and wanton monk, who follows the filthy lust of the flesh, is counted with the demons who withdrew from the Lord.

    There are three things whose perpetual observance [unclear] our [unclear], without which no one among monks is to be judged worthy of being named. The first of these is the obedience of humble and true subjection; the second, the renunciation of all property, as the rule commands; the third, the inviolate guardianship of perpetual continence and chastity. Whatever one of these the monk violates, he corrupts the purpose of his order. Chastity is sustained by two companions: fasting, namely, and temperance; if it is ever deprived of these, it quickly, without doubt, collapses. The chastity of monks is the greatest ornament, by which, adorned, it will lead them into the fellowship of the angels.

    On continence and true chastity: Homily XXI.

    On continence and true chastity.

    Nothing is more beautiful than chastity: it makes clean what has been conceived from unclean seed; it also makes an enemy into a member of the household, and an earthly man into an angel. Chastity is the most beautiful of all the virtues; when, for love of Christ, it promises that it is to be preserved even unto death, it is rewarded with an inestimable prize. Chastity is next to the fellowship of the angels, and the highest medicine of the Christian mind. Chastity is the lovable dwelling-place of Jesus Christ, the eternal king, and the wondrous beginning of future incorruption. Chastity is the fullness of heavenly grace, through which every corruption of nature is restored. Chastity is the most powerful of all virtues, through which, in a fragile vessel, nature is marvelously conquered in combat. Chastity imitates the angelic life, and, in the midst of mud, knows no sprinkling of stain.

    Blessed is the man who has merited to receive from the Lord God the true gift of chastity, and has kept it inviolate, in Christian humility, even unto death. Chaste is he who, for love of Jesus Christ, pure in mind and body, abstains from every defilement of the flesh; who, by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, burns sweetly in the charity of God; who desires nothing at all in this age, but always desires to be and to live with Christ. Chaste is he who, mindful of the profession of spiritual warfare, restrains the motions of the flesh by reason, and at once, from the beginning, strongly checks all the itching sparks of lust. Chaste is he who, as soon as carnal thought begins to strike the mind, implores divine aid with tears, and does not cease from prayers until he has felt the fire of itching ardor wholly extinguished. Chaste is he who flees every material and occasion of lust; who has made a covenant with his eyes that he should not even think about a woman; and who sets a guard over his senses, lest foul or immodest things be brought in. Chaste is he who avoids the company of the wanton, and always turns his eyes away so that he may not behold vain things. Chaste is he who detests the frequent company of all women, and who at every time regards his own frailty with fear and vigilance as suspect. Chaste indeed is he who in mind and body imitates angelic nature, and who by holy morals admits no corruption.

    Chastity is a gift of grace, and not a work of nature or of human effort. Chastity makes the humble monk most pleasing to God, since he who lives in mortal flesh without corruption is a companion of the angels. He who has attained true chastity is always humble; and he who understands its nature does not arrogate possession of it to himself, but to the Lord who gave it. For no one is chaste by his own strength, since frail man is not sufficient to conquer nature, unless he who created nature and all things has given it. For as often as nature is conquered through chastity, God manifestly works together with man. Chastity itself has, however, a difficult beginning in the young, until the motion of unlawful thought is brought into contempt. Chastity overcomes fornication by fleeing rather than by fighting, since lust is surrounded with so many subtle weapons that it must be avoided of one’s own accord before it is engaged.

    Therefore, as often as the soul is touched by the motions of lust, divine aid should be invoked without delay; no space for deliberation should be given to unclean thought, but as soon as it begins to be felt, it should be brought into contempt by the remedy of forgetfulness. With a fraudulent enemy, and one who always uses ambushes, no dealings at all are to be joined in conversation; and plans are not to be considered with the unclean thoughts of the flesh. Indeed, unless you crush the serpent’s head, it slips away; and unless you at once restrain the motions of lust, they are strengthened from the beginning. The holy apostle of Christ, Paul, admonishes that one must fight against any vices whatever; fornication alone he commands to be fled. We carry about with us the material of victory against ourselves; therefore he wills that we flee the enemy. Chastity is nourished by fasting; by gluttony it is shipwrecked. Hence, if you love chastity, love fasting, so that it may have its necessary nourishment. He who is chaste follows the industry of the bee; and he who is truly a monk, adorned as if with all flowers, is decorated with all virtues.

    Not everyone who does not know lust is chaste, but he who, in pure and clean flesh, for love of Christ alone, also obtains holiness of mind. Otherwise, what does the purity of the dwelling profit, if the inhabitant is foul and unclean? Blind paganism too once had its virgins, sacrificing in garments; but because they did not sacrifice the modesty of their bodies to the true God, nor hold the right faith in their mind, they descended into the depth of hell with their demons whom they worshiped. For he is chaste who, for love of the Creator, restrains even the flesh from every lust, and sacrifices the mind to God himself, adorned in every way with holy virtues. Outside fi

    All Things, XXI.

    [unclear] of Jesus Christ, today there is no true chastity, nor any that is meritorious for eternal salvation. Although you live chastely, O monk, pure and holy, and as long as the spirit remains in the body, do not presume to have confidence in chastity from clay. The food of chastity is fasting and abstinence, and, in every action, the support of wholesome continence. But when you have attained all things, do not trust in yourself, because he whom we know to have eaten nothing fell from heaven. The mortification of the body is both very necessary and useful for preserving the beauty of chastity; but however much you have advanced in either, do not trust in yourself, but, always watchful and hoping in the Lord's help, be afraid. For unless you keep yourself continually and most earnestly in the fear of the Lord, the house of your conscience will quickly be overthrown. He runs in vain who presumes to guard chastity by his own strength. For unless the Lord causes the dwelling-place of chastity to be built, the one who builds the wall of abstinence labors in vain. And unless you become, with all your strength, a co-worker with divine grace, you will in no way obtain the beauty of chastity. For God will not make you chaste without your will, nor will you attain this great gift unless he, through his mercy, comes to the aid of your weakness. Therefore yours it will be, O monk, to offer the desire for chastity with good will, and, in humble confidence, to await certain increase from the Lord. Apply fasting, and the Lord's help will not be lacking. Chastity is a gift of grace, not of nature; and to live in the flesh as though beyond the flesh belongs to angelic strength, not human. Nevertheless it is not difficult for a man of good will to preserve chastity, especially one who is separated from the tumult of worldly people and lives solitary in the midst of monks. A monk, too, who, young and innocent, enters a monastery of good reform, if he keeps his mind continually occupied in the fear of the Lord, is less assailed by lust. For the experience of lust is pernicious, since, as someone truly said, it seeks to conquer souls, not to satisfy the veins. But a monk who is a lover of lust can easily extinguish the heat if, fleeing idleness and fullness, he is willing to occupy himself continually in spiritual exercise. For among all vices none assaults chastity more greatly and more dangerously than fullness and idleness. If a monk overcomes these two evils, he will easily preserve chastity. Hence the most holy princes of monks, wishing to cut away the causes of lust, established for us a spare and meager diet according to a fixed measure, by which the body is sustained for necessity and is not fattened for lust. They also decreed that scantiness of sleep was useful for monks, because immoderate rest expands the flesh no less than gluttony. But they wished idleness, as the most pernicious plague of the soul, to be far from cloistered persons, dividing the time most wisely so that a monk would never be found idle. Hear these things, brothers, and grasp them in your mind, you who carry a great treasure in a fragile little body. Always flee idleness; do something good, so that whenever the tempter, the devil, approaches, he may find you usefully occupied. For truly, he who is idle lies open to the snares of the tempter; but he who is occupied in good work has closed every entrance to snares. Therefore the mind must be occupied with continual exercise, so that it is never found idle. Blessed is that monk who occupies his mind at all times in good exercises and never sleeps in the sleep of torpor and sloth. Blessed is the spiritual soldier of Christ who always keeps watch in the fear of the Lord and immediately restrains, from the beginning, all the disordered motions of the flesh. For it is not enough to guard true chastity unharmed, if someone plays with unclean thoughts as though deliberately. It belongs to strong men to [unclear] the first motions of wicked [unclear], because where delay creates danger, one must fight strongly at once. There must always be vigilance against the adversary of our salvation, who is never conquered more quickly than if he is choked off immediately from the beginning. Continual exercise is needed, brothers, because a mind always occupied in holy studies is like a very high [unclear] of strength, in which the soldier of Jesus, set as most watchful, fears no hostile snares. Therefore I beseech you, my dearest brothers, do not consume time in idleness, lest you increase in yourselves material for vices, you who are not ignorant of the wiles of the malignant spirit. Preserve continence in all things, and apply temperance, the guide of virtues, to all your [unclear].
