    On continence and true chastity.

    to God, by whose words you have sworn; and so live that you do not fear to appear at his judgment.

    You are monks, set apart from the world for the service of our Lord Jesus Christ by a voluntary promise; hence, under necessity of salvation, you must lead a life higher and holier than the rest of your fellow Christians, and overcome every depravity of flesh and soul. For you must always be most chaste in mind and body alike, and stained by no filth of corruptible flesh. An incontinent monk is an apostate; and he who defiles his flesh with the filth of women is like one violating an oath. Lust is a lake of hell, and despair is always very near to incontinence. A monk who once slips into the pit of the flesh is rarely kindled to true compunction of heart. For the vice of fornication, strengthened by long habit, is not easily conquered unless it is corrected by force through contrary remedies. It is a matter of greater difficulty to rise again after a fall of the flesh to true chastity than to remain in continence once possessed. It is very easy to fall from the state of uprightness into any vice whatever, rather than to amend a sin strengthened by habit. For, as a certain pagan truthfully says, easy is the descent to Avernus; but to recall the step and escape upward to the breezes: this is the work, this is the labor.

    Let us consider those who have fallen into this most shameful pit and afterward, by the authority of their superiors, were compelled to penance: how do they live among the brothers? They do not have the signs of true compunction, but pass a restless life in dryness of heart. No devotion of mind is seen in them, but everywhere they follow the comforts of the flesh. O how rarely is one converted to the sweetness of inward love who has once been cast down into the lake of fornication. For unless, before he comes into this misery, he has been grounded in the fear of the Lord, when fallen he returns with difficulty to true compunction.

    Therefore live soberly, dearest brothers, and always keep watch in holy prayers, since unless you walk most cautiously in all things, you will by no means be able to escape the snares of demons. Love abstinence; guard humility above all things. For no one can suppress the movements of his flesh who has disdained to subdue gluttony and pride. The insolent demon of fornication is never better conquered than if true humility of heart is preserved in the fullness of all virtues. For just as almighty God, resisting the proud, gives grace to the humble, so the devil, fleeing the humble, casts the proud down into fornication. Therefore he who, being gluttonous, eating and drinking to satiety, desires to conquer the spirit of fornication, is as one carrying oil to a fire. And he who strives to extinguish the movements of lust by abstinence alone is like a man who is seen swimming in the midst of waves with one hand. Let continual prayer to God be joined to abstinence, and in the ship of holy humility one will sail securely.

    Let prayer always be in the mouth of the monk, and the memory of the passion and death of the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore whenever you feel a disordered movement of the flesh, whenever you perceive the invisible enemy to be present to do harm, immediately flee to the Son of God hanging on the cross, and, with your knees bent to the ground, let such a prayer be formed to him: O crucified Jesus, my love, through the pain of your wounds have mercy on me; through the outpouring of your most holy blood help me in this struggle, and through the power of your most innocent death free me from every contagion of mind and body.

    Nothing is more salutary than this manner of prayer, in which the memory of Christ’s passion is cherished and petitions are strengthened in the power of the Savior of all. Nothing weakens the snares of the ancient enemy more; nothing more quickly enfeebles the forces of his malignity, than if a devout servant of Christ humbly perseveres in meditation on the most bitter passion of the Lord. Just as some thief flees before the face of a pursuing judge, so the devil quickly vanishes from the sight of a monk who attentively meditates on the passion and death of the Savior. He quickly extinguishes the movement of wicked thought when the bitterness of Christ’s passion is recalled to mind. Just as snow melts when the sun grows warm, so the devil is driven away by meditation on the Lord’s passion.

    The greatest protection of chastity is always to invoke divine aid. And unless immediately at the beginning of temptation you run back to the Lord, you will little by little incur harm from delay. For if you admit delay in pernicious thoughts, demons soon cast a perceptible blindness into the mind.

    All Things XXI. Fol. LII.

    [unclear]. For unless the mind has first been blinded, the will does not yield to the demon. The spirit of fornication first gravely darkens the mind; afterward it fights until it has hurled it, blinded, into sin. But afterward, when it has cast the monk into the mire of unspeakable crime, it sets two means in the way, lest he rise again to repentance. For either it subtly tries to make light of the gravity of the sin, so that he may not fear a great penalty; or it brings back to the fallen man’s memory the severity of judgment, so that he may fall into the pit of despair. By these snares the sinful soul is caught; and the longer it has lain in the depth of misery, the more hardened it is rendered.

    Flee idleness, O cloistered men, and avoid gluttony and the excess of the belly with the greatest care, because the monk who stuffs his belly with food and drink provides the demon of fornication with matter for doing harm. Put on true contrition of heart, and restrain the illicit motions of the flesh through tears of prayer. For no one is able rightly to conquer his body who has not first taken up the goad of contrition. But he cannot attain to the grace of holy contrition who [unclear] has perfectly despised himself to deny himself. Whoever, however, has perfectly denied himself for the love of Christ, already overcoming the assault of the flesh, will more easily [unclear] contrition. For he who has been mortified in will desires nothing carnal, nothing base.

    But who among us, brothers, is there who would dare say that he has arrived at this grace of mortification? Which of us does not feel himself weak? We run in the arena of spiritual warfare, and in daily combat we fight against vices. We have received no confidence of peace, even if at times we have peace. The more familiar to us is the weakness of the flesh, the harder are the battles of chastity. Here we must be especially watchful, since we carry about a familiar enemy and sustain, as it were, a domestic instigator of evil. Therefore, so long as we live in this mortality, let us always fear the most relentless enemies of chastity. Let us beware of everything that arouses lust; as much as we can, let us flee sloth and idleness. For fullness of bread and idleness are the strongest enemies of true chastity; unless they have been driven far away by abstinence and the labor of salutary exercise, they threaten immediate shipwreck to chastity.

    Keep your hearts with divine guard, O most dear [unclear], and always keep watch in spirit against your adversary. Arm yourselves with the breastplate of perfect faith in Jesus Christ, so that in deed and belief you may be true Christians. Always be of one mind in brotherly charity, and united without pretense in the true observance of regular discipline. Love fasting and continence; pray without ceasing. Flee idleness as the pernicious plague of the soul, and continually exercise yourselves in holy works. Love silence, and do not flee monastic solitude, if you desire to obtain true purity of mind and body. Keep continual guard over your eyes, ears, and speech, lest through the windows of the body [evil] enter into the soul. Flee conversations with women, and avoid even the touch of holy women as the burning of fire. No one safely looks willingly upon what brings the sting of death to the desirous man. Always behold with faithful eyes of the mind, through love, our Lord Jesus Christ dying for you; occupy yourselves daily in salutary fashion with his evangelical teaching; give humble thanks for his passion and likewise for his death. If you do these things with continued perseverance in true simplicity of heart until death, we trust that you will be rewarded with the fellowship of the saints.

    On Brotherly Charity and the State of Monks. All Things XXII.

    Let us hear, my dearest brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ commanding in the holy Gospel: Whatever you wish men to do to you, do the same also to them. This is indeed a brief but solid commendation of brotherly charity, without which no one can ascend to the love of God. For no one can love God who is shown not to love his fellow Christian. Hence the blessed apostle John says: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him. Hence, if anyone has said that I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. Therefore Paul, the holy lover of Christ, exhorts us, saying: Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. And Peter, prince of the apostles, admonished us thus: Before all things, he says, having continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity

    On the brotherly charity of monks.

    It covers a multitude of sins. How necessary brotherly charity is for salvation, the Lord of all, Jesus Christ, revealed, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. The second is like to this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.” For whatever is commanded anywhere in the whole course of the Scriptures is without doubt referred to these two commandments.

    By “neighbor” here we understand not one joined by closeness of blood, but every human being by the fellowship of reason, and especially the Christian, whom each person is commanded to love as himself, with whom he is seen to await eternal salvation. But it is especially fitting for you, brothers, to love one another in the true charity of the Savior Jesus Christ, since monastic profession enjoins you to strive with all your strength toward the height of perfection. For just as covetousness is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all goods. In the first place you ought to love God above all things with a pure heart for his own sake, because he is the highest good, and then to love your neighbor with sincere charity for the Lord’s sake. These two precepts of charity are joined by the authority of Christ, so that one can in no way be fulfilled without the other. For he who truly loves God cannot hate his neighbor. If he hates his neighbor, he does not truly love God. The love of God begets in him love of neighbor, and through love of neighbor the love of God is nourished. If one of the loves is lacking, the other by no means grows strong. For he who certainly does not love his neighbor shows himself empty of the love of God. Therefore we truly love God when we love our neighbor, that is, every Christian human being, more diligently with sincere intention.

    For brotherly charity is the bond of peace, which alone nourishes concord in the dwelling and preserves Christian unity among brothers. Charity is the begetter of meekness and the noble mother of Catholic piety. Brotherly charity is fearsome to demons, since it makes victorious all whose inner chamber of the heart it embraces. Charity extinguishes the fire of lust and covers every multitude of sins. Charity renders good people most dear to God and makes them companions of the holy angels. Charity preserves the Church in the unity of the saints, outside which no one obtains eternal salvation. Brotherly charity orders the morals of cloistered men and makes God dwell in the midst of monks. Charity does injury to no one, but supplies help to all through compassion. Charity drives out every vice, because it is the sole nurse of all virtues. Charity preserves the reform of brotherhood in vigor among cloistered men and works a great salvation of souls. Mutual charity confirms obedience and makes brotherly correction fruitful. True charity nourishes concord among brothers and preserves a sweet-smelling chastity of both minds and bodies. Charity makes monks of one mind in the house of God, and laudably concordant in every good work. Mutual charity lightens the rigor of the order, and all things that seem hard and harsh to the carnal it changes through custom into nature, as though they were something very gentle. Charity is the most beautiful beauty of monks, adorned with all virtues. Charity utterly drives hatred and envy out of the monasteries of God’s servants, and by its presence puts to flight far away the remaining crimes of death. The charity of brothers is a fitting dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and a fortress of serene conscience. Charity is the handmaid of justice and the sole preserver of regular discipline in a monastery. Charity keeps the mind innocent of cruelty and provides for all a peaceful lightness of spirit. Brotherly charity seeks the salvation of all, and does not allow the one who has it to grow sluggish in idleness. Charity does not loathe poverty, but for love of the brothers is ready to endure every poverty. Charity is the water of heavenly sweetness; if anyone drinks it in the fervor of the Holy Spirit, he does not fear the perpetual thirst of hell. Brotherly charity does not seek the enticements of the flesh, but directs pure, holy, and unstained affections toward the neighbor. Charity has the name of chaste beauty, which cannot be shared with things or actions of most impure pleasure. Charity loves purity and cleanness, and admits no impurity. Charity, in the working of love, considers not the flesh of the neighbor but the soul, which it does not doubt was created in the image of God. Brotherly charity raises up a delinquent neighbor with pious admonitions, and keeps all its own actions pure and innocent of every malice. Charity walks in peace and tranquility of mind, and saddens the neighbor neither by word nor deed nor sign. Charity humbles itself as much as it can in all things, and ministers most lovingly to an infirm neighbor as to a son of God. Cha

    Homily XXII.

    Fol. LIII.

    Charity judges no one rashly, but humbly corrects erring neighbors with the gentlest admonitions. Charity is terrible and fearsome to the reprobate, but tender and kindly to the meek. Charity reckons another’s misfortune as its own, and weeps over a brother’s tribulation as though it suffered it itself. Charity suffers with all who are placed in necessity, and is no less saddened by others’ adversities than by its own. Charity imputes nothing evil first, but for the love of God always bears the infirmities of all with equanimity. Charity is diligent in good works, and as long as it remains in the heart it is never idle. Charity neglects none of the things to which it is bound, but guards all things most diligently. Brotherly charity is the fulfillment of the law, since whatever is commanded after the worship of God is referred to love of neighbor. Hence the holy love of Christ says: He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the laws. For, You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet another’s property; and if there is any other commandment, it is renewed in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love of neighbor does not work evil. Therefore the fullness of the law is love.

    And so, my dearest brothers, we beseech you through our Lord and Savior Christ, who is to judge the living and the dead, that you always keep brotherly charity unharmed, without which you can neither truly love God nor in any other way fulfill his commandment. The keeping of brotherly charity is as necessary for your salvation as the nourishment of food and drink is for preserving the body’s life. For the body dies without necessary nourishment, and all the virtues of the soul are scattered without brotherly charity. For brotherly charity preserves a multitude of monks in unity of spirit; for without the bond of mutual love, no cloistered man perseveres content without disturbance. The monk who persecutes his brother with hatred is far removed from God’s charity. For the holy evangelist John says: He who hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes. But the chaste and prudent lover of his neighbor walks safely in the light of the Holy Spirit, and he is not disturbed by another, nor does he disturb anyone else. For true love of neighbor is gentle, sweet, and most tender, and in all its intercourse meek, peaceable, and tranquil.

    Yet the vigor of discipline directs the meekness of a chaste ruler, and the clemency of brotherly consideration beautifully tempers vigor. For one must be struck from the other in such a way that vigor is not rigid, nor love slack. The lover of brotherly charity does not abandon the way of justice; he who rightly loves his neighbor introduces no corruption. For true first love neither covets gold nor requires the services of ministry, but, content with all things that could overthrow the condition of the mind, pursues only the increase of the soul. For charity is not sincere when it seeks gifts because of corrupt morals, or [unclear] a boy because of a little gift, so as to love with an affection of likeness one who runs together for distributions. The friendship of monks among good men who are zealous for the same purpose ought to be common, and far removed from every affection of the flesh. Let it be pure, simple, upright, and durable without injury to anyone, and let it have in itself nothing of suspicious conspiracy.

    This is not the rule of brotherly charity: to seek forbidden private gatherings for consolation, and without the prior’s blessing to be occupied with furtive, indeed prohibited, conversations. You do not rightly and [unclear] hinder love of your neighbor whenever you come together for the comforts of the flesh against the rule of regular observance. A monk’s love ought to be solid and very far removed from every transgression of regular discipline, since unless charity has been much [unclear] by the signs of carnal conversation, it does not have within itself the mark of divine love. Now examine your conversations, brothers, to see whether you have them rooted in your heart even in true charity. For charity that either gives or receives consolations harmful to the spirit was never sincere. Therefore take care to direct the eye of the mind not toward the beauties of the flesh, but rather toward contemplation of the soul, if you wish rightly and laudably to love your neighbors mutually. For when the flesh is loved without regard for the soul, not sincere but carnal and impure love is generated. Consider that your brother has a soul like yours, and always think that you both equally await happiness. [unclear] without the soul we understand; in soul, not in body, we are immortal. What is immor-

    On the brotherly charity of monks.

    It is [unclear] to love one another mutually, and, with regard to charity, to direct one’s attention rather to the soul than to the body. Thus by reason and understanding one is distinguished from brute animals, so that the regard of our love is referred to the mind, by which we understand, not to the body, which we have in common with beasts. And far from holy monks be all affections of the flesh, for they are not ignorant of the rule of mutual and sincere charity.

    If love for one another is pure, upright, and conceived solely from the fear of God, so that no advantage of any corruptible thing intervenes, but the simple intention of charity remains; and true charity, simple and pure, does not seek the byways of evil conspiracies, nor arm itself with the murmur of contention for the devising of iniquity. He who possesses true charity of brotherhood in his heart preserves peace in all things and stirs up no matter or causes of destructive dissension. Charity, spending its one [unclear], does injury to no one, and whatever it does not wish to be done to itself, transfers to the person of no other.

    Do not think that you have true brotherly charity when you love one another mutually for the sake of the flesh or the advantage of any temporal thing whatever; for where the cause of love is not the Lord, the affection of the one who loves is always vicious, either in part or in whole. But he will rightly love his brother who loves him with the love of God, and for the sake of the common participation in the kingdom which we await. Therefore, as Saint John the bishop says, we have been baptized into one body of the Church, so that we may not be dissolved; in that harmony and friendship which exists mutually, let us preserve forever the charity and mutual agreement of one body. Just as no one outside the unity of the Catholic Church can obtain salvation, so no one is believed able to be saved without brotherly charity.

    Charity, therefore, is necessary for you before all things for salvation; without it, the remaining works of virtues are altogether fruitless. For there can be no good thing, no reward salutary unto life, which has not drawn its origin from it. Charity is a certain road to the compendium of virtue; if anyone enters upon it by the straight path of the journey, he will need no guidance of a leader. Pure, simple, and upright charity is not accustomed to harm one’s neighbor, nor to bring evil upon anyone. Charity is accustomed to spend upon all the affection which it grants to its own advantages, and whatever it hopes may conduce to its own salvation, this it desires to be common to all people in Christ Jesus.

    Charity, free from any disturbance, is exercised in the office of love; and though it loves all people most greatly, nevertheless it is provoked on behalf of none to a zeal of bitterness. It is always solid, always constant, always stable and firm, because it is neither touched by passions nor agitated by movements of unrest. It offers itself common to all, and so spends its love upon each individual that it sees its own as common to all. Charity does not neglect itself in those things that pertain to the reason of being and of the soul; but in those things which regard the advantage of the body, it often puts the causes of others before its own interests. Great indeed is the dominion of charity, which compels a person to make another’s disadvantage his own.

    Thus you also, my brothers, who have solemnly taken up the service of Christ, who through the steep path of obedience pant after eternal life: if you do not wish to run in vain in the [unclear] of so laborious a contest, take care before all things, we exhort you, always to preserve brotherly charity inviolate among you. For unless you have sincere and perfect charity toward one another, you labor without fruit in regular observance. Abstinence from eating flesh will contribute nothing to the salvation of your souls; the renunciation of all private property will profit nothing toward the attainment of eternal happiness, if brotherly love does not hold a place in your hearts.

    Therefore, desiring to be saved with Christ in truth, love one another mutually; and as Christ loved you, so, we pray, love one another. What each one of you desires to be done to himself, let him, without envy and for the love of God, bestow that very thing upon his brother at all times. Let divine love conquer in you all quarrels of the flesh and all [unclear] contentions; nor let destructive dissension of the flesh find a place where the fullness of brotherly charity ought continually to dwell. And unless all in the monastery, according to the law of Christian institution, are [unclear], each of you must always necessarily abstain from harming another. But if through contentions and injuries you harm one another mutually, you are certainly neither monks nor true Christians. For it befits all cloistered persons and monks to be outstanding in the observance of charity, and to be far removed from envy, hatred, and rancor. Let the monk, therefore, be stable in the purpose of holiness even unto death; let him be faithful in the service of God, so that also in love

    Homily XXIII. Folio LIV.

    may sweetly burn for the Creator, and may never withdraw from purity of conscience. For whoever perfectly loves the Lord God from his whole heart, and preserves his conscience clean and pure from every pollution of sin, and always shows sincere charity to his neighbor. But he whom either envy burns or hatred stirs up against his brother, it is clear that he neither truly loves God nor has a conscience pure from sin. Therefore everyone who persecutes his brother with hatred and indignation is neither a true monk nor worthy of the name Christian, but by merit and conduct a servant and companion of demons. Therefore let hatreds depart far from this holy congregation of yours; let there be no destructive contests of contention in your midst; let no zeal of bitterness be found here, let no word of displeasing pride be heard. Let the concord of brotherly unity flourish here continually; let the innocence of Christian purity adorn the consciences of each, so that we may live in this short time in such a way that after death we may be glorified with Christ in eternity.

    Homily XXIV.

    Nothing is so just, nothing so holy, nothing in human actions can be so honorable, as always to love God above all things from the whole heart, and in the whole mind, and with the whole strength, and for love of him to fear neither death nor any kinds of punishments. There is no greater cause of action in us than divine love, because, since God is the author of all things, nothing is loved more justly than he; and since he is the greatest of all goods, nothing is loved more fruitfully than he. God first loved us: we are lowest, he greatest; we little, he almighty; we weak. Therefore, my brothers, let us love the Lord God with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength, by whom we are most sweetly loved, who not only made us in his image and likeness, but, which is a sign of the greatest love, mercifully called us to the kingdom of eternal happiness through the teaching and death of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. No fleshly mother ever loved her only-begotten son so tenderly, sweetly, and strongly as almighty God loved us, who not only willed to become man for our instruction, but also deigned to undergo death in the flesh he had assumed for our salvation. No greater love ever existed, if we rightly weigh who it was who endured such things for us. For out of love for us, free from the debt of death, he voluntarily dies; and he who always remained immune from every sin, innocent and just, willingly is condemned for our sins. By the most just reason, therefore, we are commanded to love the Lord our God with our whole heart: he who, when we did not exist, made us from his goodness alone, and when we had perished, mercifully freed us. Love of God is the greatest of all virtues, because whatever good, whatever virtue is done in this world, if it is not done from charity toward God, is emptied of reward. Charity toward God purifies the conscience from every fault, since he who truly loves the Lord his God from his whole soul and in his whole heart and with all his strength undoubtedly grants no place in his conscience to vices. For the heart which the love of God occupies, no uncleanness of vices enters. The love of God is an unfailing treasure: whoever possesses it is richer than all the wealthy of the world; whoever lacks it is more wretched than all the poor. Hence the holy apostle of Christ says: To those who love God, all things work together for good, since nothing is lacking to those who fear him. Happy is the man in whose heart no bond of earthly affection dwells except the love of Christ, who sighs for the memory of no human being, in whose conscience purity resides and divine love always burns most ardently. Love him, O my brothers, who for love of you descended into the Virgin's womb; always carry him in your hearts, who by his death opened heaven for you. Let the love of Christ be in you at all times, brothers, as strong as death, so that your life may be conformed to Christ's teaching, and, if at any time it should be necessary to die for love of him, you may not fear, just as he first deigned calmly and kindly to undergo death for us. For the love of Christ makes a monk near to God, and he who is always fervent in the charity of the Lord will obtain the fellowship of the angels. The love of Christ makes a man most strong against all assaults of demons, and no less in adversities than

    On the love of man toward God.

    ...in prosperity long-suffering and at the same time tranquil. The love of Christ teaches one truly to despise the world, and to reckon as nothing all its delights and all the comforts of the flesh. The love of Christ swiftly suppresses the illicit movements of the flesh and brings the purest chastity into the mind. The love of Christ sweetly lifts the mind with desire to heavenly things, and keeps it, separated from earthly things, in spiritual exercise.

    The love of God lightens all hard and harsh things, for where Christ is loved in truth, tribulations and any adversities whatever are counted as delights. The love of God is always constant in good works and is never idle. The love of God despises present things and strongly raises the mind to eternal things. The love of God neither seeks honors nor seeks riches, but, joined to Christ by desire, covets nothing at all except him. The love of God covers the multitude of sins and remits all offenses to the penitent. The love of God suddenly justifies the impious; and the more love has increased, the more quickly and strongly perfection also rises up.

    The love of God is a tower of strength, to which all the ministers of diabolical wickedness cannot draw near. The love of God is the consummation of all justice and the end of monastic discipline. The love of God perfects the monk and makes him consummate in all good works. The love of God is the sweet yoke of inward sweetness, by which all filth of earthly corruption is driven out from the mind. The love of God honors souls and makes them pure and immaculate from all stains. The love of God perfectly illuminates the mind in every knowledge of heavenly honors, and purges the very affection from all unclean vanities.

    The love of God makes those who truly have it most learned and wondrously instructed in all Scripture. The love of God renders the monk fearsome to all enemies and bestows angelic power on those who persevere. The love of God defends a man in dangers, since whoever truly loves God fears no opposing things. The love of God makes the one who has it secure in the hour of death and safe from demons, and joins the soul to the heavenly hosts. The love of God leads its possessor back to the heavenly homeland and bestows everlasting glory on those who love God.

    The love of God is the greatest of all good works and the single foundation of all virtues in the faith of Christ. The love of God is the best ointment, in which all wounds of languishing souls are healed. The love of God is an abundant remedy for poverty and want, and an effective consolation above every possession of riches. The love of Christ far surpasses all the learning of this world, and forms those who have it most perfectly for every knowledge necessary to salvation. The love of God prepares a delightful dwelling for the Holy Spirit in the heart of man, and preserves him, as he perseveres, in all purity.

    The love of God is the swiftest of all teachers, because what carnal men learn over time and with much study, the Holy Spirit has handed on in a moment to those who love God. The love of God gives knowledge to little ones and makes rustics more learned than the educated. The love of God is stronger than all things and by its power rules over all things. The love of God commands demons by a single word and puts them to flight from bodies possessed by the sign of the cross. The love of God bestowed eternal blessedness on the holy spirits in heaven, whom the grace of the Creator confirmed as lovers.

    The love of God beatifies in eternal felicity [unclear] baptized in the faith of Jesus Christ, because no one has ever been able to reach the fellowship of angels unless the persevering love of God was proved to have inflamed him. For the love of God alone is what makes works both good and meritorious, since God accepts from us only that gift of a good work which the flame of charity has made worthy in his sight. Whatever is done outside charity is judged unworthy in the sight of God.

    Now attend, my brothers, to our admonitions, and carefully consider how necessary it is for you to love God above all things, if you desire to arrive at his kingdom and to triumph happily with him forever. Let none of you deceive his soul with empty words, so that he believes that he truly loves God whose commandments he either despises or neglects to keep. You have heard the Lord Jesus saying in the holy Gospel: “He who loves me will keep my words.” And as the holy pope Gregory says, the performance of the commanded work is the proof of the love enjoined. For then we truly love the Lord our God with our whole heart, when, having despised worldly pleasures, we perfectly keep all his commandments even unto death. Likewise, then we love him above all things, when out of love for him, not according to the flesh but according...

    Homily XXIII.

    Fol. lv.

    while we walk innocently in the spirit. He truly loves God who, always intent upon good works, keeps himself pure and unstained from this world. But he loves the Lord God rightly who desires absolutely nothing in this world. He truly loves God with his whole heart who, for love of him, resolutely despises worldly honors, riches, pleasures, and all the comforts of the flesh. He loves God with his whole soul who, at all times careful in observing his commandments, omits to do none of the things that are pleasing to him. For the love of God neglects nothing, but is accustomed most diligently to keep and fulfill everything that he has commanded. He who loves God in true charity has fulfilled the law, the prophets, and the Gospel. Therefore by your works you will give testimony whether you truly love God. For everyone who has deserved to receive a ray of divine love always shows great and manifest signs of love. Indeed, the fire of divine love makes its possessor pious in all things, chaste, gentle, and very humble, and, both in adversity and in prosperity, always calm in the same constancy of mind, without disturbance.

    The monk who truly loves the Lord God, according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict, always obeys the commands of his seniors cheerfully in all things; in hard and contrary circumstances he embraces patience, and everywhere preserves true humility. The love of God makes its possessor richest in all good works, and renders him far removed from any vices whatever. The lover of God does not murmur at the command of obedience; in [reproofs?] he does not rashly excuse himself; he does not touch his neighbor with the gall of bitterness, nor is he disturbed even when injured. He who is a true lover of God keeps his life irreproachable in all purity of mind and body, and demonstrates in himself a fervent charity not only in word but also in deed and in truth.

    Whatever in the world is beautiful, whatever is pleasant or delightful to behold, whatever flatters the wantonness of lascivious flesh, the true lover of God most steadfastly despises it all, and desires nothing other than to please Christ and to live with him [unclear]. Great and incredible to those who do not know it is the force of divine love, which always impels a man to work well, and never permits him to live idle. For what else is the inward love of God than a sweet drunkenness of the soul, by which a man is snatched away from all the consolations of the world, and, as though he felt nothing of what mortals do, feasts in the banquet of the Holy Spirit alone?

    The monk who is a true lover of God has put aside, for Christ’s sake, every curiosity of the world and concern for worldly things; and, as though he did not feel them, he transcends in his mind all the stings of cares. He cries out with the apostle: “The world is naked and crucified to me, and I to the world.” O wine of divine love, how sweetly you intoxicate, how innocently you satisfy, how wisely you make foolish, how chastely you inflame. For everyone who has been intoxicated by your savor, separated from every tumult of carnal pleasures, rests sweetly in the shadow of the Holy Spirit. Because of the excessive drunkenness of the spirit, he speaks things alien to carnal and worldly people, and nothing contrary to God is heard from his mouth. This is the unstained satiety of spiritual wine, which is extended by desire the more, the longer it is continued.

    O holy and venerable simplicity of the lover of Christ, which, although to many who savor earthly things it may seem to be folly, nevertheless before God and all his saints is the greatest and truly highest wisdom. Let the world have its prudence, let it have honors, dignities, and riches; but I would choose the merit of one simple monk truly loving God rather than the sovereignty of the whole world. The love of God is both the highest pleasure of the soul and always the most chaste; its fire illuminates the mind and gently inflames the affection. The love of God is the fountain of heavenly grace, because the grace of the Holy Spirit makes fruitful, with the fruits of all the virtues, the mind which the charity of Christ purifies by plowing. The love of Christ wins the friendship of almighty God for men, and reveals to mortals the will of the highest majesty.

    The love of God makes a monk acceptable to God, because he requires from us not knowledge, not learning, not eloquence, but charity. Therefore the monk who has publicly offered himself to the Lord God ought to care for nothing except God, lest he seem to have a divided heart; since, just as God is one, so love directed toward God cannot be divided. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: “He loves you less, Lord, who loves anything together with you which he does not love for your sake.” Just as God is perfect, so he must be loved by us with all our strength, because he is not rightly

    On the charity of a person toward God.

    [unclear] is loved: whenever anything besides him is loved together with him. Love of God advances rightly when nothing is mixed with it that could weaken it. Let each one of you, as much as he can, strive with the whole strength of his mind to love the Lord his God above all things, because love alone toward God is what will open for you the gate of paradise. For the more ardently you now love God, the greater the glory in which you will be received in the heavenly homeland.

    Happy is that monk in whose conscience, besides the love of Christ, there remains no imagining of any occupation; who, waking, thinks of nothing but Christ; sleeping, dreams of Christ; living and dying, most steadfastly sighs after Christ. O how well and securely he dies who has always been solicitous in the exercise of divine love, and at all times zealous in observing the commandments of God. For love of God alone is admitted into the kingdom of heaven, and the more fervent the mind has been in loving. He who loves much receives much; and he who now loves less is also then to receive less in glory. Therefore let each person, as much as he can, love with his whole heart and with his whole soul and with all his strength, because our God is not to be loved lukewarmly or sluggishly, but fervently, wisely, and sweetly.

    But love of God grows and is increased by spiritual exercises, just as a burning fire spreads when supplied with wood. For truly, if the wood is withdrawn the fire is extinguished; and if spiritual exercises are interrupted, charity is soon shipwrecked. True love of God is never idle, but at all times is delightfully occupied in those things that nourish and preserve charity. For the lover of his God never forgets his beloved, but always meditates on his presence and beauty; and now, most devout in prayers, he admires him as Jesus speaking to him. The true lover of Christ meditates day and night on the law of the Lord, and does with the greatest diligence all things that he understands to be pleasing to God.

    O how sweetly he burns whom the love of God has truly inflamed; how pleasantly he glows whose mind the flame of the Holy Spirit kindles. Blessed is that monk who, full of divine love, withdraws himself entirely from earthly vanities and rests in the shade of heavenly desire. O if only we had love toward God as strong, whole, and vehement as mad and foolish lovers have toward their corruptible mistresses, for desire of whom lovers often grow shamefully mad and fear no scandals of this world. But the love of God is stronger than all things, if it has truly been rooted in us. Whoever truly loves the Lord God always keeps in his memory his most bitter passion, because nothing so causes perfect love of God in the human heart, nothing so brings on true compunction, as the never-interrupted recollection of God’s benefits. Therefore let the written sequence of Christ’s passion always be in your memory, and let this word never depart from your mouth: O Jesus crucified, my love, by the power of your most innocent death have mercy on me and make me your faithful servant.

    On Serenity of Conscience.

    Homily 24.

    Most beloved brothers, we must keep watch with great solicitude, and must take care with continual meditation that we always guard our conscience, whose testimony we cannot escape, clean from every contagion of sin and unstained. Nothing is more beautiful, nothing more pleasing, nothing finally more precious than a good conscience, when the mind has in itself a manifest testimony of rectitude; it suffers no remorse of destructive unrest. An upright and good conscience is an incredible exultation of the mind and a sure consolation in every adversity. The monk who has obtained the testimony of a good conscience neither refuses to live nor fears the coming of future death. A good conscience is always glad, always joyful, always fearless, and truly tranquil in the peace of Jesus Christ. In a good conscience there is always peace, piety, goodness, light, virtue, honor, joy, gladness, sweetness, and delight without dissipation. Conscience is the treasury of the soul, because whatever is placed in it is reserved as provision for the life to come. A good conscience is the best treasure; if anyone has neglected to have it, he must be judged the most wretched and unhappy of all men. A good conscience is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and the earthly paradise of all graces. A good conscience does not fear the detractions of the impious, and a mind conscious of rectitude scorns the lies of rumor. A good conscience is always cheerful, and

    Homily 24.

    Fol. LVI.

    ... works the righteousness of God; he is not uselessly sorrowful. A good conscience always advances in the love of the Lord, and he who lives innocently will not fear danger. A good conscience has peace and concord with all in God, and in humble simplicity cares for its own salvation. A good conscience strengthens the soul; but he who is constant in evils will fall into despair. A good conscience confidently rebukes the foolish man; but he who is evil keeps a bitter silence. A good conscience gladdens the soul; but he who is conscious of his own evils continually suffers desolation of mind. A good conscience safely rebukes the impious man; but he who has lost the testimony of uprightness always fears reproof. A good conscience is the most beautiful adornment of the soul; and he who does not care for wisdom in this life will die in want.

    A good conscience is the dwelling-place of the virtues and the true mansion of heavenly mysteries. A good conscience is the consummation of all philosophy and the fullness of all sciences. A good conscience is the best teacher of the virtues, and the perfected discipline of all studies. A good conscience bears the best fruit of holiness, and, standing founded in the fear of the Lord, admits no sin. A good conscience is more precious than all the riches of the world, and much sweeter than all desirable things that can be had in this life. A good conscience is the merit of Christian perfection and the humbly presumable beginning of future happiness. A good conscience is a fertile field of virtues, and the sweet and pleasant fragrance of the paradise of God. A good conscience is a very sweet companion to the good man, and a glorious mediator between God and man. A good conscience is very fearful to demons, but a pleasing friend to the holy angels. A good conscience makes the dying man secure against the snares of demons, and he merits having the escort of angels. A good conscience does not fear to appear in the sight of judgment, nor does it dread the judgment of an accusing synteresis. A good conscience has hope in God and, without the unrest of hesitation, the best confidence, because he who remembers having committed no evil comes confidently to the examination of judgment. A good conscience will be richly rewarded by the Lord God, and is changed into everlasting joy.

    A good conscience is not one that perpetrates no evil, but one that, preserving purity for the love of God from every sin, also adorns itself most fittingly by the exercise of all good works. For a good conscience, according to the prophet’s admonition, wholly declines from evil, and with most zealous intention always and continually does good. A good conscience especially adorns the monk, and makes him far removed from secular actions. A good conscience follows the Lord Jesus in simple purity, and is stained by no spots of errors. For a conscience that is good, and so long as it is good, cannot be erroneous, but always remains founded in the truth of the Holy Spirit. But a conscience that has been erroneous is not good. For error both opposes truth and in no way shares in goodness. But when conscience is in error, danger is close at hand, and the descent to hell very steep.

    There are many among cloistered persons who are weak and exceedingly feeble in mind, who are not always directed by the right judgment of their consciences, being preoccupied by various causes. And often indeed a small or great error of conscience arises from ignorance, whenever, that is, one less skilled in spiritual exercise doubts whether what he is considering in his mind is good or evil. For who, walking rightly in his simplicity, understands everything? In doubtful matters the counsels of elders are to be sought, and what they have decided the monk must embrace without doubt as the truth of the opinion. Sometimes conscience errs from negligence, when the monk neglects to examine himself by the scrutiny of reason and does not labor in doubtful matters to investigate the truth. Hence a punishable error arises in the conscience, through which reason is gradually clouded. Frequently also pride of conscience arises from singularity, to which presumption is always joined [unclear]. And this plague often [unclear] among monks and those who profess holiness without the necessary foundation of humility. For the sheep that walks singular paths is more quickly caught and strangled by wolves. Sometimes also an excessively disordered affection casts the conscience down into error, namely when a man loves his own will more than is expedient. For he who is led by the affection of his own sensuality is frequently blinded in the judgment of truth.

    On Serenity of Conscience.

    Hence there is no doubt that it comes about that many have erroneous consciences, because they love too much the pleasures of their own flesh. Every proud, lustful, impure person, and anyone entangled in great or public crimes, clouds his conscience by deliberate perversity; and how erroneously he thinks about the future repayment of merits he frequently shows both by words and by deeds. A malicious affection perverts the judgment of rectitude, and the disordered concupiscence of the flesh clouds the understanding. Sometimes, moreover, excessive and immoderate faint-heartedness makes the conscience err; this evil is born partly from ignorance and partly generated from one’s own sensuality.

    In this scrupulosity, however, let the monk follow the counsel either of the abbot or of some elder more experienced, and let him not rashly defend the opinion of his own head. Excessive scrupulosity is dangerous, because it casts the conscience into error and unhappily causes many to stumble. For everything that is done against conscience is said to build toward hell. Excessive perplexity of mind has also harmed many, and has driven them headlong into various errors. But he who is truly a humble monk submits himself to the examination of his rector. For whoever, in doubts that arise, makes use of his superior’s counsel is not easily overthrown by the snares of demons. For the more the consciences of monks have been exposed to the examination of a wise prelate, the more secure and more brightly shining they will gleam.

    Therefore, dearest brothers, care must be taken first of all that you have consciences free from every error; then pure from all vices; and finally adorned with the holy works of all the virtues. Therefore let the monk who desires to advance in truth guard his heart with every watchfulness, and, as far as can be done, let him set a barrier before his senses and not permit anything deadly to enter. But if, by any occasion, he recognizes that he has fallen into some sin, let him at once strive to wipe it away by true penance, and let him not grant time to the wicked seed in which it may grow stronger for the worse. While the wound is small, let a remedy be applied, for if it is neglected it grows beyond measure.

    Therefore, my brothers, strongly resist the first motions of demonic suggestion, and overcome the enemy when he is small and weak. But if the sensuality of the body has become altogether wanton, let it be brought back to obedience by harsh mortification, just as we know our holy father Benedict did, when he rooted out the slippery wantonness of the flesh by the prickings of nettles and thorns. Then, too, if you diligently recall to memory the dreadful future punishments of the impious, you will easily overcome the unlawful motions of the flesh. For there is no one who does not fear pain more than he loves pleasure.

    Also bring often to mind the joys of heavenly blessedness, to which you desire to come, for if you faithfully consider them, you will strongly lessen the fire of the flesh. Whatever delights in the world is corruptible and momentary; but the joys of eternal pleasure remain without end forever. It is therefore foolish, and a matter of extreme madness, to choose a passing advantage and to despise that good which remains eternally. He is judged foolish among men who prefers dross to gold; but he is held most senseless before God who sets temporal pleasure before everlasting goods.

    He who loves a serene conscience should flee idleness, since, as Scripture says, every idle man is in desire, and idleness has taught much malice. The soul must be occupied with good exercises, and the fire of holy conduct, which burns with charity, must be nourished by continual use. For the idle man lives neither for himself nor for his neighbor, but is always given over to the belly or to sleep; he opens his mind to vice, and keeps it closed and empty of virtues. Idleness, the kindler of lust, quickly extinguishes the fervor of spiritual devotion.

    Abstinence also is especially necessary for a monk, so that his conscience may remain clean. For, as Saint Jerome says, a filled belly easily foams into lust; and he who nourishes his servant delicately will find him disobedient. The lover of serenity of conscience becomes constant in holy prayers, since, as dogs flee a stone, so demons flee devout and continual prayer. Let him also carefully beware of acedia together with sadness of mind; and as soon as he senses some temptation creeping in, let him have recourse to the consolation of the Scriptures. Indeed, the mind which the word of God has filled [unclear] foul thought will enter. Whatever we do, whatever we think, whatever we perform, let us always know that the presence of God is at hand, and we shall easily overcome disordered delight. A good conscience never forgets the presence of God, but always meditates that its judge is present.

    All Things. XXV. Fol. LVII.

    Act now, my brothers, so that you may have consciences pure from every crime; and if anyone feels himself burdened in some fault, let him return without delay through true penitence to necessary purity. For unless you have consciences clean and good at all times, you live as apostates, not as monks.

    On Continual Preparation for Death. All Things. XXV.

    The supreme philosophy of cloistered religious, my dearest brothers, is continual meditation on death. Hence a certain wise man, considering the usefulness of this philosophy, admonished every mortal, saying: “Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Meditation on death draws men back from the pleasures of the flesh and brings on contempt for all corruptible things. Meditation on death despises present things by voluntary poverty and drives the mind toward desire for future things. Meditation on death banishes pride far away and plants true humility in the heart of the one meditating. Meditation on death makes the monk solicitous about preserving regular discipline and never permits him to be idle. Meditation on death cuts away all the vanities of the world and preserves the mind in the highest temperance. Meditation on death makes one despise the vain and transitory honors of the world and think of nothing other than the future judgment of God. Meditation on death does not fear the poverty of this life, because with its whole desire it longs for everlasting riches. Meditation on death endures all adversities of this world most patiently for the love of Christ, because it hopes for nothing other than the heavenly reward. Meditation on death makes the monk humble and obedient in all the commandments of righteousness. Meditation on death makes the monk quiet and stable in the congregation, and in good harmony with all in Christ. Meditation on death makes the monk quiet and peaceable, and tranquil without any disturbance of mind. Meditation on death drives out all dissoluteness and frivolity, and preserves the monk mature and wholesomely sorrowful in all things. Meditation on death makes the monk solitary and continually devoted in holy prayers. Meditation on death hastens penitence and brings on true compunction. Meditation on death withdraws desire from every vanity and keeps the conscience serene and most pure. Meditation on death makes a person despise all the consolations of this world and prepare daily for departure. Meditation on death teaches one to flee idleness and makes a person keep watch constantly in the fear of the Lord. Meditation on death does injury to no one, because it always fears the strict accounting of judgment. Meditation on death softens anger and all disordered motions, because when a person thinks that he will soon die, nothing external disturbs the mind. Meditation on death makes the heart contrite and humble, because intent remembrance of future things permits no one to be proud. Continual meditation on death makes one’s departure safe at the last, because it renders prepared the one who has meditated for a long time. Meditation on death especially befits cloistered religious and monks, whom renunciation of all earthly things and regular profession itself have already made dead and buried to the world. Meditation on death makes the monk run prudently in the course of spiritual warfare and renew daily the purpose of holy fervor. Continual meditation on death is very useful to cloistered religious, because it powerfully represses the vices of the flesh and grants no entrance to perverse thoughts of the mind. For the holy bishop Augustine says: Fear of future death necessarily shakes the mind, and, like a nail of the flesh, fastens all motions of pride to the wood of the cross. And the holy champion of the Church, Jerome, says: Nothing will benefit you as much for temperance in all things as frequent thought of the shortness of life; its end is certain, but nothing is more uncertain than its hour. Therefore meditation on death corrects all intemperance and sets in order the character of the one meditating, stable in beautiful variety. Meditation on death gives a person true wisdom and perfects the highest philosophy among cloistered religious. For Plato too held the opinion that the whole life of wise men is a meditation on death, because we are all born on this condition, that we should again depart from here through death. For Scripture says: We all die, and like waters we flow down into the earth, which do not return any more. And the holy apostle of Christ, Paul: It is appointed, he says, for men to die once [unclear]

    On Continual Preparation for Death:

    The continual meditation on necessary death makes a man not trust in earthly things, but with foresight await his departure in every place and time. Meditation on death always awaits the end of life in every place, because it is wholly ignorant of the moment of dying. He who daily meditates on the coming of future death disposes himself at all times for dying with as much diligence as he can. For death is certain to us; all of us are ignorant of the hour of dying. Hence, brothers, we urgently admonish your charities as much as we can, that you always think on death; with such foresight prepare yourselves diligently for dying, so that when the hour of departure comes you may not fear. Let no one promise himself a long life in this world, because nothing so deceives mortals as hope of a longer life. For what does a more advanced age accomplish in the good, except that it makes them liable for more offenses, and always less disposed for dying? The longer we live in this world, the more we fear death. A longer age accumulates greater debts of spiritual obligation, so that an old man fears all the more to come before the sight of the strict judge, the more he knows himself bound before the Lord to render account in many matters. For the soul leaves its body unconquered when it is driven by the heavier goads of its conscience. But he who is pure from every malice of iniquity and adorned for salvation with the necessary comeliness of virtues does not fear to die, because through death he goes to eternal life. Therefore, O monk, live now such as you wish to die, because death cannot be evil when the integrity of a good life has gone before. O reader, whoever loves the Lord Jesus above all things dies [well], because, despising all the goods of this world for love of him, he truly keeps his words. Securely does he depart from this life who always lives in the love of God without stain of conscience. Securely does he die whose life is defiled by no pleasures of this world. For the death of the righteous is a most sweet sleep, because it is a tranquil entrance into eternal life. But the death of sinners is very evil, whose evil life and one contrary to divine institutions has gone before. For him who lives in sins, contrary to God, death becomes a dreadful entrance into hell. Such a man does not die who lives well; rarely does he die well who has always lived badly.

    Homily XXV. Fol. LVIII.

    ... brothers, and those who have now preceded us in this monastery. Just as there is no memory among us of those who have gone before, so also we shall be in perpetual oblivion among them and among those who follow. Let us ponder these things beforehand, dearest brothers, while we live, lest we fall into death unprepared. Just as we hasten daily toward death, so daily let us prepare ourselves, as far as we are able. He dies securely who in life is adorned with good and holy works. Nor let the hope of a longer life deceive you, for the longer we live in this world, the shorter is the life you will have. Behold, daily we die as we tend toward death; daily one part of life is charged against us; and the longer our life extends, the more the remaining time of life is shortened. All the time that we have lived is wholly gone when it has passed; what we live today we divide moment by moment with death; how much time for living remains to us in the future we do not know. Why, then, do we trust in the vanity of this life, when we are soon to die? Thus let us continually think, brothers, that we shall soon come to that place to which all our elders have gone before us. We are all born under this law: that we should soon die. And let death appear terrible to him whose whole life is polluted in the pleasure of the flesh, and who stores up nothing good in heaven. But we who place all our hope in Christ Jesus our Savior, despising all the pleasures of the world for love of him: why should we fear death? Yet since the mind is most terrible of all terrors [unclear], we shall be able to drive out indiscreet fear of dying in this way, if we prepare ourselves daily as though about to die. It is one thing to have fear of death, another to have trembling. For even the Lord Jesus, the patron over death, felt the trembling of approaching death, to show the two properties of his nature. Therefore continual meditation on death is altogether necessary for us who are weak; indeed, the mind not yet perfected in the love of Christ is roused to the grace of compunction as if by a violent impulse. For the memory of future death, like a nail driven into wood, thus pierces the mind with a useful dread. The memory of death introduces arduous penitence and true sobriety of mind. The memory of death is necessary for beginners, since conversion begins from servile fear, and afterward is gradually raised in charity through filial [fear]. The memory of death and of the strict examination of the future judgment of God is especially necessary for those who, through an evil and long-standing habit, are drawn to sin. And there are among you some who are too lukewarm and negligent in the spiritual warfare; admonishing them, we exhort them as a father that they remember they are mortal, and live henceforth in such a way that they do not fear to die. For it is very dangerous to live in that state in which one would be afraid to die. We must live in such a way that we await death securely; this can finally happen if, preserving ourselves in all purity of mind and body, we continually burn in the exercises of divine charity. Let us live, as far as can be done, innocently, according to the rule of our divine father Benedict, which we have professed, and we shall have good hope that almighty God will have mercy on us, for he does not permit a man of good will to perish. Let us always think of God as present with us everywhere: he sees all things, knows all things, understands all things, rewards all things. And let us live in that purity in which we have promised to serve his most holy majesty.

    The end of the twenty-fifth homily of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to the monks.

    Here is the end of the first book of exhortations to the monks, written by my own hand, of me, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, on the day of the month of June, in the year of Christians 1486, in the fourth indiction, in the thirty-third year of my age. I have dedicated this work to my predecessor, now abbot of Seligenstadt, most dear to me.

    Letter.

    John Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Sponheim, though unworthy, to the reverend father Lord Johannes de Colenhausen, abbot of Seligenstadt and formerly of Sponheim, my most dear predecessor: with prayers, a spirit ready and prepared to give satisfaction.

    Recently, venerable teacher, I had sent to you my first book of exhortations to monks, containing twenty-five homilies. After I understood that it had been approved by your examination, I judged that this second book also, which I now send, should confidently be inscribed to your name. In the former I collected, for the instruction of the brothers, twenty-five homilies which I had delivered before them; in this one I have arranged the sermons in number according to the order in which they were spoken in their presence. I do not fear to undergo the examination of your paternity, since I have always had you as a gentle teacher, and long ago found you to be a sincere lover of truth. For you are vigorous in intellect, both gentle and profound, able easily to distinguish between true and false, and, where necessity requires, to amend everything sufficiently. Therefore I pray that, according to the gentleness innate in you, you may patiently bear the rudeness of my talent, for I am both a little child in knowledge of the Scriptures and a novice in the order of prelates. Exercise in the Scriptures will give me practice, as I trust, and continued solicitude will give progress.

    The occupation of household business and the poverty of the place very often draw me back from salutary study, and carry my mind elsewhere against the purpose of my will. Only on feast days and Sundays is leisure granted me for writing; on these, out of reverence for God, I am accustomed to admit no cases of the country people. Sometimes also, after the customary chanting of matins, I am accustomed to spend what remains of the night on the study of letters, and, as far as I can, to work by lamplight on something for the instruction of my brothers. For I desire in all things to follow your footsteps, and by teaching to be solicitous for what is praiseworthy. I submit these sermons to your examination, and with humble supplication I beg that the file of your mastery may correct them. I have collected a few out of many into order, since I neither committed them all to writing, nor did an excessive extension of the book seem to me either necessary or useful. For on feast days, when we have respite from the tumult of worldly business, we devote ourselves to reading according to the rule of the Scriptures. And lest I should seem to occupy the place of shepherd in vain, what I have worked out by night I am accustomed after none, in place of the regular study, to say and to recite from a small sheet before the brothers in chapter. For I consider that this solicitude of mine not only profits the brothers for edification, but also conduces to my skill in composition. Farewell, venerable teacher, and pray for us. From Sponheim, on the twelfth day of the month of September, in the year of the Christians one thousand four hundred eighty-six.

    Sermon I. Folio LIX.

    In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the second book of exhortations to monks, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, afterwards of [unclear]. How cautiously monks must live: Sermon One.

    Many indeed, most beloved brothers, are the things necessary for you to consider in this life, if you desire to arrive at the glory of eternal salvation. For you know, Scripture bearing witness, that your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour; and we know that he must be resisted with great vigilance in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ through works of charity. Therefore let no one presume on his own powers, lest he trust in vanity; for unless you humbly keep yourselves in the fear of the Lord, you will quickly fall into the snare of the devil. “The greater you are,” Scripture commands, “humble yourself in all things,” for God resists the proud and grants grace to the humble, and to the true despiser of this world.

    A monk must always be solicitous in the observance of regular discipline, and continually zealous in the fear of the Lord. A monk must be chaste and modest in mind and body alike, so that he may serve God just as he promised, in all purity. A monk ought not to live according to his own will, but according to the Rule and according to the direction of his pastor, conformed to the norm of cenobitic institution. A monk ought to love busy and holy silence, and usefully occupy his mind in the reading of the Scriptures. A monk must at all times, even unto death, be solicitous that he be made perfect in the observance of the commandments of God and of the Rule.

    But so that you may know what things are necessary for you, living in holy religion, for perfection, I shall describe for you a certain path of virtues, by which one must direct the way to the kingdom of heaven. All the virtues, however, cohere with one another by the bond of kinship, so that he who possesses one perfectly seems to have them all, and he who lacks even one is said to possess none at all.

    The first of all virtues necessary for salvation is the most holy Catholic faith, separated from every pollution of errors and heresies, and originally rooted in the doctrine of our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as Scripture bears witness, without faith it is impossible to please God; and he who does not believe in the only-begotten Son of God is already judged, and the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore faith is the origin of all virtues, from which all pursuits of salvation arise.

    True and right faith in God begets fear of the Lord, for if we believe God to be just, we shall rightly confess that he is to be feared. Right faith brings forth hope and confidence, because when we believe God to be merciful, soon we hope that by his goodness we can attain salvation. Faith begets charity, because if we believe God to be the highest good, without doubt we love him. For who would not love what he does not doubt to be the supreme good? Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing. Faith joins the soul to God, and through the mediation of charity makes it the friend of the eternal King.

    For the most holy prelate Augustine says: There are no greater riches, no treasures, no honors, no substance of this world greater than the Catholic faith, which saves sinful men, enlightens the blind, cures the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores penitents, increases the just, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins, widows, and married persons in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, and places believers with the holy angels in the eternal inheritance of the heavens.

    But where sound faith is not, there justice cannot be, because the just man lives by faith; and he who lacks the merit of justice will have no portion with Christ. Faith is the beginning of human salvation, without which no one can reach the number of the children of God, nor possess any share in the kingdom of God. Faith is the foundation of all virtues; whatever is done outside faith is without doubt built for Gehenna. Christian faith is a most beautiful lamp illuminating the soul, and through the observance of the commandments leading it into eternal happiness.

    Faith first brings the mind back to the knowledge of God; afterward it gives the precepts of living unto obedience; and when a man has kept the commandments of God, hope of attaining salvation follows; then charity is made firm in hearts. Faith gives knowledge to the soul, knowledge [unclear]; because when right faith is corrupted by the falsehood of heresies, by no action is one brought to the harbor of salvation. Therefore let it be in faith

    That monks must live cautiously.

    [unclear], uprightness and truth; in action, justice and sincerity; and no iniquity will have dominion. For faith without works is dead, and earns nothing toward the salvation of eternal happiness. To have faith without works of charity is to imitate the demons, who, though they are wholly estranged from all charity, nevertheless both believe that God is just and tremble. Hence concerning believers who do not show works of charity, the Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah, and afterward through himself in the holy Gospel, saying: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Whoever praises Christ with his mouth, without work, is like a man who doubts in faith. For if he truly believed, he would certainly fear God. Faith without works is like a body dead without the spirit, which, removed from the sight of the living, is hidden in the tomb. If you believe well and live badly, you destroy yourself by your own sword, because for one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin. Beware, my brothers, lest you admit any error in faith, and take the utmost care that there be no wickedness in action. Follow the faith which holy Church commends to us; live the life prescribed by the Gospel and by the cenobitic rule.

    Then have hope in the manifestation of God at all times most certain, but never divorced from fear of the Lord. Hope is the certain expectation, through the grace of the merciful God, of future goods, and solicitude for deserving the crown of justice through the exercise of charity. Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, which the grace of God works in us, accompanied by the uprightness of a good will. Hope is that by which a person hopes to come to the life of eternal happiness which he desires, and, through the mediation of God’s grace, also disposes and prepares his own will to meet it.

    Hope concerns good things, difficult things, future things, and possible things; in these no one hopes for the contrary. For no one hopes for evil, nor for something trivial, nor for what is present or past; nor are we ignorant that hope is not of impossible things. Hope is the moderator of all labors, and the sole consoler amid tribulations. For hope of future goods gives rest to those laboring for Christ in this life, just as expectation of the crown, through continual victory, softens the pain of wounds for those contending in the contest. Hope strengthened the martyrs in torments, and made them, in the power of Christ, stronger than all persecutors. Hope of eternal blessedness preserves the Church, and gave the holy confessors and virgins true charity in Christ. Hope strongly raises up the soul cast down by grief; and the higher it has lifted itself through love, the less it feels the contrary things of this world. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, because hope does not confound, as the holy Apostle promised, by which we have been made saved.

    But so that hope may not break out into presumption, fear of the Lord is necessary for our salvation, so that we may not doubt that he whom we believe merciful and compassionate is also just and upright. For the most blessed Pope Gregory says: Nothing is safer for us than to tremble humbly under hope, lest the incautious mind either cast itself into the depth of vices by despairing, or fall presumptuously by being exalted. For the more humbly it trembles before the eyes of the strict judge under hope, the more robustly it stands in him. Fear of God corrects the mind and keeps it pure from all malice. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, because on the way of God one begins from fear, so that little by little one may come to the strength of charity. Fear of the Lord orders the monk, and makes him zealous in the observance of regular discipline. Fear of the Lord guards the rule and preserves true purity of mind and body. Fear of the Lord neglects none of the things that are commanded, but is solicitous in all things. Walls are [unclear]. A city without the protection of walls is quickly taken by enemies, and the monk who does not have the fear of God is easily overcome by demons. For the fear of God alone is what corrects minds, drives away crimes, preserves the innocent, and makes the monk persevering in the purpose of holiness.

    From fear there gradually arises charity; when, with God’s help, it has truly been rooted in the mind, overcoming servile fear, it now casts it out. The root of all goods is charity, since whatever good is done in this life is ordered by charity alone, so that it may please God. Charity is the greatest of all virtues; without it all deeds of mortals are nothing. For the most holy Apostle of Christ says: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so that [unclear]

    [unclear]. Hope strongly raises up the soul cast down by grief; and the higher it has lifted itself through love, the less it feels the contrary things of this world. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, because hope does not confound, as the holy Apostle promised, by which we have been made saved.

    But so that hope may not break out into presumption, fear of the Lord is [unclear] necessary for our salvation, so that we may not doubt that he whom we believe merciful and compassionate is also just and upright. For the most blessed Pope Gregory says [unclear]: the more humbly it trembles under hope, the more robustly it stands in him. Fear of God corrects the mind and keeps it pure from all malice. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, because on the way of God one begins from fear, so that little by little one may come to the strength of charity. Fear of the Lord [unclear]. For [unclear] is the fear of God which corrects minds, drives away crimes, preserves the innocent, and makes [unclear]. The root of all goods is charity, since whatever [unclear] deeds of mortals.     [unclear]. Hope strongly raises up the soul cast down by grief; and the higher it has lifted itself through love, the less it feels the contrary things of this world. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, because hope does not confound, as the holy Apostle [unclear].

    Sermon I. Folio LX.

    “... so that I might move mountains, but if I have not charity, I am nothing. And if I should distribute all my goods as food for the poor, and if I should hand over my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.” Consider carefully, now, my brothers, your own selves, and ask your consciences whether you have the true charity of God, without which all other things avail nothing for salvation. For you have heard the clear judgment of the Apostle, by which he says that charity is necessary for salvation. Let no one put confidence in the wisdom of this world; let no one vainly exalt himself over the natural gifts he has received; let no one presume upon bodily continence, since, if charity is lacking, the observance of the other things contributes nothing to salvation.
