But lest anyone presume a false opinion of himself, the holy Apostle set forth certain signs and operations of charity, saying: “Charity is patient, is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, and does not seek what is its own; it is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.” Have the charity of God in you, my brothers; unless you keep it, you labor in vain by striving.

    Humility is very necessary for you, and often so: it is not only a great virtue, but also the nurse of the other virtues and the foremost guardian of them all. For Pope Gregory the Great says: “He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.” For the greatest virtue of monks is humility, since they are bound to be so much humbler than others living their life in the world, as by profession they are bound to strive and tend toward greater perfection. Humility is the stable foundation of the virtues; whatever is built upon it will be overturned by no whirlwind of tempest. Through pride the devil fell from heaven; through humility man ascends. In vain are we called monks if we have not been humble, for just as fire is extinguished if it lacks the fuel of wood, so a monk without humility is judged very unworthy of his name. By Christian humility the devil is conquered, and, as if struck by a nail, is overcome as he flees. No more splendid jewel is seen in monastic adornment than humility; if a monk has despised it, he has denied both his profession and the humble Christ.

    Prudence follows upon humility; it always directs all things to the standard of reason and does nothing except what is right, honorable, and praiseworthy. Prudence knows what it ought virtuously to seek, and knows well what, according to the right judgment of reason, it ought to avoid. True and perfect prudence is that by which we seek that highest, unchangeable good, and order all things to their due and right end. Prudence preserves the observance of regular discipline stable in vigor, and brings wandering monks back to the complete restoration of their lost purpose. Prudence directs the monk in the right way of salvation, and does not allow him to decline to either side. Prudence preserves peace and concord among brothers, and orders right action in each matter. Prudence, O my brothers, is very necessary for you; by it you will know in every action what things are to be undertaken by you, and what in turn are to be fled. True prudence, not of the flesh but of the spirit, teaches you to despise the world, and to desire only those things that are future and eternal. Prudence teaches a man to stand firm in himself, and neither in prosperity nor in adversity to decline from the purpose of holiness. Prudence teaches how to order present things beautifully; it brings past things back to memory for instruction; and it foresees future things, lest anything happen unexpectedly. Prudence corrects offenders usefully and fruitfully, and composes all that it either does, says, or thinks, according to the judgment of reason, toward its due end. Therefore be prudent as serpents and simple as doves, because prudence without goodness is malice, and simplicity without rational prudence is called foolishness. For the most holy Paul, Apostle of Christ, says: “The prudence of the flesh is death.” Be prudent, lest you be circumvented by the deceit of others, but simple, lest you circumvent anyone. For this is the duty of the prudent man: neither to be capable of being deceived, nor to wish to deceive anyone. [unclear] By foreseeing, indeed, one is called prudent.

    Justice accompanies prudence; it is the most splendid of all the virtues. For without justice all the remaining virtues are nothing. Justice is the preserver of religion, the mother of grace, the nurse of observance, the nourisher of truth, the begetter of peace, and the origin of piety.

    That monks must live cautiously.

    Justice is the virtue which distributes and preserves for each person what is his own; by it private advantage is neglected so that it may preserve the common advantage and equity, without which no commonwealth can subsist in divine peace. For the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “A kingdom is transferred from one nation to another because of injustices, and injuries, and insults, and various deceits.” The order of justice looks first to God, then to the fatherland, thereafter to parents, afterwards to all in common according to the distinctions of ranks and the merits of dignities. To God, in the first place, at the dictation of justice, we owe religion, faith, worship, devotion, and thanksgivings, and true love from the whole heart with obedient submission. Then to ourselves, purity of mind and body, continence with zeal for perfection, so that through obedience it may be permitted us to return to him by whom we were created. In the third place, to the fatherland we owe advantage, honor, and defense, and, insofar as we can, to procure its benefit together with justice itself. Fourth, we are bound to our parents by honor and obedience, and in their necessity by care and support of every kind. Fifth, to prelates [unclear], to subjects teaching and nourishment, and correction to those who offend. In the seventh place, however, we are bound to give honor to elders and princes, and, without fault, subjection for the love of God. Eighth, we owe reverence to venerable persons, and honor to priests. Consequently we are bound to equals by friendship, to inferiors by condescension, to benefactors by reciprocation, to friends by fellowship, to enemies by patience, to the poor by mercy, to the wretched by consolation, to all by charity. This, however, is true justice: by it we love God from the whole heart for his own sake, and our neighbor in God as ourselves, but enemies for God’s sake, distributing to each person what is owed to him by right and providing for the advantage of all.

    But since excessive justice easily incurs sin, temperance is necessary for you in all things; it alone makes men more perfect. Temperance is the virtue which by reason discerns and conquers the motions of the soul and every lust, lest impulse in acting exceed the equity of the law. Temperance is a most excellent virtue: it governs pleasures and preserves all things in due order. Apply temperance to all your actions, words, and also thoughts, and the discretion necessary to the virtues. Whatever good you do with discretion receives the name by the merit of virtue; but what is done without discretion must be called vice. Discretion is the moderator of all virtues, and the greatest ornament of prudence and justice. Discretion is necessary not only for prelates but also for subjects, since it gives order to those exercising virtue, grants modesty to affections, and bestows on all human counsels most beautiful grace and honorableness. Hence a certain wise man said: “There is a measure in things; there are, finally, fixed limits, beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.”

    For this, brothers, strength of soul is necessary for you, through which you may become not only steadfast in adversities but also ready and cheerful in difficult things. For who, especially without strength of soul, could despise this world with its pleasures, and persevere in holy monastic religion under the laws of obedience even unto death? Strength of soul takes its powers from the charity of Christ, and stands constant, no less in adversities than in prosperity, in desire for virtue. Strength walks the way of uprightness without fear, and to enemies it appears terrifying with a certain holy pride. But strength of soul seems fearful of [unclear]. Strength despises the injuries of the small and easily overcomes all the pleasures of the flesh. Strength lies hidden in patience, is shown in adversity, and is openly declared through patience. Strong of soul is not the man who avenges injuries brought upon him, but the man who patiently tolerates them; and if he has received his adversary into his power, he thinks that he has been able to take vengeance. The strength of monks is to despise the world, to conquer the flesh, to spurn all the honors and pleasures of the world, and to place all hope and confidence in God alone. The measure of strength is to be necessary, neither rash nor [unclear], because, walking on the right way, it declines neither to the right nor to the left. That monk must be judged strong who is temperate in all things, and moderate and just. Hence the most holy pope Gregory says: “The strength of the just is to conquer the flesh, to oppose their own pleasures, to extinguish the delight of the present life [unclear] strengthen; they despise earthly things, seek heavenly things; they can be killed, they cannot be bent, nor can they endure falsehoods. Through weakness they fear [unclear], nor, when harmed, do they ever keep silent from the truth.”

    The monk, therefore, who is strong with true virtue neither ventures rashly nor fears imprudently. For fortitude together with constancy is the royal road; from it the rash and obstinate man turns aside to the right, but the fearful, faint-hearted, and timid man to the left. The monk, constant and strong in spirit, never withdraws from the purpose of holiness, but is neither cast down by adversities nor lifted up by prosperities. Hence also the most holy bishop Ambrose says: “The fool is changed like the moon. But the wise man is not broken by fear, not changed by power, not puffed up by prosperities, not overwhelmed by sorrows.” For where wisdom and virtue are, there is constancy and fortitude of spirit. Therefore the wise man is always the same in spirit; he is not diminished or increased by changes of affairs, nor does he waver like a little child so as to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but he remains perfect in Christ, founded in charity and rooted in the perfection of faith.

    Lastly, my dearest brothers, there must be perseverance. Take away perseverance, and neither will virtue have a reward, nor service a recompense, nor a benefit merit grace. For he alone who has persevered to the end will be saved. No virtue has merit if perseverance does not bring it to its increase. The kingdom of eternal blessedness is promised not to those who begin the good, but to those who persevere in the good even unto death, because not in the morning, not at midday, but when evening had come, the denarius was paid to those laboring in the vineyard.

    For it is not he who began well who is to be praised, but he who continued well to the end is more honorably regarded. Therefore, my brothers, I am accustomed earnestly to admonish you, and I must never cease, that you should diligently attend to your vocation and walk cautiously in all religion and holiness, as befits sworn soldiers of Christ. For now is the time for doing good, because when the hour of death has arrived it will cut off entirely every capacity for working. And therefore, as long as you live sound and unharmed, do good; always consider the future repayment, and daily grow from spiritual progress. Seek the Lord while he can be found. The life of Christ the Savior should be your imitation; you are bound, from the foundation of your institution, to follow him not by bodily steps, but by your powers, by likeness of affections. Walk cautiously in all things; always place the fear of God before the gaze of your mind in true humility. For great purity is needed by you who have consented, in mind and body, to the holy warfare of Christ. It now belongs to you, O brothers, to despise the world and all things that are in the world for God’s sake with perpetual fortitude; to overcome all motions of fleshly pleasures; to flee sin; to occupy yourselves constantly in good and holy works. Your life also, as far as human weakness allows, ought to be made righteous in angelic purity, and to flee and detest every [unclear]. But the holy angels are never idle, but are always intent, without weariness or tedium, upon the praises of God. The holy angels love God above all things, and do not withdraw from his charity even for a moment. In imitation of them the monk ought to be assiduous in the service of Christ, and always occupied in good works according to the Gospel and the Rule. The monk ought to have most fervent charity for God, and it is proper that he have true and sincere love of neighbor. For burning love toward God perfects the monk and does not allow him to be idle. For the four-times most holy pope Gregory says: “The love of God is never idle. For it works great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it was never true love of God.” For if the mad poet spoke truth concerning carnal love, “let him love who does not wish to become idle,” how much more powerfully does the most chaste love of God drive the mind that it possesses toward arduous things. Love God, brothers, with the whole heart, as far as the strength of desire can extend itself, and you will be able most easily to observe all things that have been commanded you. For nothing is difficult to one who loves; but all hard things, all grave and arduous things, burning love makes easy.

    What the ordering of a good monastic life is: Sermon Two.

    We have set forth that the institution of our most holy father Benedict, which by the customary term we call religion or order, shone forth as most excellent at the beginning of its foundation, and was very greatly and manifoldly spread throughout the whole church of the Latins. Hence for very many years in this same order many wise, learned, and most holy men flourished.

    What the good ordering of monastic life is.

    who magnificently illuminated the whole Church. For there are some who write that from this monastic religion of ours fifteen thousand six hundred, men as well as nuns, have been entered in the catalogue of the saints. The multitude of these saints in the order, brothers, is set before us for imitation, not for vain glorying. What can their multitude contribute to our salvation, if we do not imitate the manner of life in which they went before us? Whenever we desire profitably to praise the most holy men of our order, let us hasten by holy conduct to come into their fellowship. For then we shall glory fruitfully in the multitude of the saints of our order, if, living rightly, we earnestly strive to increase their number. Therefore indeed we set before you so great a multitude of saints, so that, when you see that many before you in this very order conquered the world and the flesh, you may at last rise up from your lukewarm manner of life. The virtue that God’s mercy granted to them he will not deny to you, if you ask in true charity.

    They conquered the world because they loved Christ with entire devotion, despising all things for love of him. They despised all things, and the Lord Jesus provided for them whatever seemed necessary to them for the sustenance of life. This fervor of devotion among monks endured after the first institution of the order for many years with great constancy, and converted the souls of many thousands of people to the Lord. But nothing among human things is stable; nothing among perishable things is everlasting. Holy religion brought riches upon the monks, until in time the daughter suffocated the mother. For, as Scripture says, all those who wish to become rich fall into the temptations of the devil. The beloved grew fat and kicked back; made fat and enlarged with earthly possessions, he abandoned the holy pursuits of the first institution, went after vanities and false madnesses, and an abundance of temporal things made him needy and wretched in spiritual riches.

    This pitiable deformity of our order began almost two hundred years after the passing of the divine father Benedict, and with time it grew more and more, until at last the harmful poison spread through the whole order. But this deformity occupied the order not suddenly, but through the succession of many years, until it had taken over almost the whole of it, although almighty God never left it wholly without good men, but always reserved for himself some who had by no means bent their knees to Baal. For men of mercy arose, whose righteous deeds will never be handed over to oblivion; pitying the ruin of the order, they put their shoulder under the labor and, the Lord generously granting aid, restored it in many places.

    Indeed many varied particular reformations flourished often in the order at different times, but there was never any general one that brought the whole order back to the integrity of regular observance. Finally, we now see that the particular restorations, which we have said were many, have almost all collapsed again. Most recently, however, namely in the year of the Christians one thousand four hundred and twenty, when the general council was being celebrated at Constance, a certain new and, up to now, last particular reformation took its beginning in Germany. It took its name from a certain monastery in the regions of Saxony, then indeed the poorest of all, which is called Bursfelde.

    The first author and leader of this most holy reformation was Johannes Rode, abbot of the distinguished monastery of Saint Matthias at Trier. Having been appointed general visitor of the order by the aforesaid Council of Constance, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should be judged reprobate, he first displayed reformation in himself. For first of all he reformed both himself and the monks of the said monastery; he issued constitutions conforming to the Rule; he obtained confirmation of the holy work from the apostolic see. But among all the monasteries of the order, Bursfelde, a humble and rather poor monastery, first received this reformation, which it afterwards extended to Reinhausen and to a few monasteries of Saxony neighboring it.

    When at last Johannes Rode, abbot of Saint Matthias and leader of our reformation, had died, since in that place no suitable successor was found for extending the undertaking that had been begun, Johannes de Hagen, abbot of Bursfelde, who had already reformed certain monasteries, a holy man and very zealous for the order, was elected at the urging of Jacob, archbishop of Trier. Content with his poverty, he did not consent to leave Bursfelde, lest he seem to have preferred riches to poverty. He therefore remained in his own monastery, and another was appointed in the place of the first reformer. Since he seemed comparable to his predecessor neither in learning nor in zeal, he was able to accomplish little for the continuation of the undertaking begun, nor to enlarge the reformation among many. Meanwhile it happened that Nicholas of Cusa, presbyter cardinal of the holy Roman Church

    legate of the apostolic see to come into Germany; and since he burned with great zeal for our order, he established and granted many things for its reformation. Hearing, moreover, of the good reputation of the aforesaid abbot in Bursfelde and of his most fervent purpose of regular discipline, he summoned [him] to himself [unclear], settled the matter, and through his diligence [unclear] many things reformed. On this occasion at last he instituted an annual chapter for the preservation of the reformation; he transferred the presidency from Saint Matthias to Bursfelde; and he commanded, through the apostolic see, that all things which he had established for the good of the reformation be confirmed.

    The first abbot of Bursfelde in the reformation was Johannes, a monk appointed from Reinhausen; the second, Johannes called de Hagen; the third, Theodericus, whom we saw; and the fourth, Johannes, who has now lately been installed in the government. We briefly touch upon the origins of our reformation, dearest brothers, for this reason: that you may know with how much labor it began, and that unto death you may persevere steadfast in the holy observance of the rule. Among all the reformations of our order that preceded it, none was more conformable and agreeable to the one rule of the divine father Benedict, and none more alien from foreign aids. We have read the statutes of nearly all other reformations; but we judge that none cleaves more than ours to the rule, to the purity of Benedict’s intention. This is the Bursfelde reformation, most holy in the order, which teaches true obedience and preserves subjection in humility. In this holy religious life the monks live poor and without private property; they live humble; they live obedient; they live chaste. O venerable union of monks, in which charity reigns doubled, obedience serves, humility complies, prayer keeps watch, perseverance fights, glad chastity triumphs. This is the school of regular discipline, the institute of Christian humility, which directs morals to rectitude and restrains the vices of the flesh. No one in this arena of virtue is permitted by his own will to follow [unclear] against the rule; no one is forbidden to do good. In this holy union one lives according to the purity of the rule; and if anyone begins to stray from the path of rectitude, the diligence of the elders immediately recalls him to the observance of justice. The rule of the most holy father Benedict is read publicly three times in the year, so that no one may try to excuse himself from observance under the pretext of ignorance.

    There are two things that promise me great hope for the perseverance of this holy reformation: namely, the annual chapter and the diligent biennial visitation of the monks. But if either of these is neglected, the reformation will soon be in danger. Consider now, dearest brothers, and take the most diligent care you can, that you do not occupy this monastery of the divine bishop Martin uselessly under the title of so venerable a reformation; for unless you live according to the rule and the statutes of the order, purely, holily, and blamelessly, you trust in the name in vain. We shall say to you a few true admonitions for salvation, through which the zealous observance of our Bursfelde reformation will possess its name by merit and dignity.

    First of all, before all things, direct the whole power of your striving and your whole desire toward monastic perfection; and as often as you feel it growing lukewarm, renew it by the intent remembrance of the Lord’s passion and most innocent death. For although we are not bound to that perfection by necessity of salvation, nevertheless we are bound to strive for perfection with all our desires. The monk who casts aside the striving to be perfected falls into the pit of failure. The second thing which the sacred custom of our reformation has established for you to keep preserves strongly the striving for perfection in its first desire. Therefore when, awakened, you rise for Prime, do these things in secret. Examine and discuss the course of the coming day; prudently consider what useful thing stands before you to be done. Set in your hearts in what caution you wish to live the whole day, and arm your spirits with patience against all things that might occur as adversities. Whatever you do, perform it in the fervor of charity, and always order all words and deeds to the praise of God. The third thing we judge useful and necessary for you is that, with most devout prayers, you always strive to implore the help of divine aid in all things. And it seems very fitting to us, as we have often said and always admonish, that each of you at least once a day make remembrance of the Lord’s passion, and for the many benefits received from God say an act of thanksgiving one time. That this may be done uniformly by each one of you, listen to this brief form which we have arranged; if you wish, write it out for yourselves.

    I adore, praise, bless, and glorify you, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, savior and life-giver of the souls of all the faithful; and I give thanks to you from the innermost part of my heart for your most holy incarnation and nativity from the most pure virgin Mary; for your circumcision; for your flight into Egypt; for your seven-year exile there; and for

    What the good ordering of monastic life is.

    ... by your return afterward into the land of your temporal birth. I give you thanks, most sweet Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for all your labors, journeys, and weariness; for hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, poverty, and want; and for the necessities, injuries, insults, mockeries, and slanders which throughout your whole life you willingly, not under compulsion, endured for us. And as often as you moved your hand to work, your foot to walk, or as often as you opened your mouth to speak, so often I bless you, praise you, glorify you, humbly adore you, and with all the powers of my heart always give thanks to you, mediator of God and men, most sweet Jesus Christ.

    I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, most merciful king of the heavens, for your most holy teaching, for the establishment of your faith and of the evangelical sacraments, for the calling of the nations, for the justification of sinners, and for all your wondrous acts and virtues, and for all your benefits, which either you have bestowed upon me in particular or upon all others together with me in general.

    I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, most benign savior, for your charity which you had toward the human race, and for your whole most bitter passion, and all the pains which you endured on account of us wretched ones. I give you thanks, Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for the grief and sorrow of your most innocent heart which you endured for us at the time of your impending passion, when you said to your disciples who were following you: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” I beseech you, by this sorrow of your heart, O God, have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death, and take from me all melancholy and disordered grief, granting me at all times a salutary sorrow for my sins.

    I give you thanks for the sadness of your most holy heart, when, placed in agony, you prayed to the Father a second and third time that he would take away from you the chalice of the passion; and, pouring forth sweat in marvelous anguish, you resigned yourself wholly to his will for us. I give you thanks, O king of heaven and earth, for your captivity, for the insults, injuries, and mockeries which you endured throughout the whole time of the passion on account of the salvation of us all.

    I give you thanks, O Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you, bound to the column, for the most harsh scourging of your most tender body, and for the shedding of your most sacred blood from the wounds, with immeasurable pain. I adore you, Lord Jesus Christ, crowned with thorns, and I give you thanks for the piercings and pains of your most holy head, for the blows, spittings, and all the mockeries cruelly inflicted upon your majesty by the wicked. I adore you, Christ Jesus, Son of the living God, bearing the very heavy weight of your cross; I adore you, stripped of your garments before the multitude; I adore you, stretched out by hands and feet with iron nails upon the cross and very cruelly fastened to it.

    I adore you, Jesus Christ, everlasting king, hanging and dying on the cross for me; and I give thanks for the pains of your wounds, I give thanks for the shedding of your most precious blood, I give thanks for your most innocent death which you willingly endured for our sins and the sins of the whole world. I give thanks to your boundless goodness, because you called me, your own, to the faith; because you caused me to be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity; and because you deigned to call me away from the vanity of the world, to serve you in true tranquillity of mind, into this holy congregation.

    I beseech you by your most holy name, O most sweet Jesus, mediator of God and men; I beseech you by the pain of your wounds and by the merits of your most bitter passion; I beseech you by the shedding of your most holy blood and by the power of your most innocent death: grant me indulgence of all my sins; pour into my heart the sweetness of your most fervent love; give me, with progress in all virtues, perseverance; and have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death, guarding me today and at all times, in your mercy, loving Jesus, from every sin and danger of mind and body. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

    And which of you, brothers, is there who cannot say this short prayer, or one like it if he has a better, once each day? It is not long nor is it wrapped in foreign words, but short and plain, gathering the life and passion of Christ in a compressed summary. A Christian person, and especially one in the cloister, is exceedingly ungrateful to God if he does not at least once in the day recall the Lord’s passion to memory, devoutly rendering acts of thanks. But if to any of you this prayer has seemed too lengthy, in the eighth homily of our exhortations to you we recently set down a shorter one, to which the weary man can have recourse. Above all, take care, I beg you, that among so many benefits of God you not be ungrateful for even one. Let this be done...

    Sermon II. Fol. LXIII.

    thanksgiving after matins, because it is a most fitting time for prayer, and the silence of the night’s rest is wont to increase devotion. For I say that [unclear] testify [unclear] more efficacious: than those which they offer to God the Father with remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and gratitude.

    Fourth, what we have judged necessary for you for regular observance is that you keep watch in the guarding of the outward senses, because no one is able to guard well the city of his own heart who disdains to close the gates. Love silence, and flee every tumult of this world. Apply holy prudence to all that you do, and love the secrecy of quiet. For a monk who loves public life and wandering excursions was never a true lover of observance.

    Fifth, we admonish you to flee idleness, destructive to the soul, because this pestiferous poison nourishes the gravest vices and always begets unclean thoughts. Therefore whoever, as a lover of virtues, loves his own salvation, whoever desires to arrive at eternal happiness, let him flee idleness as from the face of the devil, if he desires to avoid sin.

    Sixth, for the purity of regular observance there is required, by necessity of salvation, that the renunciation of property be kept inviolate by all until death. For a monk having private possessions prepares for himself a way to hell. But whoever receives and disburses money in the monastery, let him be a public minister; let no private person dare to presume this. The possession of riches does not befit monks, who are commanded to imitate the Lord Jesus in poverty of spirit. Let us hear the holy apostle of Christ saying: Having food and clothing, with these we are content. By God’s mercy we provide you with necessities: not as much as the desire of disordered pleasure demands, but as much as nature, content with little, requires. And so, just as it is not lawful for you to have anything without the abbot’s consent, so, since we minister all things, not even what is necessary [unclear].

    The seventh thing that makes a monk is humble obedience to commands. For he cannot be a true monk who despises obedience and denies to his superiors the humble subjection which he promised. This disease of disobedience arises from elation and pride of mind, just as from evil matter pus is generated in ulcers. But what does Scripture say? Pride is hateful before God and men, and is the beginning of every transgression. The warfare of monks is the imitation of Christ, who obeyed the Father even unto death.

    The eighth place is adorned by the most beautiful virtue, chastity; when this is despised, it is now necessary that all integrity of regular observance suffer shipwreck. For a monk, by the necessity of his salvation, is commanded to live chastely until death and to abstain perpetually from every venereal pollution. For let these be the three principal vows of monastic conversion: against the observance of which to live is certain damnation for monks. For the profession of monks, under sentence of eternal damnation, commands them to live without property, under obedience to a pastor, and in perpetual chastity. If one of these three is taken away, monastic integrity has been violated, and transgression condemns the one who despises it.

    In the ninth place, therefore, we admonish every person dedicated to God that he always beware his own will as a venomous serpent, because unless he has held it suspect at all times, he easily falls into the pit of damnation. Attend to the rule, which permits monks neither the will of the body nor that of their own will. No one sins unwillingly. If you have perfectly submitted your will to God and to your abbot in all things, you will easily avoid sin.

    The tenth thing, my dearest brothers, that can preserve in you the integrity of regular observance is that in all adversities and contrary things you have most steadfast patience for the love of God. For patience is a great virtue, which by another name we call endurance, without which no one will come forth victor over his temptations. Therefore the Lord said in the holy Gospel: In your patience you shall possess your souls. What is patience, if not to bear with equanimity both the injuries done by one’s own people and all other adversities whatever, out of reverence and love for God? Believe me, brothers, I speak the sentence of the Apostle: patience is very necessary for you, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise. Let the Lord Jesus be for you the living example of patience, whom you should follow with all your strength.

    Eleventh, my brothers, take care that your hearts not be weighed down in gluttony, because a monk ought not to eat and drink to satiety, but, from love of abstinence, always to cease with a certain appetite and hunger. For the wise man says: He who loves feasts will be in want, and he who loves wine and rich foods will not be made rich. Love fasting; cherish abstinence; preserve continence and frugality in all things. These are the weapons of cloistered persons; these are the insignia of the spiritual warfare of monks.

    [unclear] prevail. With an abundance of foods useless conversations keep company; and a belly filled with wine stirs up unclean promptings of the flesh and of lust. If you wish to be chaste, be abstinent. It is most shameful for a monk to serve the belly and the throat, who for the love of God has renounced all the pleasures of the world together.

    The twelfth thing that makes a monk useful and vigorous in regular observance is that he be most diligent about the service of the divinity. For he who is a true servant of God, which all monks ought to be, is always fervent and diligent in the work of his creator; and because he truly knows God to be present everywhere, he prepares himself with complete devotion for obedient service to him. For it is written: Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently. Therefore, as you approach the service of the highest and unchangeable God, dearest brothers, chant the psalms sweetly, wisely, fervently, and cheerfully, and with as much devotion and purity of mind as you can, diligently praise your creator and savior. Let all sloth be far from the hearts of those chanting the psalms; let no drowsiness be admitted while praising, for since God is present in the midst of those chanting, the fervor of devout minds ought altogether to be present. In the time of divine service let all things be clean, all things pure, all things most full of the fervor of charity, so that wicked thoughts may have no place and all things may be done fittingly.

    When the day has been completed and Compline has been sung according to custom, as soon as the monk has reached the privacy of his cell, let him examine his conscience as to what affairs he has occupied himself with. This is the very good and praiseworthy custom of the brothers of the Bursfeld reform: that no one should presume to place himself upon his bed after Compline unless he has first taken utmost care to examine his conscience concerning the faults or negligences committed during the day. But if, after making examination, you find that during the day you have offended in anything, you know, taught by long custom, what must be done. Hidden faults must at once be erased on the next day by contrition and humble confession; manifest faults, however, must be referred to the chapter of faults, which is held daily. This is the custom of the reformed order, this the holy institution of the reform: that we should never allow the faults of offending brothers to grow, but should take care to cut them off as soon as they have begun to arise. The soul must be cleansed daily; the purpose of holiness must be renewed daily; for just as we cannot remain in the same state without change, so it is necessary for us, by continual exercise, to stir up the mind more frequently to the former fervor of charity.

    What are the signs of true humility: Sermon Three.

    Let none of you, most beloved brothers, deceive himself by his own estimation of himself; let no one mislead his heart by foolish and vain presumption. Not all who desire to seem humble are humble before God, nor are those who keep silent under injuries always truly patient. For the roots of true virtues lie hidden in the heart, and not in the mere outward display of exhibition. We discern certain persons among you who seek rather to be considered humble than truly to be so; and they show many signs of pride, but either none, or certainly very few, of humility. We feel deep compassion, as rightly we ought, for those who err so greatly: they desire to have the name of virtue, but they despise virtue itself. Whom, I ask, do you deceive, wretched men? Do you not destroy yourselves by shamefully misleading yourselves, you who, despising truth, love a lie? But so that you may know how proudly you live, we shall set forth in order the indications and signs of true humility, some of which remain hidden in the heart alone, while others, breaking forth even outwardly, must become manifest to all who see them. Let this be for the monk the true mirror of perfect humility, in which, looking each day, he may examine himself.

    The first sign, then, of true humility each person can recognize in himself when he can regard himself as lower and more worthless than all men, not by painted speech, but by the humble judgment of the heart. This is the greatest sign of profound humility: that the monk, always advancing toward a better way of life, should believe himself an unprofitable and unworthy servant of God. True humility belongs to the heart, not to speech; it is the pursuit of the mind, not of bodily display alone. That monk is truly humble who loves God above all things; who always keeps himself pure in all things from every transgression of the commandments of God and of the rule; who does great deeds of piety and justice, and concerning himself, in his own judgment,

    Sermon III. Folio LXIII.

    he bears [them] continually in his heart; and, always contrite in spirit, praying and groaning to the Lord with tears, he asks pardon and mercy. Nor does he pray only for his own sins, but also for the sins of the whole world. The greatest remedy against the exaltation of the mind is the remembrance of one’s own offenses.

    The third mark of humility is that he desires to keep all the good works he does within himself in secret, and hides his own progress out of zeal for humility. He who is humble does not boast in vain glory, nor seek praise from men, because he hopes for the glory of eternal happiness. Whoever among you considers himself humble and a true monk should not on that account despise this sign of profound submission and abasement for God’s sake.

    The fourth indication of true humility is that, voluntarily descending into the abyss of contempt for himself, he considers all his brethren, even those openly sinning, better than himself before God; forgetting the good things of his own, he wisely considers his evils, while passing over the evils of others in silence, and opportunely making known whatever good things they have done. This is the condition of true humility: always to admire and proclaim the good works of others, and prudently to make little of and hide one’s own, for the avoidance of pride.

    Having attained the fifth sign of humility, he is quiet in his simplicity and does not speak of the defects of others, unless compelled either by reason of office or by the command of charity. Yet prudent humility preserves moderation in correction, so that the one whom it cannot make better by correcting him more severely, it strives to admonish gently and meekly. It also sometimes wisely dissembles rebukes, and waits for and observes a more opportune time.

    The sixth sign of humility is shown when a monk, from love of humility, is found slow and not ready to accuse and rebuke the sins of others. For he who is truly humble always considers his own weakness, and silently weighs in secret how many evils he himself has committed against God’s justice. Hence he greatly fears to rebuke the deeds of others, because he recognizes himself as a sinner and therefore unworthy to judge others. We except the prelates and rulers of monks from this norm of humility, insofar as we know them to be bound to the correction of their subjects.

    The seventh sign of true humility is that he gladly receives corrections and amendments for his faults and negligences, and is embittered by no grief against the one who rebukes him. Whenever the humble man is rebuked by someone, he rejoices in spirit with the prophet, saying: Let the just man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head. Of the proud, however, Scripture says: They hated the one who rebuked in the gate. He who is truly humble loves the one who rebukes him, but flees the flatterer.

    The eighth indication of true humility is clearly shown when, rebuked, he does not defend, deny, cloak, or excuse his fault, but confesses it with simple shamefacedness. The truly humble monk, when he is rebuked, does not murmur; he does not protest that he has exceeded the measure of equity, but at once, falling to the ground before the judge, cries out most meekly: I have sinned; I confess the fault; I beg pardon; I promise amendment.

    The ninth indication of monastic humility makes one mild, sweet, and modest in speech, and not loud in voice. The monk whom you see to be loud and hasty in speaking you will judge not humble, but proud and rash. The humble man speaks modestly and almost under silence, and is always found readier to listen than to speak before others. It is shameful for a monk to raise his voice too much when he speaks, since, crucified to the world, he is commanded to love silence.

    He possesses the tenth indication of perfect humility who is accustomed to interpret everything he has heard about his neighbor in the better part. For our Savior says in the holy Gospel: Do not judge, and you shall not be judged. And again: With what measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you. The Apostle also says: Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts. Who are you, who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls, and not to you.

    The eleventh indication of holy humility is that he despises no man in his heart on account of any excesses whatever, but places all before himself in the merit of sanctity. He also considers all who offend publicly to be better than himself, and therefore condemns no one. He always thinks with himself in his heart what evil he himself has done, but humbly weighs the good deeds of others as outweighing his own. Hence he spurns no one, makes little of no one, despises no one, because he desires all to be saved in the Lord.

    What are the signs of true humility.

    [he] has laid [it] up in heaven: he despises all the glory of this life. The thirteenth sign of true humility is not only to despise praises and favors in the truth of one’s mind, but also prudently to avoid those by whom one sees oneself being praised. Those who are truly humble flee their praisers, and whenever they are praised, they fall silent, answering nothing. The esteem of a great reputation is burdensome to the humble man, and he is confounded in himself all the more, the more he is proclaimed by men. For true humility, when blamed, advances; when praised, it runs into danger.

    The fourteenth perfect sign of monastic humility: in corrections and disparagements, if he suffers any, he conceives spiritual joy and a great increase of divine love. When wronged he is pierced with compunction, and is provoked much more to contempt of the world. Whenever he is reproved insultingly by anyone, if he is humble, he judges himself justly corrected. For he does not consider his own innocence in the accusation, but, humble and compunct, weighs that he has gravely offended God in other matters.

    The fifteenth sign of perfect humility: he never kicks back against one correcting him, but preserves silence in all tranquility of mind. He does not cast even the very well-known vices of his reprover in his face, nor does he seek any grounds for argument. He does not complain that insult is being done to him; he sets no excuse against a rash man, nor is he accustomed to answer words with words, but, as if mute, to be silent toward all things.

    The sixteenth sign of deep humiliation: he despises all comforts of the world and seeks no friendships of mortals. True serene humility, which is assumed for the love of Christ, delights nowhere but in Christ alone. But one cannot stand in the love of Christ unless he has learned to deny both his own will and the world with all its disordered pleasures. Thus the Lord says to him in the holy Gospel: If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple.

    The seventeenth sign of humility: he does not divide himself into many things; he does not greatly seek the aid and benefits of men, but humbly remains in his own moderation, or even extremity. For benefits received from men he is not accustomed to applaud much, but to show himself grateful with few and simple words. Little gifts weaken the minds of the infirm, and often render the unwary useless and superfluous in speech. Indeed, he who is truly humble does not delight in the conversations of givers, because they often hinder the purity of his purpose. The love of Christ does not love publicity.

    The eighteenth sign of humility: from the heart he suffers with all who suffer for the love of Christ, and most patiently bears the defects and infirmities of others, and prays for the correction of those who offend. For true humility shows to sinners and the weak the bowels of piety and compassion; but false and simulated humility, because it is truly pride, swells against the frail with hard and indiscreet severity, and often becomes the cause of danger when in correcting it exceeds the rule of charity. But he who is truly humble always fears to exceed the due measure of correction, and therefore is more inclined to mercy than to excessive severity.

    The nineteenth sign of true humility: the mind perseveres free from all envy, and he favors and prays for all men. He envies no one the gifts of divine kindness; he favors the grace of God in all, and rejoices together in the progress of others. He judges no one unworthy of God’s benefits; he thinks all better than himself. He considers the advantage of his neighbors his own, because he loves all as himself.

    The twentieth sign of perfect humility: with bitterness of heart he recalls to memory the multitude of his sins, and therefore thinks himself unworthy of every benefit and grace of God. Hence, seeking the depth of humility, he imitates the evangelical publican, who had remembrance of his own offenses and did not wish to lift his eyes to heaven. For the monk who is truly humble by the love of Christ always bears in his heart the holy sorrow of compunction and repentance for the evils he has done.

    The twenty-first sign of cenobitic humility: he trusts the judgment of others more than his own, and because of Christ subjects his own will wholly to another’s command. Let those among you who follow the judgment of their own head attend whether they can or will apprehend this sign of monastic humility. For today we see few observers of true monastic humility, though we see many monks professing it. O times, O morals, in which we all promise humility, and very few of us truly discern how to keep what has been promised inviolate.

    The twenty-second sign of cenobitic humility: he will abominate and despise beautiful, new, precious clothes, and [will desire?] to have all garments cast off by others and. 14 q

    Sermon M. Fol. LXV.

    he longs to put on. He willingly uses meaner garments, and takes very great delight in those things which others despise. Beautiful garments, decorously arranged, do not befit a monk, but the meanest, with which the body may be defended only from the injury of the inclemency of the air. All fastidiousness is forbidden him, as it is to cloistered men, who by reason of their profession made before God are bound to contempt of the world. Humility flees lofty things; it seeks the things that are lowly.

    The twenty-third sign of monastic humility shows a monk to be servant-like toward the brethren and voluntarily given to acts of service, and ready for all things whatsoever he has been ordered. For true humility obeys even inferiors with a most ready will, and is never indignant against the one who commands. As far as he is able, he desires to serve all for the love of Christ, who faithfully loves God with his whole heart. For whatever service he has bestowed on the brethren, he firmly believes that the whole has been shown to Christ.

    The twenty-fourth sign of humility a monk then attains in truth, when for the love of God he delights to attend to the meaner offices in the monastery, which the rest despise. We read that many once ascended to this degree of true humility; we do not doubt that they are of great merit before God. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted; for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. The humble monk imitates Christ; the proud one, the devil.

    The twenty-fifth sign of monastic humility is always to seek the lower place for sitting in the assembly of any persons whatever, and to prefer oneself neither to an equal nor to an inferior. It is not for monks to contend proudly about precedence of place; nor does it befit a soldier of Christ to wish to surpass others in honor. For the true monk, who loves humility, content with the lowest place in every respect, does not desire to excel anyone.

    The twenty-sixth indication of humility especially befits him who, although learned and educated, on account of the lowly humiliation of himself hides all learning and knowledge. For the monk who is truly humbled is always found readier to listen than to speak. For the divine priest Jerome says: The monk has the office not of one teaching, but of one lamenting, who either mourns himself or the world, and fearfully awaits the coming of the Lord. The arrogance of monks is hateful both to God and to men, and always liable to sin.

    The twenty-seventh sign of humility is perfectly attained by him who, for love of regular discipline, delights more to be silent than to speak. The humble lover of Christ loves silence, and, lest he offend in speech, is accustomed to say very few things. Humility is rarely found among the talkative; and he who is swift to speak casts down his own soul. A talkative and garrulous monk is not without pride; and he who is foolish multiplies words. Whoever in the spiritual contest desires to overcome his adversary through humility must not omit to restrain his tongue from much speaking and from every idle word. It is written in the book of Proverbs that in much speaking sin will not be lacking.

    Whoever has attained the twenty-eighth sign of perfect humility will avoid laughter and all disordered gestures of those who guffaw. Lamentation most befits a monk, not laughter, as one who is dead to all the levities of the world. But the wise man says: A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely laugh quietly.

    The twenty-ninth indication of perfect humility takes its beginning from the fear of the Lord; for the sake of his honor, as far as he is able, he flees and detests every sin. For everyone who does not fear to sin has not truly been humble. But the monk who follows Christ according to his strength in true humility is accustomed to flee every sin, and, as far as he can, to exercise himself in the pursuit of virtues. Humility confesses its sin; and as often as it has offended even in the smallest matters, it does not rest until it has amended everything through true penance. He who is truly humble is always found zealous for preserving cleanness of conscience. For the nourishment of humility is charity, which does not permit the one who has it to be idle.

    The thirtieth sign of true humility shows a monk confirmed in the purpose of holiness, and makes him subject to all the brethren, even the younger. Whatever the pastor has commanded, he obeys simply; he never debates the commands of his superior; he does not ask the reason why he so commands. If impossibilities are commanded, he is very ready in spirit; he is prepared without contradiction for whatever things are hard and arduous. He is directed by the counsel of his pastor; he believes him, trusts him, obeys him, and is willingly governed by his command. You have now heard, my dearest brethren, the thirty indications of true humility. O good God, where are the works? Which of us will boast that he has true humility, so that in these signs he suffers no defect? These, shameful to say, are

    On the arduous way that leads to life.

    our own times, in which the charity of many has grown cold; the integrity of holy religion has perished; the devotion of almost all has breathed its last. Our monks seek sanctity without the merit of virtues; they wish to have merit without the exercise of labor. Therefore a saint is not found today in the monastery. The fervor of holy compunction in many is either exceedingly rare or lukewarm; for where one lives for flesh and blood, the fervor of inward charity is not possessed. It is not enough for you, O monk, who boast of observance, to have nothing of your own, not to touch a woman, to reside in a monastery under obedience to a shepherd, not to eat meat, and in the other things that are external matters of regular discipline according to the monastic institution [unclear], unless with the utmost diligence you also strive to [order?] your inner things through true charity of God and neighbor, for the acquisition of which all the other things have chiefly been instituted. Without the charity of God, therefore, all things profit you nothing; for it is itself the one and only thing that distinguishes between good and evil works. O monk, monk, whoever you are who live lukewarmly in the monastery without the fervor of charity, do you think that the outward equipment of discipline can save you? Charity is what sanctifies the one who has it; charity commends the other virtues and all good works to God. Have charity, and all the works of piety that you do will be pleasing to God.

    On the arduous way that leads to life. Sermon 4.

    You have heard, dearly beloved brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ saying in today’s reading in the holy Gospel: “How narrow is the gate and strait the way that leads to life, and few are they who find it.” Is not Christ himself the way, who had said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life”? And how does he now say that it is strait and narrow, when he himself is the one who had said: “Take my yoke upon you and learn, for I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light”? What else is the yoke of Christ than the strait and narrow way to the kingdom of God? How, then, is it both light and narrow? Let your charity hear. The yoke of the Lord Jesus is sweet to the good, hard and unbearable to the reprobate. The way of Christ to life is broad and pleasant to those exercised in the charity of the humble, but narrow and bitter to the proud. For nothing is so hard, nothing so terrible, nothing so arduous that it is not easy and pleasant to one who loves God. Again, nothing is so light, nothing so easy, nothing so small that it is not heavy and burdensome to an evil will. Therefore the Lord said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.” If you wish to bear my yoke upon you, first learn the meekness and humility of my heart, since unless you are meek and humble, you will by no means be able to carry my load, as though it were a heavy weight and an unbearable burden. I am a humble way; I do not contain the proud. I am a narrow gate; I do not admit the swollen. Unless your soul has despised all worldly things, unless you have inflicted the necessary force upon the pleasures of the flesh, you cannot enter through me into the kingdom like an animal burdened with sins. I am a humble and meek way, and I receive the humble; I am a strait doorway, and I admit the poor in spirit and the clean of heart.

    To eternal life, brothers, we strive by the narrow way of truth; it is necessary that in time we provide for ourselves all things that are necessary for so arduous a journey. There are, moreover, four things especially necessary for travelers, without which the journey is dangerous and one rarely arrives at the goal. The first thing that we say is necessary for travelers we believe to be knowledge of the roads. For one who tries to walk far through trackless places without knowledge of the roads is sometimes entangled in dangerous errors. Therefore let the prudent traveler either first learn the road, or take to himself a companion skilled in the journey, lest he either fall into the hands of robbers or depart from the path of the right road. Therefore, desiring to return to the homeland of the heavenly kingdom by a way exceedingly narrow and known to few, we must have as guide and companion of the journey Jesus Christ himself, who called himself the way and the truth. Outside Christ there is no true knowledge of the ways. Whoever neglects to have Christ as the companion of his journey runs in vain and without fruit. Therefore let us learn the way of life, dearly beloved brothers, without knowledge of which no one reaches the homeland; no one reaches life [unclear]. For he himself says in the holy Gospel: “He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life in”

    Sermon 3. Folio 66

    [unclear] remaining. But he who does not believe in the Son: the wrath of God remains upon him. What does it mean that wrath remains upon him, except that the first, original sin is not removed from him? For after the establishment of the New Testament, original sin is removed from those who believe in him through faith in Christ alone. Circumcision was given to the fathers as a sign of future salvation; nevertheless none of them could enter the kingdom of heaven before Christ the Savior rose from the dead. Therefore outside faith in Christ there is no salvation, since, as he himself says, he who has not believed is judged and will be condemned. We remain in Christ through faith and love: he himself is the way of salvation, he the truth without error, he life without death. If we have the Lord Jesus as the guide of our journey, we walk confidently.

    Secondly, it is necessary for wayfarers to pass through the lands of their journey without injury to anyone; for if they commit theft or robbery, or any other similar sin against the commonwealth, in the end they would come to be punished by penalty and would not reach the intended destination of the journey. But we, brothers, placed on the road by which we return to the homeland of the heavenly kingdom, must most diligently take care that we commit nothing, in word, deed, or thought, contrary to the justice of God, but render to each one his right and due: to God first of all devotion in worship and charity, to our neighbor love, to ourselves the holiness of perfect purity. Indeed, if we live according to the things Christ taught, do we not remain on the straight way of salvation which leads to the kingdom? We shall remain on the way if we keep the commandments of God; we shall walk in the truth if we love the Lord our God himself with all the strength of our mind; we shall come to life if, turning aside from evil, we continually persevere in the practice of good.

    Thirdly, it is necessary to have provision for the journey, because if wayfarers lack travelling supplies, they will not be able to reach the intended place. But the prudent wayfarer, before he leaves his house, reckons within himself the time and length of the journey, and prepares travelling supplies and expenses according as necessity requires. A great and hard journey remains for us; we must prepare provisions for many years, lest we fail on this road on which we are going. The travelling provision of this journey of ours to the supercelestial homeland is not gold, not silver, not the deceitful riches of the world, but faith in Christ and love of God. The holy virtues are the unfailing travelling provision of the soul for the kingdom of heaven; strengthened by them, it walks on the way of God in gladness. The soul faithful to Christ and accompanied by the holy virtues gladly completes the hard road of this long pilgrimage. To love God above all things, to exercise oneself constantly in good works, to keep one's conscience in all purity, to do injury to no one: this provides the soul with true travelling provision for the eternal homeland in heaven.

    Fourthly, it is advised as necessary for wayfarers that they not forget the purpose undertaken before they come to the end of the journey begun. For he must be called a foolish wayfarer who is recalled from his journey by children's games and forgets where he was tending. And we, dearest brothers, who have taken up the way of monastic religion, must always think upon our end, since death hastens every day even when we do not notice it, and presents the unprepared as well as the prepared before judgment. Meanwhile let us do good while it is permitted, as much as we can, and let us not delay to be converted to the Lord with all our heart. Christ is the way by which we proceed to the kingdom of God; Christ is the truth in which, remaining, we do not err; Christ is the life for which we hope. Hear, brothers, what he himself says in the holy Gospel: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. This is the way upon which you entered at the beginning of your monastic profession; if you wish to proceed on it rightly and laudably, you will have to love Christ above all things, living purely in regular observance. It is yours, brothers, to love nothing in this world and to chastise the flesh for the love of God. It belongs to monks to despise all the delights and pleasures of the present life and to desire nothing other than the everlasting feasts. It belongs to monks to imitate Christ according to their powers, and to establish their life in evangelical purity. To imitate Christ is the highest perfection. The faithful minister of Christ follows his Lord, and where Christ is, there his minister also will be. Therefore whoever among you is a lover of his own salvation, desires to come after Christ to the kingdom of heaven, and wishes to keep and preserve until the end those things which he promised at his entrance into religion, let him keep these things. First, so that he may prevail, let the monk learn through faith and devotion; [unclear] in sincerity [unclear].

    On the arduous way that leads to life.

    [unclear] to know, and at all times to occupy himself piously and soberly with the holy Scriptures. And whatever holy mother Church of the faithful has established either to be believed or to be observed, let him faithfully and firmly both believe and keep it, nor depart in any way from her determination. All who had remained outside the ark were once destroyed by the flood; Noah alone, with those who were in the ark, escaped safe. The ark presented the figure of the Church, and the thing done prefigured a mystery. Hence there is no salvation for men outside the Church, which our Lord Jesus Christ built upon the most firm rock. Every unbeliever is not in the Church, and therefore he will necessarily perish, just as those once did who were not in the ark: pagans, gentiles, Saracens, likewise heretics and schismatics, who have withdrawn themselves from the unity of the Catholic Church, set [unclear] outside the ark of salvation; and if they persevere in error, without doubt they are to be damned forever with the demons.

    Since, therefore, faith is the foundation of salvation, without which it is impossible to please God, the monk must know what he ought to believe; and lest it happen that he err, you must learn the Gospel and the constitutions of the Church that concern him. For he who does not know will not be known. It is most shameful for a monk not to know the rules of the Christian faith [unclear] what [unclear] forever [unclear] offers proof. But this we admonish: that the things proposed to you as to be believed should not be debated by curious argumentation, since, as Saint Pope Gregory says, faith has no merit where human reason provides proof. We admonish [unclear] that a monk ought to be studious in the divine Scriptures, so that he may know [unclear] faith may wholly consume [unclear].

    Every unbeliever [unclear] without doubt with the demons forever [unclear] to be damned. Since therefore faith [unclear] you must learn [unclear] it is necessary to please God. The monk must know what he ought to believe, and lest it happen [unclear] human [unclear] offers proof. But this we admonish: that the things proposed to you as to be believed, by curious argumentation [unclear] the monk ought to be studious, so that he may know [unclear] faith may wholly consume [unclear]. [unclear] forever for the monk [unclear] offers proof. We admonish [unclear] that the monk in the divine Scriptures [unclear] ought to be studious, so that he may know [unclear] faith consumes wholly [unclear] he must [unclear] offers proof. But this [unclear] we admonish that the monk in the divine Scriptures [unclear] ought to be studious, so that he may know [unclear] faith consumes wholly [unclear] he must [unclear] offers proof.

    And nothing hinders a man more from knowledge of himself than the man himself. Those who feed on the pleasures of the flesh, who are lifted up into pride by the vain knowledge of this world, whether by riches or by honors, are not permitted to come to knowledge of themselves. Yet to know many things and neglect oneself is not to be wise, but rather to be mad. It belongs to the accumulation of a graver damnation to learn many things and shamefully to be ignorant of oneself. Let each of you therefore consider what he is, whence he is, and what he is going to be. Man through himself is certainly nothing; but whatever he is, he is from God and for God. What is man but a wayfarer and pilgrim, as it were of one day upon the earth, who today lives in the world [unclear] but tomorrow, snatched away by death, is seen no more? Our whole life, every action, every day and hour, shows how nothing we are: we die by living, we are corrupted by acting; with time running on, I make comparison of us present to death. He spoke truly who compared you to the leaf of a tree. The wind, tearing it from the tree, casts it to the ground; in its place another new one afterward grows up, subject to a similar fall. But what has fallen to the ground is dissolved into the ground and never afterward returns to the tree. Hence a certain wise man of the Greeks says: as is the race of leaves, so too is the race of men. The race of men is very like the race of leaves, because it grows green for a time and is dissolved into the earth; and neither does the leaf return to the tree nor man to life.

    Now follows the third thing, which I think very necessary for a monk walking in the way of God: the man who knows himself to be a wayfarer of this life and understands that the activity of life is of a very brief time truly shows himself humble in all things. For why should earth and ashes be proud? He cannot be exalted who truly knows himself. My brothers, we have no cause at all for exaltation and pride, but much and continual cause for humility, since indeed we are earth and a certain compacting of dust, and after a few days are to return again into dust. But because true humility belongs to few, therefore the way of salvation is called narrow and is found by few. By humility one comes to the kingdom, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel: everyone who humbles himself for God’s sake will be exalted, and he who exalts himself will be humbled.

    Sermon III. Fol. LXVII

    Whoever thinks that he is walking in the sight of him who always sees all things keeps his conscience pure and observes his conduct with the greatest diligence. Let him always keep watch in the fear of the Lord; let him always chastise [his body?] with fasting and [abstinence?], for love of the heavenly Father. The monk who recognizes himself as a pilgrim and stranger in this world never forgets the heavenly homeland; he sees nothing on the road of the present life in which his soul may take delight. For the prudent traveller considers none of the sights along the roads; nothing of passing things delights him in his pilgrimage, but at every time he sighs for the end of the journey. He always thinks sweetly of his homeland; he bears it grievously that his pilgrimage is prolonged or delayed; and therefore he desires to have nothing in this world except the Lord, in whose sight he hastens earnestly to appear. [Unclear] necessary for our traveller: [unclear] of divine charity [unclear]. No one will be able to come to the heavenly homeland who departs from the path of charity. The charity of God is the way to God; if anyone has neglected to keep it burning in himself, he wanders miserably from the true road of the heavenly homeland. Scripture says: God is charity; and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. But he who is not in charity has withdrawn far from the way of salvation; and walking in outer darkness, he will never come to the kingdom.

    How Sin Is to Be Fled

    Sermon V.

    You have heard, my very dear brothers, what Saint John the Apostle says about sinners: Whoever commits sin is from the devil, for the devil sins from the beginning. A truly fearful and greatly dreaded sentence. If everyone who commits sin is from the devil, because everyone offends in many things, whom shall we find immune from sin? Yet he says subsequently: Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. But he had said before: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. What does this very contradiction mean? that no one is without sin, and that he who is born of God does not commit sin? There is no contradiction here, because it is true on both sides: no one is without sin, inasmuch as no one is without the law of sin. He who is born of God does not commit sin, because through the law of the mind, that is, through charity, which is the seed, he does not commit sin. [Charity?] therefore

    How Sin Is to Be Fled.

    the multitude of sins: without which there is no good work, and it alone is able to destroy every sin. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: No saint and just man is without sin; nor yet on that account does he cease to be just or holy, if he holds fast to holiness with affection. But those sins of the just are not to be thought mortal or enormous, but small and venial, without which the life of a man is carried on; for every mortal sin must be far from the just man, if he is to retain the name of justice. For mortal sin separates a man from God, kills the soul, and condemns it with the demons forever. This pernicious kind of mortal sin we can avoid by the grace of God, and by the rectitude of free choice we ought carefully to do so. Therefore we have been made monks, so that, living most cautiously under the rule of saving obedience, we should not fall into the pit of mortal sin. Thus a monk must always keep watch in good works, so that he may live free from mortal crime. But whoever on the way of God feels the flesh troublesome and contrary to him must make it subject to the spirit, and, as it were, obedient through fear, by the memory of punishments.

    First, therefore, the monk who loves his own salvation [unclear] the deceitful flesh. For what is the world but a great, deep, and restless sea, in which there are as many creeping things of evils as there are evil desires of men ordered against the good? O world, deceitful, deceiver, and unclean, you shamefully deceive those who cling to you; you plunge all who follow you into the depth of hell. How happy are those who despise you for the love of Christ and, making a useful separation from your vanities, depart from you in time. Whatever we perceive in the world is vain, and every lover of the world is made vain and will soon be corrupted. Think that you will shortly die, for nothing draws men back from sin as frequent and intent meditation on death does. Hence Scripture says: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. Think on the necessity of dying: it shakes the mind with fear and restrains it from vice.

    The second thing that urges one to flee sin is fear of the judgment to come, in which all men must be presented. No one can escape this dreadful judgment, but we must all appear in it. Two judgments to be feared hang over us, neither of which we shall be able to evade; necessity compels us to appear in each. One is called particular, in which immediately after death the soul is judged according to its merits either to grace or to punishment. The other is named general, which will be at the end of the world, where we shall all be judged publicly by the only-begotten Son of God. Each judgment is exceedingly terrible and greatly to be feared by all mortals. Hence the prophet Joel says: Great is the day of the Lord and very terrible, and who will endure it? Likewise in Ecclesiastes King Solomon says: All things that are done under the sun God will bring into judgment, for every error, whether it be good or evil. Likewise in Isaiah it is read thus: The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes. And in the book of the prophet Amos it is written thus: Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord. What is it to you? For that day of the Lord is darkness and not light. Likewise Zephaniah, prophet of the Lord, foretelling the bitterness of the future judgment, said: The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be troubled there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind. In the fire of the zeal of the Lord the whole earth will be devoured, because he will make a consummation with haste for all who dwell on the earth. This day, exceedingly terrible and to be dreaded by all mortals, which you believe will certainly come, always keep in memory, dearest brothers. For the most holy bishop Ambrose says: There is nothing that profits more toward an honorable life than that we believe him to be the future judge, whom neither the hidden things of minds deceive nor dishonorable things delight. For all of us, as Saint Christophilus says, must be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive the proper things of the body, as he has done, whether good or evil. How greatly that day of the future and terrible judgment is to be feared Saint Jerome the priest indicates, saying: Whether I eat or drink, or do anything else, that voice always seems to sound in my ears: Arise, dead, and come to judgment. As often as I think of the day of judgment, I tremble wholly in heart and body. Hence, if there is any joy in the present life, it must be conducted in such a way that the bitterness of the future judgment never departs from memory.

    Sermon V. Folio LXVIII.

    What shall we wretches say on that day, or where shall we stand before the strict Judge, if, as Saint Peter the apostle says, scarcely shall the righteous man be saved? If Jerome, a righteous and most holy man, feared the judgment to come, O good God, where will Trithemius, an unhappy sinner, appear? If the righteous man fears, where will the sinner stand? What, then, shall we say, or what shall we answer, when grievously accused on every side? All the elements will stand against us in testimony; earth and heaven together will accuse us. But even if all things were silent, each person’s own conscience will be a grave accuser. He who knows all things is ignorant of nothing, for there all things will be manifest to the Judge. There will be present the evil deeds we have done, grievously accusing us; there will stand round about us, as testimony against us, innumerable demons. We shall see opened before us the dreadful chaos beneath us; above us we shall behold the Judge in wrath; and from every side the utmost danger will threaten us.

    These dangers, my brothers, of the examination to come, keep always turning over in the memory of your heart, and diligently consider how dreadful it will be to fall under the future sentence of the Judge. In that terrible hour pure hearts will be of more worth than the clever words of rhetoricians; a clean conscience will profit a man more than the money of the whole world, since he who is to judge all things is not deceived; indeed, he is changed neither by a price nor by prayers. O what incredible horror will invade all the wicked when they are about to hear the fearful sentence: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” O worst of all evils, O deepest sorrow of all sorrows: to be separated from the fellowship of the saints and to be tormented with demons forever. Truly the day of judgment is dreadful, fearful for all because it is exceedingly bitter; there the synteresis of conscience dies by the worm that does not die; there one once damned to punishment is never freed.
