    Therefore the monk who desires to attain eternal salvation should keep himself, as far as he can, always clean from every sin, and that voice, “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire,” should never depart from his memory.

    Hence the third thing which we judge to be very useful for turning away from sin is diligently to consider the bitterness of the penalties of eternal damnation. For there is no temptation of carnal pleasure so vehement that it will not at once be overcome and fail, if the one tempted recalls in careful meditation what the damned suffer in hell. What do riches once possessed now profit the damned? What do past pleasures confer on the lustful placed in hell? What do the vainest honors confer on the swollen with pride? What does power once broad confer on the proud? Think, brothers, what those already damned suffer in the lower regions, and, lest similar things happen to you, persevere continually in good and holy works. If you fear hell, flee sin. For nothing in hell will harm a man if he has remained in the faith of Christ, free from sins; nor will he burn in punishment who previously, here, had not burned in guilt.

    Hell is a place to be feared, in which there is no redemption, but whoever, once damned, enters there will never again come out to salvation. The wretched cry out amid torments, placed in anguish and everlasting horror, saying: “What now does our pride profit us: riches, honors, dignities, luxury, gluttony, and all past carnal pleasures? What do they now profit us, damned forever? Behold, all things have passed away like a shadow, and all have vanished like the brief dream of one night. But we have been assigned to these eternal torments, in which we know most certainly that there is no redemption.” In hell, as Augustine testifies, even if there will be the sting of penitence, nevertheless there will be in the damned no correction of the will; in them iniquity will be blamed in such a way that the equity of justice can by no means be loved or desired by them.

    There, then, the devouring flame of hell burns those whom carnal delight now pollutes; and each person is burned in torments so much the more as he here in the flesh takes greater delight against God. In the lower regions, as Gregory testifies, there will be intolerable cold, inextinguishable fire, the immortal worm of conscience, intolerable stench, palpable darkness, pains beyond estimation, lashes without interruption, a dreadful sight of demons striking them, confusion over crimes committed, and despair of all good things. But of all the punishments in hell, that one must be considered by far the gravest: that there the damned are forever deprived of the vision of eternal light.

    Here the most blessed father John Chrysostom says: “Gehenna is an intolerable thing, and all people abhor it. For who does not know that punishment in hell to be very horrible? Yet if anyone should set down a thousand, indeed ten thousand gehennas, the whole of what he says is nothing compared with this: for the soul, exposed to Christ, to be driven away from the glory of the saints, and to hear that terrible voice from the mouth of the Judge of all: ‘Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I do not know you’; and, ‘Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for you and for the devil,’

    How sin is to be avoided.

    O voice by far the most terrible of all terrible things; O sentence to be feared and exceedingly dreaded by all mortals: to be hated by Christ for one’s deserts, to be reproached by the judge, to be separated from the fellowship of glory, and to retain no further hope of recovery. Consider now, brothers, the punishments of the impious, most certainly to come, and compare whatever pains of this life, whatever torments of this passing age, and all imaginable tortures of this world, with those everlasting punishments of the damned; and they will be as nothing to something, imagination to truth, a dream to waking. You will easily overcome the temptations of the flesh and the law of sin if you continually keep thoughts of these things in memory. O eternity, what an inconceivable time; an age without end, a world without time. Blessed is he who now, in time, foresees how he may fare well in eternity after this very brief life.

    The fourth thing that can draw a person back from sin is to have continual remembrance in the heart of future and everlasting happiness. Truly the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in the saints, where there will be no discord, no dissonance at all, but the highest peace of all and the everlasting concord of the rejoicing saints. In the heavenly blessedness of the saints there is true joy without sadness, peace without discord, goodness without malice, gladness without end, light without darkness, everlasting life without pain. There is sweetness without bitterness, rest without labor, praise without reproach, love without fault, brightness without cloud, satisfaction without weariness. Eternity remains without tedium; goodness abounds without defect; happiness continues without misery. For where God is all in all, perfect and full joy will be present to everyone.

    There the soul, or holy mind, is joined to its first principle through love; the intellect is perfectly illuminated for the knowledge of the highest good; and from these two things the enjoyment of eternal happiness is poured into those who rejoice. To know and love God in the kingdom of eternity is to possess, by enjoyment, the very glory of happiness. For this was man created: that he should understand God his creator to be the highest good; that, understanding him, he should love him above all things; and that, loving him, he should enjoy and possess him forever. [unclear] of the Christian faith: so that God, whom we now know through faith and love with our whole heart through works of charity, we may then in that life, understanding him perfectly, have as the perpetual object of our enjoyment. For the attainment of this everlasting happiness, dearest brothers, all good things must be done, even with the greatest labor; all adversities must be endured most patiently, since the very brief exercise of virtue brings forth for us an eternal reward. Hear what Saint John the bishop says on this matter: “If every day,” he says, “we had to endure torments; if, finally, we had to bear Gehenna itself for a little time, so that we might be able to see Christ reigning in eternal glory and be joined forever to the number of his saints, nothing sorrowful that could happen to us would, by any comparable reckoning, be worthy, if by it we might deserve to possess the glory of so great a good.”

    But one does not arrive at the highest good except through the greatest labors, since, as [unclear] testifies in the holy Gospel, [unclear] vice and loves the good of virtue. Every human being who lives according to the command of reason is a lover of virtue; but he who, filthy in the dung of vices, rolls about, lives like a beast and not like a human being. But for you, my brothers, vices must above all be detested, and virtues loved, since for this reason you have despised the world, that you might profitably live in the monastery a life estranged from sins and adorned with holy virtues. Therefore virtues must be cultivated by you, not images of virtues; I say cultivated not with incense, not with sacrifice, but with love and with the purpose of a most upright will. To cultivate virtues is nothing other than to embrace them in the soul and, for the love of God, to keep them inviolate even unto death. For as Lactantius says, the whole duty of virtue is not to sin; and therefore there is no true virtue except that which, through faith in Christ, tends to that end where the highest good of man is, than which nothing can be better. But he is not virtuous who does not love God, since charity is the sum of all virtues. Therefore, if you love God with your whole heart above all things, you are truly virtuous. Virtue is the way of the good, by which, through faith and love of Jesus Christ, one comes to the kingdom. He who truly loves God does not sin, out of love of virtue. Consider your dignity, my brothers, and flee sin, since everyone who is swollen with pride, who is defiled by lust, who is infected by the other plagues of the soul, does not live as a human being, but is confounded in himself and proceeds into death. And the more anyone slips into sin, the farther he withdraws from God and the nearer he approaches to hell. But since all human beings naturally seek the good, it is most shameful to love sin, since every sinner abandons the good and turns himself toward evil.

    Sermon V.

    Sixthly, it draws the mind powerfully back from sin if, by habit, it persists always occupied in meditation on the Lord’s Passion. Who will be able to devote his works to the pleasures of the flesh, if he has reflected that Jesus Christ, the ruler of the world, hung for him on the cross? The death of Christ freed the world from eternal death; whoever carries this benefit with him in memory will easily abstain from every wickedness of vices. Finally, if anyone with the whole attention of his mind has considered God present to him in every place, knowing and understanding all things, he will without doubt always abhor every sin. For God is everywhere with us, not only present, but truly most inward and most present; no secret escapes him, nothing remains hidden from him, but all lies plainly manifest to him. He searches the hearts of all; he knows the most secret thoughts, since he alone has true knowledge of all things. Who among mortals would dare, without the greatest shame, in the presence of so great a majesty, which he believes sees all things, if he weighs who and how great he is who sees? Therefore, whenever some wicked thought troubles the mind, whenever the disordered motions of the flesh disturb the soul, think of the Lord God, who is the avenger of evils, as present; recall to memory the bitterness of the Passion of Jesus Christ; devoutly implore the aid of heavenly grace. He is harder than stone whom these things, diligently considered, have not been able to recall from the purpose of sinning.

    The [seventh] thing that recalls the mind of the studious monk from the desire of sinning is that by continual reading he should run through the passions of the holy martyrs. For indeed, whoever often recalls to memory the unconquerable constancy of the holy martyrs of Christ cannot fail to become stronger and more steadfast in resisting sins. For this reason the brave deeds of the saints were committed to writing: so that whenever we, weak as we are, read such things, we may rise up to imitate those who went before. Do not look, brothers, to those who with proud rashness deny credence to the histories of the saints, and think that the glorious things narrated about the most blessed friends of Christ are fables. For the virtues and good qualities which they do not find in themselves, they scorn to believe that the saints of God possessed. For there are many, and especially among them those who think themselves great because of their learning, who very rashly reject the histories of the holy fathers; and since they themselves cannot enter upon the arduous path of virtue, they invent with windy loquacity that no one, or only a few, could have done so. Whatever is read before them concerning the lives of the saints, whether lofty or great, they cry out is invented and fabulous; and, such as they themselves live, placed in the darkness of vices, so they judge those whose histories they mock to have gone before. But the prudent and devout monk will not be shaken by the sloth of the proud, since he well understands that an effective power of exhorting is present in the histories of the saints. For, to confess meanwhile what I feel about myself, I am moved more toward the devotion of inward fervor by the life of one saint than by many curious sermons, because, as the most holy pope Leo says, examples are stronger than words, and it is more to teach by deed than by voice. But just as not all things please all people, so not all things suit all people; we advise each person to read more frequently and more studiously that by the reading of which his mind is stirred to greater perfection.

    The eighth thing that most powerfully draws a man back from sin is charity, concerning which the holy apostle says: Charity is patient, is kind; it does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek the things that are its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never falls away. He who loves God flees sin; but he who is a servant of crimes assuredly does not love God. A lover of God does not commit sin; and he who truly loves his Lord and always beholds him as present does not work iniquity. God is the highest and unchangeable good; for love of him sin must both be fled and detested, since he who fears to sin only from fear of punishments does not ascend to the heights of charity. For a slave does not sin through fear of the lash; but a son withdraws from evil out of love for his father, lest he offend his father’s heart. Let us avoid sin, my brothers, and live in the sight of the Lord with as much purity of soul as we can, since just as deadly poison, once taken, kills the body, so sin kills the soul of the offender. Hence the wise man admonishes us in Ecclesiasticus, saying: Flee sins as from the face of a serpent, because if you come near to them, they will receive you. The teeth of a lion are the teeth of sin, killing the souls of men. Like a two-edged sword is the iniquity of man; for its wound there is no healing. In Ezekiel also

    How sin is to be fled.

    ...does not imitate God but the reward of sin, the devil. Let us love God, and sin will not have dominion in us; let us love Christ, and we shall do nothing contrary to our salvation. There is nothing better, nothing stronger against sin, nothing safer, than to love God, who first loved us and washed us from all sins in the blood of his only-begotten Son. We are bound to that God, and we are obliged to love him with all the powers of the heart for many reasons.

    First, indeed, God is supremely to be loved by us for no other reason than for his own sake, who is the highest and sole good; in him alone are rest and the salvation of the soul; without him there is no salvation, no rest, no beatitude, no happiness, either in heaven or on earth. For since God is the cause, maker, and beginning of all things, he alone is the object of the soul’s beatitude; to his everlasting enjoyment one comes by charity alone, and only by purity of mind is one led to love of him. Therefore, since God is the sole and highest good of the soul, he is to be loved by us for his own sake with all our powers. Outside God there is nothing good, nothing holy, nothing by which the soul can be gladdened forever. For God alone is the center of the soul’s beatitude.

    Second, we are commanded to love the Lord our God, because he deigns to show himself to us as a most loving father. For thus he taught us to pray: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Truly God is the father of us all, who created us all, nourishes us, feeds us, and preserves us in being, lest we perish. There has never been any father so indulgent upon earth who loved his only-begotten son with such charity as God almighty, our Father, loves, cherishes, guides, and follows us with loving affection. And therefore we are bound to love him with a pure heart above all things, who gives us both being and living. For he himself is our father; and Adam, who was created the first of all men, did not know us.

    Third, we ought to love God above all things because of the likeness by which man was made in the image of God, following his creator in a certain likeness in his intellect. But God is perfect, infinite, and everlasting intellect; by participating in his goodness through grace, our intellect is made blessed in him who created all things. For although there is no comparison between God and man, yet there is, from the nobility of its condition, a likeness of the rational soul itself to its beginning, a likeness of no contemptible dignity. For the prophet says: I have said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. The Lord God also said in the beginning: Let us make man to our image and likeness. Great is the condescension of divine loving-kindness toward our race, which it befits us at all times to remember with pure mind in the observance of charity.

    Fourth, we ought to love our God above all things because of his inestimable munificence, whom we acknowledge to have bestowed such great benefits upon us when we did not deserve them. When we did not exist, he first established us in being by his goodness, and ordained us to participation in his glory, which will never end. Thus Scripture says of the nobility of man: Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels; thou hast crowned him with glory and honor, and hast set him over the works of thy hands. Do you wish to know, brothers, in what respect man is less than an angel? Attend carefully to what we say. There are two intellects created from the beginning: angelic and human. The angelic, immediately from the beginning of its creation, was made full and perfect in actuality with respect to all knowable things, and by nature knew and comprehended all that it ought to know; but the human intellect, first indeed, exists in potency with respect to all knowable things, ignorant of all, but in the end, through many actions, it will at last acquire knowledge of all things, as the angelic intellect does. For the perfect consummation of nature, which is present in the angelic intellect from the beginning, will be granted to the human intellect at the end. Hence it is clear that between these two created intellects there is only this difference: that the angelic intellect is what it can be, while the human intellect is to receive the likeness of angelic perfection in the end, that is, after the death of the flesh. For when the angelic intellect was first created, without any action of its own, immovably, substantially, and by nature, it was full and perfect with knowledge of all things. Of these, those who adhered to their beginning, namely God, through love have been confirmed in eternal happiness; but those who, glorying in themselves, withdrew from God in affection are forever wretched and unhappy. But the human intellect, since from the beginning it is created in ignorance and privation of all things, must by action, motion, and art at last arrive at the knowledge of things set before it. As long as we are in the body and are pilgrims away from the Lord, our intellect, because of its excessive commerce with the body, is confounded as if placed in the darkness of ignorance, and is by no means illumined to perfect knowledge of future things. But afterward, when the soul has been separated from the body, then the intellect will enjoy angelic perfection. Therefore we are distant from the angels only to the extent that we participate in bodily impurity.

    Fifth, God is to be loved by us especially because he first loved us and washed us

    Sermon VI. Folio LXX.

    from our sins in the blood of his only-begotten Son. The Creator loved his creature, which he made from nothing; it is fitting that the creature itself should love above all its Creator, by whose goodness it was brought into being. God loves us with the greatest charity, than which none greater can be spoken or conceived; and he loves us so greatly that he neither ought nor could love more, since in God all things are perfect, and in the immutable there is no capacity for changes.

    Consider now, my brothers, with how great fervor [of mind?], and with how great desire of heart, a man ought to love his God, by whom he is loved, even without merits, with the above-written degree of love. Let us stretch our mind toward love of him above all things, as much as we can; for he is worthy that we love him with all our strength. For however much we have loved God, who loves us, we shall still by no means have reached that measure by which he loves us. For, as we have said, he loves us supremely; nor can his love toward us, with which [unclear], increase, since it is established that he loves his creature most perfectly. But however much we have loved him, we can always make further progress in loving and love more ardently even unto death. We, weak, we, lukewarm, we, consigned to a muddy prison, what shall we render to so great a lover, who surpasses us in loving [unclear], since there is no comparison of the thing made to the maker, [and] with a few he mercifully called us to the faithful knowledge of Christianity.

    Of all benefits after the death of Christ I think this is the chief: that he made us Christians in the faith. For outside the faith of Christ no one will be saved, whether Christ is announced or is entirely unknown. How many kingdoms there are today in Asia and Africa, how many peoples, how many islands of the sea, for whom there is no knowledge of Christ and no faith; just as, with [unclear] of them left in error, he mercifully called us in Europe, with a few, to the knowledge of the Christian faith. But of all things after the death of Christ we think this is [unclear]: that we made [unclear] Christians. For outside the faith of Christ no one will be saved, whether Christ is announced or is entirely unknown. How many kingdoms there are today in Asia and Africa, how many peoples, how many islands of the sea, who [unclear] and no faith; just as [unclear] are in Europe with a few, he mercifully called to the knowledge of Christian faith. But of all things after the death of Christ we think this is [unclear]: that we made [unclear] Christians. For outside the faith of Christ no one will be saved, whether Christ is announced or is entirely unknown.

    Let us bless God the Father at every time, who poured out the gifts of the Holy Spirit upon us and did not permit us to be born removed from the unity of the Church. The seventh thing that is believed able to produce the love of God in our hearts is considered in the promise of eternal happiness. For if one considers what great goods he has promised that he will give us in heaven, love of him will deservedly burn sweetly in our hearts. He promised his whole self to us [as a reward?], he who alone is the highest and wholly immutable good. And since he is indivisible, he will grant himself to be enjoyed by all in such a way that nonetheless he is possessed whole by each. He loves all by whom he is loved, and he loves each one by whom he is possessed. The more we now love God with a pure mind, the more of the promised [reward?] we shall receive there.

    On the Knowledge of Spiritual Grace: Sermon Six.

    The holy apostle of Christ Paul teaches us that not every spirit is always to be believed, but that impulses are to be diligently examined, whether they are from God, who is true light, lest perhaps something rise up against us from the side of darkness. For since our adversary is crafty, he never sleeps, but devises ways by which he may catch us unawares. Yet he attacks those who are making progress in one way, and deals in another way with those who are still [unclear] in the torpor of negligence. The more we have advanced in the commandments of God, the more necessary it is [unclear], and that we keep watch against the devil. Finally, [unclear] those attempting to flee [unclear]; and against those who desire to please God he rages with [greater?] envy. Lying hidden in secret under the appearance of good, he attempts to suggest [unclear] to those who do not know, by which he tries to overthrow incautious minds [unclear] under the appearance of good. Against his snares the best remedy is if the monk submits all the [thoughts?] of his heart to the examination of the elders. For demons hate the public light, and are ashamed that the [thoughts?] of the young which they suggest come to the knowledge of spiritual elders. Let each one of you who thinks that he stands in good always be anxious lest, with the devil undermining him, he fall. There are among you certain men both in years and in conversion in [unclear]

    in [unclear]

    On the Knowledge of Spiritual Grace.

    ...and their sensual desires are indulged more than is expedient; by these the demons deceive them in various ways, even under the appearance of good. They desire to have sanctity without deserving it, without the necessary exercise of virtue. They seem to themselves great before God in devotion and [unclear], and in their animal passions they are not mortified. You err, O wretched men, and you shamefully deceive yourselves; without the foundation of humble subjection and obedience, [one] thinks to build a tower of sanctity. First, the disordered desires of sensuality must be mortified; the animal passions must be restrained: anger, murmuring, the spite of indignation, and all impatience. For so long as vices rule over you, whatever gifts of private singularity you offer are not pleasing to God. All things are vain where there is no pure conscience.

    The conduct of a young monk is suspect to us, however devout it may seem, when the humility of voluntary subjection does not commend it. A monk without humility and obedience cannot be good, even though by fasting and prayer they daily hunt after sanctity. The devil deceives many in the hiddenness of elation and pride, whom he permits continually to keep vigil, fast, and pray. For none of these works is pleasing to God without humility and charity: fasting, vigils, prayers, and the studies of monks without these are not feared by the devil. [Unclear] does not move the devil; [unclear] does not torment him. Nor does he greatly value the vigils of the proud man, nor does he heed the fasting of the swollen with pride; nor does he fear the prayers of the proud.

    But if he finds you humble, cheerfully obedient in all things to the commands of the elders; if he sees you doing great things and thinking humble things about yourself; if he perceives the charity of God and neighbor burning in you, then certainly he is moved against you, for he is tormented by envy of your virtues. He turns against you all the weapons of his cunning that he can, and with all his strength strives to overturn your purpose of sanctity. For nothing in a monk displeases the demons more, nothing torments them more vehemently, than if, for the love of God, he has truly humbled himself in all things and has always kept the service of the monastic institution under the guard of obedience with a cheerful spirit.

    You have been deceived by the prompting of demons, because you think yourselves to be something great without the true merit of virtues. I see you unwilling toward the commands of the elders, impatient and murmuring under correction, quick to rebuke another's life, but very slow in considering your own defects. These are the surest signs of the promptings of demons: that the necessary [things] have been despised...

    Sermon VI. Folio LXXI.

    But so that [unclear] may learn wisely to discern [unclear] from the promptings of the ancient enemy, mark what we say. First, therefore, let him reckon himself inspired by the grace of God whenever he diligently observes that he is becoming purer in conscience and that the tinder of sin is diminishing. Wherever the Spirit of God has poured himself out by the gift of heavenly grace, every inclination to sin soon withdraws. But if a horror of sin enters the mind, it is certainly manifest that the prompting of the devil has not taken possession of the man. For as soon as the Holy Spirit has penetrated the mind of a man, every spark of vice is either mitigated or utterly extinguished.

    Hence let each one of you diligently examine himself and weigh by whose prompting he is moved. For the prompting of God is accustomed to lessen sins, but that of Satan, the enemy, to increase them. In those who follow the Spirit of God, sins diminish daily; but he who follows the prompting of the devil is rarely truly amended. The second sign of divine prompting is recognized from the increase of virtues, since the grace of the Holy Spirit always produces great virtues in a man. Therefore, when you feel yourself advancing daily in the love of God and in good works; when you experience in yourself that the habit of sinning and the vices prevail less from day to day, you ought humbly to acknowledge that the grace of God is present. For the love of God, which grace brings, is never idle, but is always usefully occupied in good works; and as it covers the multitude of sins, so by the exercise of virtues it does not permit the soul to sin. For the grace of God cannot stand with sins, and is not at all accustomed to be in a man without the working of virtues.

    The third sign of the Spirit of God is shown in a man when the mind does not waver in its purpose of sanctity, but, growing stronger from day to day, is strengthened. For there are many who, touched by a passing compunction, sometimes receive the first two signs, but, despising perseverance, do not reach the third. Without perseverance there is no reward for a good work, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel: "He who has persevered to the end, he shall be saved." The devil knows how to pretend himself absent for a short time, and [unclear] the two true written signs of the Spirit of God, when he does not know how, or fears, to disguise [them]. Soon thereafter, bursting out from ambush, he attacks the devout but unwary person, and, fostering him in former negligence, either casts him headlong or wounds him more gravely.

    O what a heavy yoke is evil habit, how unjust and exceedingly dreadful, and rarely [having] an end before death. Let whoever is bound by a long habit of sin fear and shudder. For nothing is more difficult than to overcome an evil habit strengthened by long practice. For Solomon says in Proverbs

    On the recognition of spiritual grace.

    [unclear] despise the things of the present life. The soul which has God present within itself through love despises all the comforts of the flesh; it longs to come to its Lord through hardships and rough places. It does not love the riches of this world; it spurns transitory honors and dignities; it strongly contemns the pleasures of the flesh. It meditates always on the law of the Lord and never forgets the most bitter passion of Jesus.

    Who among you, brothers, does these things? Who detests all the little consolations of this age, who thinks of nothing else, seeks nothing, desires nothing except the love of God? Whoever shall have attained this sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit, if he perseveres to the end of life, shall be saved.

    The eighth indication of a good course, and a true sign of the presence of the Holy Spirit, we receive when we humbly conform our wills in all things to the divine ordinances. This degree of spiritual progress separates the monk from all the cares of the world and calls him wholly to inward things. For his will is subjected to the divine will with the affection of a peaceful mind, and is separated far from all desires which war against the spirit.

    Whoever has received this gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit, let him first give thanks with humility, and not vainly exalt himself on account of the gift; but the more he has advanced, so much the more let him learn to humble himself in all things. For often a man deserves to lose the grace of God when he neglects to preserve it in the vessel of true humility. Therefore almighty God sometimes withdraws the grace of sensible devotion from those who are advancing for a short time, so that humility may persevere in the mind and the fervor of desire may burn more strongly to seek further. But since there are many causes in human beings by which the grace of God is sometimes withdrawn, it will be worth the effort for them to be stated in order.

    First, indeed, the grace of God is withdrawn from a person because of sin, when the conscience is stained by the foulness of vices. For our God, as Scripture says, is jealous: either he is loved alone, or he is not loved with any companion. Therefore whenever the mind, by desiring in a disordered way, turns back either to itself or to something else, it is removed, alienated from its principle, which is God; whence it deserves to lose the grace which it had, because, by consenting to sin, it was unwilling to guard it inviolate. Hence the holy apostle of Christ, Paul, exhorts us not to receive the grace of God in vain; for then indeed it is received fruitlessly and in vain, when the mind of the recipient is made unworthy by the filth of vices.

    The little vessel into which we receive the grace of God is our conscience; when it is cleansed from vices and adorned with holy virtues, it becomes a worthy dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and produces great progress in us. But if the vessel of our conscience has been defiled by the rottenness of sin, at once the Spirit of God withdraws with all the gifts of grace. Is not our Lord Jesus Christ the lover and faithful spouse of the soul, which he purchased for himself by the outpouring of his own blood? With what face, with what rashness, O man, can you despise this so great lover and savior of yours, and love anything else whatsoever in this world? God, who is your creator, loves you supremely; by his death he delivered you from eternal destruction. What will you repay him, O mortal man, from whom you have received such great benefits? He asks nothing from you, seeks nothing, demands nothing, except gratitude, affection, and love. Guard innocence and purity of conscience, lest you lose the impulse of grace.

    The second cause, then, on account of which grace is withdrawn from a person is called the pride of ingratitude. But God, as Scripture testifies, resists the proud, while to the humble he gives grace. For by the just judgment of God the grace of the Holy Spirit is lost whenever the one who has it is lifted up into pride. For everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and he who exalts himself will be humbled. Hence again almighty God says: Upon whom shall my spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet man, and the one trembling at my words? The more anyone humbles himself in true purity of conscience for the love of Christ, the more fit he will be to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. But whenever the mind rises up in pride, deservedly the spirit of devotion is taken away from it as from an unclean vessel.

    Therefore, my brothers, let no one grow proud because of the grace of the Holy Spirit which he has received; let no one vainly exalt himself, because unless we have been humble, we shall by no means be able to be sharers in the mercies of the Lord. For as the holy lover of Christ Paul says: he who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself.

    Third, the grace of devotion is withdrawn from a person because of sloth

    Sermon VII.

    Our temptation is wholly upon the earth; in it, if we do not make progress in good, do we not fail? And there, as the holy pope Leo says, we fall into the danger of failing when we draw back the appetite for being made perfect. Therefore flee sloth, and always keep watch in good works. And consider what happened to the lazy servant, who hid in a napkin his lord’s money, which he had received for trading. Trade, I pray you, while there is time, and as long as you live be always occupied in good pursuits.

    Fourth, the grace of devotion is very often withdrawn from those who, placed under obedience, follow their own will. For the monk who loves his own will most justly loses the grace of God. But the man who, for God’s sake, humbly subjects himself in all things to the shepherd of obedience, who despises the will of his own heart, [God] pours into him various gifts of spiritual grace and illumines him with the light of inward fervor. We can offer nothing more precious or more acceptable to God than if, for love of him, we deny our own will. Finally, the very profession of the monastic institution enjoins on us, by necessity of salvation, to despise our own will and humbly to lie subject to him who has been set over us. Therefore the monk who follows the movement of his own will is judged like an unclean vessel and unworthy of spiritual grace. Hence the grace of God is deservedly withdrawn from the monk of his own will, who, living otherwise than he promised the Lord, lies.

    Fifth, the grace of devotion is withdrawn from a monk when he thinks that he has it from his own merits. He does not understand that sin dwells in him; if he has received any good, he ascribes it to his own merits. Against this sluggishness of mind the holy prophet said to the Lord: Lord, in thy will thou hast given strength to my beauty, because it is not of him that wills nor of him that runs, but of God who has mercy. Thou turnedst away thy face from me, and I was troubled. For no one is becoming through his own merits, no one holy by his own powers. But let us acknowledge that all the causes of the withdrawal of the grace of God which we have mentioned pertain to our weakness.

    But so far as concerns those who already walk in the way of perfection, such a reason is given, so long as they have persevered. For from them the grace of God is never withdrawn, although the sensible fervor of compunction is sometimes taken away for a time. And we shall state in order the causes of this removal.

    And first, indeed, almighty God sometimes withdraws for a time from his lovers the grace of sensible devotion, so that, when he pretends not to be present when invoked, the desire of inward love may grow. All who have felt the fire of divine love and who are true emulators of the holy fathers have known this alternation of holy ardor. For whenever the bridegroom withdraws himself from the bride, the desire of the lover grows. While she is present, she seeks him whom she loves; from every desire of love she groans.

    Second, this grace is withdrawn from the devout for an hour, lest frailty be raised up into pride. For when we lose the grace of compunction even against our will, by humble examination we judge our weakness, which can do nothing of itself. Therefore, so that devout worshippers of God may remain humble in their exaltation, it is necessary that they recognize their own frailty.

    The third cause concerns merit, because to seek inward consolations is not the mark of the strong but of the weak. The Lord must be served freely because he is good; but those who seek sensible sweetness in their devotion are less devoted and seek the Lord’s [unclear] for little consolations. The Lord is to be loved usefully, and all womanish and soft affections are to be driven far from the soul. Therefore, so that the Lord may increase merit for his worshippers in holy compunction, he sometimes denies the grace of sensible devotion to those who ask. But lest, affected by the bitterness of weariness, they grow wholly torpid in the purpose of holiness, the comforter of the deserving does not go far away, but remains nearby. He suddenly returns to his beloved, and the one whom he had pretended for an hour to be sorrowful he consoles with the sweetness of spiritual presence.

    Fourth, to these causes we join this: that we are warned to walk more cautiously. For if we fear losing the grace of compunction, let us learn to guard more diligently what we have. A rare and precious treasure, the more its possessor loves it, the more diligently he guards it. Therefore the monk who has deserved to receive from the Lord the grace of devotion ought to watch over it with the utmost zeal, lest he lose it through his own negligence. That you may know how you ought to preserve the granted grace of compunction, lest it perish, the order of what is to be said clearly makes this manifest to you. First, he who [unclear] for himself the grace of inward compunction

    On the knowledge of spiritual grace.

    Third, if you do not wish to lose the grace of inward compunction, you should strive to love the quiet of solitude. For divine Scripture says: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet?” And again it says in another place: “In silence and in hope shall be your strength.” For the grace of inward compunction is quickly lost when the secrecy of solitude is not loved. Therefore let the monk who wishes to possess the grace of God learn gladly to remain with himself in his cell.

    Fourth, one must take the greatest care that you do not despise in your heart any person, however evil; for by the just judgment of God the grace of compunction is withdrawn whenever rash judgment concerning one’s neighbor is not avoided. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned.”

    Fifth, the monk who does not wish to lose the grace of inward devotion should strive to exercise himself in the cultivation of all virtues. Let him always keep watch in the fear of the Lord, always occupy himself in the exercise of divine love; let him be constantly assiduous in good works, and, as far as he is able, devout at all times in the remembrance of the Lord’s passion. For attentive meditation on the passion of Christ strengthens a person against all vices and preserves the grace of compunction.

    Sixth, be constant in holy prayers, because he who interrupts the practice of prayer is not able to preserve the grace of compunction. For the Savior says in the holy Gospel: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation.” The help of the Lord is close at hand for those who call upon him; but he who neglects to pray loses grace. But if you lose the grace of devotion in any way, you will quickly recover it by the following same six remedies.

    First, consider that without the grace of God you cannot make progress toward salvation, but that in all the good things you are going to do you are in the greatest need of his mercy. Recognize, therefore, that you are unworthy of the grace of God for doing good, although, because of the multitude of your sins, you know yourself to be unworthy. Call upon him, for he is near; and make every time that is granted you as free from the common exercises of the brothers be spent usefully and fruitfully. The grace of God is necessary for you for doing good; it is acquired by breadth of charity, guarded by humility, and recovered by the practice of saving penance. The Lord is with you so long as you have been with him in good will. But in order that you may be able to recover the lost grace of devotion, you must submit yourself to God in true humility.

    Second, for the recovery of the lost grace of compunction it seems necessary that you never lift yourself up against the Lord, but conform your will in all things to the divine ordering. We say in the Lord’s Prayer, “May his will be done”; it is fitting that we always voluntarily agree with that very prayer in mind and affection.

    Third, he who desires to recover the lost grace of devotion must strongly despise every pleasure of this world for the love of God. For it cannot happen that he recovers the spirit of inward compunction who opens the dwelling-place of his heart to earthly joys and pleasures. Therefore you must cast away every consolation of the present life, if you wish to have the divine spirit of love with its gifts.

    Fourth, you are commanded to withdraw yourself from the vain cares and occupations of this world for your own sake, and at every time to occupy your mind delightfully in the service of God. For, as the Lord says, no one can serve God and mammon; but whoever desires to serve the Lord in truth of heart must despise all the occupations of the world.

    Fifth, we advise that you remember always to occupy your heart in meditation on the passion of Christ, because there is no other way more expedient for recovering the delay [unclear] of compunction, nor any manner of prayer more effective for obtaining from the Lord whatever we have asked.

    Sixth, you should strive daily to cleanse your conscience by true penance; and whenever you have fallen into some fault, at once come to your senses through contrition. If you have taken care to keep these things with good will, by the mercy of God you will recover the lost grace of compunction.

    On the nine degrees of ascent.

    Sermon VII.

    With the pen we describe for you, dearly beloved brothers, the nine degrees by which the ascent of the human spirit into heaven is made. And although one is higher than another, nevertheless all and each direct one to the kingdom of God, and they are distinguished according to the merits of those ascending. Therefore attend diligently to what we are going to say, and consider how much you have made progress in spiritual advancement. All, as many as reach the kingdom of God, have ascended by the degrees of this ladder. The more anyone has made progress in the love of God, the higher he has already ascended.

    The first degree is nearest to hell, and

    Sermon VII.

    [unclear] they have not avoided. For no sin is so small that it does not become greater through neglect. For although we cannot wholly avoid venial sins, nevertheless we ought to take care with all our strength that they do not multiply in us. But those who, by the Lord’s mercy, daily make progress toward better things in this degree fall into sin more rarely. And whenever they have fallen, they rise again through penitence. Yet their state is very near to danger, because just as a torn garment, often [torn], is at last rendered useless, so the man who falls by sinning more frequently is often choked by an evil habit. But if any from this degree depart this life in the Lord’s mercies, they will be saved not without the very heavy pains of purgatory. Therefore one must hasten toward higher things, so that not only mortal sins but also venial sins may be avoided with all one’s strength.

    The second degree is believed to be ascended by those who strive, as much as they can, to avoid both venial and mortal crimes. But because of excessive commerce with bodily weakness they have not advanced in their purpose, but often fall into the various negligences of this life, although they do not commit mortal sins. We who are lukewarm trust that we have somehow ascended this degree, who, established under the observance of regular discipline, keep our minds from graver sins with the Lord’s help. But since we are surnamed lukewarm, we live very negligently and are slow to perform the exercises of holy virtues. There are, moreover, many set on the threshold of this second degree whom servile fear occupies; if that alone exists, it by no means approaches the kingdom of God. For servile fear without charity will not suffice for obtaining the glory of heavenly felicity, since he is a slave who does not sin from fear of punishment, but a son does not do evil for love of God. Yet it is good to begin from servile fear, so that a person may gradually be able to arrive at filial fear, which is called chaste. For although to withdraw from evil from fear of punishments is by no means sufficient for attaining the kingdom of God, nevertheless it prepares those who act for filial fear. Hence the lowest degree of those making progress is not to transgress from fear of punishment, and not to sin lest they be damned forever. For charity alone, discerning the merits of all, is admitted as fit to enter the kingdom of God; and whatever has been done outside it is judged unworthy of the kingdom of God. Therefore whoever has merited to ascend according to this second degree, whoever has learned not to sin from fear of punishments, if you wish to arrive at the joy of eternal felicity, take care to hasten as quickly as possible toward higher things. For, with Scripture bearing witness, we grant that you are indeed beginning rightly; yet we judge it dangerous to stand long in the valley of shadows. Ascend, therefore, as much as you can, daily, and do not persist with beasts in the dung of stinking actions, since if you do not make progress, you have failed; if you do not ascend, you descend.

    The third degree is comprised by those who, persevering in a good purpose, keep themselves from every mortal sin and also withdraw from venial sins with all their strength. They love purity of conscience, and by no means commit anything that could stain it. Yet in one respect they are lower than those that follow, because, not simply withdrawing from evil for the love of God, they do good; but, still weak and far from the height of holiness, they remain among lower things. He who truly loves God with a pure mind serves and obeys him neither from fear of punishments nor with regard for reward, but only for love of him. And therefore all the degrees written above are proposed for beginners, through which, ascending gradually, they are at last joined to the perfect. It is good to withdraw from evil from fear of punishments; it is good to do good for love of reward; and although this by no means suffices for perfection, it nevertheless provides the beginning and the way for those who desire to make progress. For servile fear, if continued, begets filial and chaste fear, from whose [unclear] perfect charity flows. But holy charity, after it has once kindled minds, thereafter casts out every servile fear and [unclear] fear.

    The fourth degree strives to show the way of perfection to those ascending, and for that reason is rightly judged greater than the degrees written above. Whatever of good is seen in them is possessed more perfectly in this one. For the ascenders of this fourth degree, with every zeal, keep themselves not only from mortal sins but also from venial sins as far as is possible for them; they most diligently devote themselves to good and holy works, and desire to please God above all things. In one respect they surpass those preceding, because they turn aside from evil neither from fear of punishments nor perform good in hope of reward, but do all things for the love of God alone, and [seek] nothing other than the honor of God. For the true lover of God neither fears punishment nor thinks of reward, but, walking in breadth of heart, commends his will to the divine ordinance. For God, because he is supremely good, is to be loved not for the reward of the heavenly kingdom, nor on account of anything else, but for his very self; and in every good work [he is] principally to be held in intention.

    On the nine degrees of ascent.

    Hasten, my very dear brothers, to ascend this degree of the spiritual ladder as quickly as possible, so that you may at last be able to arrive at the summit of perfection. For if you, who have been placed under obedience of monastic perfection, have advanced to this fourth degree, you will now ascend the fifth without difficulty. For those who are placed in the fourth do [unclear], since they have not subjected themselves by vow or profession to monastic constitutions. And in this one respect they are inferior to those that follow: because a good work is so much the more acceptable to God, the more it is commended by the merit of obedience.

    Therefore those ascend the fifth degree who keep themselves from sins with all their strength, and, placed under obedience, always persevere strong and constant in the purpose of holiness. Loving God above all things with a pure mind, they do good works chiefly for love of him, and in their intention they neither fear punishments nor seek rewards. They obey their prelates humbly for love of God, yet they are somewhat obstinate. They sometimes try to defend their exercises and private observances against the determination of their prelates, and to consider themselves wiser than their rulers in the examination of spiritual matters. Flee this, monks, because the demon lies hidden in ambush; and those whom he cannot conquer in open conflict he strives to overcome by secret plotting. For the holier and more perfect a monk has been before God, the more promptly he obeys his prelate without debate. But if a perfect monk should scorn to obey his abbot, even an imperfect one, in things lawful and honorable, then surely he has lost the name of perfection. Therefore let each one take care to press on with zeal for progress in such a way that he presumes in nothing to violate obedience. Scripture says: Obedience is better than victims, and to listen is better than to offer the fat of rams. Whatever you have offered is another’s; but the truly obedient man offers himself.

    The sixth degree, then, belongs especially to those who, living in every purity of mind and body, love the Lord above all things; who do every good thing that they can for the honor of God alone; who do not depart from the commands of their prelates. Great is the virtue of obedience, which doubles the good work that has been done, and, increasing the merit of the worker, presents him to God as a tree with fruit. Do not let the words of men who despise obedience disturb you, my very dear brothers, who prefer the freedom of their will to the subjection of monks, and place a good work done from freedom before the merit of obedience. For even if a monk obeys by necessity of his profession, nevertheless the good will by which, for love of God, he bound himself to obedience commends that necessity in many ways.

    There is a necessity by which a man is compelled to do something, where the will has not consented but always resists. This necessity diminishes the praise of virtue, because the good work was never in the will. There is also another necessity, proceeding from the inward inclination of the mind, which increases the praise of a good work and does not diminish it, because it kindles the will more intensely toward that very work. There is a third necessity, which has regard to the end and does not compel the will. For if you wish to cross the Rhine by ship, the fitting necessity demands an instrument. But the necessity by which a monk is compelled to obey his shepherd is not that of the first compulsion, nor that of the second inclination, but rather of the third, since it is ordered toward the end from a preceding will. Therefore it is necessary for a monk, on account of the end, to do that which the abbot commands, so that he may be able to fulfill the vow that he made for love of God. Since, then, this end is very praiseworthy, by which the creature subjects himself to his creator out of love, the necessity of obeying in a monk is of good praise, of more excellent merit, and of more abundant reward, by reason of the vow, than if he did a good work from obedience without a vow, or if it were done without a vow from the freedom of his own will. For the monk has once offered himself wholly, and all his will with him, to God, and has reserved absolutely nothing for himself. Whatever good he does under obedience is referred back to the end of the religion he has undertaken, to be kept for love of Christ; with this no work after martyrdom is compared. He who is continent without a vow from the venereal act performs one virtue, which is called chastity; but he who observes these things by reason of a vow walks at a higher degree, because the several virtues are referred in ordered fashion to the perfection of the whole religion which he has professed. For the whole monastic religion is more than one private virtue. For he who offers to God a good work that he did without obedience offers that alone, leaving to himself what is greater: the power of acting, together with his own will. But the monk who does something for God from the vow of obedience is of more excellent merit, because he offers also the act

    Sermon VII.

    [unclear] and the power of acting. For no one has offered more to God than the monk who has given himself.

    But some who ascend this sixth degree have hidden within themselves a certain defect of pride, because, while they look back incautiously upon themselves, they do not commit themselves in all things to the divine will as they ought. This defect takes its beginning from a certain very subtle vanity, when the soul, trusting in its own purity, asks that some secret be revealed to it by the Lord. And in this one thing the climbers of the sixth heaven differ from those of the seventh, who, being devoted to God, flee the signs of vanity. For signs have been given not to believers but to unbelievers; hence the monk who asks a sign from the Lord shows that he has not yet perfectly subjected himself to the divine will.

    They ascend the seventh degree who most zealously keep all the things prescribed, and, subject to God in all things, live without the stain of vanity. They flee, as far as they can, every sin, whether venial or mortal; they do works of virtue for the love of God alone; in all things they obey their shepherds; they seek no miracles of vanity. Whatever almighty God has ordained concerning them, they receive gratefully; they do not at all depart in anything from the observance of monastic purity. Yet in one thing they are lower than those who follow, because perhaps they suffer some defect of which they are unaware, by whose impulse they sometimes commit something of their own sensuality.

    Whoever has deserved to ascend the eighth degree grants nothing further to sensuality. Here is the sweetest rest of the soul; here the perfect tranquillity of the mind. At this degree nothing vicious in beauty is left behind; here nothing is found that can sadden the soul. Here all things are clean, all things pure, all things most sweetly burning with the fervor of charity. O that we might strive to ascend to this degree; O that we might sometime deserve to arrive at this harbor of tranquillity. The more one standing on this holy ladder begins to taste the sweetness of inner delight, the more, hastening toward what lies ahead, he desires further things. O desires of holy love, always to be proclaimed; O exercises of venerable perfection, where the clean conscience of one loving God shines without sins, where the wicked battles of vices have ceased and great tranquillity has succeeded.

    They ascend the ninth degree who, already consummated in the eighth, keep all the things prescribed purely and simply for the love of God, and desire nothing other than to praise, bless, and glorify God. Whoever has ascended to this degree of perfection, as though forgetful of himself, resigning himself wholly to God, submits humbly. He reckons himself unworthy of all God’s benefits; he takes no thought at all for himself, because he has already learned to commit himself wholly to God and to be subject humbly in all things to his ordinance. Hence he asks for no miracles and seeks no consolations in this life, but with the holy apostle of Christ he truly cries: To me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. For the true monk who loves Christ has offered himself wholly to God out of charity and has despised the world with all its riches, honors, and vanities. Hence the world is said to be crucified to him, in which there is nothing that seems able to penetrate his mind.

    Happy are those monks who serve the Lord God with a pure conscience in true charity, who run without offense under the rule of humility and obedience, who ascend this last degree of perfection. These are true monks, who seek nothing other than the honor of God. Indeed, my brothers, although monks are not bound, by necessity for salvation, to be perfect, otherwise very few would be saved, nevertheless we are all bound with good will to strive toward perfection and with all the strength we can to pant after this ninth degree. For it is very contrary to the monastic profession to be unwilling to make progress, and it is a kind of apostasy, after a vow of perfection, to wish to remain in imperfection. For the enemies of our salvation are the vices that attack us, and until they either conquer or are conquered they do not cease to pursue us. Let us imitate the history of the ancient battle, when the children of promise destroyed their enemies not in one day but successively. For it is difficult to conquer all things at once, unless the charity of God suddenly overshadows the mind. Against all the vices that attack us in any way, let us wage war: let us conquer gluttony today; when it has been properly overthrown, let us overcome acedia; and so let us deal with the rest, so that at last we may come forth victors over them all. The Lord will be present with us as we fight, and God will give victory to those who love him. Amen.

    End of the second book of exhortations to monks by Johannes Trithemius, abbot, on the first day of September, 1486.

    These two books were printed at Strasbourg by Johann Knobloch, printer, at the expense of Johannes Haselberger of Reichenau, of the diocese of Constance, in the year of the Lord 1516, on the twenty-fifth day of the month of August.

    What was wrong: The published rendering opened with a fabricated psalm citation, "Have mercy on me, O God," which the print does not contain; the page opens mid-word "(no)stra tẽptatio est tota sup terrã," and the real psalm citations (Ps 29:8; Rom 9:16) occur only inside the fifth cause. The old version also scrambled the print's paragraph order (relocating the psalm material and the "causes in order" transition to the top, merging the fifth cause into the fourth) and dropped both patristic attributions (Pope Leo; Gregory).

    Key corrections (verified against the scan): - Removed the unwarranted opening 'Have mercy on me, O God': verified page 150 begins '(no)stra teptatio est tota sup terra' (continuation of 'Vita enim no-' from p. 149), rendered '[For our life] is wholly a temptation upon the earth' - Restored print order: Quarto (self-will) -> Quinto (presumption of merits, with the Ps 29:8 / Rom 9:16 citations in situ) -> transition -> four causes of temporary withdrawal -> two preservation precautions; old version had merged Quinto into Quarto unnumbered and moved its citations to the chunk opening - Restored the Leo attribution: 'ibiqz vt sact9 papa dicit leo' = 'and there, as the holy Pope Leo says, we run into the danger of failing, where we call back the appetite for advancing' (old version dropped 'Leo') - Recovered the closing Gregory attribution: 'Na vt diu9 Gre. dicit: spoliari desiderat: q thesauru i publico portat' = 'as Saint Gregory says, he who carries his treasure in public desires to be robbed' (cf. Hom. in Ev. 11); old working version missed the attribution and the public-repo 0127 rendering ('God does not wish the grace given by him to be stripped away...') was wrong - 'q aliter viues qz promisit dno metitur' (glyph 'q̃z promisit' verified) = 'living otherwise than he promised, lies to the Lord'; old rendering garbled this clause - 'dei gratiam iustissime amittit' = 'most justly loses' (old: 'very quickly') - 'Negociamini precor dum tempus est' = 'Trade, I beg you, while there is time'; old 'Trade with God's talents' invented 'God's talents' - 'Nemo ei deuot9 meritis suis: nemo sctus virib9 proprijs' = 'no one devout by his own merits, no one holy by his own strength' ('sctus'='sanctus', same abbreviation as 'sctus ppheta' three lines above); old version relocated and rendered 'strong' - 'dnm iesum pro consolaciunculis querunt' = 'seek the Lord Jesus for the sake of petty consolations' ('Iesum' omitted in both prior versions; diminutive restored) - 'vt ois iactatia caueatur' = 'that all boasting be avoided' (old: 'empty chatter') - 'ex consuetudine vnu magnu efficit' = 'out of habit brings about one great one' (OCR garbage 'ex p̄luerī die rūnī' resolved from scan) - 'in sancta compunctione' = 'in holy compunction' (public 0127 had 'dry compunction', unsupported) - Printer's signature 'm iiij' (OCR misread 'vi vi') recorded as a bracketed editorial line
